andersen-improvisatore-howitt-1847:
Hans Christian Andersen published The Improvisatore in Denmark in 1835, and Mary Howitt Englished it in 1847. The novel made Andersen famous across Europe a decade before his fairy tales ruled nurseries. Antonio, a poor Roman boy with a gift for improvised song, tells his own story from childhood onward.

Antonio rises from street singer to admired performer, through love, loss, and patronage. Rome, Naples, and Venice glow in the background of his fortunes. Andersen drew on his own Italian travels and his hunger for recognition. Howitt, a tireless carrier of Scandinavian writing into English, gave the book its English life. It stands apart from the tales, as his great novel of the artist.
arxiv-2510-00347:
Huitao Yang and Guanting Chen published this 2025 paper on teaching transformer agents to explore decision tasks. Decision-pretrained transformers learn from offline data, then act in new settings by context alone. They tend to falter when the test setting drifts from the training data's distribution. The authors add in-context curiosity, a light regularizer inspired by exploration bonuses.

Their framework, the Prediction-Powered Transformer, pairs the agent with a helper reward predictor. Prediction error becomes an intrinsic curiosity signal that rewards broader training exploration. Proof-of-concept tests used Gaussian multi-armed bandits, a classic choose-and-learn setup. When test rewards grew more variable, the curious model degraded far less than the plain one. The benefit was clearest when pretraining data had limited diversity. The authors frame the work as early evidence that curiosity can harden in-context reinforcement learning agents.
arxiv-2510-00447:
Toshiyuki Fujii, Fumio Hiroshima, and Satoshi Tanda wrote this 2025 mathematical physics paper on the Josephson junction, a workhorse superconducting device. They introduce its Hamiltonian as a self-adjoint operator on a discrete sequence space. Then they show the same physics lives naturally on functions over the unit circle. From that circle picture, a Mathieu operator falls out directly.

A fiber decomposition splits the circle Hamiltonian by total particle number. Each fiber's action can then be analyzed on its own terms. Adding a magnetic field shifts the phase and defines a magnetic junction Hamiltonian and its current. For a steady field, the local current is computed point by point along the junction. The famous Fraunhofer pattern, the current's interference-like wiggles, emerges from the math rather than being assumed. The paper ties an iconic experimental signature to a clean operator framework.
arxiv-2510-00847:
Zhu, Ruan, Chen, and Tang argue that gluon condensation inside the proton explains two puzzles at once, in this 2025 arXiv paper on particle physics. Their work on gluon evolution equations found chaotic behaviour that piles gluons up near a critical momentum, a condensation rather than the colour glass picture. When protons collide at ultrahigh energies, that condensate should release many low-momentum pions. The pions' decays would imprint a characteristic breakout shape on gamma-ray spectra.

The authors point to such features appearing across cosmic gamma-ray spectra. At the lower energies of the Large Hadron Collider, they find weaker but recognizable signs of the same effect. Some LHC events previously attributed to Bose-Einstein condensate pions fit the condensation story instead, they argue. One proton structure would then link phenomena at wildly different energy scales. The claim remains a proposal that further data must test.
arxiv-2510-01147:
Liu and Mallada tackle safety-critical control for complex nonlinear systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Control barrier functions certify that a system stays inside a safe set, but building a valid one for a high-order system is often computationally hopeless. Layered control dodges that wall by designing the barrier for a simple reduced-order model and tracking it with the full system. Classical tracking functions must shrink the tracking error monotonically, and systematic ways to build them exist only for fully actuated systems.

Their recurrent tracking functions relax monotonic decay to a finite-time recurrence condition, which tolerates temporary error growth. Combining those functions with reduced-model barrier functions yields recurrent barrier functions with provable safety for the full-order system. Numerical experiments confirm the tracking functions work as designed and keep the full system safe. The relaxation widens layered safety methods to underactuated machines.
arxiv-2510-01247:
Singh and co-authors test whether language models understand the traditional sports that most of the world actually plays. Benchmarks favor globally televised games and skip regional and indigenous traditions entirely. Their benchmark, CultSportQA, spans sixty countries across six continents and eleven languages.

Thirty-three thousand questions cover the history, rules, and game situations of traditional sports. Text and image questions probe knowledge in two modes. Leading models showed notable gaps on these culturally specific questions. The misses likely mirror blind spots in the data the models were trained on. Four cultural categories organize the sports in the collection. Zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting all faced the questions. Small and multimodal models were tested beside the large ones. Cultural sensitivity guided the curation from the start. Regional games carry rules no global dataset teaches. Benchmarks shape what models bother to learn.
arxiv-2510-01447:
Soleymani, Dadsetan, and Rudzicz soften the gradient clipping inside private training so minority groups stop paying the highest price. Differential privacy protects data by clipping each update, but hard clipping crushes the learning signal of underrepresented patients. Adaptive clipping helped utility yet kept the harsh uniform cutoff.

Their method replaces the cutoff with a smooth hyperbolic transformation that preserves relative gradient sizes. Sensitivity stays bounded, so the privacy guarantee survives the softening. Clinical and income datasets showed subgroup disparities shrinking dramatically against both baselines. The gains cleared statistical significance, not just numerical improvement. Subgroup disparity fell by up to eighty-seven percent against standard private training. Clinical text, intensive-care records, and income tables span the test beds. The hyperbolic tangent supplies the smooth bounding curve. Fairness and privacy stop trading against each other so brutally. Gradient geometry carries the fairness lever.
arxiv-2510-01747:
Almendros-Abad and nine co-authors report a rare outburst from a lonely planet-mass object in this 2025 astronomy paper. The object, Cha 1107-7626, floats alone in space with only five to ten times the mass of Jupiter. It still feeds from a disk of gas and dust around it. Telescopes watched it change sharply during 2025.

Spectra from the Very Large Telescope and the Webb telescope caught the shift. The object sat quiet in April and May, then flared into strong accretion from June through August. Its feeding rate rose six to eight times, reaching the highest level ever measured for a planet-mass body. The hydrogen line took a double-peaked shape with red-shifted absorption, a sign of magnetically funneled infall. Water vapor emission also appeared where none had been seen before.
arxiv-2510-02247:
Nibauer and co-authors use a thin stream of stars to probe dark matter clumps near the Milky Way. Their 2025 astronomy paper studies the GD-1 stream. A stellar stream forms when gravity tears a small star cluster apart. Passing dark clumps should jostle the stream stars. That jostling raises the spread in their speeds. The team measured speeds for 160 member stars. They combined four spectroscopic catalogs and used repeat visits to check for binary stars.

The stream showed a speed spread of about two to five kilometers each second. One stretch ran about four kilometers each second hotter than smooth models predict. That gap is a four sigma mismatch, well beyond chance. Perturbation models explain the heat with clumps holding about five percent of the halo mass. That share fits cold dark matter expectations.
arxiv-2510-02347:
Katharakis, Rossi, and Mukkamala test small open models as curriculum based teaching assistants. Their 2025 education paper pairs the models with retrieval. Eight small models entered the benchmark. The group included LLaMA, Granite, and Gemma systems. Each model answered from course materials through a retrieval pipeline. The giant GPT-4o served as the reference point. Fifty multi-turn tasks covered theory questions and assignments. With good prompting and targeted retrieval, small models matched the giant. Their answers stayed accurate and aligned with teaching goals.

Small models run in real time on one GPU server. Schools can host them on consumer grade hardware. That setup protects student privacy by staying local. It also cuts energy use and cloud costs sharply. Personal tutoring at campus scale becomes affordable. The authors still call for broader validation studies.
arxiv-2510-02647:
Ferreira models how charmonium states melt inside a rotating quark-gluon plasma using holography. His 2025 theoretical physics paper builds a bottom-up holographic QCD model. Charmonium probes the plasma made in heavy ion collisions. Heat partly dissociates these heavy bound states. Non-central collisions also spin the plasma strongly. The model first reviews the cold quarkonium spectrum. Equations then track heavy mesons moving through the rotation. Motion splits into directions along and across the wave vector. Quasinormal modes give the dissociation fingerprints. Charge diffusion and pole-skipping get computed in the same setup.

Mode frequencies rose with momentum in both directions. The spectral function peaks shifted in step with them. Spin alignment of the J/psi state answered the rotation too. Holography turns hard plasma questions into tractable gravity ones. Rotation is a real feature of collision fireballs. Models ignoring spin miss part of the physics.
arxiv-2510-03047:
Gómez-Ortiz and co-authors clear up a mix-up about how crystals twist light. Some materials rotate polarized light as it passes through. Textbooks often tie that rotation to the crystal's handedness. The authors show the tie is looser than assumed. They studied quartz and its cousin aluminum phosphate from first principles. Both crystals pass through a phase change as they cool. The change flips the handedness named in the space group.

Yet the sense of light rotation does not flip with it. The screw axis label reverses, but the optical sign stays. A single phonon mode drives the shift between phases. The real decider is the helix of the most polarizable atoms. In these crystals, oxygen atoms form that imperfect helix. Its twist keeps its sense across the transition. Handedness of a label, the paper argues, is not handedness of matter.
arxiv-2510-03147:
Valentine and co-authors test whether the Ariel telescope can map exoplanet skies at scale. Eclipse mapping reads a planet's glow as its star covers it. JWST can do it, but its time is fiercely contested. Ariel, a dedicated survey mission, will visit a thousand planets. The team benchmarked Ariel against JWST with simulations. Existing JWST eclipse maps served as the test cases.

Top targets gave Ariel maps much like JWST's own. It needed the same observing time for those worlds. Mid-ranked targets needed only about triple the time. Phase curves rescue the weakest targets from impossible demands. Latitude detail will stay limited for Ariel overall. Longitude detail, though, should be wide-ranging and strong. That suffices to pin down first-order air flow patterns. Nearly one hundred planets could be mapped in a quarter of the mission.
arxiv-2510-03247:
Zhang and Zhu open active learning to multimodal data where the pairs themselves are the expensive part. Active learning picks which examples deserve costly annotation. Classic methods assume each item needs one label. Multimodal pipelines like CLIP instead need aligned image-text pairs. Single-modality items are cheap, but good alignments cost real money. Their framework is the first built for that unaligned setting. The learner actively buys alignments, not labels on ready pairs.

The acquisition rule blends uncertainty with diversity in a modality-aware way. It runs in linear time, keeping big pools practical. Pool-based and streaming workflows both fit the design. Benchmark experiments showed steady annotation savings. One dataset needed up to forty percent fewer annotations. Accuracy held level with fully aligned training in those runs. Results stayed consistent across CLIP variants and model sizes. Modern multimodal pipelines drown in unpaired raw material.
arxiv-2510-03347:
Curreli and a large team present a 2025 arXiv paper on twisting stacked atomic sheets without touching them. Layers of graphene and boron nitride gain new traits when one is rotated by a few degrees against the other. Past methods turned layers with probes or complex rigs that are hard to scale. The team instead used an electron beam to plant charge on an insulating flake. The charge built a sideways field that torqued the flake around.

Across six devices, flakes turned by a few degrees under the beam. Three turned clockwise and three counter clockwise, matching the bias setup each time. Microscope images tracked the motion, and laser spectra confirmed that the layer alignment had truly changed. Once a flake settled, it stayed pinned in its new spot. Contactless twisting could lead to chips whose traits are tuned after building, a key step toward flexible nano devices.
arxiv-2510-03647:
Yoshihara and Ohzeki present a 2025 arXiv paper speeding up a decomposition method for optimization problems by handing its bottleneck to a quantum classical hybrid solver. Extended Benders decomposition splits mixed integer quadratic problems into a master problem and a subproblem. The master part, holding the integer and quadratic variables, dominates the computing time. The authors plug D-Wave's constrained quadratic model solver into that slot. The rest of the decomposition proceeds classically.

The hybrid matched the commercial solver Gurobi in solution quality in their tests. On some instances it reached near optimal answers with exponential speedups over the classical route. As problem size grew, the hybrid's advantage became clearer, without performance decay. Mixed integer quadratic models sit inside power grid scheduling and portfolio design. A solver pairing that scales could widen the problems those fields can tackle. The authors plan tests on instances to map where the benefit holds.
arxiv-2510-04047:
Imagawa, Murata, and Yamamoto present this 2025 arXiv paper on a strange echo effect in a quantum spin chain at its critical point. Theory linked to holography predicts that a sharp local kick can produce responses that reappear at localized spots in space and time. Whether that happens may depend on exactly what kind of kick is applied. The authors test this numerically on the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model.

Using a time-evolving block decimation simulation, they varied the perturbation's spatial profile and operator type. Sharply localized, periodically recurring responses appeared only for perturbations matching local density fields in the continuum limit. These results tell experimentalists which perturbations to use when probing holographic-style dynamics on quantum simulators.
arxiv-2510-04147:
Gao and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on speeding up diffusion language models without changing what they output. Diffusion models generate text in parallel, but practical parallel decoding drifts away from careful stepwise decoding and loses quality. Speculative decoding usually fixes such gaps with a separate small draft model. For diffusion models, that extra model wastes the parallelism already built in.

Their method, Self Speculative Decoding, makes the diffusion model draft for itself. The model predicts several positions at once, then verifies candidates through a hierarchical tree in a single forward pass. Accepted tokens commit progressively, and the final text is identical to stepwise decoding. On the open LLaDA and Dream models, the scheme delivered speedups of more than threefold at best. No auxiliary module means no extra memory overhead either. Lossless acceleration of this kind is what diffusion language models need for real deployment.
arxiv-2510-04447:
Lucas Happ of the RIKEN Nishina Center in Japan wrote this 2025 paper on a software package for quantum few body problems. Few body physics studies systems of just two or three particles, between the single particle and many body cases. No general, well documented solver for such systems was freely available. Happ presents FewBodyToolkit, a package written in the Julia language for that gap.

The package handles two and three body systems in several spatial dimensions. Users can set almost any pairwise force between the particles. It computes both bound states and resonant states that decay over time. The engine rests on the Gaussian expansion method, a proven way to solve such problems. Benchmarks and research examples in the paper show the package working as claimed. It ships with full documentation and worked examples. The author aims it at research, teaching, and testing new methods.
arxiv-2510-04847:
B. Mehl wrote this 2025 paper on gas detectors that multiply charge inside pure argon. Thick gaseous electron multipliers are drilled plates that avalanche electrons through holes in a gas. They serve particle physics and imaging, and they promise simple readout for noble gas detectors. The study runs plates one millimeter thick in pure argon at over three atmospheres. Computer field simulations guided the designs before the plates were built.

A modified design hides two extra electrodes inside the plate itself. Those inner electrodes calm the discharge instabilities that cap plates. The team measured gain for each design across wide ranges of field strength. Two electrode plates were measured beside the new four electrode ones. The comparison shows how geometry changes the operating range and the reachable gain. Charge readout in argon matters for neutrino and dark matter detectors. A stabler multiplier means cleaner signals and fewer sparks in long runs.
arxiv-2510-04947:
Xin Li, Kaixiang Yang, Qiang Li, and Zhiwei Wang address a gap in breast cancer screening in their 2025 arXiv paper. A standard mammogram exam takes two X-ray views of the breast. In real clinics, one view is sometimes missing, damaged, or too degraded to use. Their method rebuilds the absent view from the one that remains.

Their system, CA3D-Diff, uses a diffusion model guided by the shape of the breast. One part matches tissue that sits in the same columns across both views. Another part infers a rough 3D structure and feeds it back into image generation. On the VinDr-Mammo dataset, the method beat prior tools on fidelity and structural consistency. Views it created also improved single-view cancer classification in screening tests.
arxiv-2510-05047:
Víctor Blanco, Harshit Kothari, and James Luedtke build a new classifier for multi-category data in this 2025 arXiv paper. Support vector machines sort items by drawing a boundary that maximizes the gap between classes. Extending that idea to many classes at once takes care. The authors frame the whole task as one optimization problem.

Their model arranges several hyperplanes at once under a mixed-integer formulation. A kernel extension lets the boundaries bend for harder data. The framework can also absorb classification trees and feature selection choices. A dynamic clustering heuristic keeps large datasets tractable. In experiments on synthetic and real benchmark data, the method proved faster than an earlier formulation. Its accuracy stayed competitive with leading tools in scikit-learn.
arxiv-2510-05747:
Ma and colleagues generate T-cell receptor sequences conditioned on their targets. Designing receptor variable regions for cellular therapy usually takes months of screening. A useful receptor must fit a specific peptide presented by a specific HLA molecule. Their 2025 PhysicoGPTCR model designs candidates in minutes instead.

The Transformer conditions jointly on peptide and HLA context. Residue-level physicochemical descriptors are embedded into the generation process. Trained on curated receptor-peptide-HLA triples, it beats ANN, LSTM, VAE, and earlier GPT baselines. Its outputs score better on edit distance, similarity, and longest common subsequence. It also explores a broader region of sequence space. Novelty, diversity, and biophysical plausibility are enforced together, not traded off. Blind docking shows more binding-competent clones than the strongest baseline. Future work extends the approach to class-II HLA molecules. Top candidates await synthesis and in-vitro binding assays.
arxiv-2510-06347:
Choustikov and twelve co-authors use MEGATRON simulations to separate physics from observational bias in early galaxies in a 2025 astrophysics paper. JWST spectra of early galaxies encode gas properties, but extracting them is hard. Simulations that predict spectra directly can show which inferences are trustworthy.

MEGATRON couples radiation hydrodynamics with non-equilibrium thermochemistry at parsec-scale resolution. Multiple star formation and feedback prescriptions run side by side. Regardless of feedback, the simulated early interstellar medium is denser, metal-poorer, and more strongly irradiated than local counterparts. That pattern matches JWST interpretations. Applying standard observational methods inside the simulations revealed a trap. Gas density controls the slope of the mass–metallicity relation. At high densities the popular O32 ratio traces density, not ionization, so other ratios are recommended. Different feedback models land in different regions of strong-line diagnostic diagrams. Observers can use those diagrams to constrain feedback physics itself.
arxiv-2510-06647:
Haochen Zhang, Zhong Zheng, and Lingzhou Xue study how reinforcement learning agents learn from trial and error. Their 2025 paper works with Q-learning in simple table-based decision problems. A key measure is regret, the total loss from choosing worse actions while learning. Good bounds on regret should reflect the gap between the best action and the rest.

Existing gap-based bounds were coarse and missed much of that structure. The authors build a finer analysis that treats good and bad state-action pairs separately. That yields the first fine-grained regret bound for a classic algorithm, UCB-Hoeffding. They also design a simpler variant, ULCB-Hoeffding, which performs better in experiments. For methods outside the UCB family, they find two flaws in the leading algorithm, called AMB. Fixing its update truncation and a broken martingale step gives the first rigorous fine-grained bound there too.
arxiv-2510-06747:
I-Fan Lin, Faegheh Hasibi, and Suzan Verberne group short texts by intent without any labeled examples. Their 2025 paper serves companies whose chatbots receive floods of user messages. Those messages must be sorted into intent clusters, but nobody knows the clusters in advance. Hiring annotators to label training data is often unrealistic.

Their method, TWIST, needs no training and no labels at all. It builds sparse vectors from representative texts, then refines them step by step with guidance from a language model. The method sits on top of any existing text embedder. Results matched or beat leading methods that rely on contrastive learning. It worked across varied datasets and with relatively small language models. It also scales to large message collections while limiting how much the model is queried. That economy matters in commercial settings. The team next wants to test specialized domains and add human feedback.
arxiv-2510-07147:
Lalan and co-authors propose a team of software agents that keeps its memory while it searches. Their 2025 paper targets a weakness in one-shot model calls. Stateless calls forget prior steps, so long tasks fall apart. The team instead keeps a shared state across rounds of search. Specialized agents propose, attack, score, and test candidate answers. The test case is writing hard unit tests for code.

An actor agent suggests edge cases. An adversary probes how robust those cases are. A critic scores them, and an executor runs them in a safe sandbox. Good candidates survive across rounds, which keeps the search varied. Trials on known coding test sets found far more coverage than single-step baselines. The gains held on code the system had never seen. Stateful search suits tasks where answers improve through rounds of attack and repair.
arxiv-2510-07247:
Ravindranath, Liu, and Chen study quantum circuits whose entanglement grows with unusual slowness. Their 2025 paper mixes unitary gates with repeated measurements. Such monitored circuits show a sharp transition between entanglement regimes. In the high-entanglement phase, entanglement usually grows fast. From certain starting states, though, it grows only logarithmically. The authors trace that slowness to a matching slow growth in how widely the state spreads over basis states.

The same circuits map onto a classical spin model with positive weights. That model shows glassy behavior, freezing into sluggish patterns at finite temperature. Large, non-local symmetry operators explain both the slow quantum dynamics and the classical glassiness. The mapping turns an entanglement transition into a structural transition in the classical model. This bridge gives researchers a new geometric lens on measurement-driven transitions.It may suggest classical simulations for some monitored systems.
arxiv-2510-07647:
Chandee, Lee, and Li wrote this 2025 number theory paper on L-functions, special functions tied to prime numbers and modular forms. A famous idea from Katz and Sarnak predicts how the zeros of these functions are spaced. The prediction borrows statistics from random matrices. The authors study a large family of L-functions built from holomorphic Hecke newforms. They average over many forms at once to see the pattern clearly.

The team computes the centered moments of the one-level density of zeros, for any order. Their formulas match the Katz-Sarnak prediction across a stated range of test functions. Reaching that match required handling oversized phantom terms that hide the true off-diagonal contributions. It also required solving a matching puzzle between their main terms and random matrix predictions. The result strengthens evidence that random matrix statistics govern this family's zeros.
arxiv-2510-07747:
Crompvoets, Kirk, Gutermuth, and Di Francesco wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on sorting objects in James Webb Space Telescope catalogs. Webb data reveal many kinds of objects, but each observation uses its own filter set. That variety makes uniform classification hard. The authors built a tool named SESHAT to label objects from any Webb observation. It targets young stellar objects, field stars, brown dwarfs, white dwarfs, and galaxies.

SESHAT trains a gradient-boosted model on thousands of rows of synthetic photometry. At run time it adapts that training to whichever filters the real data used. On real star-forming regions and deep fields, it recovered every class with recall of at least eighty percent. It needs no shape or position information to do so. Proposal writers can also test whether planned filters suffice before observing. The tool ships as an open Python package for the community.
arxiv-2510-07847:
Li, Wang, and Sun wrote this 2025 paper on spotting anomalous graphs when labeled examples are few. Graph-level anomaly detection serves fraud control, review sorting, and biochemistry. Neural methods usually demand large labeled sets, which problems rarely provide. Noise in the graphs further blurs what counts as abnormal. The authors build a meta-learning framework, MA-GAD, that learns how to adapt from related networks before facing a new one.

A compression module first shrinks each graph while keeping its node information, cutting noise. Meta-learning then extracts anomaly patterns across similar networks. The result is an initialization that adapts fast with a handful of samples. A bias network sharpens the contrast between normal and anomalous nodes. On four real biochemical datasets, MA-GAD beat leading methods at whole-graph and subgraph anomaly detection. The design suits fields where anomalies are rare, costly, and hard to label in bulk.
arxiv-2510-08047:
Lin and six coauthors wrote this 2025 speech recognition paper on fixing training labels without human transcripts in the target accent. Pseudo-labeling lets recognizers learn from unlabeled speech, but the labels carry accent-specific errors. Filtering throws data away instead of repairing it. The authors correct the bias in parameter space. In a source accent with real transcripts, they fine-tune twin models on true labels and pseudo-labels.

The weight difference between the twins forms a correction vector capturing the bias. Adding it to a target-accent model trained on pseudo-labels pulls it toward real-label behavior. On a dataset spanning ten African accents, error rates fell by up to a third for the smallest Whisper model. Corrected models occasionally beat models trained on true labels. A self-corrected variant added gains. The method needs one labeled source domain, a modest price for underserved accents.
arxiv-2510-08147:
The BESIII Collaboration, the international team running the BESIII detector at China's BEPCII collider, reported in 2025 the first measurements of three rare decays of the J/psi particle. The team analyzed about ten billion J/psi events. They searched for decays producing a neutral Xi baryon with an anti-Lambda or anti-Sigma baryon and a kaon. These three-body decay rates had never been measured.

All three channels were measured for the first time, yielding their branching fractions. The team also examined whether the baryon and antibaryon cluster near threshold, a phenomenon seen in some related decays. No baryon-antibaryon threshold enhancement was observed. That negative result constrains models predicting enhancements from final-state interactions or exotic states. Each newly measured channel removes a blank spot from the decay tables theorists use.
arxiv-2510-08847:
Jia and co-authors propose a report card for AI agents, in this 2025 arXiv paper on evaluation. An agent works in a loop: it sets a goal, makes a plan, and then acts. Failures can hide in any of the three stages, and a single end score cannot say where things went wrong. The team's framework, called Agent GPA, grades each link in the chain separately with five measures.

The measures check whether the final outcome matches the goal, whether actions stay consistent with earlier ones, and whether execution wastes steps. They also grade the plan itself and whether the agent actually followed it. On two test collections, the framework caught every agent error in the public set. Automated judges agreed well with human graders and pointed to the failing stage with high agreement, which helps builders fix agents in a targeted way.
arxiv-2510-08947:
Chen, Hua, and Zhou settle where a classic nonlinear equation on a grid can and cannot have positive solutions, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Lane-Emden equation balances spreading against a self-reinforcing source. Their stage is the integer lattice, the infinite graph of whole-number points, plus its half-space and quadrant regions with the solution forced to zero at the edges.

A weight in the equation fades with distance at a rate the authors vary, alongside the source's strength. For strong sources in what they call the Sobolev super-critical region, they prove positive solutions exist, building them with variational methods that hunt for energy minima. In the Serrin sub-critical region they prove none exist, by tracking how any candidate must decay and reaching a contradiction. A band between the regimes stays open on the full grid and half-space; the quadrant has no such gap.
arxiv-2510-09147:
The Euclid Collaboration, with Goh among the lead authors, reports upgrades to the analysis pipeline of Europe's Euclid space telescope, in this 2025 arXiv preparation paper. Euclid will map billions of galaxies, charting where they sit and how they are shaped, to probe dark matter and dark energy. Squeezing answers from that flood requires a likelihood pipeline, the software that scores how well each cosmic theory fits the data. The pipeline, called CLOE, was built for the standard cosmic model and needed room for alternatives.

The team extended CLOE to handle theories beyond the standard model. They added a magnification bias effect to the clustering analysis of spectroscopic galaxies, and adapted the main photometric probes for heavy neutrinos and modified gravity. The changes were validated by forecasting on synthetic Euclid-like data and recovering the known answers, in line with earlier studies. They also flag where the pipeline still needs work.
arxiv-2510-09447:
Álvaro Álvarez-Domínguez presents his doctoral thesis in a 2025 arXiv paper on particle creation in intense electromagnetic fields. The work applies quantum field theory in curved spacetimes to the Schwinger effect, the production of particle-antiparticle pairs by very strong electric fields. The effect still lacks experimental proof, so theory carries the burden of explaining it.

The thesis builds the framework for quantising charged fields in nontrivial backgrounds, facing the ambiguity in defining the vacuum head-on. It extends states of low energy, an idea from cosmology, into the Schwinger setting. It also generalises the quantum Vlasov equation across schemes, and shows the ambiguities have physical meaning tied to measurement. Applications include analogue cosmic expansion in condensates and black holes. There, the Schwinger effect prevents black holes forming from light under current conditions, and quantum effects discharge them through fermionic superradiance.
arxiv-2510-09947:
Mir Tafseer Nayeem and co-authors question a standard metric for tokenizers in this 2025 arXiv paper on multilingual language models. Tokenizers split text into tokens, the chunks a model reads. Fertility, the average tokens per word, is the usual score for how well a tokenizer compresses a language.

The team argues that fertility hides how vocabulary is shared across languages and domains. They analyze six widely used tokenizers over seven languages and two domains, and study a metric called STRR as a richer alternative. They find fertility stays stable for English, runs high for Chinese, and barely reacts to domain shifts. Their results show a single compression number can mask real gaps in how fairly tokenizers treat different languages.
arxiv-2510-10047:
Li and co-authors introduce SwarmSys in this 2025 arXiv paper on multi-agent reasoning with language models. Single agents reason well, but teams of agents often rely on fixed roles or a central controller. Those designs limit how far the system can scale and how well it adapts on long reasoning tasks.

SwarmSys takes its cue from swarm intelligence, the way insect colonies solve problems through many simple local interactions. It is a closed-loop, decentralized framework, so agents adjust to each other's output without a boss agent. The authors aim for scalable and adaptive reasoning on long-horizon problems. Decentralization also removes the single point of failure that a central controller creates.
arxiv-2510-10147:
Khanikati and Konstantin Y. Bliokh study time-diffracting wave vortices in this 2025 arXiv paper in wave physics. Wave vortices are swirling wave patterns tied to phase singularities, points where the wave's phase is undefined, and they carry orbital angular momentum. Two families were known: vortex beams that spread in space, and spatiotemporal pulses that spread in space and time.

The authors develop a class of two-dimensional vortices whose diffraction unfolds in time. This adds a new member to the vortex family, with its own transverse angular momentum behavior. Vortices are used in optics, acoustics, and quantum systems to carry information and exert torque. A time-based variant widens the design space for those applications.
arxiv-2510-10247:
Pinteaux and Gijs M. Tuynman revisit rolling tangent spaces in this 2025 arXiv paper in differential geometry. Take a surface sitting in Euclidean space and a curve drawn on it. Rolling the tangent space along the curve, like a coin rolling without slipping, leaves an imprint of the curve on that flat space.

The authors develop this forgotten picture of geodesics and parallel transport, two core notions of curved geometry. Parallel transport moves vectors along a curve while keeping them as unrotated as the surface allows. The rolling view makes both ideas concrete and visual. Recovering an old viewpoint can refresh teaching and suggest new invariants for submanifold geometry.
arxiv-2510-10747:
Chirag Shetty and six co-authors argue that a standard cloud computing control, CPU limits, does more harm than good, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A CPU limit strictly caps how much processor a container may use. Most research on rightsizing and autoscaling assumes such limits are necessary. The authors question that assumption, drawing on practical experience from cloud users who report worse performance and higher costs with limits in place.

They argue the indiscriminate adoption of limits rests on mistaken beliefs that limits are essential for operations and safety. They provide empirical evidence for dropping CPU limits entirely from latency sensitive applications. That shift, they say, forces a rethink of autoscaling and billing models built around limits. They also identify cases where limits genuinely help, such as background jobs, when used with clear reasoning. The paper is a position piece aimed at both researchers and industry practitioners.
arxiv-2510-10847:
Ilya Fokin reports measurements aimed at the phase structure of quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Lattice calculations predict that at nearly zero net baryon density, chiral symmetry is restored through a smooth crossover between quark gluon plasma and a hadron gas. The two descriptions agree on net baryon fluctuations up to third order, but fourth order cumulants from the lattice fall significantly below the hadron gas values. That gap offers an experimental test.

Fokin presents net proton number cumulants up to sixth order in proton proton collisions at top LHC energy, recorded by the ALICE detector. The small system measurements search for signs of a chiral phase transition. Net proton measurements in lead lead collisions extend to fourth order. Beyond probing the QCD partition function, the data can distinguish between mechanisms of baryon production.
arxiv-2510-10947:
Namhoon Kim and Sara Fridovich-Keil add a warning light to AI based image reconstruction, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Generative models serve as priors that rebuild images from few measurements, as in medical scans. When a test image falls outside the training distribution, these priors can hallucinate features. Existing uncertainty methods need in distribution calibration data, give heuristic answers, or measure the wrong source of uncertainty. Their indicator needs none of that.

The hypothesis is simple: rebuilds of in distribution images stay stable when the measurements vary randomly, while out of distribution rebuilds wobble. They use that stability as the signal. In a tomography demonstration on handwritten digits, a network trained only on the digit zero was tested on all ten digits. The unfamiliar digits showed higher variability and higher error, validating the indicator. The authors propose pairing aggressive measurement reduction with such lightweight guardrails in deployment.
arxiv-2510-11147:
Self-organizing maps compress high-dimensional data onto a grid that preserves its structure, and they remain popular decades after Kohonen introduced them. Louis Berthier and co-authors introduce torchsom in this 2025 arXiv paper, an open-source Python library that implements these maps in PyTorch. The package aims to be a reference implementation that is easy to use and easy to extend.

The library offers three main features: dimensionality reduction, clustering, and friendly data visualization. Its PyTorch backend brings GPU acceleration for fast training and smooth integration with the wider PyTorch ecosystem. It also follows the scikit-learn interface, so users get a familiar way of fitting and applying models. The authors highlight uses in exploratory analysis and explainable AI workflows. The library is released under the Apache 2.0 license with 90 percent test coverage, and its source code and documentation are public on GitHub for the community.
arxiv-2510-11647:
Telling a program 'make this video look like sunset' is easy; judging whether the edit obeyed, stayed faithful, and looks good is not, and existing benchmarks barely try. Yinan Chen and co-authors build IVEBench, a benchmark suite for instruction-guided video editing, in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Earlier benchmarks suffered from limited source diversity, narrow task coverage, and incomplete metrics, so the authors rebuilt all three dimensions.

IVEBench contains six hundred source videos spanning seven semantic dimensions and lengths from thirty-two to over a thousand frames. Its editing tasks cover eight categories with thirty-five subcategories, with prompts generated and refined through large language models plus expert review. The evaluation protocol scores three things separately: video quality, instruction compliance, and fidelity to the source, combining traditional metrics with multimodal model-based assessment. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art editing methods showed the suite delivers comprehensive verdicts, .
arxiv-2510-11847:
Sam Hawke and three colleagues review a young family of data methods called contrastive dimension reduction. Ordinary dimension reduction squeezes data into fewer variables, but it often keeps variation shared by everyone. Researchers comparing a treatment group against a control group want the opposite: the signal that is unique to, or stronger in, the foreground group. That contrast matters in genomics, imaging, and time series studies.

Their 2025 arXiv review gives the first systematic overview of these methods. The authors propose a shared pipeline for analyzing case-control studies, step by step. They sort existing methods into a taxonomy based on their assumptions, goals, and mathematical formulations. That sorting unifies approaches that grew up separately under different names. The review also surveys key applications and the challenges current methods face. It closes with open questions and future directions, aiming to help the technique spread into wider scientific use.
arxiv-2510-11947:
Cristian Ivanescu and Hunter Labrecque prove a tidy preservation result in operator algebra. The way-below relation says one object sits compactly inside another, with room to spare, rather than merely being contained. It began in topology and found a second home in the Cuntz semigroup of C-star-algebras, a tool for comparing positive elements. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks whether the relation survives tensor products, the standard way of combining two systems.

The answer is yes: if each factor sits way below its partner, the tensor product does too. The authors state plainly that, after finishing, they learned the Cuntz semigroup literature had already recorded this fact. They publish their argument anyway, judging that it offers a complementary perspective. Their route uses countably generated Hilbert C-star-modules, where Kasparov stabilization applies. For researchers, an independent proof can clarify why the result is true, not just that it is.
arxiv-2510-12247:
Wang and co-authors speed up quantum state preparation by randomizing how small amplitudes are kept, in a 2025 arXiv quantum physics paper. Preparing a desired quantum state is a dominant cost in many quantum algorithms, so its price can erase any quantum advantage. Many useful states have hierarchical amplitudes, where values shrink exponentially or by a power law.

The usual approach truncates small amplitudes outright, tying error directly to circuit depth. Instead, the authors prepare an ensemble of simple circuits, each keeping all large amplitudes while boosting a single small one. They prove this randomized ensemble gains a quadratic improvement in the trace distance error over deterministic truncation. For exponential decay that halves the number of encoded amplitudes, and for power law decay it gives polynomial savings. Tests on a lithium hydride wavefunction, an Ising model ground state, and ResNet parameters confirm the approach across chemistry, physics, and machine learning.
arxiv-2510-12347:
The ATLAS Collaboration searches for emerging jets, a possible signature of a hidden dark sector, in proton proton collision data, in a 2025 arXiv particle physics paper. The proposed dark sector mirrors quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force, with its own dark quarks. These shower into many long lived dark hadrons, which later decay back into ordinary particles. A jet thus appears to emerge gradually, with multiple displaced vertices.

The analysis uses data collected at the Large Hadron Collider between 2015 and 2018. It targets events with four jets: two emerging jets and two ordinary jets from pair produced scalar mediators. No meaningful excess above the Standard Model background was observed. For a dark pion decay length of twenty millimeters and a dark pion mass of twenty giga electron volts, mediator masses between one and two tera electron volts are excluded. The result constrains how such a dark sector could behave.
arxiv-2510-12747:
Zhuang and colleagues make diffusion based video upscaling run in real time as a stream, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion models produce excellent video restoration, but their latency and computation have kept them from real world super resolution. FlashVSR is presented as the first one step diffusion framework for streaming video super resolution.

Three innovations combine. A three stage distillation pipeline enables streaming. A locality constrained sparse attention cuts redundant computation. A tiny conditional decoder speeds reconstruction without sacrificing quality. The system processes high resolution video at about seventeen frames per second on a single high end graphics processor. To train at scale the authors built a dataset of one hundred twenty thousand videos and one hundred eighty thousand images. Experiments show reliable scaling to ultra high resolutions with speedups of up to about twelvefold over earlier one step diffusion methods.
arxiv-2510-12847:
Zheng and co-authors diagnose a failure mode in language models adapted for time series forecasting in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such models often underperform simple linear methods, a puzzle the authors trace to pseudo-alignment, where time data and language representations blur together without truly matching. They connect the effect to the cone effect inside pretrained language models, which squeezes representations into a narrow region.

Because time series data live on a low-dimensional manifold, a curved surface inside a larger space, the mismatch grows worse. Their remedy, TimeSUP, lifts the time series manifold so its dimension better matches language embeddings, letting temporal signals stay distinct while shared structure is still learned. Across long-term forecasting tests, TimeSUP beat leading methods, and it plugged into four existing pipelines with clear gains.
arxiv-2510-13147:
Tahmasebi, Pelluer, and Kwon make activation compression practical for large language models in this 2025 arXiv paper on computer architecture. Low-rank decomposition can shrink models, but decomposing activations at runtime was thought to cost more latency than it saves, so earlier work decomposed only weights. The authors challenge that consensus.

They adopt the progressive Lanczos algorithm for decomposition and design a companion accelerator, D-com, around it. A compute replication method attacks the operation's memory-bound bottleneck and delivered a large speedup in evaluation, while a shape-keeping scheme removes decomposition costs in consecutive layers. A multi-track approach handles outlier channels separately to protect accuracy. Overall the accelerator improved end-to-end latency by about a fifth against a high-end data center GPU, with only a small quality loss on a reasoning benchmark.
arxiv-2510-13247:
Adlam, McQueen, and Waegell argue that agency cannot be purely quantum in this 2025 arXiv philosophy of physics paper. An agent, minimally, must build a model of its world, use that model to weigh what different actions would bring about, and reliably carry out the action maximizing expected utility. The authors test whether a system evolving purely quantum mechanically, with no decoherence or collapse, could meet those three conditions.

They show the first two conditions collide with the no-cloning theorem, which forbids copying an unknown quantum state. Building a world-model requires copying environmental information. Deliberation requires copying the model to test multiple actions. Approximate cloning lacks the needed fidelity and generality. The third condition fails separately through the linearity of quantum dynamics. The consequences reach from constraints on physical agency to how classical agents emerge in a quantum universe.
arxiv-2510-13947:
András Grabarits and Adolfo del Campo study how quantum complexity grows when a quantum system is driven through a phase transition, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They use spread complexity, a measure of how far a quantum state spreads across a special basis called Krylov space. The basis is built by applying the system's energy operator again and again.

Using a mathematical expansion for driven systems, the authors map the process onto a simple one-dimensional hopping model. In that picture, complexity moves like a particle stepping along a line. For the transverse-field Ising model, a standard chain of interacting quantum spins, they prove a sharp result. Every statistical moment of the complexity grows with the same power law as the defect density predicted by Kibble-Zurek theory. The full distribution becomes Gaussian, bell-shaped. Numerical tests on long-range Kitaev models support their scaling argument for other transitions.
arxiv-2510-14047:
David Alonso-Gutiérrez, Silouanos Brazitikos, and Giorgos Chasapis sharpen estimates for the volume of slices through convex bodies placed in John's position, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A convex body is in John's position when the ellipsoid inside it is the ball, a canonical placement making volumes comparable across shapes. Knowing how large central sections can be is a basic question in convex geometry.

The authors revisit a clever argument of Keith Ball, combining the Brascamp-Lieb inequality, a strong tool for bounding integrals of product functions, with a generalized Parseval-type identity from Fourier analysis. Their technique adds to earlier results by the first two authors. It generalizes estimates by Meyer and Pajor and by Koldobsky about extremal sections of the p-norm balls. It covers a broader family of norms built from a John decomposition of the identity. It is the structural data certifying John's position.
arxiv-2510-14147:
Gabriel Raulet and co-authors present parallel algorithms for building fixed-radius near-neighbor graphs, which link point pairs within a set distance, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such graphs are the first step in clustering, dimensionality reduction, and topological analysis. But large scientific data sets and non-Euclidean distance measures, like string edit distance, defeat many tools that assume ordinary geometry.

Their approach builds cover trees, a data structure for metric spaces, with a shared-memory algorithm competitive with state-of-the-art search structures. It then scales across distributed machines with two strategies: partitioning the points, or partitioning space itself. The algorithms scale across real and synthetic data sets under many metrics. On high-dimensional data with a million points, they report speedups of several hundred times over the state of the art using a thousand cores. Gains grow larger with more cores and denser graphs.
arxiv-2510-14247:
Kentaro Takahira and Yuki Ueno present VisAider, a work-in-progress AI assistant that suggests visualization changes during live data presentations, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In small-group settings, discussions shift quickly and presenters must adapt charts on the fly. Existing systems bind fixed actions to fixed commands. Changing chart types, transforming data, or adding a data set mid-talk is awkward.

VisAider analyzes the presentation context, the available data set, the active visualization, the ongoing conversation, and the audience profile, and generates ranked suggestions for helpful chart aids. A formative study with data analysts identified the key challenges of real-time adaptation and distilled design considerations. A prototype works in simulated settings, while testing exposes hard problems: inferring data transformations, settling ambiguous chart tasks, and responding with low latency. The authors outline ongoing work to address these limits and integrate the system into real presentation tools.
arxiv-2510-14347:
Andrej Bogdanov and co-authors show a decoding algorithm for error-correcting codes works better than believed, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The decoder is allowed a code-dependent hint. Prange's information set algorithm decodes any linear code in polynomial time, but only up to an error rate. Raising that rate matters for cryptography, where decoding hardness underpins security assumptions such as learning parities.

The authors use a polynomial-length advice string depending on the code. For codes that are balanced, meaning their codewords have near-uniform weight, they improve the tolerable error rate by a logarithmic factor. Their insight is that multiplying the received word by a matrix of dual codewords measures how close the word sits to the code. Their decoder minimizes that measure. They show the threshold-based approach is asymptotically optimal among all decoders using advice, revealing vulnerabilities in cryptographic uses of parity learning.
arxiv-2510-14447:
Mohammad Shafiei, Farhad Fazileh, and Milorad V. Milošević show that linearly polarized light, long thought useless, can switch a thin Dirac material into a topological phase with one-way edge channels, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Floquet engineering shines light on quantum materials to rewrite their phases; in three-dimensional Dirac systems, circularly polarized light opens gaps, while linear polarization was assumed ineffective.

The authors find the loophole: in quasi-two-dimensional Dirac materials, a momentum term arising from coupling between the film's two surfaces changes the symmetry analysis. That term lets the light drive a topological phase transition, producing chiral edge channels that carry current in one direction only. Studying an ultrathin film of bismuth selenide as the system, they find the transition occurs at light intensities within reach. The result promotes quasi-two-dimensional films as platforms for light-controlled topology.
arxiv-2510-14747:
Medvedev and Ushakov test, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether their calculated line lists for carbon monoxide can be trusted for lines nobody has measured yet. Line lists give the positions and strengths of a molecule's spectral lines. Astronomers rely on them to read temperature and composition from light. The strengths come from the molecule's dipole-moment function, and the authors built semi-empirical versions of it, fitted in 2022 and 2025.

A line list earns its keep by predicting, not by fitting. The authors therefore compare their predictions against recent measurements in four vibrational bands of carbon monoxide. The comparison covers lines never used in the fitting, plus lines not yet observed. The functions describe the held-out lines well and give credible intensities for the unobserved ones, so the list can be used where measurements do not yet exist.
arxiv-2510-15047:
Chen and co-authors diagnose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, why AI agents collapse when their world changes. In unfamiliar environments with rules and randomness, agents cannot ground their knowledge in the dynamics. Vanilla reinforcement learning makes it worse: the chance that at least one of several sampled attempts succeeds drops as training proceeds, a symptom of brittle exploration and generalization.

Their remedy borrows from model-based reinforcement learning: give the agent a world model, split into state representation and a transition model. The framework, SPA, cold-starts the policy with self-play supervised fine-tuning, where the agent learns the world model by interacting with the environment. It then simulates future states before policy optimization begins. This initialization outperformed the online world-modeling baseline and boosted reinforcement learning. The broader claim is that agents should internalize how a world works before being graded on acting in it.
arxiv-2510-15147:
Aditya Bhosale, Kavitha Chandrasekar, Laxmikant Kale, and Sara Kokkila-Schumacher address supercomputing jobs that move to the cloud, in this 2025 conference paper. Cloud billing rewards using exactly the machines a job needs, yet classic parallel software cannot grow or shrink a running job, so resources sit idle or jobs wait. The team's setting is Charm++, a programming system whose work units can migrate between machines.

They built a Kubernetes operator, a controller that runs Charm++ jobs on cloud clusters managed by the popular Kubernetes system. On top of it sits a priority-based scheduler that rescales jobs live as cluster conditions change. The goal is fuller use of the cluster while high-priority jobs still get quick responses. In their tests the elastic scheduler, rescaling with little overhead, clearly outperformed fixed-size schedulers. They argue such flexibility is what makes cloud supercomputing pay off.
arxiv-2511-00147:
Eyer, Huijse, Chornay, and the Gaia collaboration describe how the Gaia mission, which observed over two billion stars repeatedly for ten years. It built the largest catalogue of classified variable sources across the whole sky. Variability from seconds to years appears in its astrometric, photometric, and spectroscopic time series, down to faint magnitudes. Machine learning handles crossmatching, variability detection, and sorting at that scale.

Astronomy readers get an account of the variable universe as Gaia reveals it: pulsating stars, eclipsing systems, and transients in unprecedented numbers. The catalogue turns time-domain astronomy from case studies into population statistics, with methods other surveys can reuse.
arxiv-2511-00547:
Alain Riou proposes a simple algorithm for building binary magic squares: grids of zeros and ones where every row and every column sums to the same total. Such matrices serve combinatorics and design problems, but generating them efficiently, with a guarantee of success, takes care. An induction proof shows Riou's algorithm always returns a valid square and runs at optimal theoretical complexity.

The study then widens to non-square grids. Riou formalizes the conditions on row and column sums under which rectangular binary magic squares can exist at all. A slight variant of the first algorithm provably generates those too, whenever the conditions hold. Two implementations are released publicly as Python packages, including one that produces several squares in parallel on a GPU.
arxiv-2511-00647:
Ethan Fort, Mohamed Mousa, and Mostafa Nouh build logic gates out of sound waves in engineered materials, a bid for mechanical computing that thinks with vibrations. Older mechanical computing used slow static tricks, buckling beams or origami folds. Wave-based logic inherits the speed of sound itself, and the authors add memory: metamaterial cells infused with shape memory alloys that store elastic profiles and act when heat triggers them.

A proof-of-concept device demonstrates working, reconfigurable gates, verified by output probes and measured wavefields. The modular gates combine into larger combinational circuits, and the design points toward sequential logic, the kind with memory of past states, in wave-based analog systems. Fast, low-latency mechanical intelligence could suit places electronics cannot go.
arxiv-2511-00747:
Zixuan Ma and Chenfeng Huang generate synthetic time series by first taking real ones apart. Trend and seasonality drive temporal patterns, yet many generators never decompose their data interpretably, so the series they synthesize carry muddled patterns. Their approach, Seasonal-Trend Diffusion, joins diffusion models with a learnable decomposition that keeps the parts meaningful and visible.

Trend learning falls to a multi-layer perceptron block, while seasonality is learned through adaptive wavelet distillation across scales. A correction step then enforces internal consistency between the generated parts and preserves how they relate. Across eight real-world datasets the method reaches state-of-the-art generation quality. It also extends to multi-window generation of long sequences with reliable results, marking it as a robust, flexible tool for synthetic time data.
arxiv-2511-01047:
Yu Shi, Hao Li, Bram Adams, and Ahmed Hassan study whether a code repository's history can help an automated agent fix bugs. Earlier work showed history helps with single line bugs. Their system, HAFixAgent, feeds context drawn from blame information, which records who last changed each line, into an agent's repair loop.

The study covers hundreds of Java bugs from Defects4J and Python bugs from BugsInPy, across three base language models. History proved widely available and useful: the best heuristic added a few percent for the strongest model and far more for weaker ones. Three different history heuristics fixed different subsets of bugs, so combining them repaired greatly more than no history, at no extra cost in steps or tokens.
arxiv-2511-01247:
Md. Shariful Islam and colleagues show software orchestrated quantum networks over a campus scale testbed at Argonne National Laboratory. Quantum networks will only matter if they grow from solo experiments into infrastructure that runs shared applications on its own, much as classical networks do.

Their prototype orchestrator borrows software defined networking principles to run standard quantum network experiments across buildings linked by deployed telecom fiber. The system provides a service level view of networking tasks, shared time synchronization, and entanglement checks between remote nodes. As a demo service, it distributed entanglement nonstop and stably between remote sites for twelve hours. The authors present the result as a promising path toward scalable quantum networks.
arxiv-2511-01447:
Yong Song, Jiaqi Fu, and Yiting Cen ask whether a particle's spin can change the global pattern of its possible circular orbits around a black hole. Spin couples to spacetime curvature in the Mathisson-Papapetrou-Dixon formalism, pushing spinning particles off geodesic paths and shifting their orbital parameters, so the qualitative orbit structure might shift too.

Using a topological approach, they build an auxiliary vector field and compute a winding number for timelike circular orbits in static, spherically symmetric spacetimes. Between two horizons the winding number is minus one, guaranteeing at least one unstable orbit, and outside the outermost horizon it is zero, forcing orbits into stable unstable pairs or none. Both results hold whatever the spin's size or direction. Examples in Schwarzschild and its anti-de Sitter and de Sitter variants confirm the invariant topology under explicit spin induced shifts.
arxiv-2511-02047:
Hamidreza Sadeghsalehi builds a deep learning system for analysing how people walk, using wearable sensors, with two jobs in mind. Gait analysis helps clinicians manage nerve and joint conditions, but the models can quietly absorb biases hidden in their training data. The framework uses attention across several sensor streams, applied to a multi-cohort dataset covering Parkinson's disease, osteoarthritis, and stroke screening tasks.

The attention patterns exposed a serious flaw in the public dataset: for two screening tasks the model relied almost entirely on the right foot because the data itself was heavily one-sided. Sadeghsalehi presents the auditing ability as the main contribution, with sensor combinations suggested by the model as leads for future testing.
arxiv-2511-02247:
Hao Li and ten co-authors estimate real distances from a single endoscope camera, information that could guide autonomous medical robots. Supervised learning needs images with known depth, which real surgical footage lacks, so a common workaround translates synthetic images into a realistic style and trains on those. A stubborn gap between translated and genuinely real frames limits how well that works, especially for absolute, metric depth.

The team's method attacks the gap inside the network rather than in the images. The depth network learns features that stay consistent between synthetic and real frames of central airway videos. It uses adversarial training and a directional consistency requirement. It works regardless of which translation process produced the synthetic data. On airway phantom videos with hand-aligned depth maps, the approach beat leading methods on absolute and relative depth, across several network backbones.
arxiv-2511-02347:
Liuhao Lin and seven co-authors evaluate language models by making them draw. Standard benchmarks report opaque numbers that can hide a basic weakness: models that ace text tests may barely understand space. Their benchmark, LTD-Bench, asks models to produce pictures, either as dot matrices or as executable code, so spatial failures are visible at a glance, even to non-experts.

The tasks run in both directions, generation to test spatial imagination and recognition to test spatial perception, across three levels of difficulty. State-of-the-art models that shine on conventional benchmarks showed profound gaps in mapping between language and spatial concepts in both directions. The authors argue this undermines claims that such models are genuine world models, and they note the drawings themselves offer a diagnostic tool for comparing how different models represent space.
arxiv-2511-02947:
Clare Burhenne and eleven colleagues read the star formation histories of the two Magellanic Clouds from the Scylla survey's deep Hubble images. The survey covers large areas of both galaxies, deep enough to reach stars older than the ancient main-sequence turnoff. Their 2025 paper groups fields into eight sub-regions in the Small Cloud and seven in the Large Cloud, then hunts for bursts of star birth in each.

The Small Cloud shows two global bursts, about five and one and a half billion years ago, plus one local burst. The Large Cloud shows one global burst about three billion years ago. Against orbit models, shared triggers seem to start earlier and stronger in the Small Cloud. One Small Cloud region, the Wing and Bridge, matches the southwest Large Cloud in chemistry and growth, hinting at stripped material.
arxiv-2511-03347:
Mario Ayala, Nicolas Dirr, Grigorios A Pavliotis, and Johannes Zimmer untangle how the reading of noisy equations affects whether motion can run backward in a statistical sense. Random pushes whose strength depends on position can be read in several standard ways, named for Ito, Stratonovich, and Klimontovich. A single dial between them lets the team write one geometric condition for reversibility.

That condition ties noise choice to a Gibbs weight on a curved space. For systems with slow and fast parts, shrinking away the fast parts keeps reversibility intact. The Klimontovich reading, notably, survives that shrinking unchanged. The work gives modelers a clear rule for picking a noise reading that will not break after simplification.
arxiv-2511-03747:
Ali Safa and co-authors release OpenMENA, an open board and software stack for computing with memristor crossbars at the edge. Memristors compute where they store, promising frugal intelligence for small devices. Until now, tinkerers lacked a full open path from bare crossbar to running model.

The system joins a reproducible hardware interface with read, program, and verify loops, a firmware and software stack with high-level interfaces, and a careful method for writing trained weights into analog conductances. Chip-in-the-loop tuning then irons out device quirks. Digit recognition and a robot dodging obstacles prove the full flow. Open neuromorphic hardware can spread edge experimentation beyond a few specialist labs.
arxiv-2511-20747:
Takato Mori and Beni Yoshida revisit in 2025 a puzzle about baby universes inside holographic models of gravity. A baby universe is a small closed spacetime budding off from a larger one. Path-integral calculations hint its state space might be one-dimensional, leaving no room for entropy or inner life. Mori and Yoshida argue it can carry large entropy instead, using random encoding as their lens.

In their picture, the baby universe holds logical information that neither boundary region can read alone. Haar random encoding scrambles the data so thoroughly that reconstruction from either half is impossible. Two puzzles then dissolve: its states cannot be cloned, and no single observer can witness their fate at the singularity. The heavy operator that creates the universe also serves as its observer, making each microstate observer-dependent.
arxiv-2511-20947:
Tianyi Hao and colleagues build in 2025 a compiler pipeline that predicts when error correction starts paying off for real quantum algorithms. Their target is early fault-tolerant machines using the surface code, where logical operations run as lattice surgery. The pipeline chains open-source tools, error-aware gate synthesis, and magic state cultivation to turn logical circuits into physical ones. They compile two flagship algorithms, QAOA and quantum phase estimation, and simulate the resulting Clifford proxy circuits.

Both test algorithms reach break-even, the point where error correction beats no correction, at modest scale. A 5-qubit instance needs 2,517 physical qubits at code distance 11 when physical error rates sit at one in a thousand. At half that error rate, 1,737 physical qubits and distance 9 suffice. The numbers give hardware teams concrete targets for the first machines where correction helps algorithms, not just memory.
arxiv-2511-21047:
Changjian Xie introduces in 2025 a faster, sturdier way to simulate how magnetisation swirls and settles inside magnetic nanostructures. The governing Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation is stiff, and conventional schemes trade accuracy against stability. Xie's method reaches strict third-order accuracy in time, beyond most current techniques, while cutting the cost of the linear solves that made an existing third-order scheme slow. Nanostrip simulations validate the design against established benchmarks.

Robustness is the pleasant surprise. For Gilbert damping coefficients from 0.1 up to nearly 10, a range spanning the very large values near 9 seen in experiments, the scheme stays strongly stable and avoids non-physical magnetisation states. It reproduces domain wall motion consistent with prior validated studies, and the energies it computes sit significantly lower than the rival third-order method's, a sign of cleaner relaxation. The scheme suits quantitative studies of magnetic memory switching, where damping varies widely by material.
arxiv-2511-21247:
Jaime García-Martínez and seven coauthors release a new training ground for music technology in 2025: the Spheres dataset of multitrack orchestral recordings. Algorithms that separate a recording into its instruments have thrived on pop music but lacked clean orchestral material. The Colibrì Ensemble performed two famous works for the project, Tchaikovsky's Romeo and Juliet and Mozart's Symphony No. 40, plus scales and solo excerpts for every instrument.

García-Martínez and his coauthors recorded over an hour of music with 23 microphones, from close spot mics to room ambience, and supply each instrument section as an isolated stem from every position. They also measured the room's impulse responses, its echo fingerprint, for each instrument spot. Baseline tests with X-UMX models on separating instrument families and removing microphone bleed show both the dataset's promise and how hard full separation remains.
arxiv-2511-21847:
Wang and colleagues show that a photograph of a dripping droplet at the instant it breaks off can reveal the liquid's hidden properties. Viscosity and surface tension normally need specialized instruments, complicating quality control in printing and coating. The team filmed droplet formation at high speed for silicone oils, alcohol and glycerin solutions, and methanol, collecting 840 examples across wide flow conditions.

They trained machine learning models on each droplet's outline near pinch-off, plus the flow rate, to predict viscosity and surface tension from shape. The models succeeded, showing the break-up geometry encodes enough information to recover both properties and even to predict the droplet's shape at pinch-off for new cases. Unsupervised clustering of the learned representations grouped cases into regions matching known physical regimes in the Reynolds and Ohnesorge number planes, suggesting the method could simplify liquid testing in automated production.
arxiv-2511-22047:
Young, a researcher, stress-tests the safety guardrail models that screen prompts before they reach large language models, evaluating ten publicly available guardrails from Meta, Google, IBM, NVIDIA, Alibaba, and the Allen Institute. The test set holds 1,445 prompts across 21 attack categories, mixing benchmark items with novel attacks the models could not have memorized during training, a design meant to expose inflated benchmark scores.

Qwen3Guard-8B scored highest overall at 85.3 percent accuracy. Yet it collapsed from 91.0 percent on public prompts to 33.8 percent on unseen ones, a 57.2-point generalization gap suggesting training-data contamination. Granite-Guardian generalized best with only a 6.5-point gap. Most alarming, a 'helpful mode' jailbreak made two guardrails generate harmful content instead of blocking it. The study argues generalization to genuinely new attacks, not headline benchmark accuracy, should be the primary metric for judging guardrails.
arxiv-2511-22247:
Le, Tran, Nguyen, Zhou, and Gurrin make image search with optional text practical for small labs. In image-guided retrieval with optional text, a query is a reference picture. Sometimes with words like 'same dress but red,' and the system must handle composed retrieval, sketch-based retrieval, and plain visual search in one framework. The available flagship dataset is too heavy for modest hardware, and models tend to favor one subtask. Their FIGROTD dataset is deliberately friendly: 16,474 training and 1,262 test triplets spanning all three subtasks.

Their model adds a Variance Guided Feature Mask amplifying discriminative dimensions, trained with combined InfoNCE and triplet losses. Despite fewer training triplets than rivals, it reaches 34.8 mAP at rank 10 on the CIRCO composed-retrieval benchmark and 75.7 mAP at rank 200 on Sketchy, beating stronger baselines. Dataset and code are public.
arxiv-2511-22547:
Tan and a large collaboration compute a key quantity of proton structure directly from quantum chromodynamics. The Collins-Soper kernel controls how transverse-momentum-dependent parton distributions, maps of quark motion inside the proton, change with energy scale. Models had to guess its behaviour at large transverse separations. Using lattice QCD within large-momentum effective theory, the team simulated the needed correlations and extracted the kernel at physical pion mass and the continuum limit.

The calculation used lattice spacings from 0.052 to 0.105 femtometres and pion masses down to about 136 megaelectronvolts, with smeared operators and nonperturbative renormalisation. The resulting kernel is determined out to separations of about one femtometre with controlled uncertainties. It agrees with perturbative calculations at small separations and with phenomenological extractions. It is now the most precise first-principles constraint on its long-distance behavior. Feeding it into global fits shows an impact on them.
arxiv-2511-22647:
Bao, Cheng, Song, and Gu show that a conformal field theory's dynamics can regrow from its topological skeleton. Recent work built fixed-point tensor complexes encoding a conformal field theory, or CFT, in tensor network form, topological data from one dimension higher constraining local physics through generalised symmetries. The authors design a tensor complex renormalisation algorithm for that structure, a renormalisation-group flow respecting the generalised symmetry.

Starting from only the primary fields' three-point functions already reproduces the full fixed-point tensor. More remarkably, the flow stays stable when all conformal and geometric information is stripped out: topological input, plus partial conformal dimensions, recovers the complete tensors. They call this the topological bootstrap, validating it across the Ising, tricritical and tetracritical Ising, three-state Potts, and Yang-Lee models. Unlike classic bootstrap bounds, the method constructs conformal data, suggesting a route to algebraic descriptions of gapless states.
arxiv-2511-22947:
Chandra and colleagues study the inside of the pion, a tiny particle made of a quark and an antiquark, using a model rather than direct measurement. They compute generalized parton distributions, maps that describe how the pion's momentum is shared among its quarks and where those quarks sit inside it. They focus on the zero skewness case, a symmetric setup that makes the maps easier to interpret.

Working inside the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, a stand-in for the strong force theory, with a mathematical cutoff that also mimics quark confinement, they find their pion parton distributions match experimental data. They also match the JAM global analysis well at two energy scales. They also extract charge radii for the pion, obtaining 0.56, 0.63, and 0.83 femtometers for its scalar, vector, and tensor responses. These values are consistent with recent lattice simulations and a check on future collider measurements.
arxiv-2511-23047:
Sultanow and Hatziiliou revisit a classic question in spectral geometry, famously phrased as hearing the shape of a drum.
