The question is how much geometry is encoded in the eigenvalues, the vibration frequencies, of a shape. For a rectangle they assume the hard case: only a finite ordered list of eigenvalues is given, with no labels saying which vibration mode each number came from.

Their method splits the spectrum into a smooth part and an oscillating part and reads different facts from each. The rectangle's area comes from the high-frequency growth rate described by Weyl's law. The doubled side lengths, 2a and 2b, then appear as the peaks when the oscillating part is Fourier transformed, because they are the shortest billiard paths inside the rectangle. The recovery works even when the list starts at an unknown offset and the lowest eigenvalues are missing.
arxiv-2511-23147:
Zou and colleagues present the first systematic survey of sulfur monoxide and its rare isotope-bearing variant in Milky Way molecular clouds. They aim to measure how the ratio of sulfur-32 to sulfur-34 changes across the Galaxy. Until now that gradient rested only on carbon monosulfide measurements, a single tracer whose uncertainties could distort the picture, so an independent molecular check was needed.

Using the IRAM 30-meter telescope and the 10-meter Submillimeter Telescope, they detected the higher sulfur monoxide line in 136 of 184 clouds and derived isotope ratios for 55 sources. They found no correlation with distance or gas temperature, which argues against measurement artifacts. Ratios from the lower-energy transitions follow the rising radial trend seen earlier, while the higher-transition values sit systematically lower. Comparison with Galactic chemical evolution models suggests their star-forging recipes need revision in the low-metallicity regime.
arxiv-2511-23247:
Boukabene and Benbouzid-Si Tayeb review the literature on community detection in multilayer networks. The same people or entities are linked by several kinds of relationships at once, such as family, work, and friendship layers in a social system. Finding groups that are densely connected within themselves is much harder here than in single-layer networks, because each layer can carry a different community structure. The layers often disagree.

The survey organizes the existing methods into a taxonomy. It walks through the main types of multilayer networks and collects real-world applications across disciplines where layered data arise naturally. It then catalogues the open challenges, including how to fuse conflicting layer partitions into one defensible answer and how to evaluate results without ground truth. It closes with concrete directions for making multilayer community detection more accurate and more useful for future researchers.
arxiv-2512-00047:
Angelina Parfenova, Alexander Denzler, and Juergen Pfeffer study how language model agents converge when they annotate data together. Models are more and more deployed in shared settings, yet their teamwork as black-box agents is little understood. The team simulated thousands of multi-agent, multi-round talks on an inductive coding task.

The runs produced well over a hundred thousand messages, capturing final labels and full interaction records. Watching settling unfold shows whether agreement reflects shared understanding or mere herding. That gap matters for using agent panels as research assistants. Full records are preserved in the data, so settling can be studied as a process, not just an outcome.
arxiv-2512-00547:
Rebuilding a moving scene in three dimensions is much harder when several people interact with objects at once. Sandika Biswas, Qianyi Wu, Biplab Banerjee, and Hamid Rezatofighi present asset-driven semantic reconstruction of dynamic scenes in 2025. The scenes involve multiple humans and their complex interactions with surroundings.

Such environments matter for augmented and virtual reality, gaming, and embodied AI, yet they remain underexplored. Diverse motion patterns and frequent occlusions defeat simpler reconstruction pipelines. An asset-driven approach, reusing known object models inside the scene, could keep reconstructions stable even when people block the camera's view. Asset-driven means known objects are fitted into the scene rather than rebuilt from scratch.
arxiv-2512-00647:
Vision Mamba models promise transformer-level skill with lower cost, yet their efficiency is capped by the number of image tokens. Shanhui Liu, Rui Xu, and Yunke Wang present MambaScope in 2025, a coarse-to-fine scoping method for efficient vision Mamba. Token pruning and merging cut computation but lose information.

Discarding or compressing token representations throws away detail that fine recognition may need. A scoping approach first surveys the image coarsely, then spends tokens where detail matters. Keeping information while cutting cost would widen where state-space vision models can run, from medical scanners to mobile cameras. Coarse-to-fine mirrors how people scan a scene before examining details. Vision Mamba's promise is efficiency, so a method that protects it is on theme.
arxiv-2512-00747:
Tingjun Zhang and a large team of physicists study a magnetic material called alpha-MnTe in a 2025 paper. The material is a semiconducting altermagnet, a magnet with no net moment that still splits electron behavior by spin. The team adds lithium to it and watches what changes.

Using inelastic neutron scattering, they bounce neutrons off the material to probe its inner motions. Adding lithium flips the spin direction from in-plane to out-of-plane. It also raises the density of mobile charge carriers. The evidence points to an interplay between those roaming carriers and local magnetic moments, which shapes how the material acts.
arxiv-2512-00947:
Liyao Li and a large team study how language models can treat tables as a data type of their own in a 2025 paper. Tables run much of the world's stored data, in spreadsheets, databases, and reports. Language models shine on plain text, so researchers have worked to extend them to table reasoning tasks.

Their paper presents tables as a modality, a distinct channel like text or image that a model must learn to read. Rows, columns, and cell relations carry meaning that plain text flattens away. Framing tables this way guides how models should encode and reason over them. Better table skills matter for finance, science, and business tools.
arxiv-2512-01047:
Tanmay Ambadkar, Đorđe Žikelić, and Abhinav Verma automate the sharpening of learning specs in a 2025 paper. Logical specifications can guide reinforcement learning agents toward complex tasks by stating rules the behavior must satisfy. When a spec is under-specified, though, it leaves too much open, and agents may fail to learn useful policies.

The authors explore improving coarse-grained specs through an exploration-guided strategy. The agent's own exploration reveals which parts of the spec need refinement. Automating that loop could save the hand-tuning that now limits spec-based training. Better specs mean agents that learn intended behavior, not loopholes.
arxiv-2512-01347:
Fukunaga, Nakatsuyama, and Takahashi study odd points on translation surfaces. A translation surface sweeps one curve along another. Points where the surface pinches or folds are called singular. Past work dealt with the case where the two curves are freely set.

Here the pair handle the linked case, where the curves rest on each other. They use framed surface theory to sort the odd points. The work wraps up the full study of such surfaces. A full sort helps in geometry and in design of curved forms for art and building. The framed view sorts pinches, folds, and cusps by local form, giving each odd point a name tied to how it can unfold.
arxiv-2512-01447:
Maya Sadeler Perrin and co-authors study Hawkes processes with a drifting baseline. Hawkes processes model events that spark more events. Their baseline rate is often fixed. In brain, social, and finance data, outside factors drift over time and move that baseline.

The team lets a diffusion process drive the baseline. They study long-run acts, inference, and tests for the new class. The model spans many variables at once. It should fit event data where a slow hidden drift shapes bursts, like trades or nerve spikes. Diffusion-driven baselines also absorb seasonality, since slow outside cycles enter through the same drift term that carries trends and shocks.
arxiv-2512-01547:
Muratore and co-authors study Bootes I, a very faint dwarf galaxy, with space telescopes. Such dwarfs are old and poor in metals. Their metal spread is a fossil record of early star birth. It tests models of first stars and dark matter halos.

Data from JWST and Hubble map stars in the dwarf. The team reads the spread of metals across its stars. They also hunt for binary stars in the system. Those reads sharpen the tale of how the smallest galaxies formed and how their first stars enriched them. Binary counts matter too, since unseen companions can fake a wider metal spread if their light blends with the star being gauged.
arxiv-2512-01647:
Andrea Coccaro and co-authors learn to rebuild muon tracks at the LHC. Charged particle paths must be rebuilt with high precision. Good tracks need sharp hit picks and mass momentum gauges. Errors there blur all later physics results.

Their differentiable approach learns the rebuild step itself. It can be tuned end to end for final accuracy. Muons are clean probes of new physics at colliders. Sharper muon tracks lift searches for rare decays and new particles that show up first as small track shifts. End-to-end tuning also spots which hits hurt most, guiding detector crews toward the sensor flaws that cost the most physics reach.
arxiv-2512-01747:
Aguasca-Cabot and the LST-1 team report follow-up views of the brightest gamma-ray burst ever seen. GRB 221009A was detected in October 2022. Part of its brightness came from its close distance. That closeness makes it a unique lab for burst physics.

The LST-1 telescope chased its high-energy afterglow. Such follow-ups test how jets cool and spread after the blast. A record-bright event lets weak traits show that dim bursts hide. Results refine models of the most violent explosions known in the cosmos. Cherenkov telescopes catch the highest energies, where burst jets may hide a second component that satellite data alone cannot resolve.
arxiv-2512-02147:
EP240222a is the first tidal disruption by an intermediate-mass black hole caught in real time, with multi-wavelength observations and spectroscopic confirmation. Wenkai Li and a large team present in 2025 a five-stage model explaining why its light curves broke the usual theoretical expectations.

In their picture, the shredded star's stream circles inefficiently, meets the forming disk late, and its light is reprocessed before escaping. Each stage leaves a mark on the evolving brightness that the model reproduces. Intermediate-mass black holes are the missing link between stellar and supermassive ones, so a well-explained first event anchors a new observational field.
arxiv-2512-02347:
When many users want the same popular file from one transmitter, sending it once by multicast beats sending it user by user, but users must cooperate. Anjali Yadav and four co-authors use cooperative game theory in 2025 to find when users gain by forming coalitions for multicast reception.

A coalition can share the costs and benefits of joining a multicast group, and game theory predicts which groupings are stable. The framework of coalitional games lets the authors state precise incentive conditions. Multicast efficiency matters more as wireless traffic grows, and understanding users' incentives decides whether cooperative schemes survive outside theory.
arxiv-2512-02447:
Spiking neural networks promise brain-like, energy-sipping computation, but their object detectors often waste their temporal gift by feeding neurons nearly identical inputs at every step. Fan Luo and four co-authors add a Temporal Dynamics Enhancer in 2025 for directly trained spiking object detectors.

Conventional designs replicate the input or stack it into fixed-interval frames, flattening the time structure the spikes could exploit. Enhancing temporal dynamics gives neurons varied, informative stimulation across steps. Better spiking detectors would bring accurate vision to power-starved devices, from drones to wearable cameras.
arxiv-2512-02847:
Theodoros Katsoulas and Kyriakos Tamvakis test how the early universe might have inflated inside Einstein-Cartan gravity. Their theory lets the action depend on two curvature measures: the Ricci scalar and the Holst invariant. Einstein-Cartan gravity adds torsion, a twist of spacetime, to the usual picture.

The models studied add cubic terms of the Holst invariant to the action. The authors examine the inflationary behavior those terms produce. Viable inflation inside modified gravity widens the options for explaining the universe's smooth, flat start, and future sky surveys can test them. Twist in space time is a bold add on. The early sky is the one place such a bold move can be tried and judged.
arxiv-2512-02947:
Samuel Andrello, Daniel Alabi, and Simon J. L. Billinge organize how inorganic materials are made so machines can predict full recipes. Machine learning now predicts new materials with novel properties quickly. Working out how to synthesize those materials remains largely unsolved, though.

Earlier work predicted precursors or conditions, rarely the whole synthesis pathway. The authors present a graphical framework and datasets that represent full reactions. Structured pathways let models learn from real lab history, moving prediction from what to make toward how to make it in an actual laboratory. Full paths, not just parts, are what a lab tech must run at the bench. Data in path form meets the tech where the work is done each day.
arxiv-2512-03247:
AI image edits often leave seams and color shifts. Haitian Zheng and co-authors present PixPerfect to fix those flaws in this 2025 work. Latent diffusion models raised edit quality, but their compression can cause pixel-level mismatches at edit borders.

Past fixes often fail to remove all artifacts or do not transfer across models. The authors add a pixel-space refinement step guided by a discriminative check. Seamless edits matter for photo work, design, and film. A method that works across latent types would be widely useful. Pixel-level polish decides whether an edit looks real at a glance, especially along hair and edges.
arxiv-2512-03347:
Robots learning to handle objects often drift off course. William van den Bogert, Gregory Linkowski, and Nima Fazeli present GrOMP to fix that in this 2025 work. Imitation learning copies expert moves, but small errors compound and hurt precision.

GrOMP projects the grasped object back onto a lower-dimensional manifold, a constrained surface of valid poses. Keeping a loosely held object on that surface limits error growth. The method targets repetitive tasks like industrial assembly. More precise imitation could make robot training faster and safer. Manifold projection acts during learning, correcting drift before errors compound into failure.
arxiv-2512-03547:
Mixed-integer programs are powerful but slow to solve exactly. Stefan Clarke and Bartolomeo Stellato propose a learning-based hierarchy in this 2025 work. Such programs model scheduling, logistics, and design problems with both whole and continuous choices.

Their architecture splits the original problem into higher and lower level problems. Both are smaller, so solutions come faster while staying high in quality. Learning guides the split for structured problems. Faster mixed-integer solving could improve planning in transport, energy, and manufacturing. Hierarchy also lets planners refine only the hard parts of a schedule.
arxiv-2512-03947:
Training a support vector machine means running an optimisation algorithm, and knowing when to stop is worth money at scale. Matthew Hough and Stephen A. Vavasis analyse that stopping problem in a 2025 preprint. Their core idea: stop not at a fixed accuracy, but when the current classifier is certified to agree with the optimal one on points that matter.

For a perturbed SVM formulation, they derive a stopping condition that certifies points correctly classified by both classifiers, with no assumptions on the data at all. Under a geometric model of two clean clusters plus noise, certifying one point can guarantee the whole well-behaved set is separated. They add computable bounds for two algorithms, FISTA and coordinate descent. The analysis exposes flaws in the stopping rule of the popular LIBLINEAR package, which can stop too early or too late.
arxiv-2512-04047:
Persuasion used to be expensive, so political elites could shape public opinion only crudely, through schools and mass media. Nadav Kunievsky asks what changes when artificial intelligence makes persuasion cheap and precise, in a 2025 economics preprint. In his dynamic model, elites deliberately choose how far to reshape how policy preferences are distributed, paying persuasion costs and needing majority support.

With a single elite in charge, optimal intervention tends to push opinion toward polarised profiles. The author calls this drift the polarization pull, and better persuasion technology speeds it up. With two opposed elites alternating in power, incentives flip in places: each side may park society in cohesive semi-lock regions that rivals struggle to overturn. Depending on the setting, cheaper persuasion can then heighten or dampen polarisation. Polarisation, on this account, becomes a designed instrument of governance.
arxiv-2512-04847:
Tsai-Ning Wang and Lin-Lin Chen, working with Neil Zeghidour and co-authors, present AcuLa, a light post-training method that teaches audio models the clinical meaning of the sounds they hear. Models trained on stethoscope recordings spot acoustic patterns well, yet often miss what those patterns signify for a diagnosis. Their 2025 arXiv paper aligns an audio encoder with a medical language model that acts as a semantic teacher.

To teach at scale, the team used large language models to turn the structured metadata stored with existing recordings into readable clinical reports. Training then pulls audio features toward the matching report meanings through a contrastive objective, while a self-supervised term guards fine acoustic detail. The audio model keeps its sharp ears and gains a clinician's vocabulary. Better sound understanding could support screening tools that listen for heart and lung trouble where specialists are scarce.
arxiv-2512-05047:
Zephyr Penoyre works out where two blended stars appear to sit on the sky when their images overlap. When two stars' smeared images merge, the combined light seems to come from a position that is neither star's true home. The problem sharpens for instruments whose blur is stretched into an oval, as with the Gaia space mission, where the answer depends on the oval's angle against the line joining the pair.

Penoyre reduces the stretched case to a one-dimensional profile along that joining line, with an effective blur width set by the angle and stretch. From there the problem scales with just the separation and brightness ratio, and he derives the faintest companion still resolvable at a given separation. He also maps how the measured position wanders as the same pair is viewed from different angles, a wandering that adds noise to precision star catalogs.
arxiv-2512-05347:
Pablo Galaviz and six co-authors simulate how silica nanopores vibrate, atom by atom. The vibration density of states — how a material's atoms distribute their jiggling across frequencies — is a fingerprint measured by neutron scattering and used to identify structure. For silica riddled with nanoscale pores, the authors run molecular dynamics on pore and bulk silica alike and set the results against density-functional calculations and experimental neutron data.

They systematically test a range of force fields, the recipes that set how atoms push and pull, and probe how temperature, the pore's surrounding structure, and adsorbed water change the spectrum. The simulated spectra agree reasonably well with theory and experiment. Temperature matters little for a dry pore, but water matters a great deal. Its molecules dominate the low-energy modes, increasingly as loading rises. The study is a step toward characterizing nanoporous silica in the computer before the beamline.
arxiv-2512-05547:
Pengfei Wang and Emilia Fridman design a complete feedback controller for high-dimensional heat flow, using only boundary sensors and actuators. Semilinear heat equations in two or three dimensions are controlled from the edge of the domain. The difficulty grows with dimension, because the Laplacian's eigenvalues grow more slowly. That leaves more modes within reach of the nonlinearity. The authors build the whole loop: an observer that rebuilds the inside state from boundary readings, and a controller computed from matrix inequalities.

Their design widens the allowed boundary shapes, allows shape functions supported on part of the boundary only, and permits larger Lipschitz constants than earlier work. They analyze robustness against two kinds of noise, one fading at equilibrium and one persistent. Conditions give the smallest observer and largest nonlinearity that keep stability. Simulations in two and three dimensions confirm the gains.
arxiv-2512-05647:
Giorgos Antoniou and six co-authors release a large open dataset of Greek government decisions. The records come from Diavgeia, the national platform where public bodies must post their acts for transparency. The corpus holds about one million decisions, with clean text pulled from the original PDF files. It ships in Markdown form, together with the full pipeline used to build it, so others can reproduce or extend the work.

The team goes beyond release notes. They study repeated boilerplate patterns across decisions, and they build a test task in which a retrieval based system answers questions over the corpus. A baseline system is scored on how well it finds and reasons over the right documents. The exercise shows how a chat style assistant could answer public questions from official records. The corpus can also serve as training material for language models that work on legal and government text.
arxiv-2512-05847:
Elena Fernández-García and five co-authors present a formula for how many dark matter halos the universe holds at each mass, and test it across cosmic history. The halo mass function is basic cosmology infrastructure. Their model grows from the classic Press and Schechter idea, upgraded with triaxial collapse along three unequal axes. The count depends almost entirely on the variance of the early density field.

The formula needs no explicit redshift term, yet lands the right normalization and high mass tail alone. The team checked it against the Uchuu simulation suite, runs covering ten orders of magnitude in mass and redshifts out to twenty. Deviations stayed mostly within a tenth to a fifth. The standard Sheth-Tormen formula drifted badly at early times; this one did not. A universal halo census simplifies studies that count galaxies to weigh the universe.
arxiv-2512-06247:
Gus Henry Smith, Sandesh Adhikary, and six co authors build DUET, a method that helps AI agents grasp how a computer chip design really works. Chip designs are written in a low level language that spells out how signals change over time, step by step. Language models can read that code, yet they often miss what the design does when it runs, which hurts tasks like checking and documenting it.

DUET copies how human experts learn a design: by trying things out. The agent forms a guess about the design, then tests it with simulators, signal viewers, and formal checkers, and folds what it learns back into its picture of the chip. Step by step, a firm grasp of the design grows from the bottom up. In trials, agents using DUET did better at formal checking than agents that only read the code once.
arxiv-2512-06347:
Naoki Yoshida, Isao Ishikawa, and Masaaki Imaizumi prove a striking claim about learning machines that fit their training data exactly. Such machines, called interpolators, can still do well on fresh data, a fact that puzzled theory for years. Some credit the training method's hidden leanings. Others note that even random machines that fit data perfectly seem to generalize, pointing to a trait of the model itself.

Working in a teacher student setup, where a fixed rule generates the data, the authors prove the error on fresh data drops to exactly zero. That happens once the count of training samples passes a threshold set by the shape of the set of perfect fitting machines. Their proof leans on algebraic geometry, the study of shapes defined by polynomial equations, to describe that set. The result gives a clean reason why sheer sample count can turn exact fitting into perfect learning.
arxiv-2512-06647:
Siyu Qiu, Anqi Lin, Shiya Wang, and Xingyu Lan study how much teenagers trust AI chatbots, and what drives that trust. Most trust research samples adults, yet teenagers use chatbots often and are still forming judgment. Drawing on theories of teen education and psychology, the team picked four traits to test: AI literacy, ego identity, social anxiety, and psychological resilience.

An online survey of Chinese middle school students, joined with follow up interviews, carried the study. Resilience stood out as a strong positive predictor of trust: steadier teens trusted chatbots more. Age changed the link between social anxiety and trust. Interviews added texture: teens reported fairly high trust overall, rated their own AI skill higher than it likely is, and were swayed by outside forces such as social media. The study gives schools and designers a first map of teen trust in chatbots.
arxiv-2512-06947:
Sarah V White and co-authors continue a census of the brightest radio galaxies in the southern sky, the G4Jy sample. Each entry is a powerful radio source whose glow must be matched to the ordinary galaxy that hosts it, a step needed before distances and energies can be known. Earlier rounds of the project matched sources using infrared images. This third paper adds fresh identifications based on sharper radio maps from several surveys.

By eye, the team lays radio outlines over galaxy images and picks the true hosts, adding over a hundred matches. They also gather distance estimates: measured spectra for part of the sample, photo-based estimates for another part, and further values from a public extragalactic database, each inspected and refitted where needed. The long goal is a fully measured sample; radio power and size are reported here as a start.
arxiv-2512-07047:
Angel Naranjo and co-authors dissect the swirling chaos of active nematics, materials made of tiny self-driven rods that constantly stir themselves. Confined in a channel, such a material can flow left or right and spontaneously reverse, and the authors ask what organizes those flips. Their tools are symmetry and exact coherent structures, tidy flow patterns that persist inside the turbulence like skeletons inside a body.

At low activity they trace families of steady and repeating patterns to symmetry-constrained bifurcations, both local and global. The surfaces surrounding those patterns channel the flow between left-moving and right-moving states, sometimes through a lattice of vortices, sometimes directly. At high activity the chaos takes over, yet the same skeleton survives underneath: typical turbulent paths keep shadowing the tidy patterns and their exit routes.
arxiv-2512-07347:
Krzysztof Stempak revisits the harmonic oscillator, the most familiar system in quantum mechanics, through its inner anatomy in flat space. Its special functions can be organized into two different complete bases. Comparing the two pictures, and using only basic analytic tools, Stempak gives simple new proofs of two known results that usually demand heavier machinery.

The first is the rotational symmetry of the Hermite projection operators, a family studied by Kochneff: rotating space does not disturb the projections onto the oscillator's energy levels. The second is an identity of Hecke-Bochner type, due to Thangavelu, which relates how the oscillator's harmonics behave under rotation and scaling. Short, clear proofs matter where key facts can hide behind folklore.
arxiv-2512-07547:
Sam Adriaensen wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on families of polynomials that keep meeting. Work over a finite field, and call a family intersecting when any two members agree somewhere. A star is the obvious giant family: every polynomial pinned to one fixed value at one fixed point.

The classic Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem says stars are the largest intersecting families in its world. Adriaensen proves a stability version of that result for polynomials. Once a family grows past a stated size, it must sit inside a star. Near-maximal families, in other words, have no exotic shapes left. The proof also covers a view of the polynomials at infinity. That view turns the problem into one about homogeneous polynomials in two variables. The technique widens into a general frame for intersecting families of linear codes. Geometry of the code's projective system decides when stability holds.
arxiv-2512-07647:
Georgios Tzachristas and Renhai Chen wrote this 2025 machine learning paper with Lei Deng, Ioannis Tzachristas, and Gong Zhang. Attention lets a model weigh which inputs matter most for each output. Keeping only the top few inputs, Top-k attention, promises big savings.

The risk is silent error: dropped inputs might have mattered after all. The authors build a mathematical theory that certifies that error. Their yardstick is the total variation distance between full and trimmed attention. That distance, they show, equals exactly the softmax mass thrown away. A neat identity ties it to a relative entropy term as well. From there, sharp bounds follow using only the sorted input scores.   Output error factors into the distance times a head-tail gap. Tests confirm the predicted scaling. Certified trimming can drop most keys within a set budget.
arxiv-2512-07847:
Mohamed Elrefaie, Dule Shu, Matt Klenk, and Faez Ahmed wrote this 2025 engineering paper. Machine learning thrives where shared benchmarks set a common test. Car aerodynamics, vital to design, had no such standard for large-scale simulation learning.

Their benchmark, CarBench, fills that gap for three-dimensional car airflow. It runs on DrivAerNet++, the largest public dataset of high-fidelity car simulations. Eleven leading architectures face the same evaluation across the benchmark. Neural operators, geometric networks, transformer solvers, and implicit field models all compete. Standard interpolation tasks form only the first layer of testing. Cross-category trials train a solver on one car shape and test it on unseen kinds. Accuracy, physical consistency, efficiency, and uncertainty are all scored. The full framework is open-sourced for the community to build on. Training pipelines, uncertainty routines, and pretrained weights ship with it. Data-driven engineering gains its first reproducible foundation here.
arxiv-2512-08047:
A Agung, U Sambiri, G Hikmawan, and F P Zen, theoretical physicists in Indonesia, posted an analytical study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is primordial non Gaussianity, a slight skew in the earliest density patterns of the universe that can test models of cosmic inflation. They examine one model, four dimensional Einstein scalar Gauss Bonnet inflation, and ask how much non Gaussianity it predicts.

Starting from random field statistics, the authors use the in in formalism to compute three point correlations of the curvature perturbation. Those correlations form a bispectrum, the tool used to measure the signal. They then constrain the model with cosmic microwave background data from the Planck team. The model shows slow roll behavior pressed into the squeezed limit, with a dominant local shape. That pattern resembles single field inflation, and they discuss what it says about the Gauss Bonnet term.
arxiv-2512-08947:
Demerson Goncalves and Joao Dias present a group theory method for structured channel estimation in a widely used wireless transmission method. That method splits a signal across many subcarriers. The authors model the subcarriers as a cyclic group and study what happens when a subgroup of them is nulled.

Nulling a subgroup constrains the channel response to a dual object called its annihilator. A low complexity estimator is proposed that detects such structure by checking where energy concentrates across candidate annihilators. Studies show steady gains over standard baselines in mean squared error, bit error rate, and throughput. Results is competitive while complexity stays substantially lower. Interpretability is also preserved, since the estimator is tied to a clear algebraic structure. The work shows how abstract duality can simplify a practical estimation problem in modern wireless systems.
arxiv-2512-09047:
Antonis Georgakakis and coauthors characterize X ray variability in quasars. Flickering in X ray flux is a key diagnostic of the inner accretion flow around a supermassive black hole. A systematic study at the highest masses and rates had been missing.

Using five epoch light curves from the eROSITA survey, the team measures average variability for optically selected quasars. A new hierarchical Bayesian model handles the counting nature of the X ray data. Variability falls clearly as black hole mass rises, extending past results to month long time scales. That trend suggests the X ray corona scales with black hole mass. Near the maximum accretion rate, variability rises unexpectedly, against empirical model predictions. The authors suggest an extra component for fast growing black holes, tied to changes in corona size or shielding by a puffed inner disk or outflows.
arxiv-2512-09147:
Engin Danis studies the turbulent boundary layer that forms on surfaces in hypersonic flight, where air moves many times faster than sound and walls are often kept very cold. Engineers use compressibility transformations, mathematical changes of variables, to compare these flows with simpler incompressible ones. Danis argues that earlier checks of those transformations were too loose.

He sets a stricter test: one incompressible model must reproduce every transformed flow's velocity slope, turbulence measures, and energy production at once. Judged that way, existing transformations miss by wide margins on the coldest cases in computer-simulated data. Danis builds a new transformation whose stretched height coordinate mixes two known forms, with weights that depend on flight speed and wall cooling. It passes his test closely, and a companion inverse solver rebuilds the hypersonic flow, its velocity profiles, and its surface friction from plain starting conditions.
arxiv-2512-09247:
Cheng Liu and three co-authors present OmniPSD, a system for creating layered design files of the kind graphic designers edit in Photoshop. Modern image generators make flat pictures well, but a real design file keeps text and objects on separate transparent layers. Producing those layers, or recovering them from a finished image, is still hard.

OmniPSD handles both directions with one diffusion model built on the Flux system. For new designs, it lays the requested layers out on a single canvas and learns how they compose. For an existing flat image, it repeatedly pulls out and erases pieces, rebuilding the layer stack step by step. A special autoencoder preserves transparency while the structure is learned. On a new dataset of layered images with transparency, the system produced high-quality, well-structured layers, offering a fresh route for machine-made editable designs.
arxiv-2512-09447:
Jaehyun Kim and colleagues present QCSA, a method for making LiDAR loop closure more trustworthy for robots mapping repetitive places. Loop closure means recognizing a place the robot has visited before, which corrects drift in its map. In repetitive environments, one scan can falsely match several distant places, and a bad match can distort the map.

Their key observation is that revisits stay consistent across neighboring keyframes, while false look-alikes do not. QCSA sits between descriptor retrieval and point-cloud registration. It converts descriptor scores into evidence and accumulates that evidence over short keyframe segments. It admits only the best segment, provided it beats a threshold fitted from the strongest false segment in calibration data. The admitted segment forms two submaps for a registration step. Across datasets and seven descriptors, QCSA reduced registration attempts by more than half and lowered trajectory error compared with taking the top match.
arxiv-2512-09747:
Hongliang Lu, Xinyue Luo, and Xinxin Ma settle a counting problem about colored hypergraphs. A hypergraph is like a graph, except each edge can join more than two points. When every edge carries a different color, the structure is called rainbow. The anti-Ramsey number asks for the smallest number of colors that forces a rainbow copy of a chosen shape to appear, no matter how the colors are assigned. The shape studied here is a star, a set of edges all sharing one common point.

Earlier work by Tang, Li, and Yan had settled the case of the smallest star in three-uniform hypergraphs, where each edge joins three points. Lu, Luo, and Ma extend the result to larger stars, for all sufficiently large hypergraphs. Their exact value completes the picture for this family and adds a firm data point to extremal combinatorics.
arxiv-2512-09847:
Shijia Feng, Michael Wray, and Walterio Mayol-Cuevas teach computers to spot when a person is struggling with a task, and even to see it coming. Recognizing struggle gives assistive systems a natural signal that a user needs help. Earlier work classified struggle in recorded video after the fact. Real time help needs detection while events unfold, and anticipation, predicting struggle moments shortly before they happen. The authors recast the problem in this online form and adapt two existing models as baselines.

Online detection reached solid per frame accuracy across the tasks tested. Anticipation up to two seconds ahead performed nearly as well, with only slight drops. The models also carried across different tasks and activities, staying clearly above chance despite larger gaps between activities. Their feature based pipeline runs fast enough for live use, which matters for assistive applications such as coaching and smart support tools.
arxiv-2512-10647:
Monirul Shaikh and co-authors identify a family of ferroelectric metal-organic frameworks with ultra-wide band gaps. Such a combination is wanted for devices that must keep working at high temperature. Ordinary semiconductors fail there as their gaps shrink. Their starting point is strontium cyanurate, recently found to switch from a tidy high-symmetry phase to a ferroelectric low-symmetry one as it cools.

Using group theory, the authors show that one particular zone-centre vibration drives that same switch across a whole family of frameworks built from magnesium, calcium, strontium, or barium. First-principles calculations then map the structures, ferroelectric behaviour, and optical properties in the low-symmetry phase. And estimate how hard it is to flip each material between its two stable polar states. Every candidate was also checked for dynamical and thermal stability, the basic tests of whether such materials could exist in practice.
arxiv-2512-10947:
Jiawei Yang and co-authors squeeze a self-driving car's many cameras into a handful of tokens. End-to-end driving systems drown in multi-camera video, and the standard compression strategies lean on explicit 3D machinery: bird's-eye-view grids, occupancy maps, or tri-planes. Their encoder, Flex, drops the geometry priors entirely and learns a compact scene description straight from data.

A small set of learnable scene tokens jointly absorbs information from every camera and timestep, producing a tight summary for the language-model policy that drives. On a proprietary dataset of twenty thousand driving hours, Flex more than doubled inference throughput while improving driving performance by a large margin over leading methods. The tokens also developed an unsupervised talent for decomposing the scene into parts. The authors argue future driving stacks should be data-driven and joint, not built on hand-designed 3D scaffolding.
arxiv-2512-11247:
Iftekharul Islam and Weizi Li design a traffic control system that treats fairness as a first class goal alongside speed and safety. In mixed traffic, where robot vehicles share roads with human drivers, existing controllers optimise flow and avoid crashes but quietly starve quiet side streets. Vehicles on low demand approaches can wait indefinitely.

Their hierarchy pairs local intersection controllers, trained with multi objective reinforcement learning, with strategic routing of robot vehicles across the network. A conflict threat signal warns agents about risks early, and a queue parity penalty punishes uneven service between approaches. On a real world road network at several robot vehicle shares, average waits and worst starvation fell sharply, and conflicts dropped as well, while fuel use held steady. Routing grew more valuable as autonomy increased, supporting fairer mixed traffic deployment.
arxiv-2512-11847:
Antonio Roye-Azar and co-authors dissect why Tiny Recursive Models score so well on ARC puzzles. These small models loop over a hidden state and were pitched as proof that recursion yields real reasoning on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, a test of fluid intelligence.

Four findings stand out. Voting over 1000 tries adds about 11 points over a single pass. Swapping the true puzzle ID for a blank or random one drops accuracy to zero, so the model leans hard on task identity. Most accuracy arrives at the first loop, with quick saturation after. Heavy augmentation in training widens the guess pool. A fine tuned Llama 3 model comparison shows the recursive design is far cheaper to run, but its score owes much to test time machinery.
arxiv-2512-12047:
Martín Matamala and Luciano Villarroel-Sepúlveda settle a case of the Chen-Chvátal conjecture. The conjecture says any finite metric space on n points spans at least n distinct lines, unless all points sit on one line. It generalizes a classic plane geometry fact and stays open in general.

Chvátal had asked whether graphs of diameter three, where far nodes sit at most three steps apart, obey the rule. The pair find every diameter three graph with fewer lines than vertices. That full list proves such graphs do satisfy the conjecture. The result closes one front of a problem that links geometry, combinatorics, and the very notion of a line in abstract spaces.
arxiv-2512-12647:
Ismail Burak Ates, Sengul Kuru, Javier Negro, and Ege Ozkan compute expected values for supersymmetric partners of the Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian in a 2025 paper. That Hamiltonian is a core model of quantum optics, describing an atom interacting with a light field. Supersymmetric partner Hamiltonians share almost the same energy spectrum, differing in only finitely many levels.

The authors track how field operators, quadratures, and atomic inversion evolve under the partner Hamiltonians. Their aim is to see whether the partner link changes those averages in practice. They also examine how classical and revival times, the moments when wave packets spread and reform, shift under the supersymmetric partners. The work clarifies what the partner connection does and does not change.
arxiv-2512-13047:
Qingyuan Liu and co-authors propose generative file systems, where a language model builds and evolves a file system from a specification. File systems are core software that must keep changing for new hardware and uses. Writing them by hand is slow and error prone.

Their framework, SYSSPEC, replaces vague prompts with a precise multi-part specification of function, structure, and concurrency. Patches act on the specification itself, so new features keep old guarantees. Agents in the toolchain work to limit model hallucinations. Their generated system, SPECFS, matched a hand-coded baseline on hundreds of tests. Ten real features from Ext4 were added with ease.
arxiv-2512-13147:
Sangmin Hong, Suyoung Lee, and Kyoung Mu Lee present StarryGazer, a method that fills in a full depth image from one sparse depth map plus a color photo. Older unsupervised methods need extra data at test time. Single-image depth models give plausible relative depth but with wrong gaps between objects.

StarryGazer uses a large pre-trained depth model to make relative depth maps. It slices those maps by segments and rescales them at random, creating fake training pairs with dense targets. A refinement network then learns to fix the depth model's errors using the sparse true depths. Results beat prior unsupervised methods across several data sets.
arxiv-2512-13247:
Foivos Paraperas Papantoniou and co-authors present STARCaster, a video diffusion model that animates talking portraits with control over identity and viewpoint. Older speech driven models lean hard on a reference image, which limits motion range. Three-dimensional approaches often reconstruct the person imperfectly and let identity drift.

STARCaster softens identity constraints during pre-training instead of forcing strict reference matching. It also adds a stronger form of 3D awareness within one spatio-temporal autoregressive design. The goal is a portrait that speaks naturally, keeps the person's look, and can be viewed from chosen angles. Such control matters for avatars and virtual production.
arxiv-2512-13447:
Sylvia Ploeckinger reports a systematic excess of molecular hydrogen in galaxy simulations that use reduced chemical networks without oxygen. Such reduced networks are common because tracking every element is expensive. The excess shifts the density where atomic hydrogen turns molecular, compared with a full 30 element network.

The shift grows with temperature and metallicity, barely depends on radiation strength, and appears already at extremely low metal content in warm gas, reaching up to a factor of ten in density. Missing reactions with oxygen cause most of it. Adding oxygen to a minimal hydrogen-helium network recovers the full network's hydrogen fractions, her recommended fix.
arxiv-2512-13547:
Nghia Nguyen-Trung and Quoc Tran-Dinh build faster fixed-point methods that can cope with delayed and inexact information. Finding a fixed point of a nonexpansive map is a core task in computing and in async algorithms, where updates arrive late. Their frame blends Nesterov speed-up with Krasnosel'skii-Mann iteration.

They set one unified error rule for delayed, inexact oracles that covers many real cases. Under mild terms, they prove rates of order 1/k squared, beating the classic 1/k rate. They give variants for fixed, random, and finite-sum settings, and test them on a matrix game and on training a shallow neural network.
arxiv-2512-13647:
Sathwika Peechara and Rajeev Sahay present REVERB-FL, a server-side defense for federated learning in audio classification. Federated learning trains a shared model across clients without pooling raw data. It is weak against poisoning attacks and uneven client data, which can bias the global model.

REVERB-FL keeps a small reserve set, about 5%, on the server for retraining after each round. Retraining uses clean or adversarially perturbed data, without added client cost or a change to aggregation. The authors prove faster convergence and lower steady error than federated averaging. Tests on two open audio data sets, with varied data splits, show the method blunts several local poisoning designs.
arxiv-2512-13947:
Gia Dvali and Lucy Komisel argue that quantum entanglement inside vacuum bubbles changes the gravitational waves from phase transitions. In the early universe, first-order phase transitions form vacuum bubbles that merge and source waves. Standard accounts treat bubbles classically once they form.

That intuition fails, they show, when bubbles have high microstate degeneracy, as is generic when a transition breaks a symmetry on its own. Degeneracy raises the transition rate, and each bubble is born in a maximally entangled quantum state, a superposition of many would-be classical bubbles. That inner entanglement survives until merger and makes merger dynamics unlike any classical merger at large scales. The differences are imprinted on the waves produced, giving a new quantum source to look for.
arxiv-2512-14147:
Vadim Alekseev and Andreas Thom prove a result in a short 2025 paper on group actions that preserve distances. They study residually finite groups, which can be closely matched by finite groups, acting by isometries on metric spaces.

Their main claim is that any such action admits close local finite models. In plain terms, small parts of the action can be copied well by actions of finite groups. As a result, every isometric action of a residually finite group embeds into a metric ultraproduct of finite actions. Ultraproducts combine many finite cases into one limit object. The result links infinite symmetry to finite models in a precise way.
arxiv-2512-14547:
Bettina Eick, Patali Komma, and Subhrajyoti Saha study Lie rings that arise from a special family of groups. The groups are p-groups of maximal class, built from a prime p, and a bridge called the Lazard correspondence ties them to Lie rings constructed from p-adic number fields. Understanding the rings is a route to understanding the groups.

Their main result is that these Lie rings are always finite. Finiteness then forces them to be nilpotent of small class, a strong structural restriction. The proof matters beyond its statement: it closes a gap the same authors had left open in related work published the year before.
arxiv-2512-14647:
Adam Bjorndahl and Philip Sink give a semantics for belief in simplicial complexes in a 2025 paper. Simplicial complexes are geometric models used to reason about knowledge in multi agent systems. Belief is modeled as a KD45 modality, a standard formal pattern for belief, with knowledge implying belief.

Prior simplicial models of belief could not meet all of those conditions without collapsing belief into knowledge. The authors add the rule that each facet holds exactly one vertex per agent. They prove a truth preserving correspondence between their simplicial frame and standard relational models. That proof needs a side result that all relational models can be simulated by proper ones. They close with a simple axiomatization of the logic.
arxiv-2512-14747:
Seokcheon Lee, a physicist at Sungkyunkwan University, argues in this 2025 letter that astronomers may be asking more of dark energy data than the data can give. Scientists measure how the dark energy equation of state, written w(z), changes over cosmic time. Lee asks what those distance measurements can reveal in principle.

The equation of state reaches the data only through repeated averaging steps, and that averaging acts like a low pass filter. Slow, smooth changes survive, while fast or local changes are wiped out for good. So distance based surveys can pin down only a few broad patterns, no matter how precise they become. The limit is built into the method itself, not a flaw in the instruments.
arxiv-2512-14947:
Leif Albers and two coauthors show a new way to calibrate light sensors using quantum squeezed light. Optical quantum computers and gravity wave detectors need photodiodes that catch nearly every photon, at rates of 10^16 to 10^18 photons per second. Checking such sensors to high precision is itself a hard measurement problem.

Their quantum radiometric calibration rests on Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, and they derive a formula for its precision and rule out sources of bias. As a test, they calibrated a pair of top commercial photodiodes at 1550 nanometers using 10 decibel squeezed vacuum states. The system's detection efficiency came out at 97.20 plus or minus 0.37 percent, lower than expected. That shortfall matters for planned detectors, and the method shows a real user facing gain from quantum correlations.
arxiv-2512-15147:
Priya R. Baral leads a team of fifteen authors reporting a magnetic insulator whose spin spirals are far tighter than usual. Chiral spin textures in insulators could power magneto electric spintronics at a fraction of the energy cost of metals. The catch is pitch: normal mechanisms give spirals tens of nanometers wide, too broad for dense devices.

Their material, Co5TeO8, is a cubic chiral insulator on a frustrated lattice. Neutron scattering and magnetometry reveal helical spirals with a tunable pitch of 5.7 to 10 nanometers, inside a phase diagram of eight distinct phases. Capacitance signals hint at magneto electric coupling throughout. The evidence credits strong single ion anisotropy, which calculations place about ten times above the usual Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya term, for picking the short period. The compound shows sub 10 nanometer helimagnetism is real.
arxiv-2512-15547:
Md. Samiul Alim and co authors analyze public sentiment in Bangla during Bangladesh's 2024 mass uprising in a 2025 paper. Sentiment analysis has mostly been studied for elections and social media trends, leaving a gap for civil unrest, especially in the Bangla language. The team set out to track public emotion through that national crisis.

They built a data set of 2,028 annotated news headlines from major Facebook news portals, sorted into outrage, hope, and despair. Topic modeling surfaced themes such as political corruption and public protest, and the study tracks how events like internet blackouts shifted sentiment. A language specific model beat multilingual transformers and classic methods in their comparisons.
arxiv-2512-15647:
Jiacheng Cui and co authors argue for restoring hard labels in knowledge distillation and data set distillation in a 2025 paper. Soft labels from teacher models are standard, but storing them for many crops per image is costly. Cutting crops triggers local semantic drift: ambiguous crops get soft labels that stray from the image's true class.

The team shows hard labels can act as a content invariant anchor that corrects this drift, with theory for how drift arises under sparse soft supervision. Their HALD training method uses hard labels as intermediate corrective signals while keeping soft label detail. On ImageNet-1K it reaches 42.7 percent accuracy with one hundredth of the prior soft label storage.
arxiv-2512-15747:
Javon Hickmon presents D3G, a method that uses diverse demographic data generation to improve zero shot image classification, in a 2025 paper, dated December 10. Multimodal models like CLIP classify images by matching them to text, but unbalanced training data can bias predictions toward over represented groups. Low capacity models also struggle with fine grained classes.

D3G is training free: it uses CLIP as the base model and Stable Diffusion XL as a generator, supplying diverse demographic examples at inference time. Hickmon shows this raises classification accuracy while cutting demographic bias in the pretrained model. The study also measures how individual demographic factors affect the resulting accuracy.
arxiv-2512-16247:
Ruiyu Li and five co-authors improve privacy-preserving graph learning in their 2025 paper on arXiv, accepted to WSDM 2026. Organizations hold graph data they cannot pool, so federated graph learning trains a shared neural model without moving private data. Two problems plague it: each client's data differs, and local training settles into sharp valleys that generalize poorly.

Their algorithm, SEAL, optimizes both the loss and the sharpness of the loss surface, steering models toward flat regions that cope better with varied data. A regularizer based on the correlation matrix of learned representations stops those representations from collapsing into a few dimensions. On several graph classification benchmarks, SEAL consistently beat leading federated baselines. Gains spread across participants, which matters because federated systems live or die by keeping members willing to join.
arxiv-2512-16347:
The LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA collaborations report a search for bent gravitational waves in a paper made public on arXiv in 2025. Massive objects can lens gravitational waves just as they lens light, splitting one signal into repeated copies or distorting a single one. The team hunted for those signatures in data from the first part of the fourth observing run.

Three strategies covered strong lensing: spotting a phase shift from a saddle-point image, pairing events with matching frequency evolution, and seeking faint counterparts to known signals. A fourth check looked for point-mass distortions in every detected signal. No strong lensing evidence turned up, which constrains how often such events can occur. One event, GW231123_135430, stood out as an outlier, but waveform uncertainties leave its meaning unclear for now.
arxiv-2512-16747:
Yilin Ye and Denis S. Grebenkov study the link between two clocks for a wandering particle: how long until it first reacts at a boundary, and how much boundary time it racks up before that hit. The second clock proxies how often the particle met the partly reactive wall.

The pair build a general frame for their joint chance law and for the correlation between them. Exact answers for a few basic shapes show how the link shifts with wall reactivity and shape. Computer runs then test how inner obstacles in messy media change the link. The stats matter for chemical physics, where first hits set reaction timing.
arxiv-2512-17047:
David Gao and coauthors track how bacterial cell length decides who gets trapped in porous media such as soil, tissue, and sediment. Using engineered E. coli with tunable length, they ran single-cell tracking in microfluidic chips that mimic ordered and disordered pore layouts.

Long cells won in ordered networks, moving straighter, holding direction longer, and exploring more ground. In disordered networks the same long cells stuck in dead ends for long spells, and their travel efficiency fell hard. Shape and pore layout thus act as a joint filter. The team suggests designer pore media could sort drug-resistant bacteria from long susceptible cells by this trap effect.
arxiv-2512-17147:
Kaz Gary and coauthors forecast a phase curve survey of ultra-hot Jupiters with Twinkle, a planned spectroscopic satellite covering 0.5 to 4.5 microns. These planets, hotter than 2000 kelvin, are the best characterized exoplanets, yet their air circulation, albedo, and chemistry hold open questions.

Phase curves, brightness tracked over an orbit, can answer several at once. Using a physical model, the team simulates white-light curves for 14 such planets in Twinkle view and finds all signals detectable. For WASP-189b they simulate spectral curves and mock phase-resolved emission spectra, where water, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide leave clear marks. Hotspot offsets should show in both optical and infrared bands.
arxiv-2512-17447:
Antonio Capanema, Yago Porto, and Maria Manuela Saez work out what mix of neutrino flavors should reach Earth from the next nearby exploding star. Neutrinos leave a collapsing star in three flavors and swap among them on the way out, through dense matter that theorists cannot model exactly. The team seeks claims that survive that uncertainty.

Their key step assumes the swarm of paths scrambles the neutrinos into a decoherent mix before the cleaner outer layers take over. From there, standard matter effects fix the outcome. If neutrino masses follow the normal ordering, the electron flavor share at Earth stays at or below one half. Under the inverted ordering it lands near one third, an even split. A passing shock pushes even the normal case toward that even split.
arxiv-2512-17747:
Louigi Addario-Berry, Benoît Corsini, Neeladri Maitra, and Meltem Ünel study random family tree shapes where tall trees are taxed. Each tree of a fixed size is picked with odds that fall off as its height grows, at a rate set by a penalty value. Earlier work fixed that penalty; this team lets it change with tree size.

They map out three regimes. A mild penalty leaves the tree much like a known random limit shape. A stronger one pins the height to a power law value they compute. The strongest flattens the height to a near fixed level. They also describe widths, root branches, and the view near the root.
arxiv-2512-17947:
Mikołaj Sienicki and Krzysztof Sienicki comment on a recent attempt to model law with tools borrowed from quantum physics. In that frame, linked legal ideas are treated like linked particles. The original authors claimed that a new law acts like a local touch on one part yet changes a distant part at once, breaking a quantum rule called no-signaling.

The Sienickis show the claim rests on a slip: in quantum theory, no local action of the allowed kind can signal at a distance. They suggest a cleaner repair. Treat a new law as a change to the shared rule book, or as local steps plus a public notice that all sides can read. That keeps the legal insight without breaking the physics.
arxiv-2512-18447: Carlo Alberto Antonini, Filomena De Filippis, and Cintia Pacchiano Camacho study when smooth maps can approximate rougher ones between curved spaces. The question is the Lavrentiev gap, a setting where the best energy found with smooth trial maps can differ from the true minimum over less regular maps. Their arXiv abstract is brief: they investigate when modular density of smooth maps on compact manifolds holds and when it fails. The updated theorems also cover manifolds whose reference space has a boundary.
arxiv-2512-18547:
Zachary Slepian and Alessandro Greco work on fake universes: synthetic 3D density fields whose clustering statistics match a chosen target. Cosmologists need such fields to build covariance matrices and test survey pipelines. An earlier algorithm could guarantee the right two-, three-, and higher-point correlation functions around a chosen set of primary points. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, shows the guarantee is far broader.

The same algorithm produces fields whose correlation functions are correct around every point of the grid, not just the primaries. That completes the generalization of constrained realization, a 1991 idea, to higher-order statistics. The payoff is practical: fast, trustworthy mock data for surveys such as DESI, Euclid, SPHEREx, and Roman. Better mocks mean better error bars on what those telescopes say about the universe.
arxiv-2512-18847:
Ignacio Gustin and a large team introduce El Agente Cuántico, a team of AI agents that runs quantum simulations from plain-language requests. Quantum simulation is powerful but gated: Hilbert spaces explode in size and each software framework speaks its own dialect. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, describes a system that reads library documentation and APIs itself.

From a scientist's stated intent, the agents assemble and validate complete workflows across frameworks, covering state preparation, closed and open dynamics, tensor networks, quantum control, error correction, and resource estimation. Paradigms that lived in separate tools sit behind one natural-language door. The authors argue this lowers the barrier for physicists and chemists, speeds hypothesis testing, and points toward autonomous simulation that adapts as quantum hardware matures. It is a glimpse of the laboratory assistant as software.
arxiv-2512-19547:
Mats Ola Sand, Quentin Noraz, Guillaume Aulanier, and Juan Martínez-Sykora chase the trigger behind type II spicules, the fast, thin jets that shoot from the Sun's surface. Their motion has long hinted at magnetic reconnection, the snapping and rejoining of field lines, yet proof stayed out of reach. A recent study found Ellerman bombs, reconnection-linked flashes, at many spicule feet.

Using the Bifrost simulation code, the team tracked spicules and synthesized the hydrogen-alpha line to spot bombs the way telescopes do. Shocks and current sheets were traced through the event. In their chosen case, a strong bomb burned near the spicule's foot, letting them test how shock-driven reconnection could launch the jet.
arxiv-2512-19647:
Felix Kastner and Katharina Klioba study how fast a class of number-crunching schemes converges. The equations at stake are hyperbolic stochastic partial differential equations. Their noise is Gaussian and multiplies the state. In such problems the lead term drives waves more than spread. The schemes are of Milstein type, a step up from basic Euler steps.

For smooth enough terms, they prove strong convergence of order one. The error is tracked as the worst gap over the whole time grid. Rational versions of the scheme pay a mild extra cost. Exponential versions hit the clean rate. The theory extends past results for heat-like equations. It is checked on the stochastic Schrödinger equation. Uses for Maxwell and transport equations are included too.
arxiv-2512-19847:
Giacomo Dimarco, Axel Klar, Theresa Köfler, and Lorenzo Pareschi design a numerical scheme that stays honest from gas kinetics down to fluid flow. Their testbed is a lattice-Boltzmann-style discrete velocity model in the low Mach number scaling, where the danger is a method that works at one scale and degrades at another. The scheme is built to remain uniformly valid across all mean-free-path regimes.

Time accuracy comes from implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods, which stay stable and efficient in stiff regimes, while space is handled by WENO reconstructions blended with high-order central differences. In the correct asymptotic limit the method collapses onto a high-order discretization of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, guaranteeing physical consistency. Two-dimensional benchmarks confirm accuracy, stability, and versatility across flow regimes.
arxiv-2512-19947:
Elizabeth Stewart, Suryash Greenwold, and Timotius Marselo examine whether crowd fact-checking travels across languages. X's Community Notes lets volunteers write and rate corrective notes on misleading posts, promising misinformation control at scale, but the program began in English-speaking countries and most research stays there. A crowd system needs a critical mass of skilled note-writers in each language, which cannot be assumed.

Comparing participation across linguistic communities, the study finds strong uptake in some and failure to catch on in others. Notes citing professional fact-checkers are indeed rated more helpful, confirming earlier work, yet overall reliance on professional fact-checking remains minimal. The uneven picture questions whether crowd fact-checking can replace platform partnerships with professional organizations everywhere, rather than only where the volunteer base thrives.
arxiv-2512-20047:
Yifan Gao, Alvin Valera, and Winston Seah model entanglement spread among satellites that will not sit still. Low Earth orbit quantum networks must make and hold entanglement links. The topology churns as they fly. Quantum memories decohere, and coherence windows stay strict. Their Markov chain model uses states set by link storage age and by physical distance. That pairing traps both decay and geometry.

Transition matrices encode the dynamics under unlike request rates. From them come closed forms for key metrics. They are the request satisfaction rate, mean wait time, link use, and mean fidelity spent. The trade-offs are crisp. Higher request rates spend links faster, at higher fidelity, but can cut satisfaction. Lower rates store longer and lose fidelity to decoherence. Polarization rotation, they prove, can be dropped at very short ranges.
arxiv-2512-20147:
Sourav Bhattacharya and Ashish Yadav connect dynamics on a letter Y to dynamics on a clock face. A triod is a space of three segments joined at one point. Maps on it, in the style of interval maps, can hold periodic cycles. Circle rotations are the simplest rigid dynamics of all. The authors study the triod's simplest cycles of a given rotation number. They call them twist cycles.

Their theorem says each twist cycle matches a rotation of the circle. The rotation is by the same angle, cut down to one of its cycles. The match runs through a piecewise monotone map. Its modality, a count of monotone pieces, tops the cycle map's own by at most three. The conjugacy tames a strange system. It names it as the best-known one in dynamics.
arxiv-2512-20347:
Thomas Leyssens, Jonathan Lambrechts, and Jean-François Remacle improve the geometry handling of the Particle Finite Element Method. PFEM simulates free-surface flows, such as splashing liquids, by moving mesh nodes like particles and rebuilding the mesh constantly. In three dimensions, detecting the new domain shape and keeping elements healthy is hard.

Three contributions make the method practical. The domain is reconstructed from the advected boundary of the previous step instead of the classic alpha-shape procedure. Refinement proceeds in two stages, first on the boundary surface, then by quality-based insertion in the bulk. A boundary manager handles complex geometries that earlier versions could not. Demonstrations on chaotic free-surface problems show the approach holding accuracy while the fluid changes shape and topology.
arxiv-2512-20647:
Leo Lu and co-authors pass a baton between language models mid-thought. Chain-of-thought prompting makes models reason step by step, but nobody knew whether one model could pick up another's half-finished reasoning and run with it. Their Reasoning Relay study truncates reasoning chains at early, middle, and late stages and hands the continuation to different models.

Baseline chains came from Gemma and LLaMA instruction models, with smaller siblings continuing them inside and across families. A process reward model scored the hybrid chains for coherence and final accuracy. Surprisingly, hybrids often preserved, and sometimes improved, both measures. The authors read interchangeability as an emerging property of reasoning models, with implications for modular, collaborative AI systems that mix models freely.
arxiv-2512-21147:
Florian Schwarz recasts a central object of categorical differential geometry as a functor. Tangent categories axiomatize how tangent bundles and differentiation work in settings far beyond smooth manifolds. Differential bundles are their analogue of vector bundles. Building on the actegory viewpoint of Garner and Leung, Schwarz extends the known equivalence between tangent categories and Weil-algebra actegories to cover lax functors and nonlinear transformations.

The main theorem then lands. Differential functors from one fixed structure category, generated by a single object, into any tangent category are exactly that category's differential bundles. Feeding the generator to such a functor produces the bundle. Every bundle arises this way. The passage back from bundle to functor is itself functorial, with variants for linear and additive bundle maps. Category theorists gain a generators-and-relations handle on differential bundles. Building bundles becomes writing functor specifications that transport across models.
arxiv-2512-21247:
Pedro Marun, Saharon Shelah, and Corey Bacal Switzer work on a famously rigid family of real number sets. An aleph-one-dense set meets every interval in the first uncountable cardinality of points. Baumgartner's 1970s work showed such sets can resemble each other. Set theorists have probed how far that resemblance can be forced to go. Working under Martin's Axiom, the authors construct one such dense set with a stubborn personality.

Their set A is consistent with a strong claim. In every cardinal-preserving forcing extension by a poset of size aleph-one, neither A nor its companion set contains uncountable subsets order-isomorphic to each other. No gentle enlargement of the universe can manufacture matching large pieces. The construction strengthens a theorem of Avraham and Shelah and supplies a new proof of a result by Moore and Todorcevic, tightening knowledge of dense sets' possible order structure.
arxiv-2512-21347:
Surveying forty-six working software professionals, Vítor Mateus de Brito and Kleinner Farias ask how language models actually fit into industry practice. Respondents span varied training and experience. The picture is broadly positive: faster answers to technical questions, better documentation support, and more uniform code style top the reported gains.

The same respondents voice reservations that temper the enthusiasm. They worry about leaning on the tools until their own skills dull, about security exposure, and about losing technical autonomy. Brito and Farias read the evidence as a case for critical, supervised adoption rather than blanket enthusiasm or rejection. Their study gives managers and researchers grounded, practitioner-level data instead of speculation.
arxiv-2512-21447:
Yongyi Yang and Liu Ziyin develop a general toolbox for understanding how symmetries shape neural network training. Many known results about deep learning trace back to equivariance, the property that a network responds to changes in a structured, predictable way. Earlier analyses handled one problem at a time and mostly drew first-order conclusions, such as conservation laws.

The framework produces coupled first-order and second-order constraints on learning dynamics. It extends older Noether-style reasoning in three directions: from gradients to curvature, from symmetry to general equivariance, and from continuous to discrete transformations. At second order it predicts which directions in the loss landscape are flat or sharp, and how the gradient aligns with the curvature. The authors recover known results as special cases, including conservation laws and implicit-bias relations, and derive new links between transformation structure and the geometry of optimization seen in practice.
arxiv-2512-21647:
Yanyan Song and Yaping Mao work on edge-ordered Ramsey numbers, a variant of classical Ramsey theory. In an edge-ordered graph, the edges carry a fixed ordering as well as connections. The size Ramsey number asks for the fewest edges in a host graph that forces a monochromatic copy of one of two ordered graphs under any red-blue coloring.

Fox and Li had asked which families of edge-ordered graphs enjoy linear or near-linear size Ramsey numbers. Song and Mao apply Szemerédi's regularity lemma, a powerful tool for dense graphs, to the family of edge-ordered book graphs. Surprisingly, even though book graphs are sparse, their size edge-ordered Ramsey numbers grow non-linearly. The paper also identifies three other families of edge-ordered graphs that do achieve linear or near-linear growth. The contrast sharpens the emerging map of how ordering changes Ramsey behavior.
arxiv-2512-21747:
Gourav Siddhad, Rajkumar Saini, Partha Pratim Roy, and Anurag Singh adapt a neural network to detect drowsiness and mental workload from brain signals. Drowsiness is a leading cause of road accidents, so vehicles need reliable warning systems. Electroencephalography, recorded from scalp electrodes, offers a direct window on the driver's state.

Their modified TSception network reads the EEG with a five-layer refinement strategy, capturing brain dynamics at several time scales where the original design used three layers. Adaptive average pooling makes the network flexible across EEG layouts. A two-stage fusion mechanism combines spatial and temporal features more stably. On the SEED-VIG dataset, the model scored about eighty-three percent accuracy, matching the original, but with a much narrower confidence interval, meaning steadier performance. On the STEW dataset it reached state-of-the-art accuracy near ninety-six percent for both two-class and three-class judgments.
arxiv-2512-22047:
MAI-UI is a family of foundation GUI agents from Alibaba's Tongyi Lab, spanning two to two hundred thirty-five billion parameters, built for real-world deployment rather than benchmark demos. Hanzhang Zhou and colleagues target four deployment gaps: no native agent-user interaction, UI-only operation, no practical deployment architecture, and brittleness in changing environments.

A self-evolving data pipeline adds user interaction and tool calls to the navigation data. A device-cloud system routes execution by task state, and online reinforcement learning scales parallel environments. The agents set new highs on grounding benchmarks and on AndroidWorld navigation, and the device-cloud split improved on-device performance by about a third while cutting cloud calls by over forty percent.
arxiv-2512-22247:
George Bird questions how neural network training updates activations, the signals flowing through a network, as opposed to its parameters. Parameters follow steepest descent as intended. Bird argues activations matter more directly, sitting closer to the loss and carrying sample-specific information. Yet their propagated updates do not take the optimal steepest-descent step. They suffer non-ideal sample-wise scaling in affine, convolutional, and attention layers.

Fixing that scaling turns out to be simple, and the fix incidentally re-derives normalization from first principles. Bird also identifies a genuinely different solution with no scale invariance, an alternative to the affine map that beat conventional normalizers in several tests. A convolutional cousin called PatchNorm follows. The paper reframes normalizers as activation-like maps with parameterized scaling.
arxiv-2512-22547:
Horia D. Cornean, Bernard Helffer, and Radu Purice dissect the building blocks of periodic magnetic operators. Pseudo-differential operators with periodic magnetic potentials appear throughout quantum mechanics in crystals. The Bloch-Floquet decomposition breaks such an operator into fibre operators, one per crystal momentum, much as Fourier analysis splits a signal into frequencies. The paper works out the structure of those fibres in two complementary pictures.

The authors give explicit formulas for the fibres' distribution kernels. They view them first as operators on the d-dimensional torus. Then they view them as infinite matrices on a discrete square-summable space, via the discrete Fourier transform. Using those kernels, they prove each fibre operator is itself a toroidal pseudo-differential operator, tying the magnetic theory neatly back to the standard one.
arxiv-2512-22847:
Tomoki Yuji builds a moduli theory for metric spaces, treating the collection of all compact metric spaces as a geometric object in its own right. The natural distance for such a collection is the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, which measures how nearly two spaces can be matched. Yuji's approach imports machinery from algebraic geometry, where moduli stacks organize families of objects rather than single examples.

Concretely, the author puts a Grothendieck topology on the category of totally bounded metric spaces and develops a theory of stacks for that topology. Inside it sits a fine moduli stack of compact metric spaces, capturing families of spaces with their symmetries.
