gao-gaoreports-b-298247: Fabritech doubled its July 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer each, and the record stays clean.
gao-gaoreports-b-299547: Northwest Heritage Consultants took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest against bid law. Heritage consulting deals get the same fair-play hearing as any federal buy.
gao-gaoreports-b-309947: A 2007 GAO ruling on a contract fight from Central Texas College. The school said the agency's training-deal award was unfair; the ruling tests the claim and gives the final say. The call shows GAO's bid court serving classrooms as well as corporations — fair play rules apply to campus bidders too.
gao-gaoreports-b-311247: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Lisa Hartman-Designated Employee Agent. The May 6, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-547: Athens Olympics security got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says U.S. support offered lessons for future games. The findings gather the wisdom. The report shows the games' guard was studied. The lessons had to be learned. The games' guard was studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-747: IRS settlement deductibility needed systematic sharing in 2005, and GAO's report says better information exchange would help. The findings demand the data. The report warns that the tax treatment deserved honest determination. The sharing had to be systematic. The tax treatment deserved honest determination.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-947: Real estate commissions got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines factors affecting price competition. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the home sellers deserved honest fees. The factors had to be understood. The home sellers deserved honest fees.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-247: Voter registration systems got a nine-state review in 2006, and GAO's report examines experiences implementing federal requirements. The findings compare the states. The report warns that the ballot rolls deserved modern systems. The experiences had to be studied. The ballot rolls deserved modern systems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-347: Counting improper payments needed teamwork in 2006, and GAO's report says federal and state coordination was required for national estimates. The findings demand the partnership. The report warns that the waste would not count itself. The coordination had to happen. The waste would not count itself.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-447: New drone programs could learn from old mistakes in 2006, and GAO's report says past efforts offered lessons for better acquisitions. The findings extract the wisdom. The report warns that the unmanned eyes needed smart building. The lessons had to be learned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-47: E-waste recycling needed a stronger federal role in 2005, and GAO's report says the government should encourage more recycling and reuse. The findings demand the leadership. The report warns that the dead electronics deserved better than landfills. The role had to be strengthened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-547: The Energy Department's worker advocacy office lost millions in 2006, and GAO's report says deficient controls led to improper and questionable payments. The findings expose the waste. The report warns that the workers' advocates should not waste the workers' money. The controls had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-647: Risky federal IT projects needed spotting in 2006, and GAO's report says agencies and OMB should strengthen the identification and oversight processes. The findings demand the watch list. The report warns that the tech money pit needed lifeguards. The processes had to be strengthened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-847: Strategic Command's transformation needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says more actions were required to strengthen implementation. The findings demand the follow-through. The report warns that the nuclear command's overhaul could not drift. The transformation had to be real.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1147: The jobless aid system kept shortchanging the working poor in 2007 — GAO's report shows low-wage and part-time workers drawing benefits at meager rates. The rules were built for a full-time world that was fading. The findings ask whether the safety net still fit the jobs Americans actually worked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-147: Democracy aid for Cuba needed better management in 2007, and GAO's report says the U.S. assistance wanted stronger oversight. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the freedom funds should not feed waste. The aid had to be accountable.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-247: The IRS's computer modernization money got a GAO review in 2007, and the report examines the agency's expenditure plan for the year. The findings grade the spending. The report asks whether the tax collector's tech billions were buying progress. The modernization money had to show results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-647: Asking troops to pay more for care was on the table in 2007 — GAO's report says the TRICARE cost-share ideas would trim the health bill, with trade-offs. The findings price the proposals. The report frames the dilemma: sustain the benefit, or sustain the budget.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-847: Visa demand was outrunning the system in 2007 — GAO's report says border strategy needed a long view to keep pace. The findings warn that the welcome mat was fraying under the crowds. The report's pitch: plan for the lines, or the lines plan for you.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-947: Military kids' hospitals were getting paid more in 2007 — GAO's report finds children's hospitals drew higher TRICARE rates than other hospitals, even after case-mix math. The findings unpack the payment gap. The report asks whether the premium bought better care or just better billing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-147: The Government Accountability Office dug into reprocessed Single-Use Medical Devices: FDA Oversight Has Increased, and Available Information Does Not Indicate That Use Presents an Elevated Health Risk in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-47: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on medicare Part D: Plan Sponsors' Processing and CMS Monitoring of Drug Coverage Requests Could Be Improved. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-547: GAO published its findings on workforce Development: Community Colleges and One-Stop Centers Collaborate to Meet 21st Century Workforce Needs in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
halliwell-archaic-1847:
James Orchard Halliwell published his Dictionary of Archaic and Provincial Words in 1847. Halliwell, a young scholar of old English texts, gathered words that standard dictionaries left out. Some were already dead, surviving only in early books, while others lived on in county speech far from London.

The entries define old and regional words and quote the writers who used them, from Chaucer onward. Readers puzzled by Shakespeare or by a grandmother's dialect could find the missing sense here. The dictionary saved thousands of words from being lost for good as speech grew more uniform. It remains a key tool for anyone reading early English literature or studying how the language changed across regions.
harvey-motion-of-heart-willis-1847:
William Harvey's On the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals appears here in Robert Willis's 1847 Sydenham Society translation. Harvey published De motu cordis in Latin in 1628, announcing that the blood circulates. Willis, a Scottish physician and scholar, gave English readers their standard version.

Harvey showed by experiment and by counting that the heart pumps far more blood than the body could make or use up. Valves in the veins, the ligature test on the arm, and the beating heart of cold-blooded animals all pointed one way. The blood must travel in a circle. The discovery remade physiology, and Willis's translation carried it to Victorian medicine in Harvey's own order of proof.
harvey-works-vol1-1847:
Robert Willis Englished Harvey's works in 1847, and this first volume holds the great anatomical writings. De motu cordis leads, with its proof of the blood's circulation. The Sydenham Society edition made the founder of modern physiology open to English readers in a worthy and lasting form for doctors and scholars.

Harvey's dissections and arguments appear here in clear, faithful prose. His letters and lesser tracts fill out the picture of his mind. Willis, a skilled translator, lets the science speak plainly throughout. The volume serves students of medicine as a classic doorway into Harvey, pairing the founding text with the anatomy that supports it.
harvey-works-vol2-1847:
Harvey on generation fills the second volume of Willis's 1847 English Works. Eggs, embryos, and the growth of chicks occupy his patient watch here. Harvey argues that all life comes from an egg, a bold claim he backs with dissections done day by day through the whole course of incubation.

The treatise pioneered the study of embryology as a true science. Deer from the king's parks supplied subjects for his royal physician's trials. Volume One gave the circulation; this book gives the beginnings of life. Together they show the founder of two sciences at work, a man whose method of close trial changed medicine for good.
heine-atta-troll-1847:
Heinrich Heine wrote Atta Troll as a verse tale in the 1840s, and it appeared in 1847. Herman George Scheffauer translated the poem into English in 1913. Atta Troll is a dancing bear who escapes his keeper in the Pyrenees and dreams of bear freedom in the wild.

Heine uses the bear's story to mock the earnest political verse of his day. Hunters, witches, and the Wild Hunt cross the bear's path in wild scenes. The verse dances even while the satire bites. Heine called the poem a last free forest song of Romanticism. It stands as his great verse satire, funny on its face and sharp underneath, aimed at German complacency.
hopkins-discovery-of-witches-1647:
Matthew Hopkins defends his hunt in The Discovery of Witches, his brief tract of 1647. Hopkins had roamed East Anglia in the war years, paid by towns to find witches. Scores were hanged on his word. Foes in print charged him with fraud and cruel tests: no sleep, bound swims, and pricks for the Devil's mark on the skin of the charged.

His tract replies ask by ask, in a cool, prim tone. He died the same year, young and much cursed. The tract is the chief hunt man's own word. It is a grim self portrait.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machorro-spelle:
Machorro, a Sephardic family name spelled many ways, is traced in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. The family flourished in Brazil, Germany, Holland, Hungary, and Italy. Thirteen of its members lie buried at Altona, with gravestones running from 1620 to 1782. The entry gathers scattered mentions across three centuries.

The article picks out individual Machorros from the record. Abraham and Moses flourished at Amsterdam in the mid-seventeenth century, and Abraham won praise as flutist and writer alike. Elijah lived in Brazil about the same time. Moses ben Daniel served as rabbi in Venice around 1693, and one of his legal decisions was printed at Amsterdam. A darker note names Juan Pacheco de Leon, alias Solomon Machorro, among the Maranos tried in Mexico in the 1640s. The entry shows one family's spread across the Sephardic world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manasseh-ben-jo:
Manasseh ben Joseph of Ilye, a Russian rabbinical writer, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Smorgony in 1767, he knew rabbinic sources by age seven. His father barred him from Bible and Hebrew grammar, fearing they would crowd out Talmud. He married at thirteen and settled in Ilye. He died there in 1831.

The article stresses his independence of mind. Among his disciples he criticized even the Shulhan Aruk and Rashi. He read some Mishnah passages against the Gemara's own reading. Only a powerful rabbi's protection kept the ban from him. Elijah of Wilna welcomed him yearly until hearing he also visited the Hasidic leader Zalman of Liozna. Then the gaon held aloof, though Manasseh protested that love of knowledge alone drew him. Still, he credited Elijah with teaching him the plain-sense method. The entry portrays a mind caught between orthodoxy, Hasidism, and new learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-martyrs-the-ten:
The Ten Martyrs were ten great teachers said to have been executed under the emperor Hadrian. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote their Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Tradition says the ten were killed for teaching the Law to their pupils. They taught in defiance of a Roman edict. Legend soon added detail and drama to their deaths.

The article compares the older Talmudic accounts with a special midrash on the story, the Midrash Eleh Ezkerah. That midrash survives in four versions. Where the Talmud spreads the executions over time, the midrash gathers them into a single day. It also invents the charge against them. An emperor cites the Bible's death penalty for man-stealing and blames the teachers for the ancient sale of Joseph.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medina-sir-solo:
Sir Solomon de Medina, who bankrolled Marlborough's armies, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind. A wealthy Jew who came to England with William III, he was known simply as "the Jew Medina." Through the War of the Spanish Succession he marched with the Duke of Marlborough, advancing him funds and furnishing the troops. His private couriers ran faster than the government's, so his agents often held great news before the ministers of the crown did.

That closeness made scandal. In 1711 Parliament attacked Marlborough for taking 6,000 pounds a year from Medina; the duke answered that the money bought trustworthy information. Medina was knighted for his services, the first Jew in England so honored, and he remained the largest contributor to the Bevis Marks Synagogue. The entry adds, dryly, that his descendants abandoned Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-vardima:
Menahem Vardimas ben Perez the Elder was a French tosafist and liturgist. He died at Dreux in 1224. Solomon Schechter and Isaac Broydé profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His strange second name comes from the Talmud itself. There, Vardimas appears as a by-name of a Menahem bar Jose. This later Menahem likely adopted it to stand apart. His age held many Menahems.

His authority carried weight. Moses of Coucy invokes him in the "Semag." The famous medieval discussion on the order of the phylacteries was held, by one tradition, in his own house. Samuel of Falaise called him master and "the Holy One." Gross reads that phrase as "the Pious," not "the Martyr." A liturgical poem of his treats the binding of Isaac. It found its way into the New Year ritual. A manuscript commentary cites him on the Bible as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-adolph-10:
Adolph Meyer, born at New Orleans on October 19, 1842, was a Louisiana congressman whose life is sketched in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Cyrus Adler, published in 1906. He was studying at the University of Virginia when the Civil War broke out. In 1862 he joined the Confederate army and rose to assistant adjutant-general.

After the war Meyer grew sugar and cotton and worked in finance in New Orleans, while leading the state National Guard as colonel and then brigadier-general. Elected as a Democrat from Louisiana's First District to the Fifty-second Congress, he was reelected through the Fifty-eighth. The entry notes his service on the committees on Naval Affairs and the District of Columbia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minden-judah-lo:
Judah Löb ben Joel Minden, a German lexicographer working in Berlin in the 1760s, made the first Hebrew dictionary ever produced by a Jew with German translations. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. His Millim le-Eloah appeared in 1760 with the approval of the Berlin and Halberstadt rabbinates.

Zunz called the book the first attempt to bring High German into Jewish national literature, the article notes. Minden built on David Ḳimḥi's dictionary, added material from the Concordance, and discussed what each Hebrew letter does in grammar. Five years later he reissued Musafia's Zeker Rab as a supplement to his own work, rounding out the toolkit for German readers of Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monies-david-10:
David Monies, a Danish portrait and genre painter born at Copenhagen on June 3, 1812, is entered by Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Academy of Arts took him at twelve and gave him silver medals at fifteen and twenty. Portraits of eminent contemporaries made his start in 1830.

A public grant of four hundred rix-dollars a year sent him to Munich in 1835 to continue his studies. He entered the Danish Academy in 1848 and became professor in 1859. His best-known canvas, the homecoming of the troops after the Three Years' War, caught the nation's joy mixed with grief and hangs at Frederiksborg Castle. He died at Copenhagen in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moser-plural-mo:
Moser, plural moserim, is the Hebrew word for an informer, and this Jewish Encyclopedia article treats the informer in Jewish law and history. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote it in 1906. No figure was held in greater contempt: the Talmud compared the informer to a serpent, because his words could bring death and ruin.

The article follows the law from Talmudic times, when informing was punished with death even after Jewish courts lost their criminal powers. It gives cases from Spain, where the word malshin entered the Spanish language itself. Isaac Alfasi fled his home in 1088 after being denounced, and a Barcelona informer was executed in 1280. Later sections gather the statutes by which Spanish communities pledged to root out informers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-barnett-: Barnett Nathan was an English showman known as Baron Nathan. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in 1793, he died in London on Dec. 6, 1856. He ran music and drama shows and taught dancing from 1844. For years he directed events at Rosherville Gardens near Gravesend. On his benefit nights he danced the egg-hornpipe while blindfolded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nesek-11447:
Nesek is wine bound up with idol worship. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such wine is forbidden to a Jew outright. In a wider sense, the term covers Gentile wine. It also covers Jewish wine a Gentile has touched.

Consecrated wine defiles persons and vessels alike. An olive's worth of it in a tent defiles. Even carrying it as a porter is banned. Plain heathen wine, setam yenam, is also barred. One reason was to guard against contact with true nesek. Another was to limit social ties leading to intermarriage. Practice later eased where no idolaters lived. Non-idolater wine was then barred only as a drink.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nimes-hebrew-or:
Nîmes is the chief town of France's Gard department. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there in very remote times. Count Hilderic welcomed Jews driven from Spain in 672. Its twelfth-century community ranked among Languedoc's best.

Its academy was headed by Abraham ben David, the RABaD. A famed letter calls Nîmes the Temple itself. From it, the Law spread throughout Israel, it says. Bishop Bertrand passed harsh measures in 1284. He protected the Jews in 1295 for his own interests. Expulsions came in 1306 and again in 1394. The ghetto guarded them from Christian neighbors' abuse. In 1806 the town counted 371 Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-obed-11647:
Obed is a name borne by five men in the Bible. The entry was written for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its authors were the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser. The first Obed was the son of Boaz and Ruth. Ruth was the daughter of Naomi, a widow. His aunts and kin gave him his name.

Obed was the father of Jesse, by the old lists. He was thus the grandfather of King David. A second Obed was kin to Sheshan, a chief. A third was one of the thirty captains of David. A fourth kept guard at the Temple in Jerusalem. The fifth was father of Azariah, a captain. Azariah helped a priest set young Joash on the throne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pagay-hans-1184:
Hans Pagay was an Austrian actor born at Vienna. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there on November 11, 1845. His father was a broker in the trade of funds. The father meant his son for that same line of work.

Hans chose the stage in place of the funds trade. He began as a singer in the chorus of a house. He went on to Linz and to Odessa for work. There he sang comic parts in light operas for crowds. He roamed through Austria, Hungary, and south Germany for years. In 1887 he took a post at the Residenztheater, Berlin. There he won a strong place as a man of parts. His wife Sophie was a stage player of note too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-patriotism-hebr:
Patriotism means love for and devotion to one's country. Isidore Singer and Henry Cohen wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew Bible never uses the word itself. Its writers still praise the virtue in many places. The article gathers the proof texts in order.

Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of their new city. He said their own welfare rested on its welfare. The Talmud went further for life in the Diaspora. It taught that the law of the country is the law. It ordered prayer for the kingdom and payment of taxes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pertuis-or-1204:
Pertuis is a small town in the Vaucluse, in France. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews had settled there by the thirteenth century. In 1283 they won leave for a synagogue and cemetery.

The yearly rent was two pounds of pepper. In 1436 a cruel charge shook the region. A Jew of Aix was accused of blaspheming the Virgin. He was sentenced to be flayed alive. Jews offered the king a fortune to save him. The king took more money, and the man still died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pilate-pontius-:
Pontius Pilate ruled Judea as Rome's fifth procurator there. He held the post from 26 to 36 of the common era. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Philo paints his rule as cruel and corrupt.

His soldiers smuggled images into Jerusalem by night. Crowds begged five days at Caesarea for their removal. Pilate backed down when Jews chose death instead. He seized Temple funds to build an aqueduct. Disguised soldiers then cut down rioters and bystanders. His massacre of Samaritans on Gerizim ended his rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollak-joachim-:
Joachim Pollak, called Hayyim Joseph, was an Austrian rabbi born in Hungary in 1798. Isidore Singer and Moses Löb Bamberger wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. From 1828 he served as rabbi at Trebitsch in Moravia. He held that post until his death there in 1879.

Pollak wrote a long note on a famed work of Isaac Arama. His book, Mekor Hayyim, came out at Presburg in 1849. It reached a third edition at Warsaw in 1885. He also wrote a life of Arama himself. His Hebrew songs ran in the yearly Bikkure ha-Ittim. He wrote on Talmudic rules as well. Hebrew journals often printed his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-presburg-hungar:
Presburg, called Pozsony in Hungarian, is a city on the Danube. Gotthard Deutsch wrote its long article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its place on a trade road points to an old community. It may be one of the oldest in Hungary. The first clear record of its Jews dates from 1251.

In 1291 the Jews of Presburg won a charter from King Andrew. In 1360 they were driven out of the city. They settled at nearby Heimburg and came back in 1368. Their first synagogue was built in 1399. By 1517 their head tax reached a set sum each year. The article traces bans, returns, and growth across the centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rehoboam-12647:
Rehoboam was Solomon's son and his successor as king in Jerusalem. Emil G. Hirsch, Ira Maurice Price, Wilhelm Bacher, and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His mother was Naamah the Ammonitess. He inherited a kingdom already under strain.

The article blames Solomon's taxes and forced levies for unrest. Foreign customs at court added further harm, it argues. Border cities had already broken away under Solomon. Jeroboam waited in Egypt for his chance to return. The coronation assembly met at Shechem. There the tribes asked Rehoboam for needed reforms. He was forty one years old at that point. The entry sets up the split of Israel's kingdom. It shows a crown passing to a weaker hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riddle-12747:
A riddle, among the ancients, was a serious matter of wager. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The tale of Oedipus and the Sphinx shows that weight. Samson's riddle to the Philistines fits the same kind.

The article suggests some proverb lists began as riddles. Ezekiel offers a symbolic riddle about Babylon's king. He compares that king to an eagle in the text. Riddles were a favorite table amusement for early Hebrews. Many gathered around the Queen of Sheba's visit. She tested Solomon's wisdom chiefly with riddles. Records preserve three in one Targum and nineteen in another. Two true riddles are quoted with their answers. One answer is a tree made into a ship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenfeld-jacob:
Jacob Rosenfeld was a Russian journalist and publisher born in Austria in 1839. Herman Rosenthal and S. Hurwitz wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied law at Kiev and practised in St. Petersburg, writing for Russian papers.

The attacks on Jews in South Russia in 1881 changed Rosenfeld's course. From then on he was an ardent Jewish nationalist. That year he bought Razsvyet, a Russian-language Jewish paper he had helped edit. Under him it spoke for nationalism and the Palestinian movement. Money troubles forced him to close it in 1883, and he returned to law at Minsk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ruth-book-of-12:
The Book of Ruth is a short Bible book, an idyllic tale told in prose. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and George A. Barton wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its story is set in the period of the Judges.

In the Hebrew Bible, Ruth stands in the Writings after the Song of Solomon. Greek and English Bibles place it right after Judges instead. The heroines are Naomi and her daughter-in-law Ruth, a woman of Moab. Famine drives Naomi's family to Moab, where her husband and sons die. The entry also weighs when this much later book was written.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-simon-13:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Simon Samuel. He was a German pathologist, a doctor who studies disease. Samuel was born at Glogau on October 5, 1833. He died at Königsberg, in East Prussia, on May 9, 1899. He studied medicine at Berlin and Vienna.

Samuel took his medical degree in 1855. He set up as a physician at Königsberg in 1856. He became a privat-docent in 1864. Ten years later he rose to assistant professor. His books treat the process of inflammation and the origin of fever and body heat. In 1879 he published a handbook of general pathology. With A. Eulenburg he also issued a handbook of general therapy in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schaikewitz-nah:
Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Nahum Meïr Schaikewitz. He wrote under the name Shomer. Schaikewitz was a Russian novelist and playwright in Judæo-German. He was born at Nesvizh, in the government of Minsk, on December 18, 1849. Even as a boy he told stories well. His first pieces were Hebrew tales for Ha-Meliẓ.

At Bucharest the Jewish theater captured Schaikewitz. He settled in Odessa as a theater manager and playwright. When Russia closed the Jewish theater, he moved to New York in 1888. There he edited two Judæo-German weeklies. He wrote over two hundred novels in Judæo-German. They picture small-town Russian Jewish life in plain, spoken language. His books reached everyone, from householder to servant girl. Over thirty of his plays were staged in Russia and New York.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-servia-13447:
Servia, a kingdom in southeast Europe, stayed a Turkish vassal state until 1876. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on its Jews. Their story centers on Belgrade and Nish, the two oldest communities. No firm congregation formed at Belgrade until 1530.

Don Joseph Nasi helped found that Belgrade community. Nish followed much later, in 1728. Smaller groups lived at Semendria and Shabats, though unrest drove many away. All these communities looked to Salonica for religious guidance. In troubled years Jews there suffered attacks from Turks and neighbors alike. Full legal equality came only under Prince Milos and later rulers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheep-12547:
Sheep held a central place in the farming life of ancient Palestine. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the animal. Hebrew has many words for sheep at each life stage. Terms name the lamb, suckling, ram, and ewe apart.

One word covers small cattle, sheep and goats together. The Bible mentions sheep hundreds of times, the entry notes. Sheep are the first animals it names at all. In patriarchal days they formed the chief wealth of families. Great flocks appear from Genesis through Job and Chronicles. Even kings bred sheep without shame. Readers learn why flocks measured riches, food, clothing, and sacrifice in Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sifre-known-als:
Sifre is a midrash, or rabbinic commentary, on Numbers and Deuteronomy together. Wilhelm Bacher and S. Horovitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. It is also known as Sifre debe Rab in old sources. Rashi, Alfasi, and Hananeel all cite it under that title.

Hard questions surround the Sifre named in the Talmud. A passage in Sanhedrin links a Sifre to Rabbi Simeon's school. Scholars ask how far that link truly applies here. The surviving Sifre is not the Talmudic one, they conclude. On close study it is not even one uniform work. Parts from different hands were joined into it over time. The entry models source criticism at work on a classic text. It separates layers that readers long took as one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-magus-137:
Simon Magus is a figure often named in the history of early Christianity. Kaufmann Kohler and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Acts says he was feared across Samaria for his magic powers. He let himself be baptized by the apostles. He then tried to buy the gift of the Holy Ghost.

Peter cursed him for that bold offer. Later writers made him the father of all heresy. They linked his teaching to Gnosticism itself. Some critics doubted that he ever lived at all. The article weighs those doubts and the early sources. It also notes his claim to be a Messiah, and later a god.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-abraham:
Abraham Solomon was an English artist born in London in May 1824. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. At eighteen he entered the school of the Royal Academy. There he won a medal for drawing from the antique. From 1843 until his death he showed work each year.

His picture The Breakfast Table brought him fame in 1846. Later works showed growing originality and found ready buyers. They included Waiting for the Verdict and its sequel, The Verdict. First and Third Class also won wide notice. Many of his pictures spread through engravings to a broad public. He died at Biarritz in 1862, still under forty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stieglitz-heinr:
Heinrich Stieglitz was a German writer born at Arolsen on February 22, 1801. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at Göttingen and Leipsic. In 1828 he became a teacher at a Berlin gymnasium. He also served as keeper of the Royal Library there.

Poor health forced Stieglitz to give up both Berlin posts. After his wife died, he spent much time traveling. He became a Christian during his life. His works include Pictures of the Orient, printed in 1831 to 1833. Songs of the time followed in 1834. He died at Venice on August 23, 1849. The short entry lists a poet whose career illness cut short. His books still mark his place in German letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sweden-14147:
Sweden is a kingdom of northern Europe with a late Jewish history. Joseph Jacobs and Gustave Lindner wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Church records show Jews in Stockholm in the 1600s. Settlement then required joining the Lutheran Church. Baptism was the price of residence for Jews.

In 1681 two Stockholm Jews and their families were baptized. Twenty-eight people converted before the king himself. A 1680 petition for free residence failed. Charles the Eleventh ordered Jews out within fourteen days in 1685. He feared Jewish influence on the evangelical faith. Later sections trace how settlement rights slowly opened. Court patronage let some Jewish merchants work meanwhile. The entry shows faith, not race, driving early Swedish policy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taharah-12447:
Taharah is the rite of washing a dead body before burial. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Members of the burial society perform the washing. The body rests on a special cleansing table. Its feet point toward the door.

Workers remove the black cover and old garments first. A white sheet slides under the body. They recite a verse from Zechariah about clean garments. Warm water then washes the body with care. The mouth stays covered so no water enters. Water poured on the head brings a verse from Ezekiel. Each limb is washed downward in turn. Verses from the Song of Songs accompany the washing. The entry describes a tender duty done by custom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tarfon-greek-ye:
Tarfon was a tanna of the third generation of sages. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He lived between the Temple's fall and Bethar's fall. He came from a priestly family line. He said he had officiated in the Temple himself.

Tarfon's devotion to his mother became a model tale. He placed his hands under her bare feet crossing the yard. His generosity matched that filial care. He returned first-born redemption money though it was his by right. In famine he wed 800 women to feed them from tithes. Priest's wives could share tithes by law. For a poor bridal parade he had the bride anointed. Though rich, he was famously modest in spirit. The entry gathers kindness stories around one priest-sage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tetrarch-greek-:
A tetrarch governed a quarter of a province under Rome. Samuel Krauss wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The rank sat below that of ethnarch. Several Jewish princes of the Herodian family held the title.

Herod the Great held it before he became king. His brother Phasael held it as well. Pheroras ruled Perea as tetrarch from 20 B.C. Herod Antipas governed Galilee, and Philip ruled Iturea and Trachonitis. Lysanias ruled Abilene in the same rank. Over time the word lost its strict sense of a quarter. It came to mean any ruler below a king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-turteltaub-wilh:
Wilhelm Turteltaub was an Austrian physician and poet born at Rzeszow in 1816. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. At twelve he wrote a comedy imitating Kotzebue. He entered Vienna University for medicine in 1830. He took his degree in 1840 and practiced at home.

While studying, he wrote for several Vienna journals. His first book, Wiener Fresko-Skizzen, appeared in 1835. His one-act comedy pleased audiences at the Leopoldstadt theater. Saphir drew him into the periodical Der Humorist. Later plays reached the Hofburg Theater stage in Vienna. One comedy played across Austria and Germany in 1837. In 1859 he edited the Wiener Volksbühne journal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-varus-quintiliu:
Quintilius Varus was the Roman governor of Syria from 6 to 4 B.C. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Varus first appears in Jewish history at a trial. King Herod put his own son Antipater before Varus's court. That court condemned the prince.

After Herod died, revolt broke out across Judea. Varus marched back from Antioch with two legions. His troops burned Sepphoris and sold its people as slaves. They burned Emmaus as well. At Jerusalem the rebels gave up when he arrived. Still, about two thousand rebels were crucified. The entry shows Rome's harsh answer to unrest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wagner-wilhelm-:
Richard Wagner was a German composer of operas. He was born at Leipsic on May 22, 1813. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Venice on February 13, 1883. Meyerbeer helped him stage works in Paris. Heine helped with a libretto as well.

The entry centers on Wagner's attack on Jewish music. In 1850 he published Das Judenthum in der Musik. It appeared under a false name. He charged that Mendelssohn and Meyerbeer wrote sweet but shallow music. Replies poured in when the essay was reprinted. Yet Wagner kept many Jewish friends. His favorite choirmaster was the Jew Herman Levi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiss-leopold-w:
Leopold W. Weiss was a German eye doctor. He was born at Giessen in 1849. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Giessen, Tübingen, and Vienna. He took his medical degree in 1874. He then assisted at Heidelberg's eye institute.

In 1876 Weiss won the right to lecture at Heidelberg. Since 1878 he has practiced at Heidelberg and Mannheim. His papers study how the eye's turning points are found. Others treat the growth of nearsightedness. He also wrote on tuberculosis of the eye. His work on fluid drainage in the eye drew notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-winterstein-sim:
Simon Winterstein was an Austrian railroad magnate. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Prague in 1819. He died at Vöslau on June 11, 1883. Born poor, he had to support himself early. He worked as a clerk in Prague and Vienna.

Winterstein later ran a business of his own. He served the Nordbahn railroad as shipping agent. He rose to its executive board, then its presidency. Rothschild links put him on other boards too. He sat for the Südbahn and the Creditanstalt. He also served as president of Vienna's Jewish community. He held a seat in Austria's House of Lords.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yad-lit-hand-ju:
Yad, which means hand in Hebrew, is a pointer for Torah reading. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The reader of the Law uses it in the synagogue. A deputy points to each word as it is read.

The tool is as old as the schools of old. Teachers used like sticks to point at maps and boards. The first tale of its use comes from Bethar. That town fell in the Bar Kokba war of old. Teachers there fought foes with their pointers in hand. In east Europe the tool served in grade schools still. Its use by the deputy is a custom, not a strict law. Fine yads of silver are now part of Torah dress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zadok-15147:
Zadok was a tanna who lived through the fall of the Jewish state. Richard Gottheil, Samuel Krauss, Joseph Jacobs, and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He stood with two great sages at a feast in Jabneh. There the host poured the wine with his own hand.

Two sages praised the host at that feast in song. Zadok grew wroth at that show of praise then. God made all for man, he said in that hour. Men should not turn from God to praise a mere man. His whole life fell in the years of the state's death. He fasted forty years to stave off the Temple's fall. When it fell, he was too weak to walk or eat. Johanan ben Zakkai pled for his life with Titus then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zered-brook-or-:
Zered is a brook and vale where the Israelites camped in the wilds. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. That camp marks the end of the thirty-eighth year of the trek. It stands in the Books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.

One old gloss reads the name as vale of willows. The Greek text form backs that sense of the name. The vale lies east of the Jordan on a set line. That line splits the lands of Moab and Edom in the south. It stands ere the trek crossed the River Arnon at last. Most minds of this age place it at Wadi Karak. That is a deep and thin gorge that runs to the Dead Sea. The entry rests on the work of Dillmann and peers.
la-phrenologie-le-geste-et-la-physionomi:
Hippolyte Bruyères wrote this French work on phrenology, gesture, and facial expression in 1847. Its subtitle promises proof through 120 portraits. Those portraits, subjects, and scenes were engraved on steel.

Phrenology claimed that bumps on the skull reveal character. Physiognomy made similar claims from faces and gestures. Bruyères combined both popular sciences in one picture-rich volume. The book now serves as a record of beliefs that once drew wide public interest in France. Steel engravings made the claims feel solid and visible. Modern readers can study the pictures as period evidence, not proof.
lilly-christian-astrology-1647:
William Lilly was the best known astrologer in England during the Civil War years. His Christian Astrology, printed in 1647, taught the craft in plain English for the first time. It gave working rules that any reader could test at home. The book made Lilly famous across the country.

Three main arts fill the pages. Horary work answers a direct question from a chart cast for the moment it is asked. Election work picks the best time to start a task, and natal work reads a birth chart. Students of the old craft still treat Lilly as their chief guide.
longfellow-evangeline-1847:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published Evangeline in 1847, and it made him the most beloved poet in America. Longfellow, a Harvard professor, heard the story of the Acadian exiles at a dinner party. He shaped it into an epic in English hexameters, a bold experiment for the time.

In 1755 the British expelled the French Acadians from Nova Scotia, scattering families across America. Evangeline Bellefontaine is parted from her betrothed, Gabriel, on their wedding day. She searches for him for years, through wilderness and new settlements, aging into a Sister of Mercy. The lovers meet at last in a Philadelphia hospital, too late. Generations of schoolchildren memorized the poem, and Acadia still keeps her shrine.
mapp-clavicula-1847:
Mappae Clavicula was presented to the world by Sir Thomas Phillipps in 1847. His letter appeared in Archaeologia, the antiquaries' journal, volume thirty-two. Phillipps was a baronet, a Fellow of the Royal Society, and a famous collector. He printed the text from an old manuscript in his vast library.

The Mappae Clavicula is a medieval Latin book of craft recipes. Its name means 'a little key' to the secrets of making. Recipes teach pigments, dyes, glass, and work in gold and silver. Monks and craftsmen guarded such knowledge for centuries. Phillipps's printing opened the workshop door to scholars. The text remains a chief source for medieval arts and trades.
michelet-french-revolution-1847:
Jules Michelet's History of the French Revolution appears in C. Cocks's translation of 1847. Michelet writes the Revolution as France's national epic, with the people as hero. Bastille Day, the festivals, and the great journées glow with patriotic fire. He worked from archives and from the memories of survivors.

Michelet's style is lyrical, swift, and deeply emotional. He loves the Revolution's early hope and grieves its violence. Critics note his bias, yet few deny his power. The history shaped how France remembers 1789 to this day. English readers met romantic history at its height in this version. It remains a moving, partisan classic.
morte-arthure-alliterative-halliwell-184:
An unknown poet of the north of England told Arthur's last wars in hard, pounding verse. The Alliterative Morte Arthure, in James Halliwell's 1847 edition, prints the Middle English poem complete. Its Arthur is a great king of war, not a dreamer of courts.

Arthur marches on Rome itself, wins an empire in hard fights, then hears that Mordred has seized his throne and queen. He turns home to a last battle that kills him and the flower of his knights. The tale is darker and bloodier than Malory's later telling. The poem ranks among the peaks of medieval English verse.
notions-de-phrenologie-1847: Notions de phrénologie, in French, is a book by Julien Le Rousseau, dated 1847 in the record. The record counts more than six hundred pages for the volume. The hosted sample holds only a digitization notice from a scanning project, so it preserves no readable content from the book itself. The title alone names the subject: phrenology, the study that read character from the shape of the head. Readers should treat this note as a title level guide only.
openalex-w1603226747:
Betty Abelev and the ALICE Collaboration reported this measurement. It appeared in Physical Review Letters in November 2013. The team counted two strange particles in lead collisions. They are called K-short and Lambda in the paper. Counts were taken near the central rapidity region.

Spectra were shown for several classes of collision strength. The Lambda to K-short ratio peaked at mid momentum. Those peaks shifted higher in more central collisions. The peak size grew nearly threefold toward central events. No such excess appeared in proton collision data, they note. Flow and quark joining models partly explain the pattern.
openalex-w1981821647:
Jonathan Friedlaender and a large team studied Pacific genetics. Their paper appeared in PLoS Genetics in the year 2008. Human diversity in the Pacific was poorly sampled before. Melanesia in particular lacked adequate genetic coverage. Population relationships there stayed open to debate.

The team ran a genome scan on nearly a thousand people. Hundreds of markers of two kinds were measured. Samples spanned Pacific islands, with Melanesian depth. Such scans reveal how island groups relate and mixed. The data test stories of voyaging and settlement. It remains a base dataset for Pacific population history.
openalex-w2004268547:
Brian Grimberg, Rachanee Udomsangpetch, Jia Xainli and colleagues studied how one malaria parasite enters red blood cells. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2007. The parasite is Plasmodium vivax. It must attach to the Duffy marker on red cells to get inside.

People without the Duffy marker resist this parasite. The parasite uses its own Duffy binding protein to attach. The team tested antibodies aimed at that protein. The antibodies blocked the parasite from invading red blood cells. The result points to the binding protein as a vaccine target. Blocking that single attachment step could stop infection before it starts.
openalex-w2011445647:
Mohsen Kayal, Julie Vercelloni, Thierry Lison de Loma and colleagues tracked a crown-of-thorns starfish outbreak. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. The starfish eats reef-building corals. Large swarms can devastate a reef. The outbreak struck the island of Moorea in French Polynesia.

The team showed that the outbreak moved in a slow, ordered way. Dense starfish groups began at the outer base of the reef. They then spread to nearby and shallower areas in waves. The starfish ate coral species in a set order of preference. Reefs lost living coral fast where the waves passed. The authors call it among the most intense outbreaks ever reported. Reef fish and bottom life changed in its wake.
openalex-w2122161847:
Lea Karatheodoris Davis, Dongmei Yu, Clare Keenan, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Genetics in 2013. They asked how much of the risk for Tourette syndrome and for obsessive compulsive disorder comes from common gene variants. The two conditions are related, but the team wanted to know whether their genetic makeup differs.

Using genome-wide data, the authors estimated the share of risk explained by all tested common variants together. Tourette syndrome showed a higher share than obsessive compulsive disorder. Splitting the genome by chromosome, variant frequency, and function showed further contrasts. Rare variants counted for part of Tourette risk but not for the other disorder, so their genetic structures differ.
openalex-w2153508247:
Selma Forni, Ignacio Aguilar, and Ignacy Misztal published this study in Genetics Selection Evolution in 2011. Animal breeders now blend DNA data with pedigrees to estimate breeding values in one single-step analysis. That blend only works if the DNA-based and pedigree-based relationship tables sit on the same scale, and builders can choose many DNA recipes.

The team tested several recipes on litter size records from hundreds of thousands of sows. Some recipes produced relationship values larger than pedigree values, others smaller. Mismatched scales biased variance estimates and inflated accuracy claims. A normalized table avoided the inflation. The authors conclude that careful scaling, using observed allele frequencies, keeps the combined analysis honest.
openalex-w2170375547:
Ted Feldpausch, Lindsay Banin, Oliver Phillips, and colleagues published this study in Biogeosciences in 2011. They built a global database linking tropical tree height to trunk diameter. Biomass estimates lean on such shape rules, and using one rule everywhere can bias results if tree shapes differ by region or forest type.

Nearly forty thousand paired measurements came from two hundred eighty-three sites in twenty-two countries. Rainfall variation, dry season length, and temperature emerged as key drivers of shape differences. Crowded, high-biomass forests also grew taller trees at any given trunk width. After accounting for climate and structure, two broad regional groups remained, and the team offers fitted equations to cut biomass errors.
openalex-w2237531247:
Rocheli de Souza, Adriana Ambrosini, and Luciane Passaglia published this review in Genetics and Molecular Biology in 2015. They cover plant growth-promoting bacteria, microbes that live around or inside roots and help crops grow. Such bacteria can also shield plants from disease and from stresses like drought and salt.

The review lists the traits that make a bacterium helpful: fixing nitrogen, freeing locked phosphate, and making iron carriers and plant hormones. Bacteria living inside plant tissue may promote growth most reliably. Working inoculants could cut farm costs and pollution by replacing some chemical fertilizer. Success in the field, though, hinges on root secretions, root colonization, and overall soil health, the authors stress.
openalex-w2346336047:
Mélissa Mialon, Boyd Swinburn, and Jillian Wate led this 2016 study in Globalization and Health. They tracked how big food firms in Fiji work to shape public policy. Ills that do not spread from person to person are Fiji's top killer. Processed food feeds those ills, and the firms' political play there was barely studied.

For three months the team read public records and spoke with ten people in food and health policy. They found proof of all six known firm tactics, from ad messaging to splitting critics. Those spoken with saw a real risk that this work could weaken the fight against these ills. Gifts and lobbying stay poorly shown in public, yet the watch still surfaced many firm moves.
openalex-w2495827047:
The ALICE Collaboration reported these results in Physical Review Letters in 2016, with J. Adam as first author. The paper gives the first measurements of anisotropic flow for charged particles in lead-lead collisions. The collisions took place at the Large Hadron Collider at an energy of 5.02 TeV. Flow describes how particles spray out unevenly after two heavy nuclei collide.

The team measured three flow patterns, called elliptic, triangular, and quadrangular flow. These patterns reflect the shape of the overlap zone when the nuclei strike off-center. They also respond to ripples in the starting energy density. Reading them helps physicists pin down properties of the quark-gluon plasma formed in the crash. Earlier work found that this hot matter flows almost like a liquid, with very low viscosity.
openalex-w2604165347:
Kenneth Verstraete, Frank Peelman, and Harald Braun, with colleagues, published this 2017 study in Nature Communications. It examines TSLP, a signaling protein that drives allergic inflammation in asthma and eczema. TSLP is released by skin and airway lining cells when they meet triggers. It switches on immune cells that push the body toward the type 2 responses behind most allergies.

TSLP works by docking onto a two-part receptor on immune cells. That receptor pairs its own specific chain with a chain shared with interleukin-7 signaling. The paper's title announces its twin goals: mapping the structure of this receptor complex, and finding ways to block it. Such blocking matters because faulty TSLP signaling feeds widespread diseases of airways, skin, and gut. A clear structural picture gives drug designers exact targets for stopping the signal.
openalex-w2613751647:
Rimena R. Domingues, Paulo Fernando Trugilho, and Carlos Alberto Silva, with colleagues, published this 2017 study in PLoS ONE. It characterizes biochar, charcoal made by heating plant waste without full burning. The team made biochars from wood, sugarcane bagasse, coffee husk, and chicken manure. Each feedstock was heated to three different temperatures for comparison.

Biochars from nutrient-rich coffee husk and chicken manure carried high ash and mineral loads. Their chemistry made them promising liming agents for acidic soils. They could also replace imported potassium and calcium sources in Brazil. Made at lower temperatures, these biochars held nutrients well, thanks to high exchange capacity. Heating to the top temperature strongly cut that capacity. Overall, the authors show a biochar's farm value depends mostly on its feedstock. Choosing waste streams wisely turns disposal problems into soil benefits.
openalex-w2809515747:
Rainer Willi Bussmann, Narel Y. Paniagua-Zambrana, and Carolina Romero surveyed Bogotá's medicinal plant markets for this 2018 study in the Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine. Markets are a major source of herbal medicine in Colombia. Yet few studies had inventoried what the capital's markets actually sell. The team expected species and uses to differ between markets across the sprawling city.

Between late 2014 and early 2016, they interviewed thirty-eight vendors in twenty-four markets. They recorded four hundred nine plant species from one hundred twenty-two families. The plants treated nineteen disease categories across three hundred eighteen distinct applications. Differences between markets proved far larger than expected, even between nearby ones. The authors credit Bogotá's mix of migrant origins, each bringing distinct plant knowledge. The inventory documents a living pharmacopoeia that varies neighborhood by neighborhood.
openalex-w3004647847:
Moritz Gerstung, Clemency Jolly, Ignaty Leshchiner, and colleagues published this study in Nature in 2020. It reconstructs the evolutionary history of two thousand six hundred fifty-eight cancers from their DNA. The work forms part of the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes project.

Scientists knew the types of mutation cancers carry, but not when those changes arose during a tumor's life. By reading the full mutation record of each sample, the team could order events in time. Their inferences cover early chromosome gains, the family trees of late cancer growth, and the sequence in which driver mutations appeared. Drawing the line between normal cell change and cancer progression is a central aim.
openalex-w3029661147:
Konrad Karczewski, Laurent Francioli, Grace Tiao, and colleagues published this study in Nature in 2020. It measures mutational constraint across the human genome using natural variation in more than one hundred forty thousand people. Constraint marks the genes that evolution keeps most tightly unchanged.

Breaking genes in lab animals teaches much about gene function, but such experiments cannot be done in humans. Nature, though, has already run the experiment: large sequencing projects reveal many people carrying gene-breaking variants. By counting where such variants are rarer than chance predicts, the team quantified how strongly each gene resists damage. The resulting spectrum guides the hunt for disease genes and for drug targets that humans can safely lose.
openalex-w4321458747:
Patricia Bovio-Winkler, Leandro Guerrero, Leonardo Erijman, and colleagues read the genomes of Chloroflexi bacteria in wastewater reactors, in BMC Microbiology in 2023. Chloroflexi are abundant in treatment bioreactors worldwide. They seem to help break down carbon compounds and shape the clumps that reactors depend on. Yet most species have never been grown alone in a lab, so their roles stayed murky.

Using metagenomics, the team rebuilt genomes from three very different reactors, including one that removes nitrogen by anammox. They assembled seventeen new species, two of them proposed as a new genus. The genomes share fermenting, carbon-degrading toolkits and genes for stickiness. In the anammox reactor they also hint at a role in nitrogen removal, widening the group's known jobs.
openalex-w7160334247:
Ryoi Ohashi, of Kyushu University, led a 2026 theoretical physics study of tunneling in fractional quantum Hall states, exotic quantum fluids that form in flat electron systems under strong magnetic fields. The focus is the Read-Rezayi state, whose excitations behave as non-Abelian anyons, particles of interest for future quantum computing. The authors study how quasiparticles and electrons trade places as the drivers of electrical flow through a narrow contact.

They introduce a method called the phase-shift instanton, which builds phase factors into the standard tunneling framework. With it they reformulate a known duality for the Moore-Read state and derive an explicit dual picture for the Read-Rezayi case. Both states, they show, share a universal transport pattern at strong coupling, revealing a deep constraint on these quantum edges.
openalex-w7161687547:
Tomomi Tateishi, of the Open University of Japan, led a 2026 theoretical study of how twisting phonons in helical crystals can steer electrons' orbital motion. Phonons are vibrations of a crystal lattice; in a helical crystal some vibrations rotate like a corkscrew. The authors build a microscopic theory for a crystal with threefold helical symmetry, asking how such chiral phonons hand angular momentum to electrons.

Local rotations from the phonons create an interaction that shifts electrons between orbital states while conserving crystal angular momentum. The orbital response, they calculate, is weak at the zone center and boundary but strong at wave vectors in between, a pattern tied to how the phonon bands cross. The theory gives the debated chirality effect a concrete microscopic mechanism.
openalex-w7204190147:
João Gabriel Gomes Santos led a Portuguese-language study, in Brazil in 2026, on whether players recognize the mathematics inside the game Minecraft. The data come from a workshop called Learning Statistics Using Minecraft, held at the 2022 National Mathematics Festival in Brazil. A questionnaire reached 851 participants aged seven to nineteen, and the team studied the answers with a statistical method that maps associations among age, sex, schooling, and responses.

Most participants did not spontaneously recognize mathematical concepts in the game, with sets and the relation between speed and time hardest to spot. Older and more schooled participants recognized more, mainly about mathematics teaching and geometric figures. Teacher mediation, the authors conclude, is what turns play into mathematical learning.
openalex-w7204216547:
Maria José Almeida Santiago and André Domingues dos Santos published a Portuguese-language paper in Brazil in 2026 on funk music, youth. Quilombola culture in Helvécia, a community in the far south of Bahia descended from escaped enslaved people. Their case is a youth group called Os Brutos. Using ethnographic and methods, and producing a documentary as an school product, the team joined events, interviewed young people and elders, and recorded the group's online space.

Some young people skip traditional practices yet keep community ties, joining the raising of the Saint Sebastian mast as an act of faith and belonging. Funk, the authors find, works as sociability and expression without breaking quilombola identity. Culture there is dynamic and hybrid, continually rebuilt by its own people.
openalex-w7206208247:
Arthur Pereira da Costa, Igor Cavalcante Torres, and Wellinsilvio Costa dos Santos measure what a forced electricity tariff change costs, and saves, a Brazilian university. The A. C. Simoes campus of the Federal University of Alagoas had to move from a lower-voltage tariff class to a higher one under rules from the national energy agency for very large users. The team compared electricity bills from July 2024 to June 2025 under two contract setups.

The higher-voltage connection, they found, cut total electricity costs by more than a fifth. The saving came to roughly two million reais per year for the campus. A rules change that looked like a burden turned out to pay: the case shows how tariff class, not just energy use, shapes the bills of large public institutions.
openalex-w7211987947:
Gessika Demetrio de Alcantara leads a team that holds far-off school can open top school to autistic kids, if it is built for them. Their read of books and rule texts holds that web reach is more than tech tools. It takes fresh class craft, firm school plans, and staff growth that never stops. The team lists screen voice tools, live word subs, web class rooms fit for all, talk apps of next kinds, and game and layered-view tools.

Used well, these tools lower walls in talk, thought, and heart life with peers. Joint and fit-to-child ways, with plan for all from the start and open lore, back free stance, sure days, and true part for such kids. The close is a call for a whole-frame vow: tech, fair shares, and the school's charge as one. Then reach turns to stay, and stay to gain.
openalex-w7213395347:
Ana Cláudia dos Santos Barão leads a team linking digital literacy with science literacy. Their 2026 review asks what digital skills add to science teaching in an age of fast online information. Sources came from Google Scholar, Scopus, PubMed, and SciELO.

Digital literacy, the review finds, goes well beyond using devices. It includes judging information, working with others, creating content, solving problems, and acting ethically online. Digital media and extended reality can make science ideas easier to see and discuss. Project-based learning helps tie those tools to real questions. Benefits depend, the authors stress, on clear teaching aims and skilled teacher guidance.
openalex-w7214911347:
Yoichiro Uchida led a Japanese team in a 2026 prospective study of a blood-saving technique for major liver surgery. In hemodilutional autologous transfusion, some of the patient's own blood is drawn and diluted before surgery, then returned during the operation, reducing the need for donor blood. Fifty patients scheduled for intermediate to advanced liver resection were enrolled in 2022 and 2023.

Forty-eight patients completed the protocol operation with the technique, and the rate of donor blood transfusion during surgery was low, with no adverse events tied to the technique itself. Compared with an earlier historical group, outcomes did not differ clearly overall, though patients with massive bleeding tended to need less donor blood. The authors are cautious: safety looked acceptable, but the technique's benefit remains unproven and needs further study.
openalex-w7215780247:
Rafael da Silva Costa led a 2026 experience report on a rocket olympiad as a physics teaching strategy in a Brazilian high school. Students on education scholarships ran the event at a full-time state school in Pau dos Ferros through the Brazilian rocket exhibition program. Students built and launched rockets from plastic bottles and low-cost materials, meeting Newton's laws, pressure, velocity, aerodynamics, and conservation of momentum with their hands.

Framed by meaningful learning and inquiry-based teaching, the intervention linked prior knowledge, hands-on trials, and asking questions. Data came from a student questionnaire plus notes and records kept during the work. Students' first ideas changed, and participation and autonomy grew, the team reports. The rocket exhibition made physics teaching more tied to real life and more hands-on, they conclude, and it strengthened the future teachers' own training.
openalex-w7218714047:
Claudia A. Arias and Wiliam A. Ramirez Mesias compared denture cleaning products against the fungus Candida albicans in a 2026 laboratory study in Spanish. Denture wearers rely on cleaning solutions and effervescent tablets to control fungal biofilm on acrylic. The team contaminated acrylic resin discs with a standard strain of the fungus. They soaked them in distilled water, an active oxygen foam, or one of two commercial effervescent tablet solutions, for fifteen or sixty minutes.

All commercial solutions reduced fungal growth compared with the water control. At the shorter soak the active oxygen foam left the fewest colonies; at the longer soak one tablet product did, but differences among the commercial products were not statistically clear. Exposure time was a decisive factor, the authors conclude, and under the tested conditions the commercial solutions reached comparable antifungal activity, a practical result for judging marketing claims.
owen-death-of-death-1647:
Owen's Death of Death in the Death of Christ, published in 1647, is the definitive Puritan defense of definite atonement. The question at stake is simple to state: did Christ die for all people, or for the elect in particular? Owen, then a young pastor, argues the second with relentless logic.

He holds that Christ's death actually saves those it was meant for, rather than merely making salvation possible for everyone. His famous trilemma presses opponents to choose what the cross truly achieved. Reformed readers still cite the book as the classic case against universal redemption.
phrenological-and-physiological-almanac-: In the hosted sample, only the front matter of the Phrenological and Physiological Almanac for 1848, the title page and the first customary notes, with no further pages visible. The title page prices it at six cents. It names Fowlers and Wells of the Phrenological Cabinet, 131 Nassau Street, New York, under the motto: to believe is well, to know is better. The notes begin with the year's astronomy, Venus as morning star and the moon's highest and lowest runs.
plos-pbio-0020247:
Seth Blackshaw, Sanjiv Harpavat, Jeff Trimarchi, and a large team charted eye development in mice in PLOS Biology in 2004. The retina, the light-sensing sheet at the back of the eye, grows from a pool of stem-like cells. The team measured gene activity across that growth, stage by stage.

Their atlas shows which genes turn on as retinal cells split into the many types a working eye needs. Such a timeline is a base map for the whole field. It helps labs spot the genes behind inherited blindness and check whether stem cell work is on the right track. It also offers a model of how any complex tissue sorts itself out over time.
plos-pone-0000047:
Jizhou Yan, Ya-Xiong Chen, Angela Desmond, and co-authors traced a partnership that controls a blood gene in a 2006 study. Hoxa9 is a gene that helps direct the making of blood cells, and it must be switched on and off at the right times. In hematopoietic cells, the blood-forming cells of the marrow, two regulators share that job.

Cdx4 and Menin co-regulate Hoxa9 expression, each shaping how strongly the gene runs. The pairing matters because Hoxa9 also shows up in leukemia, where blood formation goes wrong. Knowing who controls the gene, and how they cooperate, marks the control points where a treatment might one day intervene.
plos-pone-0000147:
Shixi Chen, Yu Wang, Fuyong Chen, and colleagues published this veterinary study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It reports that a highly pathogenic strain of the bacterium Staphylococcus sciuri caused fatal exudative epidermitis in piglets. That skin disease, known on farms for its greasy, crusting sores, can kill young pigs quickly.

S. sciuri is usually a mild organism found on animal skin, so a deadly strain stands out. The authors document the outbreak strain and its effects. The report warns pig producers and vets that a familiar bacterium can turn dangerous, and it adds to the record of emerging animal pathogens.
plos-pone-0000247:
Vincenzo D'Angiolella, Luca Palazzo, Concetta Santarpia, and colleagues published this cell cycle paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. M-phase promoting factor is the engine that drives a cell through mitosis, and it must be switched off for the cell to exit division. The authors report a role for non-proteolytic control, switching the engine off without destroying its parts.

Cells were known to exit mitosis by breaking down key proteins. A non-destructive off-switch adds another layer to that control. The finding refines the model of how division ends cleanly, a process whose failure can scramble chromosomes and feed cancer.
plos-pone-0000347:
Laurent Gillet, Heiko Adler, and Philip G. Stevenson published this virology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Glycosaminoglycans are sugary chains on cell surfaces that many viruses grab as a first handhold. The authors study their interactions in infection by murine gammaherpesvirus-68, a mouse virus used to model human herpesviruses like Epstein-Barr.

A model virus lets researchers dissect infection steps that are hard to study in humans. The paper clarifies how much this virus depends on those surface sugars. The findings apply to the wider herpesvirus family, whose members infect most people for life.
plos-pone-0000447:
Laurent Jannière and colleagues presented genetic evidence connecting two core processes of the bacterial cell, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The processes are glycolysis, the breakdown of sugar for energy, and DNA replication, the copying of the genome before division. The link between them emerged from genetics rather than from chemistry alone.

That a sugar-burning pathway should talk to the genome-copying machinery is not obvious. Evidence of such a link suggests the cell coordinates its energy supply with its growth program instead of running each in isolation. Genetic evidence of this type often opens a field, inviting others to find the physical connection behind it.
plos-pone-0000547:
Diego Calzolari and colleagues took selective control of the cell's suicide network, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Apoptosis is the orderly self-destruction of a cell, run by a network of signaling proteins. Real cell populations are heterogeneous, a mix of types, and the team worked on selective control of the apoptosis signaling network in such mixed populations.

Selectivity is the crux of cancer therapy: trigger apoptosis in tumor cells while sparing the rest. A method that reads and steers the network cell by cell could find the exact lever for each type. The work is computational and systems-level, treating cell death as a controllable circuit.
plos-pone-0000647:
Fanny Mochel, Perrine Charles, François Seguin and colleagues searched blood for an early sign of Huntington disease, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Huntington's is a fatal brain disorder with no effective treatment, and its root mechanisms remain unclear. Weight loss is a characteristic feature, appearing alongside chorea, the jerky movements, and cognitive decline.

The team reports an early energy deficit in patients and identifies a plasma biomarker that can be traced as disease progresses. A measurable blood sign matters when a disease is otherwise tracked by symptoms alone. It could help doctors follow progression and give future trials a way to tell whether a treatment changes the disease course.
plos-pone-0000747:
Luca Bolzoni, Leslie Real and Giulio De Leo modeled how uneven spread changes the control of new diseases, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Controlling the emergence and spread of infections depends on many details at once. Pathogen and host genetics both matter, as do immunity, behavior, and ecology. So does the pattern of contacts over time and space among age and stage groups. Transmission heterogeneity means some cases infect many others while most infect few.

When spread is that lopsided, average-based strategies misfire. Targeting the settings and groups that drive transmission can beat blanket measures. Modelers built this study to compare control strategies under realistic unevenness, a question every emerging outbreak poses to health authorities.
plos-pone-0000847:
Gabriela Moura and colleagues compared codon pairs across many genomes, hunting the rules of the genetic code's usage, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Codon usage and codon-pair context are important features of gene structure that influence how faithfully messenger RNA is decoded into protein. To identify general rules shaping codon-pair context and minimizing decoding error, the team carried out a large-scale comparative analysis.

Their title says the analysis unveils general rules that fine-tune the evolution of mRNA primary structure. Genes are not written in any codon order that works; neighboring codon choices are tuned. Such rules matter for designing synthetic genes that cells need to read accurately.
plos-pone-0000947:
Stephen Beckstrom-Sternberg, Raymond Auerbach, Shubhada Godbole and colleagues fully characterized the genome of a dangerous tularemia strain, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia, a disease that can kill and could be used as a weapon. The type A branch, found in North America, is the most severe form.

The team present a complete genomic characterization of a pathogenic A.II strain. A full genome lets scientists compare strains, trace outbreaks and spot what makes this branch so harmful. It also supports work on detection and vaccines. For a germ on watch lists, open reference data is a basic defense tool.
plos-pone-0001047:
Martin van Vliet, Christiaan Klijn, Lodewyk Wessels and colleagues predicted breast cancer outcomes using gene modules, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Labs had gathered large collections of tumor gene data, called compendia, yet outcome predictors rarely used them. Grouping genes into pathways, or modules, was also usually ignored in training.

The authors build prediction around modules instead of single genes. A compendium enlarges the training ground, and modules keep the model tied to biology rather than noise. Predicting which breast cancers turn dangerous guides treatment intensity. A method that uses public data better is a gain for every clinic that cannot gather its own.
plos-pone-0001147:
Early birth is a leading cause of death in newborns. About 40 percent of early births follow the premature rupture of the amnion, the membrane sac around the fetus. Che Connon and co-authors probed why that membrane breaks, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Rupture is thought to involve loss of collagen, the protein that gives the membrane strength.

Using X-ray diffraction, a method that reveals molecular structure, the authors studied the biomechanics of the amnion. Their work connects the membrane's collagen architecture to its breaking point. Understanding that structure is a step toward predicting or preventing dangerous early rupture.
plos-pone-0001247:
Light does more than let us see: it also sets alertness and cognition, through special cells in the retina that respond best to blue light. Gilles Vandewalle and colleagues compared brain responses to violet, blue, and green light in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. These nonvisual responses are thought to be mediated partly by melanopsin-expressing retinal ganglion cells.

The authors report a prominent role for blue light and for the brainstem in these responses. Long retinal light exposure modulated brain activity even though the task was not visual. Their findings support the design of lighting that works with, not against, the brain's light sensors.
plos-pone-0001347:
Heart failure is usually studied one data type at a time. Anyela Camargo and Francisco Azuaje combined two: gene expression and functional network data, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Gene expression profiling and protein-protein interaction network analysis may together support the identification of disease biomarkers and potential drug targets.

The authors link the two data types for human heart failure, asking which network positions and expression changes coincide. That joint view is the point of their approach. A gene that both changes activity and sits at a network hub is a stronger candidate than either signal alone. Their study develops systems approaches to medicine.
plos-pone-0001447:
Yuan Wang and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on eye growth in fruit flies. Cell surface sensors must be switched on to send growth signals, then switched off at the right time and place. A protein called Cbl helps with that shut off. The team studied its role as the fly eye forms.

They show the fly form of Cbl is vital for cell death and cell fate choices in the eye. When it fails, cells live or take fates they should not. The eye is a classic test bed for growth control. Findings there often map to broader rules for how tissues build themselves in the right pattern.
plos-pone-0001547:
R. Brad Jones and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on HIV drugs and a human jumping gene. The jumping gene, LINE-1, is the sole one in our genome that can copy itself on its own.
