plos-pone-0345947:
Naeemeh Haddadi Esfahani and colleagues tested whether mild brain stimulation helps athletes regain thigh strength after knee ligament surgery. Weak thigh muscles and poor voluntary drive often linger after the operation. Twenty male amateur athletes in early recovery were split by chance. Both groups did standard therapy for ten sessions, with real or sham stimulation added.

Real stimulation used a weak current for twenty minutes per session, while sham faded after thirty seconds, so neither side knew its group. Voluntary drive of the thigh muscle rose clearly with real stimulation, by about seven points more than sham. Raw strength did not differ between groups. Brain help may wake the muscle up, even before strength itself pulls ahead.
plos-pone-0346347:
Drugs that may slow aging itself, nicknamed geroprotectors, are the focus of the REPROGRAM trial described by Daisy Wilson and colleagues. This 2026 PLOS One paper is a protocol, setting out how sixty healthy adults aged seventy and over in England will test three such drugs over three weeks.

Volunteers will receive metformin, fisetin, or spermidine, with blood, fat, and stool samples taken before and after. The main question is whether the drugs cut the number of worn-out, senescent cells in fat tissue. The team will also track inflammation, cell cleanup systems, and gut microbes. No results are reported yet.
plos-pone-0346447:
Solomon Wireko led a team of eight authors tracking tuberculosis trends in northern Ghana, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their records came from a regional referral hospital and covered the years from 2019 to 2024. They counted how often the TB germ was found, and how often it resisted rifampicin, a key drug.

Wireko's group read the six-year pattern year by year. Rising or falling detection can reflect better testing, true changes in spread, or both, and drug resistance trends warn whether standard treatment still works. For Ghana's TB program, a clear local record like this shows where control efforts are gaining ground and where clinics need more support.
plos-pone-0347047:
Qi Fu and Xiaotong Li build a pricing model for financial assets that learns from very fast market data. Older pricing models struggle to keep up with high-frequency trading, where prices move in minutes. Their 2026 study fuses a transformer network, which reads sequences, with a dynamic probability network that links big economic factors to small market moves.

On minute-level data for large Chinese stocks over six years, the fused model priced more accurately than a static version. In simulated trading that charged realistic costs, it earned solid yearly returns with a fair balance of risk. The design keeps some structure visible, so traders can see why prices move rather than trusting a black box blindly.
plos-pone-0347347:
McClaran Shirley and Amber Dawn Stubler measured shells in a museum collection to see how tiny sea snails off Oahu, Hawai'i changed over three decades. Their 2026 paper covers more than fifteen hundred specimens from thirty-seven species, gathered between 1974 and 2007 near Waianae. Most of the snails were smaller than a grain of rice and rarely studied.

For each shell the pair compared weight against length across the collection years. Thirty species showed no clear change over time. Seven species became lighter for their size, a shift that may signal stress as local conditions changed. Because the data come from collected specimens rather than a controlled experiment, the study points to possible vulnerability without proving a cause.
plos-pone-0347547:
Ioannis Karapanos and colleagues interviewed twenty members of a fetal medicine team in East London about breaking unexpected news to pregnant patients, above all those with mental health problems. Scans sometimes reveal serious problems, and how that news is delivered shapes everything after. The group included fetal specialists, newborn doctors, midwives, and specialist nurses.

Five themes emerged, covering helping patients truly understand, offering support, tailoring care to the person, supporting staff themselves, and the weight of inequality. Clear settings, plain words, and involving partners helped; language barriers and low health know-how got in the way. Some clinicians avoided mental health topics for lack of training, and repeated distressing talks took a toll with little formal support. The authors call for training and staff care to match the task's emotional weight.
plos-pone-0347647:
Sophia Gimple and co-workers time the dance between the brain's movement and feeling areas during hand motion. Textbooks cast the feeling area as merely reporting back after movement starts, but that order has been questioned. Their 2026 study uses dense electrode grids placed on the brain surface of patients to compare signal start times in the two areas.

In fast brain signals, the movement area switched on before the feeling area, reliably across participants. Slower signals showed no clear order. Two participants who tried to move with little feedback showed the same fast-signal pattern. The feeling area may help start movement, not just grade it afterward. Such timing maps guide brain-computer tools that read movement intent.
plos-pone-0347747:
Behrouz Ghazi Esfahani, M Elizabeth Stroupe, and co-authors solved the structure of an oversized bacterial enzyme that loads the amino acid methionine onto transfer RNA. The bacterium Mycoplasma penetrans runs a stripped-down genome, yet this enzyme's gene is nearly double the normal size because evolution fused extra domains onto it. Their 2026 study used cryo-electron microscopy to picture the assembled protein.

The enzyme proved to be three fused parts: a mystery domain, a second enzyme that normally works elsewhere in metabolism, and the methionine loader itself. Only the first two parts pair up symmetrically. Modeling suggests the loader section must swing around to accept its transfer RNA partner. The authors discuss whether the unusual assembly lets the parts pass materials directly between them.
plos-pone-0347847:
Shiming Hao proposed a new statistical method in 2026 for judging policy effects from time series when no clean comparison group or helper variable exists. Staggered start dates and hidden influences usually break standard approaches to such questions.

The method leans on a symmetry condition built from a shared stand-in variable to strip out hidden bias. A flexible expansion then supports consistent estimates for several treatments with varied effects. Theory links the estimator's behaviour to a long memory process, and a resampling plan handles the tricky inference. Computer trials suggest the approach works well in the settings it was built for.
plos-pone-0348147:
Henry Techie-Menson and his team tuned a deep learning model that spots sick cocoa pods in photos. Sick pods can ruin a crop if found too late. Most models weigh clues in a fixed order. This one learns a gate that strikes its own mix of two clue types: where a mark sits, and what sort of mark it is.

On a Ghana set, the model hit near ninety-nine per cent right. On three more sets from far spots, it stayed strong. It dipped just on a mixed set of coffee and cocoa. The team calls it a firm tool for farm work where crops are checked by phone or drone.
plos-pone-0348347:
Ambika Kormoker and co-workers lay out a plan for a clinical trial on nerve damage caused by diabetes. The condition dulls feeling in the legs and feet and can lead to serious foot problems. Their 2026 protocol describes a blinded trial in Bangladesh testing gentle nerve-glide therapy, given with mild electric stimulation and home exercises, against a sham version.

Ninety patients will be split evenly between the two groups for twelve sessions across four weeks. Feeling, symptoms, and quality of life will be checked before treatment, right after, and again weeks later. Any harms will be recorded as well. Because the plan is a protocol, it reports no results yet; its value is a careful design for care that avoids adding more drugs.
plos-pone-0348447:
Ratinan Dangwilailert and co-workers test whether a painless light-based finger sensor can judge blood hemoglobin in donors as well as needle tests. Donor screening must catch anemia without wasting willing donors. Their 2026 study at a Bangkok hospital measures three hundred donors three ways: the light sensor, a bedside blood test, and the lab's automatic analyzer.

The bedside test agreed closely with the lab analyzer, while the light sensor agreed only moderately. At the donation cut-off, the light sensor missed too many anemic donors to trust alone. Donors liked it far more, since nothing pricks the skin. Comfort alone cannot carry screening; accuracy must catch up before painless testing can replace the finger stick.
plos-pone-0348947:
Stephanie Chamberlin used population survey data from seven southern and eastern African countries to test a widely held assumption: that more schooling helps people living with HIV stick to treatment. Adherence was judged by whether the virus stayed suppressed in blood tests, a stricter measure than self-report. More than twelve thousand people were included, and the analysis checked whether gender or age changed the picture.

No link appeared. Years of education neither predicted suppression in the pooled sample nor in any single country, and the flat result survived every alternative way of measuring schooling. Chamberlin treats the surprise seriously, suggesting that whatever schooling does for health may be cancelled or bypassed in the specific grind of lifelong daily treatment. She calls for research into the local forces that actually keep people on therapy.
plos-pone-0349147:
Chenggui Duan and Billy Wong interview in 2026 teachers at one Hong Kong higher education institution about open educational resources, teaching materials shared for free reuse. Global open education promises wider access and fresh teaching, yet uptake inside institutions stays hard. Eight faculty members from varied fields gave semi structured interviews for this case study.

Many teachers confused free commercial tools with truly open licensed material, and picked resources for practical teaching value rather than belief in openness. Time to curate, quality doubts, and missing rewards blocked wider use. Artificial intelligence was seen as a future co creator. Policy should build copyright skill and reward the work, the authors say.
plos-pone-0349247:
Alicia Sasser Modestino and Gary J Young led a study of opioid prescribing in Massachusetts. Rural patients got the drugs more often than city patients did. The team used claims data from 2010 to 2014. They focused on back pain, joint disease, and car crashes. Then they split the rural gap into two parts. One part is who the patients are. The other is how local care is run.

Rural patients were about ten points more apt to get an opioid. Near half the gap came from poorer local health. Of the rest, a bit less than half traced to the care system. Veteran status and insurance type also counted. The team says no one fix will close the gap.
plos-pone-0349347:
Jonathan Santana and colleagues dug into a coastal site at Playa Chica on Gran Canaria, in the Canary Islands, focused on layers from the eleven hundreds and twelve hundreds. Island settlers came from northwest Africa in the first millennium. Sediments yielded shells, sea urchin remains, fish bones and scales, seeds, hearths, and worked bone and horn tools.

Fish scales in bulk and horn flakes used as scrapers point to heavy on site fish processing. Low, smoky fires and many hearths fit drying or smoking fish for storage. Goat horn tools, pig tooth hooks, and crops like barley and figs round out the scene. The shore camp looks like a specialist work yard feeding trade with inland villages.
plos-pone-0349447:
Alan López Leal and co-authors measured how changeable the human papillomavirus genome is, position by position, using virus sequences collected across South America. The virus causes cervical and other cancers, and its variety can trip up the DNA tests used to detect it. Their measure, borrowed from information theory, scores each spot in the genome from frozen to highly variable.

Within any one virus type, nearly every position proved rock stable. Between types, a clear split appeared: three early genes that drive cell growth varied a lot, while the two shell genes used by most tests stayed comparatively steady. The authors stress this is groundwork, not a finished test, giving laboratories a map of where detection targets are safest and where regional variants deserve watching.
plos-pone-0349747:
Zhou Ye led a stock-take of crop straw in Anhui Province, China. The aim was climate math. If all straw were used, not burned or left, how much carbon could be saved? The team used 2023 province data. Wheat, rice, and corn straw made up near nine tenths of the pool. The pool topped fifty million tonnes in all.

Use as soil feed saved the most carbon, near four million tonnes. Feed for animals came next. Power, goods, and growth beds for crops saved less each. The team says city-level counts are the base for smart plans. They offer the Anhui count as a model for other regions with the same climate goals.
plos-pone-0349947:
Mai Shirakami and coauthors published a 2026 eye study in PLOS ONE on treating the wet form of age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of central vision loss. Standard care starts with three monthly injections of a drug that blocks blood-vessel growth. The team asked whether a newer, stronger dose could cut that loading phase to two injections, comparing recent patients on the shorter plan with matched earlier patients on the standard plan.

One month after loading, the share of eyes with a dry central retina was somewhat higher in the two-dose group, but the gap was small enough to be chance. Both plans thinned the swollen retina and related structures similarly. Fluid inside the retina at the start did predict worse vision a month later in the high-dose group. The shorter plan looks promising for reducing early treatment burden, pending prospective trials.
plos-pone-0350047:
Xiaomeng Qu and co-authors hunted for gene signs of atherosclerosis tied to stress inside cells' protein factories in 2026. The artery clogging disease is driven partly by that stress, but a reliable gene signature from it had not been built.

Several public data sets were merged, and three learning methods together nominated five genes. The set separated diseased from healthy samples with high accuracy in the discovery data. Lab tests in a cell injury model checked the genes at message and protein level, and pathway work tied them to oxidative stress and immunity. A five gene panel is a candidate for future blood based detection.
plos-pone-0350147:
Shao-Yun Chien and colleagues measured hand squeeze strength in just over five hundred university students in Taiwan, aged eighteen to twenty five. Students also answered questions on exercise, sitting time, and eating habits. Body size measures included height, weight, and the girth of the upper arm. Weak grip was judged with Asian cut points set for each sex.

About six in one hundred students had a weak grip, a bit more often in men than in women. Upper arm girth tracked grip strength most closely in both sexes. Students who did little hard exercise were also more likely to be weak. Food habits and sitting time showed no clear link. The team urges early checks and strength training while students are still young.
plos-pone-0350247:
Fayez Alanazi and co-authors designed a traffic control system that pairs roadside computing with a cloud-based mirror of the road network. City traffic shifts by the minute, and signals timed on old patterns waste drivers' time. Their 2026 framework forecasts flow, density, and congestion at the street level, then feeds those forecasts into a virtual copy of the network where signal plans can be tested.

A learning module uses the forecasts to adjust signal timing, aiming to cut waiting and raise throughput at junctions. In evaluations, average vehicle waiting time fell by about seventeen percent, and forecasts stayed dependable even when sensor data were noisy or missing. The authors present the closed loop of sensing, mirroring, and control as a scalable path for smarter city traffic management.
plos-pone-0350447:
Retraction notice: The PLOS One editors have withdrawn a study of tuberculosis knowledge in Myanmar. The study used survey data from adults aged fifteen to forty-nine. It claimed to measure how many people now have the disease. But the survey question it used only asks if a doctor ever said the person had it. That cannot show current spread. The tables also list answer choices the methods never explain.

A closer check found a deeper flaw. The study counted all who took the survey. Yet the tuberculosis questions were asked only of people who had heard of the disease. So the sums mix in people who never answered. For these reasons, the paper's numbers should not be used.
plos-pone-0350547:
Cristina Toscano Fonseca and co-authors set out a study plan in 2026 for judging tests for schistosomiasis in Brazil. This worm disease persists partly because standard stool checks miss light infections, especially where the disease is fading.

The plan will gather every test registered for use in Brazil, plus prototypes, and compare them head to head. New molecular tests using stool, blood, and urine will also be built and checked. The reference standard will be an unusually thorough version of the standard stool method. Better tests are central to confirming where the disease is truly gone.
plos-pone-0350647:
Fei Liu and colleagues surveyed Chinese Super League soccer spectators to map how league quality shapes loyalty. Just under three hundred valid responses from match day surveys fed a model linking felt league quality, satisfaction, trust, belonging to a team, and loyalty. Expert review and a pilot run polished the questions first.

Felt quality lifted satisfaction, trust, and team belonging strongly, but did not lift loyalty directly. Satisfaction and trust alone also failed to move loyalty. Belonging was the bridge: fans who feel part of a team stay loyal, and quality reaches loyalty through that bond. League managers should sell identity and belonging, not just match quality and service.
plos-pone-0350747:
Robinson and colleagues presented a computing framework for fitting disease models with built-in uncertainty in a 2026 paper. Outbreak models simplify real spread, so fitting them to noisy data must allow for model error itself. Their method estimates hidden states, changing settings, fixed settings, and the simplest model structure all at once.

Letting settings drift over time absorbs some mismatch between model and reality. A penalty for complexity guards against chasing noise. The framework targets compartment models of infection, where officials need honest ranges, not single numbers. Careful handling of model error can keep forecasts humble and more useful for planning hospital and vaccine needs.
plos-pone-0350847:
Dorra Abdelmalek and colleagues went hunting for a new use for old cancer drugs: blocking the normal, non-mutated form of a growth receptor that many tumors lean on. Most approved blockers target mutated versions of the receptor, leaving patients whose tumors use the normal form with few options. From a library of approved kinase drugs first built against another target, computer screening pulled five candidates.

All five fit the receptor's fuel pocket in simulation, and one, labeled D4, gripped the key hinge and switch residues best. A hundred-nanosecond molecular movie showed the pairing held steady, and energy calculations backed it. Everything here is in silico, a ranked shortlist rather than a medicine. Still, repurposing approved compounds starts years ahead of new chemistry, so a credible shortlist is worth the laboratory tests it now invites.
plos-pone-0350947:
Soumya Ranjan Das and colleagues tackled dirty power that appears when solar panels and electric cars join the same local grid. Sun power swings with clouds, and car charging jumps without warning, so voltage waves can distort. Their fix uses a neural network controller that learns how to clean the wave, tested in computer simulation under heavy, uneven loads.

Without help, distortion sat near twenty six percent. A simple passive filter cut it by about half, and an adaptive method cut it much further. The neural network did best, bringing distortion down close to one percent with faster settling. Cleaner power protects gear, cuts waste, and helps grids welcome more solar power and cars at once.
plos-pone-0351147:
Marie A Brault and colleagues present a protocol, with no results yet, for mapping how puberty teaching for young teens is judged. Puberty shapes lifelong health habits, yet courses for eight to fourteen year olds vary widely and share no agreed skill list. The review will chart which outcomes, topics, and test tools past courses for this age group have used.

Searches will span ten sources, covering journals, theses, and broad indexes. Two reviewers will screen and extract with a shared tool, following standard scoping guidance. Results will feed a shared framework for building and judging puberty courses. A common yardstick could help schools compare courses and spot missing topics early.
plos-pone-0351247:
Namrata Ahuja and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One genome study of siphonophores. These drifting ocean colonies are made of many specialized bodies acting as one animal. The team produced a chromosome-level genome for one species, Nanomia septata. They sequenced twenty more specimens from around the world for comparison.

The genome is large. Yet it is packed into far fewer chromosomes than its relatives have. That is proof of repeated chromosome fusions. Surprisingly, nothing in the genome clearly explains the colony's elaborate division of labor. Key gene families had not expanded. Gene position rarely matched where genes are active, except in male reproductive bodies. Population data supported three known species, plus one undescribed species. Genome size had shrunk again in some lines.
plos-pone-0351547:
Sofie Jespersen and colleagues tested hard interval exercise in a hard-to-treat group. Their patients lived with both chronic hepatitis B and a fatty liver. That pairing raises the risk of serious liver harm. Patients were assigned by chance to twelve weeks of interval training or to no program. Liver fat was measured by MRI scans.

Recruitment went slowly, and the trial stopped early. Only nineteen patients joined, and fourteen finished. Liver fat fell a bit more in the training group. The gap was small and not close to firm proof. The study reads as a lesson in feasibility. The question is fair, but far more patients are needed to answer it.
plos-pone-0351747:
John Amoah-Mensah and colleagues built a math model of typhoid fever that gives dirty water a central role in spreading the disease. Typhoid thrives where sanitation is poor and clean water is scarce, yet many models skip the environment and count only person-to-person spread. Their equations track people and the contaminated water that links them.

The team worked out the threshold at which typhoid settles in for good and checked which factors push spread hardest. They then tested two levers inside the model: teaching the public about hygiene and treating contaminated water. Models like this cannot replace field data, but they help officials see which mix of education and water treatment might cut cases most before money is spent.
plos-pone-0351847:
Pinpin Jiang and colleagues chased a driver of osteoarthritis, the joint disease that wears cartilage away. Their suspect is a protein that senses low oxygen, called HIF-2α. Cartilage lives short of oxygen by design, so its oxygen sensors matter. The team measured the protein in human cartilage. They then turned it down and up in cartilage cells inflamed to mimic disease. In rats, they silenced it in knees injured to trigger joint decay.

The protein ran high in diseased cartilage. It worked by suppressing a protective chain of signals inside the cells. With that chain muted, cartilage cells moved toward programmed death. Cell and animal results line up: the protein speeds the disease rather than watching it. A named accelerator is a target drug hunters can aim at.
plos-pone-0351947:
Depression and compulsive gaming feed each other in teenagers, and Qian Li and colleagues asked whether parents are pulled into the same loop. Their 2026 PLOS One study surveyed more than twelve hundred parent and child pairs in Hong Kong, with teens answering at school and parents replying online or by phone.

Each person's low mood lined up with their own gaming problems. Teen depression also lined up with parents' gaming problems, a cross effect within the family. How warm the family relationship felt, and how long the teen gamed, carried part of these links. The authors argue help should treat the household, not the teenager alone.
plos-pone-0352147:
Eric Osoro and seven colleagues screen thousands of compounds for a kinder way to kill malaria mosquitoes. Their 2026 study targets the mosquito's juvenile hormone system. Blocking the protein that carries this hormone can derail mosquito development. The team virtually screened nearly twenty-nine hundred agrochemical compounds on the computer. Docking tests ranked how tightly each gripped the target protein. Energy calculations, chemistry checks, and toxicity predictions narrowed the list further. Fifteen lead compounds survived.

The best of them bound as strongly as the natural reference compound in simulations. Long dynamics runs tested whether those grips held over time. Electronic structure analysis favoured the same shortlist. The study pairs this computing with laboratory larvicide evaluation, per its design. Mosquito control leans heavily on a few insecticides, and resistance keeps growing. Hormone-targeted candidates, screened early for environmental safety, widen the arsenal before field resistance closes the current one.
plos-pone-0352247:
Xavier Perrier and seven colleagues collect bananas across northern Vietnam, Laos, and China's Yunnan region to rewrite the crop's origin story, in this 2026 genetic study. Cultivated banana diversity is only partly catalogued, yet new varieties with useful traits are urgently needed as diseases and climate stress mount. The team gathered ninety-one specimens, including four native wild relatives, and read their DNA for signatures of ancestry.

Farmers in the region grow many previously undescribed local varieties. Every one carried genomic traces of the endemic wild species, including the first polyploid varieties holding a complete set of genes from one local wild relative. The landraces were not domesticated on the spot. They arose when local wild plants crossed with already-domesticated bananas that arrived from farther south, possibly by an eastern route through southern China or the Philippines. Diversity, the authors say, accumulated after domestication.
plos-pone-0352347:
Jimena Fritz and seven colleagues build instruments to measure the quality of maternity care in Mexico, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Mexico lacked a thorough, culturally grounded way to judge care across pregnancy, birth, and the newborn period. Seventy-eight national experts — researchers, decision-makers, and advocates — worked through two workshops, starting from more than a thousand candidate indicators and winnowing them by structured rating.

The final set holds just under five hundred indicators across five domains, from the woman's experience to supplies and medicines. They were shaped into three tools: an interview guide for mothers, an observation checklist for births, and a hospital survey. The instruments give Mexico a common yardstick for finding care gaps.
plos-pone-0352647:
Hieu Giang Le and four colleagues tune the settings of an injection-moulding machine to make plastic parts stronger, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering study. Their materials were a common moulding plastic, plain and reinforced with woven carbon fibre, made by a two-step process that moulds around the fabric. Five settings — two pressures, two timings, and melt temperature — were varied systematically across a designed set of runs.

Adding carbon fibre raised bending strength modestly and pulling strength by roughly a sixth. Filling pressure dominated all others in influence. A combined statistical method picked the best setting recipe, and confirmation runs landed within a few percent of predictions. Small setting changes, it turns out, are free strength.
plos-pone-0353347:
Xiaoxi Huang and seven colleagues published this 2026 protein study on how stomach lining changes on the road to cancer. Infection with Helicobacter pylori bacteria drives a slow sequence from inflamed tissue to cancer, but the protein steps are poorly mapped. The team measured proteins in tissue from twenty-two patients across four stages of that sequence.

Protein groups tied to building ribosomes, the cell's protein factories, rose with progression and stand out as candidate warning markers. Meanwhile proteins for energy production steadily fell, pointing to failing cell power plants. Huang's stage-by-stage map may help doctors spot dangerous change earlier.
plos-pone-0353847:
Thomas and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Malaysia, compare behavior and feelings in teenage boys who were born with color vision deficiency and boys with normal color vision. Seeing color differently can complicate school and social life, yet its emotional effects in the teen years are little studied. The team screened schoolboys and matched forty-four boys in each group by age and class.

Parents rated behavior on a standard checklist. Boys with color deficiency scored higher on most problem scales, including anxiety and low mood, withdrawal, attention trouble, and aggressive and rule-breaking behavior. Attention problems showed the strongest tie. More of these boys fell into the borderline or clinical range on several scales. One twist stood out: among boys with color deficiency, those whose parents had more education showed more difficulties on some scales, perhaps because expectations run higher. The authors call for awareness and support in schools.
plos-pone-0354147:
Kennedy and colleagues, in a 2026 national survey, ask American parents whether they talk other parents into or out of vaccinating their children. The question gained urgency as the United States recorded its worst measles year in a quarter century. About thirteen hundred parents of children aged nine to twelve answered, weighted to stand for the country.

More than a third said they at least sometimes encourage other parents to vaccinate, while about one in ten said they discourage it; a small share did both. Confidence that vaccines matter for their own child's health predicted encouraging and protected against discouraging. Encouragers most often championed the measles and flu shots, speaking to family and close friends and sharing their own experience. Discouragers aimed mostly at COVID and flu shots, rarely measles. The authors suggest public health campaigns recruit the much larger pool of parent encouragers as partners.
plos-pone-0354247:
Waqar Shah and six colleagues tackle message routing in networks formed by moving vehicles, an area of research aimed at cutting road accidents. Cars in these networks relay warnings to each other, but the connections keep breaking as vehicles move, and urgent safety messages can get crowded out by ordinary traffic. Earlier routing methods, the authors argue, handle these problems poorly.

Their new protocol, called PDBFS, chooses routes using direction, the relative speed between vehicles, and how much traffic each route already carries. It also gives time-critical safety messages priority over other data. In computer simulations, PDBFS lost fewer packets, moved data faster, cut delays, and kept links alive longer than three rival protocols. The gains suggest smarter route choice could make vehicle warnings more dependable.
plos-pone-0354347:
Pavitra Jindahra, Stefano Starita, and Pinnaree Tea-makorn published this 2026 analysis of how chronic diseases cluster in Thailand. A national health survey of well over a hundred thousand people covered nine long-term conditions. Statistical grouping searched for natural bundles of illness, then linked each bundle to age, sex, residence, weight, and habits.

Four patterns emerged, from low burden to heavy combined illness. Older age raised the odds of every illness pattern, while city living and excess weight shaped particular bundles. Jindahra argues prevention should target these distinct risk profiles, not single diseases alone.
plos-pone-0354747:
Noa Gluskinos is first author on a 2026 PLOS ONE qualitative study of HIV outreach care in rural Zimbabwe. Moving antiretroviral therapy, the drug treatment for HIV, from central hospitals to local clinics brought care to millions. Its side effects on patients and providers were less clear.

Sixty interviews with leaders, providers, patients, and community members around a mission hospital were coded for themes. Participants agreed access had improved under treatment-for-all rules. But outreach also brought unintended harms. Stigma and tangled social relations shaped how care worked in practice and could raise social barriers to treatment. Understanding these local consequences, the authors argue, is needed for truly accessible care.
plos-pone-0355047:
Khanh Nguyen tackles in 2026 a control theory problem: keeping a fuzzy modelled system stable when its parts are sampled at different rates. Real controllers often read some signals faster than others, and the model's fuzzy rules may not match the controller's rules. Earlier proofs could waste useful information about timing delays between samples.

Nguyen builds a richer stability test that uses the newest readings and the delay tied to each state. A softer relaxation step makes the mismatched rules easier to handle without losing rigour. Two worked examples show the test holds in practice. The result is aimed at engineers designing sampled control systems.
plos-pone-0355547:
Linda Lait and colleagues mapped the family structure of the Plains Sucker, a freshwater fish of rivers east of the Rockies that was only recently recognized as its own species. Their 2026 study sequenced DNA from 371 fish at twenty-one sites in Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Montana, comparing two great drainage systems, the Missouri Basin and the Saskatchewan-Nelson Basin.

The basins hold clearly separate populations. Missouri tributaries were fragmented from each other, while Saskatchewan-Nelson fish mixed freely, suggesting recent connection. One population, in the Frenchman River, stood apart from all others and carried thinned genetic diversity, a fingerprint of drought-driven isolation. The authors argue Missouri populations, boxed in and genetically poor, need the most urgent protection from barriers and climate stress.
plos-pone-0355847:
Richmond Kwakye and coauthors published a 2026 case-control study in PLOS ONE on pregnant women in Ghana, examining a tolerance molecule called HLA-G alongside malaria and miscarriage. HLA-G helps the immune system accept the fetus, but that quieting may let the malaria parasite thrive and may relate to pregnancy loss. The team compared forty-six infected women with forty-six uninfected women, confirming parasite tests by microscope and measuring blood chemistry.

Infected women showed a liver enzyme pattern pointing to strain, with one enzyme still elevated after adjustment, plus higher inflammatory blood ratios. Skipping the preventive malaria medicine given in pregnancy was strongly tied to being infected. Women with a history of miscarriage carried considerably higher HLA-G levels than women without that history. HLA-G deserves prospective study as a marker of pregnancy risk in malaria regions, they suggest, though their sample was small.
plos-pone-0355947:
Rampukar Sah and six colleagues document violence in the lives of adolescent psychiatric patients in Nepal, in this 2026 study. Their sample was eight hundred ten patients aged eleven to fifteen at Kathmandu's Kanti Children's Hospital. Teenagers reported their past-year exposure to physical, emotional, and sexual abuse, neglect, and domestic violence, while parents supplied family background. The team modeled which social and family traits accompanied each kind of exposure.

Patterns were sharply social. Physical abuse fell more often on Dalit adolescents; neglect and domestic violence on Indigenous and minority groups relative to the highest castes. Girls faced far more emotional abuse, sexual abuse, and neglect than boys. Urban residence, single-parent homes, younger mothers, and parental illiteracy each raised particular risks, while rural and semi-urban settings lowered some. The authors call for culturally informed, trauma-focused prevention aimed at the families carrying the heaviest load.
plos-pone-0356147:
Gabriel Budel, Robert E. Kooij, and Michiel Tjepkema published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on the Beatles hiding in scientific paper titles. Researchers love a catchy title, and Beatles songs offer shared cultural shorthand. From a curated list of songs and lyrics, the team searched a major database, screened candidates with large language models, and verified survivors by hand.

They cataloged well over two thousand exact references to Beatles titles and lyrics, plus nearly a thousand creative wordplays bending the words into scientific puns. Use has grown over the decades faster than scientific publishing itself, and it clusters unevenly across disciplines, some fields punning far more than others. The paper is, the authors note, the first systematic cross-disciplinary account of this particular cultural borrowing. Beyond the fun, it shows how pop culture quietly frames serious work, and how language models help catch wordplay keyword searches miss.
plos-pone-0356247:
Lana Sallam and colleagues tested whether pressurised oxygen can shield healthy cells from radiation damage. Pelvic radiotherapy can scar tissue and cause lasting pain, so protection matters. Their 2026 laboratory study irradiated three kinds of surface and lining cells, then applied hyperbaric oxygen treatment.

Oxygen treatment reduced radiation-driven cell death. Radiation had lowered several protective genes, including an immune sensor and antioxidant controls; oxygen restored their activity. A drug that switches that sensor on also protected cells, while a blocker removed the benefit. Sallam and colleagues conclude the sensor pathway helps explain the protection, and they propose combining both approaches in future mucosal protection research.
plos-pone-0356547:
Xi Gong and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE that treats late-night tweeting as a public health sensor. Sleeplessness is common and worsened during COVID, yet health systems have no real-time way to watch population sleep. The team analyzed geotagged American tweets posted between ten at night and six in the morning, from March 2020 to mid 2021, against a pre-pandemic baseline, mapping state patterns and topics.

States fell into three rhythm types: single-peak, multi-peak, and smooth nighttime patterns. Links between night tweeting and daily case counts shifted by state and pandemic stage. More negative emotion in night tweets went with greater inferred sleep disturbance, while night owls talked more about local news, and states with more diverse nighttime topics suffered less emotional damage. The framework is presented as a cheap, scalable complement to sleep surveys, transferable to other nighttime behavior.
plos-pone-0356647:
Samia Yaqoob and colleagues cooked up a wound dressing gel from chia seed mucilage, a slippery natural polymer, chemically married to a synthetic building block. Their 2026 study verified the new material's structure, then put it through a battery of tests: blood compatibility, antioxidant power, germ killing, safety in animals, and finally healing speed on rabbit wounds.

The gel spared red blood cells and clotting, fought both major classes of bacteria plus two fungi, and showed antioxidant activity throughout. Rabbits dosed orally, on skin, and near the eye showed no harm, and treated wounds closed about as fast as with a standard product, reaching most of the way in two weeks. A seed-based, non-toxic dressing could suit low-cost wound care.
plos-pone-0356747:
Lin Xie, Jialian Li, Yuan Xing, and Yuhui Wang pulled apart a near-alpha titanium alloy, the kind used in jet engines. They wanted to understand an extra strengthening effect that appears when hard and soft regions deform together. Their 2026 study compared two internal architectures of the same alloy: layered plates versus rounded grains. It measured the internal stress that builds as the mixed structure stretches.

Both architectures generated the extra stress early on. The rounded-grain version kept hardening far better as strain grew. The reasons were geometric. Rounded grains offer more boundary area per volume to anchor the dislocations involved. Their larger scale gives those dislocations room to pile up. The layered version's thin plates cramped the process. Alloy designers now know which architecture to favor.
plos-pone-0357047:
Hafez Mohammad Nazmul Ahsan and colleagues assessed how much disability leprosy still causes in Bangladesh. They surveyed 176 patients at two specialist treatment centers in spring 2024. Their 2026 hospital-based study graded physical impairment with the World Health Organization scale. It also measured depression symptoms, activity limits, and experiences of discrimination.

Nearly three quarters of these patients already had the most serious grade of impairment. Claw hands, foot drop, and eye damage were the commonest problems. Almost all had the multibacillary form of the disease. Because the sample comes from referral centers, the figures describe severe, late-presenting disease rather than the national picture. The authors argue earlier detection in rural areas is the lever that prevents lifelong disability.
plos-pone-0357247:
Correction notice: Giuseppe Battaglia and colleagues amend an earlier mouse brain study on a receptor that prompts production of a neuron-supporting factor. After publication, concerns arose over two figures. In one, lanes of a protein blot had been spliced from non-adjacent positions. The splice was not clearly marked. The authors now give the original loading order in full. One lane pair also looks alike. The lead author blames a possible slip while rearranging lanes for the figure.

Original blots are supplied with the notice. The authors state that contrast handling differed between panels for display. The underlying measurements, expressed as ratios, stand. The notice keeps the study in the record with its figure history made explicit for readers weighing the evidence.
plos-pone-0357447:
Aitor Ugena and five colleagues watch sea life rebuild itself on underwater lava flows near La Palma in the Canary Islands, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The island offers a rare natural experiment: three flows of very different ages, one under a year old, one from the mid twentieth century, and one about five centuries old. The team sampled algae, tiny settling invertebrates on artificial collectors, and established rock dwelling microinvertebrates on each flow.

The parts of the community recovered on different clocks. Algae were sparsest on the newest flow but looked much alike on the two older ones, settling early. Established microinvertebrates peaked in richness on the middle aged flow, while the oldest flow favored specialized and predatory species. Recovery after a volcanic disturbance, the authors show, is not one process but several running at different speeds side by side.
plos-pone-0358247:
Keiko Ikuta led a team of eight authors studying shared work in Japanese cancer care, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cancer services in Japan are stretched, and pharmacists could take over some tasks now done by doctors in chemotherapy care. The team used a qualitative study to ask what helps and what hinders that shift.

Ikuta's findings map the practical and cultural factors at play, from trust and training to rules and workload. Safe task sharing could free doctors for work only they can do, while pharmacists use their drug expertise more fully. Other countries facing doctor shortages face the same choice. Japan's careful evidence on barriers gives them a checklist for making the shift safely.
plos-pone-0358347:
Qunting Chen, Xinhui Chen, and Geng Chen built a gesture control system for a bionic hand, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The hand is palm-scale with fifteen degrees of freedom, meaning many joints to coordinate. Controlling that many joints with human gestures in real time is a hard mapping problem.

The team's system translates a person's hand movements into matching robotic motion as they happen. Smooth, intuitive control matters most for prosthetics, where a user needs the hand to follow intent without conscious effort. It also serves robotics tasks where an operator guides a delicate gripper. A palm-scale testbed keeps the work close to the size of real prosthetic hands.
plos-pone-0358447:
Hanna Söderström Lindström leads a team of five assessing whether flu drugs flushed into waterways could breed resistant viruses, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Ducks, the natural home of influenza A, swim in water containing traces of the same antivirals used in people. If those traces train resistance, tomorrow's pandemic strains might inherit it. The team combined new experiments on drug release and breakdown with earlier duck studies of resistance, scoring four medicines on release, stability, and resistance risk.

Release into the environment rated high for three drugs and very high for the fourth. Stability in water varied widely, with peramivir lasting longest. Two drugs, peramivir and the active form of oseltamivir, carried the highest overall risk ranking, since both persist and can drive resistance at low concentrations. The authors call for prudent prescribing that weighs this environmental ledger alongside patient benefit, especially during outbreaks.
plos-pone-0358647:
Hristo Dimitrov and three co-workers present TrackStudio, a motion tracking toolkit built for those who do not code, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Marker free tracking follows body motion from ordinary video. It has grown strong but usually demands coding skill. TrackStudio wraps proven open source engines in one visual pipeline. It covers recording, camera syncing, two and 3D pose estimation, and display, ready out of the box.

The team validated it across three settings, from cheap webcams to high resolution cameras, with awkward postures, poor light, and obstructions included. Across seventy-six participants, frame to frame consistency was very high and 3D errors stayed small, around a centimeter for hand tracking. A practical guide warns users about common setup mistakes. The pitch is simple: clinics and behavior labs can now run serious motion studies without an in house coder.
plos-pone-0358747: Huang and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how a jelly ear fungus thickens as it grows. The fungus is Auricularia polytricha, grown as food. By comparing gene activity across growth stages, the team found pathways that switch on only at certain stages. Knowing which pathways drive thickening could help growers raise meatier, higher-value crops.
plos-pone-0358847:
Zahra Aliabadi and Alireza Mohebbi simulate, atom by atom, how a powerful natural compound grips its target protein, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The protein, cyclophilin A, helps fold other proteins and is implicated in viral infection and cancer. The compound, sanglifehrin A, shuts it down at extremely low doses. Running hundred nanosecond simulations of the protein alone and with the compound bound, the authors watched stability, motion, and bonding patterns shift.

Binding stiffened the loop at the protein's active site, even coaxing part of it into a more ordered strand shape. At the same time, distant loops loosened and the protein's overall range of shapes widened, raising its disorder in a measured way. A small, shifting network of hydrogen bonds anchored the compound. The computed binding strength matched the compound's known potency, supporting a picture where it works by selecting and holding one preferred protein shape.
plos-pone-0358947:
Wenna Xu leads a team of eight speeding up the identification of germs in infected blood, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Bloodstream infections kill quickly, and standard cultures leave doctors guessing antibiotics for days. The group tested a shortcut. They spin positive culture broth through gel tubes. They identify the organism directly by laser based mass spectrometry. Then they run rapid drug sensitivity checks from bacterial membranes or the broth itself.

Across two hundred ten specimens, the rapid route named gram negative bacteria correctly about three quarters of the time, but managed only about a third of gram positive bacteria and few fungi. The sensitivity shortcuts, though, agreed with standard testing in well over ninety percent of drug checks. The mixed verdict is useful: the membrane method is nearly ready to accelerate treatment for the commonest bloodstream germs, while identification still needs work.
pmc-13190447:
Thomas Aston, Georgios Machtsiras, and Filipe Teixeira-Dias benchmark deep learning models for head pose estimation in sports impacts in a 2026 study. Measuring head movement from video, called videogrammetry, can quantify collisions, but standard training data lack the big rotations, speed, and blocking views of real play. Ten participants performed controlled football headers.

Fast infrared cameras gave true head orientations while two video cameras filmed front and side views. All three models estimated pose with mean errors in single digits of degrees. A full-body mesh recovery model scored lowest and coped best with blocked views, beating dedicated head-only models. Errors grew for side views, rotational headers, and low face visibility.
pmc-13198447: Heather L Gelhorn and colleagues are authors of a study corrected in a 2026 note in Quality of Life Research. The study used mixed methods to define meaningful change for patients with tenosynovial giant cell tumor, drawing on exit interviews and trial data. During publication, spacing, capitalization, and table and figure header and footer errors crept in. The note states that the original article has been corrected.
pmc-13198547:
Manon Giraudier and colleagues tested nerve stimulation to aid recall of emotional memories in a 2026 study. The vagus nerve links the gut and brain and helps set arousal. It shapes how emotional memories form, but its role at recall was less clear, so the team applied gentle ear stimulation during a memory test.

Volunteers had viewed unpleasant and neutral scenes a week before, with no task attached. During recall, real stimulation was compared with a sham version. Real stimulation selectively boosted vivid recall of the unpleasant images. The effect was modest in size. The authors offer first human proof that this nerve helps retrieve emotional memories, a lead for future therapy work.
pmc-13202747:
A questionnaire about how people trust information gets a skeptical audit in a 2026 psychometric study authored by Nicola-Hans Schwarzer. The research article evaluates the German version of the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust, and Credulity Questionnaire in 567 university students, comparing its original structure with published shortened models.

Confirmatory factor analyses found that neither the fifteen-item nor the twelve-item version fit the data acceptably. Reliability and variance measures fell below accepted thresholds for all three subscales in every model tested. Links with related traits behaved as theory expects for mistrust and credulity but diverged for trust, leading the authors to recommend thorough item revision before wider use.
pmc-13238247:
Pambis and colleagues review stem cell and cell-free strategies for osteoarthritis, the world's most common joint disease. Worn cartilage brings pain and disability to hundreds of millions. Current care eases symptoms but does not stop the joint from worsening, so a therapy that truly repaired cartilage would change the field.

Mesenchymal stem cells are the most advanced candidate, tested for both their repair signals and their calming effect on joint inflammation. Cell-free options, using only the healing cargo cells release, promise fewer risks and easier storage. The review weighs the evidence for both, and what durable regeneration, rather than brief relief, would require.
pmc-13241247:
Zhao and co-authors at Ningxia Medical reviewed 3D-printed bone scaffolds built on triply periodic minimal surfaces. These lattices promise strength, cell-friendly curves, and open channels in one print. It pulls in work from many labs. The review stresses versions that also fight infection. Mixed materials and germ-fighting plans receive detailed treatment.

Pairings like polylactic acid with magnesium titanate show the mixed path. The authors explain how scaffold surfaces and released agents suppress germs. Bone growth and infection control, they argue, can reinforce rather than trade off. The survey aims to guide next-generation repair materials.
pmc-13242447:
Akemu Xiamusiya and colleagues surveyed Singapore households to update national benchmarks for the EQ-5D-5L health questionnaire. Their paper appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026, using responses gathered from May to July 2024. Just over two thousand citizens and permanent residents aged fifteen and older described their mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain, and mood. Earlier Singapore norms dated from before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Just over half of respondents reported no health problems at all, while pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression were the most common complaints. Average scores remained high overall. Older age tracked most strongly with lower quality of life, and higher income and better housing tracked with higher scores, while gender showed no clear link. The new norms give health economists a post-pandemic yardstick for judging treatments.
pmc-13244247:
Xiaorui Zhao, Xiaoqing Fu, and Wenqiang Li report a lung clot that dressed itself as a heart attack on the ECG. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Cardiology in 2026. A seventy-four-year-old man arrived with chest tightness and breathlessness, and his tracing showed ST-segment elevation across both front and lower leads, the signature of a blocked heart artery. Yet he described no crushing ischemic pain.

Other clues pointed elsewhere. His D-dimer was raised, a clot sat in a calf vein, and ultrasound showed lung pressure strain without the wall damage a heart attack leaves. Emergency CT angiography settled it, showing clots in both pulmonary arteries. He received intravenous heparin, moved to oral blood thinners, and went home after nine days. The authors urge teams to keep pulmonary embolism on the list whenever ST elevation appears. The mimic is rare but deadly if missed.
pmc-13244847:
Kristin Byström and colleagues translated a questionnaire on fear of movement in injured athletes into Swedish and tested whether it measures well. Their psychometric study appeared in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation in 2026. Ninety-five amateur soccer players injured within the past year completed the Athletic Fear Avoidance Questionnaire alongside the Tampa kinesiophobia scale. A subset retook it later so scores could be checked for stability.

The Swedish version held up. Its scores tracked the Tampa scale strongly, matching the team's preset hypothesis. Individual items proved good to substantially stable on retest, and the total score's reliability rated excellent, with internal consistency judged satisfactory. Players and clinicians gain a short, user-friendly tool in their language for spotting fear that can stall rehabilitation. One gap remains: whether high scores predict unsafe or delayed return to sport is untested, and the authors flag that as the next study.
pmc-13244947:
Yiyi Shan and colleagues show that a pig virus borrows the cell's own gene-silencing machinery to copy itself faster. Their study appeared in Veterinary Research in 2026. Porcine circovirus type 2 attacks the pig immune system and costs the swine industry heavily. The host protein EZH2, which switches genes off by tagging their packaging, was the suspect. The team raised and lowered EZH2 in infected cells and measured both the virus and the genes EZH2 controls.

More EZH2 meant more virus; blocking its enzyme activity or silencing it meant less. Gene sequencing fingered two matrix-chewing enzymes, MMP1 and MMP12, as the mediators: EZH2 sits on their promoters and keeps them quiet, and those enzymes normally suppress the virus. Release the brake, by disabling EZH2's tagging domain, and the enzymes rise and replication falls. The finding hands drug designers a host-side target against a stubborn farm virus.
pmc-13245547:
Connell and co-authors ran a pilot health program for Bangladeshi-American adults in Atlanta in this 2026 JMIR Formative Research study. South Asian Americans face high rates of prediabetes and type 2 diabetes. The program's twist was to enroll each patient's social partners, trusted household members who joined five long health-education sessions in English and Bengali.

Fifty-four patients and over one hundred partners took part. After six months the patients' average blood-sugar marker had fallen clearly, systolic blood pressure had improved, and partners reported healthier eating and activity habits of their own. The authors say the family-based approach is feasible, though larger controlled trials must prove the partners are what made the difference.
pmc-13246247:
Burbelo and co-authors asked whether low blood pressure during hip replacement surgery harms patients afterward, in this 2026 Bone and Joint Open study. Drops in pressure are common under anesthesia and have been linked to complications in other operations. The team reviewed nearly four hundred primary hip replacements at one academic hospital, tracking pressure in two ways: against a fixed floor, and as a fall from each patient's own baseline.

Crossing the fixed floor showed no link to readmission or longer stays, however it was measured. A relative drop from baseline, though, came with clearly more repeat operations within ninety days, and heavier blood loss predicted longer stays. The authors argue for watching pressure relative to the individual patient.
pmc-13246547:
Andelieri and co-authors studied feeding economics on a robotic-milking dairy farm in southern Brazil, in this 2026 Tropical Animal Health and Production paper. Their measure was revenue minus feed cost: what each cow earns in milk minus what her feed costs. The farm's seventy-six Holstein cows were managed as one group in 2022, then split into high- and low-production groups with targeted rations in 2023.

The high-production group earned the best margin and used feed most efficiently despite eating the most expensive ration. Low producers lagged, especially late in lactation. The authors conclude that grouping cows by output, and feeding each group to its needs, pays under commercial robotic-milking conditions, while single-group results need cautious reading.
pmc-13247847:
Vaughan and colleagues test a team model of diabetes care for low-income Hispanic adults. Community health workers, local staff trained to support patients, visit and coach people at home. Phone and video links tie the workers to clinic doctors in a set feedback loop.

In the trial, more than two hundred fifty adults were split between the new model and usual care. After one year, the new model cut average blood sugar by about one full point. That drop is twice the level doctors count as a real gain. Care steps in national guides were also done more often. The team reports yearly net savings from the model as well.
pmc-13250247:
Sun and colleagues review tiny engineered carriers that could deliver drugs straight into the jaw joint. Their 2026 International Journal of Nanomedicine paper covers temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis, where cartilage breaks down and the joint lining stays inflamed. Standard treatments reach the joint poorly and wash out quickly, limiting their benefit.

The review surveys liposomes, polymer particles, micelles, metal-organic frameworks, and hydrogels designed to stay longer and release drugs slowly or on cue. Newer materials such as nanozymes may also calm inflammation and help cartilage repair. The authors caution that most evidence comes from other joints, not the jaw itself. They call for jaw-specific testing, smarter responsive systems, and standard ways to judge results.
pmc-13250447:
Calarco argues in this 2026 PNAS editorial that open data rules built for numbers can endanger interview-based research. Journal policy requires authors to share all data, materials, and code with reviewers and, after publication, in public repositories. Exceptions exist in theory, but the grounds for granting them are left unclear.

Calarco explains the exemption won by a study based on deep interviews with ninety-nine young Black and Hispanic men in a Chicago violence prevention program. Even with false names, full transcripts could expose histories of violence, victimization, and incarceration, with legal and ethical risks. Sharing such data could also chill future participation. The piece asks editors to protect sensitive qualitative work rather than force it into quantitative norms.
pmc-13252747:
Georgina Mathlin and colleagues explore a resettlement support service in open prisons in this 2026 qualitative study from England. People with a likely personality disorder diagnosis face a risky stretch when leaving prison, and the service studied supports those at high risk of being sent back.

The team interviewed ten staff and nine service users across male open prisons. Three themes emerged. Arriving in open conditions felt like a shock, a halfway world between locked prison and community. Users prized support built around their own needs, which grew trusting relationships. Staff then used that trust to help men face inner barriers and move through their sentences. Personal plans, not one-size rules, drove the progress.
pmc-13252847:
Mengistie Tariku and a large team pool hookworm data for pregnant women in Ethiopia in this 2026 review. Hookworm, a gut parasite picked up from soil, is a chief cause of anaemia in pregnancy, yet a national summary for Ethiopia was missing.

Following standard review methods, the team combined 33 studies with 13,367 pregnant women published between 2010 and 2024. About twelve percent carried hookworm, and among women with any gut worm, hookworm made up 44 percent of infections. Rates peaked in the Amhara region at about 13 percent and bottomed out in Gambella near four percent. Test method also shifted the numbers, a caution for comparing regions.
pmc-13253047:
Tomáš Figura and colleagues ask why two Asian orchids spread so well abroad in this 2026 study. The bamboo orchid and the Philippine ground orchid have expanded into the Americas, the Pacific, and Africa, and the team tested whether seed traits and fungus partnerships explain the success.

Both orchids carry unusually large seeds stocked with fats and proteins, yet seedlings still need a fungus partner or a sugar supply to start. In the lab, both sprouted with fungus strains from several continents, one species pairing with a wider range. That flexibility, plus self-pollination in one species and larger seed reserves in the other, likely fuels their spread into disturbed ground.
pmc-13253847:
Julian Schumann and co-authors model how drivers dodge crashes in a 2026 paper. Avoiding a collision needs fast threat spotting and a quick, apt move, yet past models covered only parts of that skill. Their model uses active inference, a theory that the brain acts to cut surprise and uncertainty.

The model was tested on three crash setups: a lead car braking, an oncoming car drifting in, and a car failing to yield. It matched broad findings from past reviews and fine details from two simulator studies, covering timing, choice of move, and execution. The authors offer it as a general frame for driver behavior.
pmc-13255947:
Sriphuthorn, Dabseepai, and Senasri tested whether dry feed mixes can replace fresh algae for farming the fairy shrimp Streptocephalus sirindhornae. Seven diets were compared over twenty days: fresh Chlorella as control, and six blends of spirulina powder, commercial shrimp feed, fish meal, and rice bran. Growth and survival were checked across three early life stages.

A half-spirulina, half-shrimp-feed blend matched the fresh algae control at every stage and beat the other dry diets, with late-stage survival just above sixty percent in both groups. Shrimp raised on that blend also carried more protein, lipid, carotenoids, and amino acids than algae-fed shrimp. The authors recommend it as a practical hatchery diet.
pmc-13257647:
Boyang Chen and co-authors grew titanium-doped gallium oxide crystals and tested them as X-ray detectors. Gallium oxide resists heat and detects radiation well, but stray donors in the raw stock spoil its blocking quality. Doping with titanium was their 2026 route to a high-resistance crystal.

Crystals grown by the edge-defined film-fed method showed sharp diffraction peaks and a slightly slimmer bandgap. Titanium curbed free electrons without shaking the crystal's basic chemistry. A detector built on the smoothed crystal reacted quickly to X-rays and beat known sensitivity marks for similar bulk detectors. The team sees strong promise for high-end detection devices.
pmc-13262547:
Pei Dong and colleagues build a prognosis score for the commonest kidney cancer from genes of vitamin metabolism. Nicotinamide processing shapes tumor behavior in several cancers but was unmapped in clear cell kidney cancer. Their 2026 analysis mines over five hundred tumor profiles from a public atlas.

The resulting signature sorted patients into risk groups with clearly different survival. It predicted one, three, and five-year outcomes respectably, and held up in an independent European dataset. Immune landscapes differed between the risk groups, as did checkpoint gene patterns. A companion network of small and long RNAs suggests fresh drug targets behind the score.
pmc-13262847:
Gebremedhin B Gebretekle and co-authors weigh infant protection plans against respiratory syncytial virus in Canada in a 2026 journal article. The virus is a leading cause of lung infection and hospital care in infants. New options include a vaccine in late pregnancy and long-acting antibody shots for infants. The team updated a cost model to compare seven seasonal plans.

The best value plan combined both tools by season, their model found. Pregnant patients due in the virus season got the vaccine, and high-risk infants got antibody shots, including catch-up doses. Its cost per quality-adjusted life year, a healthy-year measure, was 35,408 Canadian dollars. Covering all infants was not good value at list prices, they report.
pmc-13263347:
Christopher Nelke and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on muscle inflammation that resists treatment in myositis, a group of autoimmune muscle diseases. They focus on fibro-adipogenic progenitors, support cells that live inside muscle. Using single-nucleus and spatial gene mapping in 24 patients and six healthy controls, they traced how these cells change.

The support cells adapted to their surroundings, backing T-cell programs near T cells and macrophage programs near macrophages. They clustered with muscle stem cells and active macrophages, forming inflammatory niches. Two signals, TGF-beta from immune cells and growth factor EGF from muscle fibers, combined to push the support cells toward a harmful, scar-forming state.
pmc-13263647:
Marwa Mady and a multinational team gather what is known about test anxiety among medical students. Exam dread can derail performance and wellbeing in a famously pressured degree. Their 2026 systematic review screens six databases for studies from twenty nineteen to mid twenty twenty-five.

Thirteen cross-sectional studies from Asia, Africa, and Europe qualified, with samples up to seven hundred thirty-five students. Moderate-to-high test anxiety struck anywhere from about one in seven to nearly three in four, depending on setting. Being female, early in the course, overloaded, poorly supported, or short on coping skills consistently raised risk. Mixed measurement tools blocked a single pooled number, they note.
pmc-13263747:
Handar Bakhtiar and colleagues examine the awkward legal status of forensic evidence in Indonesian courts. Science-based proof is not named as its own evidence type in the criminal procedure code, sheltering instead under expert testimony and documents. Their 2026 study pairs legal analysis with court decisions from four district courts.

Across twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four, forensic evidence decided cases most often in narcotics matters, followed by assault and weapons offenses. Corruption cases leaned on it least among the top five categories. Judges and prosecutors, they argue, undervalue what forensics can prove because the law leaves it ambiguous. Naming it an independent evidence category is their central recommendation.
pmc-13263947:
Pamela R Matías-García and a large team reported in 2026 on DNA methylation, a chemical mark on DNA, after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection. Using data from four large population cohorts, they asked whether marks in blood stay changed for months. The study sits inside the wider ORCHESTRA project.

The team compared 675 cases and matched controls up to four months after infection. They found changes at 16 single sites and 21 regions, and most marks were lower in people who had been ill. Many linked genes help the body fight viruses, and four sites matched changes seen in the first days of illness. The authors call the shifts modest but lasting.
pmc-13264447:
Daniil Lisik and co-authors wrote a 2026 paper proposing a way to judge whether machine learning clusters are truly useful in care. Such clusters sort patients into subgroups from data, but many never help doctors in practice. No shared guide existed for checking their real value.

The authors set out three tests. First, a cluster must be relevant to care and tied to outcomes that matter. Second, it must stay stable and hold up in new groups of patients. Third, doctors must be able to spot it with ease in daily work. They argue these checks would help readers sort strong cluster papers from weak ones and guide future work toward patient benefit.
pmc-13264847:
Zufar Mulyukov and colleagues published a 2026 modeling study on dosing of brolucizumab, an eye drug for wet age-related macular degeneration, a sight-stealing disease of older adults. The approved start is three monthly injections. The team asked whether starting with doses six weeks apart would work as well and ease the burden on patients.

They joined two kinds of computer models, one for drug levels and effect, one for disease biology, and checked results against two large past trials. Both schedules shut down the growth signal that drives the disease during loading. At week 48, vision and retina thickness gains matched the monthly schedule. Only about one in five patients seemed to need a third loading dose. The new schedule gained approval in several countries, the authors report.
pmc-13264947:
Nuala D M Calder led a 2026 protocol for the LIMITS trial, on how much fluid to give children after a kidney transplant. Practice varies widely, and up to 52 percent of children suffer fluid overload problems. No evidence-based rule sets the right amount, so this UK trial compares a tight fluid plan with a generous one.

The trial will enroll 140 children at many centers and split them by chance. The tight plan caps fluid for the first 18 hours, then sets a fixed daily target. The generous plan replaces urine and other losses for at least 48 hours. The main outcome is days at home in the first 30 days after transplant. Costs and value for money will also be judged. The trial includes a pilot phase and a patient group to help share findings.
pmc-13266047:
Seongbeom Park and a large team published a 2026 study predicting which patients with mild cognitive impairment will progress to dementia, using CT scans instead of costly MRI or spinal fluid tests. Up to forty percent convert within three years, yet clinics cannot easily tell who. Their model mixes scan measures of brain fluid spaces with age, a clinical rating, and a known risk gene.
