Six predictors carried the model, including the clinical rating sum, the risk gene, age, and three scan measures from the left side of the brain. Patients who converted were older, more often female, and more often gene carriers. The authors offer CT modeling as a scalable option for ordinary clinics.
pmc-13267247:
Sarandeep K Marwaha leads a 2026 heart study of athletes whose enlarged hearts are hard to judge. Heavy endurance training can stretch the heart's main pumping chamber and lower its resting strength. That healthy change can look just like early dilated cardiomyopathy, a real disease, on resting scans alone.

The team ran exercise ultrasound tests on 182 athletes in three groups. Healthy and grey-zone athletes raised their pumping strength strongly during exercise, while those with disease barely did. Adding a check between hard and peak effort caught nearly all disease cases. The combined test reached about 98 percent accuracy both ways. The authors say the extra step prevents needless worry and missed disease.
pmc-13267547:
Ayman Elmahjoubi and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare tumor of the facial nerve. Schwannomas grow from the insulation cells of nerves. Their patient was a 35-year-old woman whose left face slowly lost movement over fifteen months, reaching the most severe grade of weakness. Such slow palsy can delay diagnosis, since these tumors often cause vague signs.

Detailed CT and MRI scans showed a clear-cut growth on the middle ear segment of the nerve, reaching its knee-like bend. A biopsy taken through the ear canal confirmed the tumor, with two marker proteins testing positive. Since nerve function was already badly lost, the team planned staged repair, joining the tongue nerve to the facial nerve later. Early imaging in odd facial palsy is their main lesson.
pmc-13268147:
Grace Dickel and colleagues present a 2026 study of neighborhood hardship and chronic hepatitis B near Puget Sound, Washington. This lasting liver infection falls hardest on immigrants and poorer groups. Using University of Washington health records from 2018 to 2023, the team compared 5,729 infected adults with 6,143 similar patients without the infection. Home addresses were matched to a census-based hardship score.

Infection was more common among Asian, Black, and Pacific Islander patients and those with public or no insurance. After adjusting for personal factors, people in the hardest-hit neighborhoods had about twice the odds of infection as those in the best-off areas. Finer hardship bands showed the clearest steady rise. The authors urge place-based screening and care linkage aimed at disadvantaged neighborhoods.
pmc-13269647:
Lina M Escobar and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 comparing ways to push stem cells from dental pulp and bone-forming cells toward making bone. Cells were grown together, either touching or separated by a filter, or treated with liquid in which the other cells had grown. Shape, growth, and bone markers were measured.

Liquid treatment lowered cell numbers for both cell types, while shared growth raised numbers after eight days. All treated cells stretched out with more extensions than controls. Calcium nodules formed in every treatment group, and three bone-related genes rose in activity. The authors conclude that both shared growth and the used liquid can drive bone-like change.
pmc-13270747:
Basma Abd Alkader Alshikh is lead author of a 2026 randomized clinical trial on rebuilding a thin upper jaw ridge before dental implants. Two mesh covers were compared: a pre-bent titanium mesh, the established option, and a custom-made PEEK mesh, a strong plastic fitted to the patient.

Fourteen patients with 28 treated sites were split evenly between the groups, and both received a mix of the patient's own bone and a graft material. Scans before surgery, just after, and at six months measured bone gain. Horizontal gain was 3.02 millimetres for titanium and 2.42 for PEEK, and vertical gain was nearly equal. No statistically clear difference appeared on those main measures.
pmc-13270847:
Yating Chen is lead author of a 2026 journal article on feeding citrulline, a substance the body turns into arginine, to lactating sows and the effect on their piglets. The team used several molecular profiling methods to trace how the supplement might act through milk and gut health.

Sows fed arginine or citrulline ate more each day, and piglets gained weight faster over the 21-day nursing period. Milk fat rose in the arginine group and in the group where citrulline replaced 40 percent of arginine. In piglets, that same diet strengthened the gut lining, changed gut microbes, and improved cell energy structures, the authors report.
pmc-13271147:
Philipp Och is lead author of a 2026 single-case report of a successful pregnancy after therapeutic apheresis, a procedure that filters blood outside the body, in a woman with complex infertility. She was 33, had polycystic ovary syndrome and Hashimoto thyroiditis, an autoimmune thyroid condition, and had been infertile since 2020 despite several treatment cycles.

Fertility treatment with in vitro fertilisation and repeated embryo transfers began in 2023 without success. Apheresis was then added, aiming to lower markers of oxidative stress and possible workplace exposures, including mercury and anaesthetic gases from her work as a dentist. Pregnancy was documented in December 2024, and a healthy girl was born in September 2025. The authors stress a time link, not proof of cause.
pmc-13272847:
Zongliang Zhang leads a 2026 study of engineered T cells for glioblastoma, the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults. Cell therapy for this cancer is limited because tumor cells vary in their surface markers and can escape. The team targeted a marker called B7-H3, while also arming the cells against a second marker, EGFR.

The engineered cells carried a B7-H3 receptor and released a small engager that pulls other T cells onto EGFR-bearing tumor cells. In mouse models, including mixed tumors, they controlled cancer better and extended survival compared with standard B7-H3 cells alone. Benefit fell when many tumor cells lacked B7-H3, showing a limit of the approach.
pmc-13273447:
Mountadem and co-authors ask whether a known astrocyte signalling route still works in the adult brain. Their 2026 paper concerns mGluR5, a receptor on astrocytes, the star-shaped support cells of the brain. In young rats, astrocytes sense glutamate through this receptor and release purines that strengthen nearby synapses, the junctions between nerve cells.

Combining tissue staining, gene labelling, and electrical recordings in adult rat hippocampus slices, the team confirmed the pathway persists in adults. When only a few synapses were active, astrocyte signalling boosted glutamate release as expected. Surprisingly, when many inputs fired at once, the boost vanished entirely. The authors argue that astrocytes weigh the overall level of network activity and adjust their response to match it.
pmc-13273947: Meagan Mooney and co-authors issued a 2026 correction notice for their study protocol on scaling up point-of-care hepatitis C testing in Canada. The original protocol appeared in Implementation Science Communications in 2025. Such bedside tests give results during the visit rather than days later. The notice fixes only the competing interests statement, which lists study funding and fees from drug firms for several authors. One added line states that author Guillaume Fontaine is an associate editor of the journal. The notice says the original article has been corrected.
pmc-13274147:
Nemo Ikonen and co-authors report a 2026 journal article, written as a letter, on a drug weakness in a high-risk blood disorder. Myelodysplastic syndromes are bone marrow diseases, and patients missing part of chromosome seven fare poorly. That missing stretch holds NAMPT, a gene cells need to recycle a vital molecule called NAD+.

With only one copy left, these cancer cells make less NAMPT and lean hard on what remains. In patient bone marrow samples, drugs blocking NAMPT killed the abnormal blasts far more readily than healthy cells. Pairing the blocker KPT-9274 with the drug venetoclax worked even better. Low NAMPT levels may flag which patients could benefit.
pmc-13274847:
Ursel Heudorf and Bernd Kowall report a 2026 journal article comparing excess deaths in Germany during COVID-19 waves and a later flu wave. A city-level look at Frankfurt had hinted the flu wave at the end of 2022 was deadlier than the pandemic peaks. The authors tested that claim nationwide using official death and infection data for 2020 to 2023.

Overall excess mortality was highest in 2022 by two estimation methods. During the flu wave from late November 2022 into the new year, relative excess reached about twenty-five to thirty-seven percent above expected, exceeding every COVID-19 wave. Weekly excess deaths also peaked then, averaging roughly five to seven thousand. People aged seventy and older bore the largest share.
pmc-13275147:
Andreas Arkudas, Raymund E Horch, and Luca Kümmerl present a 2026 case report of breast reconstruction with every tiny blood vessel join sewn by a surgical robot. Rebuilding a breast from the patient's own belly tissue requires microsurgery to reconnect arteries and veins. Using the da Vinci Xi robot, the team completed both joins of the transplanted flap: the vein with a 3.0-millimeter coupler and the artery with fine 8-0 sutures. Dye imaging built into the robot confirmed blood was flowing. Recovery was uneventful with no complications. The authors argue the widely installed da Vinci system is well suited to such microsurgery.
pmc-13276147:
Annelise Huynh and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on precision music medicine for people with cancer. Music can calm the body's stress response, and cancer brings pain, fatigue, and thinking problems. The authors focus on music medicine: listening to music without a therapist guiding the session.

They note that studies often blur music medicine with music therapy, which does involve a certified therapist. Past music studies also leaned on what patients said they felt, rather than measurable body signals. The authors recommend pairing patient reports with brain and body assays in ongoing trials. They also propose using artificial intelligence to pick the right music for each symptom in a systematic way. Clearer definitions, they argue, would make results repeatable and easier to scale.
pmc-13276247:
Suchitra Biswal and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on whether eye scan measurements can predict vision in an inflammatory eye disease. Intermediate uveitis inflames the middle of the eye and threatens sight over time. The team tracked the choroid, a blood-rich layer under the retina, using light-based scans.

Ninety-one eyes from fifty-two patients had at least one follow-up visit. Eyes were classed as worsened, stable, or improved by clinical signs. Choroid thickness barely changed over time and did not differ between those groups. Still, thickness at the first visit predicted later sharpness of vision, after accounting for age and sex. Average thickness also predicted later central retina thickness. The authors propose baseline choroid measures as an early warning marker for this disease.
pmc-13276347:
David McWilliams and co-authors report a 2026 feasibility trial on pairing exercise therapy with optimized feeding after intensive care. Survivors of critical illness often leave the ICU weak from muscle wasting and poor nutrition. Calorie and protein targets were also met often enough to pass preset thresholds. The authors say a full trial of clinical and cost benefits is now warranted.
pmc-13276547:
Jianhua Liang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how the paths of breathing muscle weakness forecast chronic disease in older Chinese adults. Respiratory sarcopenia means loss of both general muscle and breathing strength. Single measurements miss how people change over time, so the team modeled trajectories instead.

Nearly forty-eight hundred middle-aged and older adults from a national aging study were followed. Breathing flow and arm-and-leg muscle mass defined the condition. Modeling sorted people into three paths: both measures high, one impaired, or both persistently low. About a fifth fell in the dual-low group. Versus the healthiest path, they faced much higher risks of new arthritis, asthma, chronic lung disease, and hypertension. The two declines amplified each other. The authors propose these paths as markers for sorting older adults by disease risk.
pmc-13277247:
Nayera S Khatab leads a 2026 rat study of two treatments against chemically induced liver cancer. The cancer-causing chemical raised liver enzymes and oxidative stress, meaning cell damage from reactive molecules, while weakening natural defenses.

Each treatment alone eased liver injury, lowered inflammation, and pushed damaged cells toward death. The combined treatment worked strongest, bringing most measures closest to normal and beating either single treatment. Tissue exams and cell tests matched the blood findings. Work in rats cannot prove benefit in people, but the pairing is the clear lead the study offers.
pmc-13277347:
Joyce Assunção Barros leads a 2026 study of training for nursing staff on palliative care, care that eases suffering in life-threatening illness. The work ran in a teaching hospital with nurses who care for adults and older people. Staff took a knowledge and confidence test, received teaching on the topic, and retook the test four weeks later.

A total of 179 nursing professionals took part, with an average age of about forty. Knowledge scores rose clearly after the teaching. Confidence scores also rose, though the authors' summary reports the gain in mixed terms. Both changes passed standard statistical checks. pmc-13277747:

pmc-13278447:

Task-sharing could widen screening, the authors argue.
pmc-13278847:

Staff at the journal, its publisher, and the Society for Experimental Biology are credited for its strong position.

A call for papers on modeling in conservation continues the push for breadth.
pmc-13278947:
B. Langley and co-authors report a 2026 study of carbon stored in sea floor mud in the far north. They ask where organic carbon, meaning carbon from living things, builds up most in Arctic and sub-Arctic seas. Those seas warm at least three times faster than the world mean rate.

pmc-13279447:

pmc-13280747:
Zhenyu Yang and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on better ways to deliver melatonin, the sleep hormone. Melatonin can fight cell damage and swelling and may help many diseases. The authors close with blocks to clinic use, such as making the carriers at scale and proving long-term safety.
pmc-13281547:

pmc-13281947:

pmc-13282247:

The authors argue that selection by type should cut failures and spare mild cases needless big operations.
pmc-13282347:
Juliane Silberschmidt Freitas and Renan Nunes Costa report a 2026 study on how warming changes the harm of metals to tropical tadpoles. One species could not be fully tested for lead, for lack of tadpoles. Lead-exposed tadpoles developed body swelling. Both study species ranked among the most sensitive overall. The authors argue that safe water limits should account for heat, especially in warm regions facing climate change.
pmc-13282547:

Heart failure affected about six percent of this group, and those with it had higher ratio values. After full adjustment for age, lifestyle, and other diseases, higher values still meant greater odds of heart failure, rising in a roughly linear way. The ratio sorted cases with acceptable accuracy, and a best cut-off value was identified. Drinking habits and past stroke changed the strength of the link in subgroups.
pmc-13282847:

Standardised asthma prevalence rose then fell across the period, and asthma antibody prescribing matched insurance benchmarks almost exactly. pmc-13283147:

A strong teacher model drafted new labels, and a human checked and fixed them. Clean labels lifted detection scores sharply under the same training setup. The authors argue that data quality, not model size alone, limits all-weather driving vision.
pmc-13283947:
Whether CT scans judge vessel invasion in pancreas cancer as well as surgery and tissue checks is tested by Gala Nacul Mora and colleagues in 2026. Correct staging shapes whether removal surgery should proceed at all. Three radiologists read scans independently for fair comparison.

Reader agreement was strong for vein invasion and moderate for artery invasion. Surgeons found vein involvement in about a third of patients during operations. Tissue checks found vein invasion in a smaller share than scans suggested.
pmc-13284447:

The authors say the approach can probe how blood and fluid dynamics interact to keep the brain in balance.
pmc-13284547:
Elena Gloria Torres García and co-authors describe a 2026 case of a rare fungal prostate infection in a man with type 2 diabetes. The authors note his dapagliflozin treatment, which raises urine sugar, may have added risk alongside blockage and diabetes. They urge alert care when several such risks meet.
pmc-13285747:
Binjin Zhao and co-authors probe blood markers that may link metabolic syndrome with thinking decline in older adults, in a cross-sectional study from 2026. Thirteen molecules stood out between the groups, among them amino acids, lactate, and a marker of inflammation. Several of these molecules carried part of the link between the syndrome and weaker delayed recall. Lactate alone carried the whole link with attention, a clue the authors say needs tests over time.
pmc-13286147:

Labs can test such pairs directly, but the cost and time make wide screening impractical. Their model reads a drug as a graph of atoms and a protein as a chain of letters, then uses shared attention to fuse the two views before judging the pair.
