Cutting out the shared attention step hurt accuracy, which confirmed that the fusion does real work. High-confidence calls from the model also lined up with pairs that make biological sense on inspection. Code is posted in public, and the authors pitch the tool as a way to rank pairs for costly wet-lab checks.
pmc-13286247:
Xiyuan Li and colleagues test farm-belt dust against human immune cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Airborne particles from California's Imperial Valley and San Joaquin Valley rank among the nation's dirtiest, and their size and recipe shift with field work. Human macrophage cells met three size grades of dust from both valleys while the team read inflammation genes, cell survival, and a chemical-sensing receptor.

Gene responses shifted with dust source, size grade, and exposure length all at once. Imperial Valley dust generally stirred stronger gene activity than Parlier dust of matching size. The smallest and largest grades hit hardest in twelve-hour runs, while the tiny and fine grades switched on the chemical-sensing pathway most. Coarse dust instead drove a separate inflammation route, evidence the authors tie to distinct particle mixtures calling on distinct cell machinery.
pmc-13286347:
Ashley N Peterson and Matthew J McHenry model how small fish dodge a slow stalker in a 2026 simulation study. Lionfish hunt damselfish not by speed but by dogged pursuit and a sudden sucking strike, so classic flee-fast math misses the contest. Their agent-based model pairs a lionfish that steers straight at its target with a damselfish that darts in bursts, biased away from danger.

Simulated chases lasted about as long as real ones recorded in tanks. Probing which traits mattered most flipped the expected answer: prey lasted longest by swimming toward the predator, not away. A lionfish turns sluggishly, so a bold dash past its nose buys escape room that flight cannot. The work shows how coupled models can surface survival tricks that distance-based theories overlook.
pmc-13287147:
Ana Beatriz de Almeida Duarte and colleagues ran a 2026 laboratory feeding study on whether adding the enzyme xylanase to tropical grass haylage could cut methane output in rumen fluid. Four grass cultivars, Andropogon, Mombaça, Massai, and Marandu, were each tested with and without the enzyme.

Forty baled lots were opened after ninety days and mixed into complete rations for bench incubations. Cultivars differed in protein level and in the mix of fermentation acids produced. Xylanase left breakdown of organic matter and total gas unchanged, though methane showed a downward tendency. The authors say other enzyme doses still need testing before firm claims can be made.
pmc-13288447:
Ting and co-authors test a theory about how people reason through close and distant relationships. Their 2026 study uses strong-ties and weak-ties rationality scales, which measure logic centred on family and close friends versus logic centred on wider contacts. They asked whether these outlooks predicted stigma, help-seeking, and health behaviour during COVID-19 in four societies.

The team surveyed 918 people drawn from Han-Chinese, Chinese-Malaysian, Malay-Malaysian, and White-Australian groups. Strong-ties reasoning was linked more strongly to public stigma, to seeking help from close ties, and to personal care habits. Weak-ties reasoning was linked more strongly to public health behaviours such as following population-level guidance. The strength of these links also differed between the Han-Chinese and White-Australian samples.
pmc-13288547:
Peng Liu and co-authors mine intensive care databases in a 2026 retrospective study of a lipid ratio called the atherogenic index of plasma. They analyzed 5,872 critically ill patients with cardiovascular disease in the MIMIC-IV database, checked findings again in the eICU database, and focused on the most severe stage of acute kidney injury.

Severe kidney injury struck 20.7 percent of patients overall and climbed steadily across index quarters, as did the need for dialysis treatment. Higher index values stayed tied to severe injury and dialysis after adjustment, to longer hospital and unit stays, and, partly through kidney injury, to dying in hospital. Prediction models performed especially well for dialysis need, supporting the index as a cheap early warning marker.
pmc-13288947:
Liangshan Mu and colleagues describe a 2026 trial plan for a malaria drug in PCOS. Polycystic ovary syndrome disrupts periods and hormones. A past small trial gave hopeful signs for dihydroartemisinin. That drug is known by the short name DHA. No fair test against placebo exists yet.

The new trial will enroll 150 people with PCOS. Half will get DHA pills for 90 days. Half will get placebo pills instead. Neither group will know which they take. The main goal is return of regular periods. Staff will also track ovary counts and metabolism. Results should show if the drug truly helps.
pmc-13289347:
Joseph V Sakran and coauthors propose a 2026 framework for hospitals facing immigration enforcement inside care spaces. Emergency rooms, wards, and restricted areas have seen enforcement activity that can scare patients and disrupt urgent care. Trauma bays and operating areas face the highest risk of delay and lost trust during such encounters.

The nonpartisan plan rests on duties to keep patient information private, follow emergency care law, and guard clinical areas. Three phases guide action: prepare ahead, respond step by step during an encounter, and support patients and staff after. Concrete steps include a written policy, a round-the-clock legal contact, staff training, and keeping immigration status out of records unless truly needed.
pmc-13289447:
Asmaa Wafeeq Abdelaziz led a 2026 comparison study on a fat-related blood protein, FABP4, as a possible marker for autism spectrum disorder in children. Fat metabolism and its hormone-like signals draw growing interest in autism research. The team tested whether blood levels separate autism from intellectual disability and from typical development in young children.

Ninety children aged 3 to 12 were split evenly into autism, intellectual disability, and healthy control groups of 30 each. Blood levels ran much lower in both autism and disability groups than in controls. Levels separated either group from controls almost perfectly in this small sample. They separated autism from intellectual disability poorly, however, and did not track with age, body mass, or autism severity.
pmc-13289947:
Sai Veena Sunkara and coauthors assess a 2026 grid study on how hydropower loss affects resource adequacy in the western United States grid. Hydropower supplied about a quarter of nameplate capacity in 2020, yet drought, operating limits, aging dams, and water needs squeeze output. The team simulated 16,384 loss scenarios mixing fourteen major water regions to find which regions matter most for keeping the lights on.

Full regional loss is unlikely, but stress tests expose outsized roles clearly. Even after accounting for installed size, Pacific Northwest hydropower contributed most to system-wide adequacy in the results. Northern California and the Desert Southwest added moderate support on top. Tree models also revealed compounding when regions fail together.
pmc-13290447:
Sixty-one cases of thyroid lymphoma, a rare cancer that is hard to recognize, are reviewed by Shuchang Li and colleagues in a 2026 cohort study. The cases come from the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, diagnosed between 2014 and 2025, and were analyzed for presentation and treatment.

Two-thirds of patients also had Hashimoto's thyroiditis, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common subtype, at 60.7% of cases in the series. Survival stood at 85.0% after one year, 78.4% after three years, and 75.6% after five years. Within the B-cell group, chemotherapy was independently tied to longer survival, while age of 60 or more and high C-myc expression predicted earlier progression. Li and colleagues argue that staging should guide management when disease extends beyond the thyroid.
pmc-13290947:
A rare blue plant oil can be made sweeter-smelling without losing its punch, Ting Fang and colleagues show in a process study from 2026. Artemisia umbrosa yields a chamazulene-rich blue essential oil, but extraction is inefficient and the raw odor is pungent, blocking industrial use.

The team tuned ultrasound-assisted distillation to a 1:13 material-to-liquid ratio, 3 hours 20 minutes, and 2% salt. Then they polished the oil with silica gel to strip harsh notes while keeping the blue color and chamazulene steady. The finished oil held 36 volatile constituents with chamazulene at 50.68%. It beat a related yellow oil on antioxidant tests and killed Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli at low doses, before and after deodorizing. Fang and colleagues warn the blue pigment frays under heat, light, and oxygen, but offer the route as scalable for natural preservation and cosmetics.
pmc-13291047:
Consent that people can change over time, built for a lung screening program in Taoyuan, Taiwan, is designed in a 2026 framework paper led by Jui-Chu Lin. Low-dose CT screening creates imaging and biobank data that may be reused for years, and one-time paper consent fits that long life poorly under privacy law.

A Web 3.0 platform lets participants in the Taoyuan screening program view and update their choices digitally at any point. Blockchain hashes lock each consent record for tracing, de-identified data sit in certified secure storage, and artificial intelligence helps with risk checks and governance. The system is being piloted toward an enrollment target of 15,000 people, offering a model other screening and biobank programs could copy.
pmc-13291247:
A rare kidney tumor of childhood still defies strong treatment. Zhigang Yao leads a 2026 mini review of care for this cancer. It strikes mostly in infancy and spreads early. Survival stays poor despite surgery and strong drug mixes.

Most tumors share loss of one gene, SMARCB1. That loss shapes the cell control system in tumors. It also gives doctors a firm test for the disease. New drugs aim at weak points the loss creates. Two drug classes show early proof of concept. Immune drugs are also being tried. Clear markers to pick patients are still lacking. Kidney-specific trial data remain very thin.
pmc-13291547:
Drug-proof gut bacteria need a fresh kind of blocker. Soumyadip Ghosh and Sudha Ramaiah hunt one by computer in a 2026 study. Shigella flexneri causes severe diarrheal disease worldwide. Young children in poor lands bear the highest burden.

Standard drugs fail as the germ mutates its targets. Two enzyme targets change shape and shrug drugs off. The team trained learning models on known drug strength data. A library of drug cousins was screened in silico. Top picks faced toxicity and quantum checks. One molecule aims to block both targets at once. Mutant forms are included in that aim. Lab proof must come before any clinic hope.
pmc-13292447:
Türkan Akyol Güner surveys a 2026 digital health tangle among older adults in Zonguldak, Türkiye, at a family health center. Three hundred three internet-using adults aged 65 and over, seen between March and December 2025, completed scales for online health literacy, cyberchondria, and perceived stress. Cyberchondria means health anxiety fed by repeated online searching.

All three measures sat at moderate levels on average. Literacy ran higher in women, the younger-old, and richer, better-educated, heavier internet users. Oddly, stronger eHealth literacy came with stronger cyberchondria, a firm positive link in the regression models. Cyberchondria in turn showed a small negative tie to perceived stress, while stress mostly followed health variables. Güner says teaching older adults to judge online health content may matter as much as teaching them to find it.
pmc-13292547:
Danny Tagle-Freire and colleagues test a 2026 processing puzzle: how the way oat protein is separated, and later heated, changes how well people could digest it. Three ingredients went head to head: a dry-fractionated concentrate, an alkali-extracted isolate, and a water-only extracted isolate, plus plain oat flour. Lab digestion followed the INFOGEST protocol, and hydrated samples were heated at two temperatures.

Protein digestibility spread widely, from 26.3 percent for the water-only isolate to 66.2 percent for the flour, with the concentrate at 61.4 percent in between. Starch digestion barely varied. Mild heating at 70 degrees changed nothing for protein, but 110 degrees cut flour digestibility by roughly 30 percent and concentrate by about 21 percent in their runs. Composition alone could not explain the gaps; particle shape and prior processing did.
pmc-13292647:
Sylvain Marcel Lybrecht Llinares sets out a 2026 scoping review protocol on a neglected intensive care question: how nurses adapt humanized care for migrant patients. The protocol, registered on the Open Science Framework before screening began, promises the first map joining three separate literatures on migration, ICU humanization models, and care across cultures in critical care. Searches in English, Spanish, and French will cover seven databases.

The review follows JBI methods and PRISMA-ScR reporting, with screening in Rayyan and thematic grouping across five objectives. The stakes are concrete: missing professional interpretation in ICUs is independently tied to higher mortality and readmission odds in the cited background. The protocol also answers 2024 critical care guidelines urging units to hunt down equity barriers in family-centered care. No results exist yet; the value lies in the map to come.
pmc-13292847:
Zijun Yan and co-authors test a Chinese version of a daily-life flexibility scale in a 2026 study with people who have obsessive-compulsive disorder. Rigidity in thought and routine is central to the disorder, yet standard lab tasks may miss how it feels day to day.

The 37-item scale was translated and given to 157 people, split between patients and healthy controls, with some patients repeating it after one month. The original five-part layout fit poorly in this group. Analysis instead supported 25 items in three parts, covering adapting to context, rigid thinking and behavior, and routine and control. Scores held steady over time, supporting careful use in clinics.
pmc-13293447:
Suraj Sapkota and co-authors hunt, in a 2026 study, for oat genes that resist crown rust, a leaf disease caused by a fungus that keeps evolving new strains. Lasting, broad resistance would help breeders build tougher oat varieties for farmers.

A breeding population from a cross of northern and southern parent lines was scored in four field settings over two years and mapped with 956 DNA markers. Six regions on five chromosomes shaped resistance, and two held up in a separate oat set. One major region on chromosome 7C worked across all settings. Linked markers could guide selection of resistant plants in breeding programs.
pmc-13293847:
Rudong Li and colleagues use large gene datasets in a 2026 study to hunt for fibroblast-linked genes that matter in colorectal cancer. Fibroblasts sit around tumors and can help them grow. The team combined single-cell sequencing, cell communication tools, network analysis, and five bulk datasets, then tested one lead gene in lab and animal work.

Single-cell data revealed 17 clusters across 10 cell lineages, with fibroblasts central in signaling. Network work produced 123 candidate genes, narrowed to five core genes. One gene, DRAM1, was higher in tumor tissue and chosen for validation tests covering growth, movement, and tumor formation.
pmc-13294147:
Mario Pescatori reviews surgery for anismus in a 2026 article. In anismus, the puborectalis muscle fails to relax during straining, blocking bowel emptying. The problem affects 44% of constipated patients with obstructed defecation in the cited figure and often travels with anxiety and depression, which lower cure chances. First-line care stays conservative, with biofeedback training and botulinum toxin shots.

Cutting the tense muscle can free emptying, but full division at St Mark's Hospital was abandoned after frequent incontinence. A gentler bilateral partial cut gave better function, though a Wexner group review found disordered continence in 12% of cases. Cure at 1 year was about 70%, so patient selection matters greatly.
pmc-13294447:
Felix Chelslín and colleagues link placental growth signals to birth weight in a 2026 study. Babies classed as small, average, or large for age numbered 60, 109, and 55 in the term cohort, with strict weight score cutoffs. Placental gene activity for 22 genes, protein staining in 78 samples, and blood levels in cord and mothers were compared across groups.

Five placental signals ran lower in small babies, and staining matched for most. Cord levels of two growth factors climbed steadily from small to large babies, while a binding protein fell. Maternal blood showed no group gaps. Placental tuning, not mother blood levels, tracks fetal growth most closely.
pmc-13294847:
Hui Sun and colleagues describe low mood in people with vascular cognitive impairment after stroke in a 2026 study. They also ask which features predict a good reply to antidepressant treatment. Damage location in the brain was a special focus, since effects may differ by where a stroke lands.

Altogether 224 patients received eight weeks of antidepressant medicine plus thinking rehabilitation, and about two thirds responded well. Starting anxiety level, time since stroke, and thinking test scores each predicted who responded. Depression severity varied clearly across eight lesion locations, while anxiety severity did not, underlining that place of damage shapes the clinical picture.
pmc-13295347:
Yoshiki Nakatsuka and Kazuhiko Ohshima trace jumping genes in reptile genomes in a 2026 study. Bov-B LINE elements likely jumped from snakes into early ruminants long ago, an unusual sideways transfer. The authors examine how long the reptile versions stayed active and what marks their insertions leave.

A shared insertion signature appears in the reptile LINE and its partner SINE elements, closely matching a signature known from plant LINEs. The pattern suggests the copying mechanism behind it began extremely early in evolution. Finding fresh signatures in distant element families may sharpen understanding of how these mobile pieces reshape genomes.
pmc-13295747:
Firdavs Khaydarov and Kennon A Lattal study delayed rewards on teamwork in pigeons in a 2026 article. Social coordination means partners acting together to earn rewards neither could get alone. Most earlier work paid partners instantly, leaving the effect of waiting almost untested.

Pairs worked under rewards that arrived later and later across two experiments. Coordination dipped when payment waited, compared with instant payment conditions. Persistence stayed higher when rewards truly depended on coordinating rather than arriving anyway. Signalling the wait with a cue softened the damage, keeping joint behaviour closer to instant-reward levels and showing that warning signs help partners hold together.
pmc-13295847:
Sofia Östensson and colleagues map the literature in a 2026 scoping review on how registered nurses talk with patients and share decisions in primary care. Nurse-led visits are growing worldwide, yet most communication research has centred on doctors.

Searching four databases in March 2025, the team screened over twelve thousand records and kept sixteen studies based on observed visits. Included work covered phone triage, long-term condition care, mental health and walk-in clinics. Four themes emerged, from drawing out patient concerns to shaping choices together. The authors find the evidence thin and call for fuller studies to guide practice and training.
pmc-13295947:
Valentina Escott-Price and colleagues use genetics in 2026 to ask whether psychosis and depression themselves raise dementia risk, or whether early dementia just looks like mental illness. Telling the two apart matters because brain changes can precede diagnosis by decades.

In UK Biobank data, dementia cases with earlier psychosis or depression carried lower inherited risk for Alzheimer's disease than cases without such history. That pattern argues against hidden dementia causing the mental illness link. Other checks found no sign that inherited liability alone explains the tie, pointing instead to the disorders themselves adding risk.
pmc-13300547:
Canadian yew stores its chemistry unevenly across its organs, Svetlana M. Zaytseva and colleagues show in a 2026 plant study. They collected the generative organs of Taxus canadensis from the Moscow region across the April-to-October season. Microscopy with histochemical stains mapped where polyphenols sit, and ethanol extracts were tested for biological activity.

Polyphenols proved abundant in the plant's cones, seeds, and fleshy arils, with flavans dominating the aril at every growth stage. Shoot extracts showed the strongest antibacterial action and the highest overall activity, ahead of seed extracts. Aril extracts, by contrast, were the least toxic to cells. The mapping helps growers and pharmacologists judge which yew tissues merit harvest or culture.
pmc-13303847:
Adina-Andreea Pop leads a 2026 review of kidney harm in children with small-vessel vasculitis, where inflamed tiny blood vessels damage organs. Kidney involvement drives most long-term illness in these disorders, so early action matters greatly.

Diagnosis blends symptoms, lab tests, and tissue findings, and new evidence has reshaped views of ANCA-linked disease. Care for IgA vasculitis follows risk levels, while one rare type requires removing its trigger. Across all forms, doctors aim to cut steroid exposure and tailor plans to each child. Biomarker-guided care and targeted biologic drugs are presented as the path forward.
pmc-13304047:
Pengpeng Ren leads a 2026 report naming Chinese sprangletop, a common rice-field weed, as a new hidden host of a damaging rice virus. The virus spreads through the white-backed planthopper and devastates rice across Asia.

Weed samples from sick rice paddies tested positive, and gene, particle, and small-RNA evidence showed quiet, low-level infection without symptoms. Slight gene changes hinted the virus adapts to the weed without losing spread ability. Planthoppers injected with virus from the weed passed it to rice seedlings in about one case in three. Weed control now joins the defense plan.
pmc-13305647:
Wasihun Seyoum headed a 2026 field study of Brucella infection in goats kept by herding communities in Benatsemay District, southern Ethiopia. Work ran from March 2021 to February 2022 and paired blood testing with questions about what owners knew and did.

Among 390 goat samples, screening flagged 22 and confirmatory testing verified 10, giving an overall rate of 2.56%. Past abortion, retained membranes and stillbirth each linked strongly to positive status. Surveys of 150 owners showed very weak awareness of the disease and its threat to people, so the authors call for joint animal and human health action.
pmc-13306947:
Yuanxin Wu catalogued tobacco genes that produce small defence peptides in a 2026 genome study. PR1 proteins guard plants and release CAPE peptides that signal immunity and stress, yet the full tobacco family had not been mapped.

Seventeen genes, named NtCAPE1 through NtCAPE17, share a conserved cap region and entry tags, with most predicted to sit in cell storage sacs in reported analysis. Family trees, gene layouts and chromosome maps showed both shared ancestry and growth by duplication. Promoter scans found many hormone, growth and stress response switches, guiding later functional tests.
pmc-13307147:
Anna A. Kamenskikh modelled heat and stretch behaviour of low-friction polymers for bridge bearings in a 2026 study. Five modified PTFE variants faced classic PTFE and a high-weight polyethylene as controls across bridge temperatures from −40 to +80 °C.

Dynamic tests mapped stiffness and loss curves plus the limits of linear behaviour for each stock. Fitted models then predicted contact stress inside a spherical bearing part, matching experiments with a score of 0.97 in reported checks. The work guides sliding layer choice where bridges flex under weather swings. The fits held across the full heat range used for steel bridge parts in service.
pmc-13308547:
Ahmed Abdi Hersi leads a 2026 case report on systemic lupus in a young Somali woman whose illness was first read as tuberculosis. The woman, aged 19 years, had three months of joint pain, a malar rash, and discoid skin marks before fluid built up around both lungs.

A gene test for tuberculosis came back negative, yet drugs for that disease were tried first due to its local spread. She then grew confused, agitated, and had a seizure, which pushed a referral for deeper checks. Blood tests confirmed lupus, and strong steroid care plus two further drugs brought clear recovery. Missed lupus can mimic tuberculosis where tests are scarce.
pmc-13309447:
László Szabados and colleagues review gene editing for tougher crops in a 2026 article. Drought, salty soil, cold, and metal-laced soil all cut farm output, and normal breeding is slow for traits ruled by many genes. Editing can change single letters of DNA or tune gene activity with care.

Lists gathered for the review cover 73 genes in a model plant and 97 edited crop lines with better stress tolerance. Editing several genes at once suits traits that no single gene controls. Twenty programs held up in field tests, which the authors cite as proof the method can enter breeding. Friendlier rules for such edits may speed farm use.
pmc-13309747:
Yingqi Li and co-authors study how fertility stress feeds low mood in women facing infertility in China in a 2026 survey. Depressive symptoms are common in this group, yet the paths from stress to mood stay debated. Shame around infertility and family support are two candidate paths.

Questionnaires from 1,294 women at two large hospitals in Hainan measured stress, mood, stigma, and family function. Depressive symptoms appeared in 26.35 percent of respondents in the survey results. Modeling showed stress linked to low mood both directly and through the two paths, with stigma carrying the larger share. Stronger family function softened the chain. The authors suggest care that cuts stigma and backs family support.
pmc-13310647:
Ihsan Fadilah and co-authors pool patient data on malaria relapse prevention in Indonesia in a 2026 review. Plasmodium vivax malaria hides in the liver and relapses weeks later unless primaquine clears it. The best total dose for Indonesia varied settings was unknown, and higher doses strain the stomach and blood.

Studies from 2000 to 2024 that enrolled acute vivax patients on primaquine were pooled at the individual patient level, with seven of ten eligible studies supplying data. Doses were compared on time to first relapse over 180 days, gut discomfort, and hemoglobin drops, among patients with adequate enzyme activity. The pooled models weigh relapse protection against side effects by dose. The authors aim to settle a national dosing choice.
pmc-13310747:
Chang Liu and co-authors test how past nitrogen feeding of soil shapes leaf litter breakdown in a 2026 lab study. Litter decay drives carbon and nutrient cycles in grassland. Extra nitrogen may change decay through soil traits or through litter traits, and telling those apart is hard in field work.

Soil came from a four year field trial in southwest China, with four nitrogen levels. Clean litter from three grass types was placed on each soil for 30 days in jars. Added nitrogen sped decay for all types, most for poor litter. Soils held more mineral nitrogen and grew more acidic, which drove faster carbon release.
pmc-13310947:
Lazaridis Georgios and colleagues publish a standard set of cave ground plans in a 2026 dataset paper. Cave maps from many sources vary in style and access, which blocks fair comparison of cave shapes. A uniform set with rock type and origin labels could support shape, geology, and map based studies.

The set holds 562 cave plans redrawn in one format, each with key facts on rock and cave origin class. Open access through a public data store lets scholars reuse the plans for shape measurement and cave growth studies. Shared data may also guide cave care choices. New plans can extend the set over time.
pmc-13311147:
Enming Qiu and colleagues review mitochondria cleanup as a two sided force in digestive cancer in a 2026 paper. Cells digest faulty mitochondria through a selective cleanup called mitophagy, which works hand in hand with new mitochondria building and with shape shifts such as fusion and splitting. Faulty balance in that system links to cancer growth.

Cleanup can starve tumors by cutting energy or shield them by removing damaged parts under stress. Building and shape programs tune how much cleanup occurs in gut, liver, and pancreas tumors. Past work is summed to guide drug plans that push the balance toward tumor harm.
pmc-13311247:
Maria Luiza S. Silva, Cristal J. Toghi, and Carlos Alan C. Dias-Junior introduce a 2026 journal collection on new drug approaches and molecular pathways in heart and vessel disease. Heart disease remains a top cause of death worldwide.

The editors set out the themes the collection sought: new or reused drugs, the cell pathways they act on, and markers for early detection. They stress the need to link lab findings with patient care and to bring fields together. The piece frames the papers that follow rather than reporting new data. It maps where heart drug research is heading and what gaps remain.
pmc-13311947:
Axel Kylhammar and co-authors give a 2026 umbrella review of risk and protective factors for stroke in people with atrial fibrillation. Stroke is a leading cause of death in this rhythm disorder.

The review gathered 35 meta-analyses covering over 7.2 million participants, split between observational work and trial work. Among observational links, only high levels of the heart marker NT-proBNP earned the top grade of convincing proof. Prior stroke and age 65 to 74 also tied to stroke with strong support. Trial-based links were graded with standard certainty tools. The harvest shows how thin firm proof is beyond classic factors.
pmc-13312247:
Reinaldo Perez and colleagues present a 2026 roadmap for training infectious diseases fellows in antibiotic stewardship through entrustable professional activities. Fellowship programs are expected to produce stewardship leaders, and a national core curriculum already exists, but trainees have said it builds knowledge more than the hands-on skill real stewardship work demands.

Working from the Duke stewardship center, the authors list core activities fellows can be trusted to perform, each broken into concrete tasks that build toward competence. The set is designed to flex: fellows aiming at general infectious diseases practice can stop at basic competence, while those headed for program leadership take on advanced activities. The authors offer the list as an adaptable template other training programs can adopt and adjust to their own settings.
pmc-13312447:
Matyas Pal Timari and a large team report a 2026 structure-based drug discovery study of new inhibitors of BCL-XL, a protein that helps cancer cells evade programmed death. Blocking this member of the BCL-2 family can reopen the cell's own self-destruct pathway, but fresh chemical scaffolds are needed to keep affinity high and leave room for further tuning.

The team redesigned the inhibitors around novel single-ring and fused-ring cores, optimizing the new shapes for binding efficiency and for open directions where extra groups could later be attached. Lead compounds bound BCL-XL at picomolar strength and killed BCL-XL-dependent MOLT-4 leukemia cells effectively. The potency carried into animals, with marked tumor growth inhibition in a xenograft study. The authors present the rescaffolded series as a promising base for cancer drug development.
pmc-13312847:
Yunuen Avalos-Padilla and co-authors uncover, in a 2026 study, an unsuspected survival trick the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum uses when fever strikes. Human malaria brings repeated heat shocks above 40 degrees, a protein-damaging stress the parasite must survive, and its defense was thought to rest on chaperone proteins alone.

The team disabled PfVps60, a protein of the ESCRT machinery that sorts cargo into vesicles, and watched what changed under heat. Nearly half the proteins found in the parasite's released vesicles matched a known aggregation-prone set. Without the sorting protein, vesicles failed to export key chaperones, protein clumps piled up in the wrong place, and parasites died early after heat shock. Feeding the mutants vesicles from heat-stressed normal parasites partly restored their tolerance. The authors cast stress vesicles as a shared lifeline and a possible drug target.
pmc-13314447:
Helen S. Philp, Steven E. Epstein, and Kate Hopper chart low blood calcium in sick dogs and cats in a study out in 2026. They focused on pets with azotemia, a buildup of waste in blood that signals kidney trouble, where low ionized calcium is a known but poorly mapped partner.

The team reviewed records from one hospital over ten years, from January 2014 to December 2023. Low calcium was set below 1.21 mmol per liter in cats and 1.30 mmol per liter in dogs, with deeper bands for moderate and severe drops, as defined in the report. They logged how low it fell, when, what drove the kidney problem, and whether the pet lived to leave the hospital. Kidney causes were sorted by world guidelines for acute and chronic disease. The map aids vets in spotting risky calcium drops.
pmc-13314747:
Hriddhi Sarker and co-workers hunt plant compounds that block a key ovarian cancer protein, in a computer-based study published in 2026. Ovarian cancer is among the deadliest cancers of women, often found late, prone to return, and quick to resist standard drugs.

The team merged gene data from three public sets, named GSE14407, GSE18520, and GSE26712 in the report, to find genes shared across the cancer. Those genes clustered in cell-cycle and division control. A protein network then flagged AURKA, a kinase that runs cell division, as a central hub. Network drug methods and docking tests screened natural compounds that might grip AURKA and stall it. The in silico path offers cheaper, gentler leads for a cancer that badly needs new options, pending lab proof.
pmc-13314947:
Debora Di Mauro and colleagues study mental toughness in university students in a paper from 2026. They ask how a general grit for life and a sport-specific grit relate to each other and to personality, sport habits, grades, and contest anxiety.

The study drew 239 students, as counted in the report, who filled three standard surveys on toughness and the Big Five personality traits. Students who played sport often also took an anxiety test for competition. General and sport toughness tracked each other strongly, sharing much ground while keeping their own flavors. Conscientiousness stood out as the top trait behind both kinds, as the authors report. Grades also rose with general toughness. The work helps coaches and counselors build grit through steady habits.
pmc-13315647:
Rabab Mohamed El Hanefi and co-authors surveyed heart patients in 2026 at the National Cardiology Center in Nouakchott, Mauritania, for vitamin D shortage. Blood levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D were measured in 170 patients, with shortage set below 20 nanograms per milliliter, and links with daily life and health traits were tested.

Shortage was very common, found in 74.71 percent of patients. Higher education, greater household wealth, low regular activity, and inactive status each linked with higher rates after adjustment, some against common expectation. Sex-split checks were exploratory. The authors used a modified Poisson method to estimate prevalence ratios directly.
pmc-13316647:
Tahreem Sajjad and colleagues ran a 2026 single-center study asking whether two cheap blood ratios can flag severe ischemic stroke on arrival. The ratios divide white cell counts, monocytes or neutrophils, by protective HDL cholesterol, mixing inflammation and lipid signals in one number.

Patients were split into mild and moderate-to-severe groups by a standard stroke scale. The monocyte ratio rose weakly alongside stroke scores, and it separated the groups with high rule-in accuracy but low sensitivity in the reported figures. After full adjustment, though, the ratio lost its solo link with severity. The authors still see promise in the low-cost marker, while the mixed math calls for bigger, sharper studies before clinical use.
pmc-13317547:
Zhe Jia and co-authors compare, in a 2026 randomized study, two ways of giving oxygen as patients at high risk of sleep apnea are put under anesthesia. One is a nasal high-flow method called THRIVE; the other is mask breathing with a throat airway. Air forced into the stomach, a known hazard in these patients, was the main measure.

Of 100 patients enrolled, 94 finished, split evenly. After the breathing tube went in, stomach air entry showed in 23.4 percent of the nasal group versus 44.7 percent of the mask group in the final tally, and stomach stretch grew less as well. The nasal method also loaded oxygen better before sleep, though carbon dioxide rose mildly during the pause. Comfort scores favored the nasal route.
pmc-13318647:
Qi Sun and Jiahao Chen report a 2026 retrospective study of stroke treatment risk. They focus on bleeding into the brain after clot-busting therapy. Their measure is a simple blood ratio of platelets to white cells. Records came from one hospital stroke database and covered 790 patients.

Bleeding was checked by brain imaging within 24 hours of treatment. Standard criteria graded its severity. Patients who bled had lower ratios than those who did not. The highest ratio quarter had 67 percent lower odds of bleeding in adjusted analysis. The lowest quarter served as the comparison group. A chart combining the ratio with other factors reached an AUC of 0.767 for prediction in their testing. It offers a practical way to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13318747:
Fei Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study of MCM8 gene variants in primary ovarian insufficiency starting in childhood. Two patients carried paired variants, p.C242R and p.S445*, in this DNA repair gene. The team had earlier described the family. Now they test what the double change does inside cells.

HeLa cells were made to produce normal or double-mutant MCM8. Patient ovarian tissue showed less MCM8 and more cell death. Mutant cells cleared DNA damage slowly, with damage marks lingering. Repair partners DMC1 and RAD51 were recruited abnormally. Cells piled up in S-phase and died more often. Protein partner patterns and gene activity also shifted, touching ovary survival pathways. The findings suggest how MCM8 faults may drive early ovarian failure.
pmc-13319947:
Naziba Nuha and co-authors describe a single case from 2026 involving the return of a very rare gland cancer near the urine channel in women. Fewer than a few dozen firm cases of this cancer sit in past reports, and its traits mimic gut and prostate cancers, which makes it hard to name. Care for a return has no set path and rests on scant proof.

A 62 year old woman first treated in 2017 cleared the cancer with drug and beam care in 2018, but a local return was proven in 2020. Inward beam care was followed by bone harm, infection, and a large pelvic abscess. Wide surgery removed the bladder and part of the pelvis, with new urine and vaginal routes built. Five years on she lives with no sign of disease.
pmc-13320347: Karolina Frachowicz-Guerreiro and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their study on signaling protein levels and symptom types in people whose breathing illness worsens with common pain drugs or alcohol. The notice itself is brief and is the whole item here. It states that the wrong version of Figure 1 ran during production, shows the corrected figure, and notes that the swap leaves the findings of the study unchanged. The study groups in the figure cover asthma patients who tolerate such drugs and patients with the worsened illness.
pmc-13320447:
Rachel Verweij and co-authors run a realist review of group parenting plans for hard pressed parents of babies in a 2026 article. Most plans for this group still run one to one, even though groups cost less, need fewer scarce nurses, and are liked by lonely parents. What makes groups work, for whom, and in which settings was the guiding puzzle, built with parent and staff advisors at each step.

Five group plans built for hard pressed parents of infants were found across school and grey sources, with twenty eight papers read in full. Their workings were sorted into sixteen linked chains of setting, spark, and outcome, then grouped under six broad accounts. A kind, non judging tone and a safe group feel stood among the sparks that let parents learn and grow.
pmc-13321247:
U Suwannasual and AK Lund probe how traffic fumes and fatty food push fat cells toward obesity in a 2026 cell study. Vehicle emissions have been tied to metabolic illness, and exposed mice showed higher angiotensin II, a hormone signal, plus swollen fat cells. The team asked whether blood from exposed mice carries that signal to fat cells in a dish.

Fat cells treated with blood plasma from high fat fed or fume exposed mice grew larger. Plasma from mice with both exposures raised gene activity for hormone and fat storage pathways, including leptin and PPAR gamma targets. A drug blocking the main angiotensin receptor, losartan, undid most of those shifts, which implicates that pathway.
pmc-13322947:
Chengxun Jin, Bingya Zhang and Yihang Gao review chemical tags that tune influenza virus behaviour, in a 2026 article on post-translational modification networks. Beyond gene change, these tags add a control layer that shapes how the virus copies itself, adapts to hosts and dodges immunity.

Tags covered include phosphorylation, ubiquitination, glycosylation, SUMOylation, acetylation and lipidation, plus RNA methylation, acting across the viral life cycle. Some fine-tune the copying machinery, others alter coat proteins in ways tied to antigen change and immune escape. Much proof comes from cells or model systems, so human relevance stays partly open. The authors highlight tag-setting enzymes as possible targets for host-directed antivirals and better vaccines.
pmc-13323147:
Christian Schlunk and colleagues report sensor-guided insulin pump care for a very small preterm baby, in a 2026 case report. The infant weighed 510 grams at birth. High blood sugar appeared on the second day of life. Most babies of this size face the same problem.

Standard care uses insulin through a vein, which needs dedicated access. After a short vein-based bridge, the team switched to a skin sensor with a pump under the skin. The set was placed by hand at a shallow angle. Fat depth was only 1 to 2 millimetres, so standard tools did not fit. Over 14 days the system logged thousands of readings. It also cut skin punctures sharply and ran through bowel surgery without a break.
pmc-13323247:
Wenting Gong, Chuang Xu and Jian-Hong Ye study teacher support and student willingness to write with AI help, in a 2026 survey. Their group held 503 Chinese university learners of English as a foreign language. All had used AI tools for writing in a second language.

Perceived teacher support linked directly to stronger willingness to engage in joint writing. Support also worked through two side paths. One ran through how readily learners accepted the tools. The other ran through their sense of task flow. Those two paths also chained together. The authors advise teachers to stay visibly involved. Handing writing practice over to AI tools alone, they warn, would waste the support effect.
pmc-13325447:
Zee Albeshir and colleagues show that a trusted lab probe quietly eats gold electrodes in a 2026 study. Ferri and ferrocyanide solutions are treated as a harmless benchmark for electron transfer tests.

A quartz crystal microbalance weighed the gold during exposure. Without the cyanide couple, salt solutions alone caused no loss. With it, etching swung widely with salt type, acidity, and buffer choice. Starving the solution of oxygen cut the loss sharply, while aging and light exposure raised it. Neat long-chain surface films slowed the attack, but charged or short films sped it up. Labs must now treat the benchmark as an active etchant.
pmc-13327547:
Ayse Mubine Turkmen and co-authors trace how progerin warps the nuclear envelope in two stages in a 2026 study. Progerin, the faulty lamin behind Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome, builds up in the membrane around the nucleus. Using cells where progerin could be switched on, they watched the damage unfold.

Before division, progerin hit mainly the inner membrane, causing local swelling, folds, and stacked membrane pockets rich in the pore protein NUP153, while the outer membrane stayed near normal. After division and reassembly, nuclei turned strongly lobed, the classic disease shape. Removing NUP153 cut the early pocket formation, suggesting it helps start the folding, with lessons for aging cells that divide or rest.
pmc-13327947:
Wei Xuan Hu and co-authors model why university students adopt generative AI tools in a 2026 survey study. Working from the Technology Acceptance Model, they propose a chain running from ease of use through usefulness, satisfaction, and trust to intention. A questionnaire gathered 334 valid replies from college students.

Modeling confirmed the chain: feeling that a tool is easy and useful raised satisfaction, satisfaction built trust, and trust proved the key driver of the intention to use. Each link in the sequence carried weight, so platforms gain users by being simple and clearly useful first, then dependable. The results guide how campuses and developers should present and promote such tools.
pmc-13330547:
Sungyeon Chin and colleagues feed curcumin-loaded nanoparticles to weaned piglets in a 2026 study. Curcumin was packed into mesoporous silica particles and added to the diet. The team checked growth, blood chemistry, gut barrier strength, gut microbes, and gases in droppings.

Piglets on the diet gained more weight and showed higher muscle gene activity in the reported results. Blood triglyceride and total cholesterol fell, pointing to better fat handling. Gut barrier proteins rose, which the authors read as a tighter gut wall. Helpful gut microbes increased, while ammonia and hydrogen sulfide output dropped. The feed may thus aid growth and cut farm odour gases at once.
pmc-13330847:
Paul R. Palme and colleagues report the crystal structure of a morpholine building block for drug design in a 2026 article. Dimethylmorpholine units appear in approved drugs and help tune fat solubility and stability. The team made the bromopyrimidine version in two steps for their anti-mycobacterial work and grew crystals for analysis.

The compound packs in a monoclinic lattice with four molecules per unit cell in the reported structure. Its shape holds near mirror symmetry across the molecule. Synthesis ran through a substitution step then bromination, giving the target in good yield. Patent routes to the same compound exist, the authors note. Solid geometry data can guide later drug fitting work.
pmc-13333347:
Yufei Zhang and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2026 on adding lidocaine to epidural pain relief during labor. They aimed at a known side effect: fever in the mother, which raises oxygen demand for mother and baby and is thought to stem from sterile inflammation.

Of 400 women enrolled, 184 received the standard mix of ropivacaine and fentanyl while 186 received the same mix plus 0.3 percent lidocaine. Fever during labor struck 3.8 percent of the lidocaine group against 9.2 percent of controls, with an odds ratio of 0.384. Pain relief also began faster, at 9.8 minutes against 10.8 minutes, and pain scores four hours in were lower with lidocaine. No extra complications appeared for mothers or babies. The authors conclude the supplement both cools fever risk and quickens relief.
pmc-13333747:
Kayleigh A. Berthiaume Fox and co-authors reviewed CC16, a protein made by airway club cells, and its role in keeping the airways balanced, in a 2026 article. Long treated mainly as a marker of airway lining damage, CC16 now looks like an active defender.

Levels of the protein fall in cystic fibrosis, asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and shift during respiratory infections in ways that mirror injury and severity. The review describes how CC16 calms inflammation, fights microbes through integrin and lipid pathways, supports antioxidant defense, and steadies mitochondria. Tobacco smoke and air pollutants suppress it, while retinoids can restore production and aid repair. The authors argue CC16 deserves study as a treatment target, not only a biomarker.
pmc-13336747:
Disheng Xie and a wide team present a portable soft robotic glove in a 2026 study aimed at stroke survivors with stiff, weak hands. Fine moves like pinching, twisting caps, and swiping a phone are often lost. Older gloves tend to be bulky and give the thumb, key to most grips, too little help.

A folded, two-chamber thumb actuator drives the thumb through its full range and delivers 18 N of tip force, about twice what stiff post-stroke thumbs need. Sensors and an assist-as-needed controller give only the help each user lacks. Three chronic stroke users completed all test tasks, lateral pinch force rose by 62.9% and thumb motion range grew ninefold.
pmc-13337647:
Hasan Buğra Ekinci leads a 2026 survey study of team sport athletes and their habits online. The work asks how heavy social media use relates to awareness of cyberbullying. It also tests whether digital skills carry that link and whether trouble managing emotions changes it.

Questionnaires from 265 licensed athletes in Erzincan, Türkiye, supplied the data. Analysis with factor checks and mediation models showed heavier social media use linked to stronger digital skills. Stronger digital skills in turn linked to greater sensitivity to cyberbullying. That indirect path was clearest among athletes who reported fewer problems handling emotions, pointing to skills training as one lever for prevention.
pmc-13337747:
Emer Hunt and Gerardine Doyle tackle a methods puzzle for social theory in a 2026 article. Niklas Luhmann's systems theory treats society as linked systems such as law, politics, and media, not as a sum of people. Interview methods center on individuals, which seems to clash with that view.

Hunt and Doyle argue interviews can still fit if people are treated as observers of a system. Researcher and interviewee watch how the legal system builds its own options and communications. Framing interviews that way keeps the theory intact while giving it a workable research method. The argument matters for anyone using systems theory to study courts and legal practice.
pmc-13341447:
Telling benign from malignant thyroid nodules with a blended prediction model is the aim of Yafei Zhang and co-investigators in a 2026 study. The retrospective project enrolled 172 patients, 87 with malignant and 85 with benign nodules, all scanned with dual-energy CT.

Candidate inputs spanned clinical traits, a panel of blood markers, and spectral CT measures such as iodine concentration and effective atomic number. Two selection algorithms narrowed the field, and the final model leaned on age, TSH, and nodule volume as independent predictors. Performance was judged by discrimination, calibration, and decision curves in training and validation groups.
pmc-13341547:
Mental health support in German schools lags rising demand, in a 2026 survey by Hannah Elisabeth Köhler and colleagues. Questionnaires went to 486 principals across 13 federal states in spring 2024, covering provision versus estimated need for guidance counseling, psychology services, and school social work.

Demand had climbed from the prior year while provision stood still, and fewer than half of schools employed guidance counselors at all. Where services were missing, unmet demand was consistently high, reaching up to twice the supply in some domains. Differences by school type added texture. The authors argue systematic monitoring is needed before gaps harden into harm.
pmc-13341847:
A simple blood index predicts throat cancer recurrence, in a 2026 cohort study by Ke Du and colleagues. The retrospective analysis covered 306 nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients treated with chemoradiotherapy between February 2017 and April 2023, followed to April 2025.

The pan-immune-inflammation value, built from neutrophil, platelet, monocyte, and lymphocyte counts, ran higher in patients who recurred within two years, at 380.88 on average versus 329.76 for those who stayed recurrence-free. Its predictive accuracy was modest, with an AUC of 0.582 on the curve and a best cutoff value of 381.55 on the index. Recurrence-free survival split clearly by that line. Cheap routine blood counts could thus add a rough risk signal beside staging and viral DNA testing.
pmc-13342047:
Speakers in bigger groups sharpen their vocal identity, in a 2026 study by Elisa Pellegrino and Volker Dellwo. Animal research shows larger social groups carry more individual vocal signatures, so the team tested people in an online game played in groups of three and five.

Players cooperated on a task while trying to recognize each other by voice, with a prize for the best recognized. Three players did both sessions, letting the analysis track harmonicity, jitter, pitch, formant spread, and duration through dimensionality reduction capturing 52.9% of variance. The work probes how people stay recognizable while still aligning enough to cooperate.
pmc-13343947:
Liam Gracia and co-authors uncover how a friendly gut bacterium settles into intestinal mucus in 2026. Akkermansia muciniphila supports metabolic and immune health, yet what lets it colonize the gut was murky, so the team focused on its sugar capsule and the genes that build it.

One capsule locus, cps1, flips on and off through invertible DNA switches, so growing populations always mix coated and bare cells. Mutants unable to make any capsule still colonized mouse guts but clung poorly to the mucus layer and clumped into biofilms instead. This built-in variety lets the species balance free mucus life against sticky group living, tuning its foothold.
pmc-13344847:
Toshinori Chiba and co-authors build a machine learning model to forecast which defibrillator patients will actually need treatment in 2026. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators prevent sudden death, yet many recipients never receive a needed shock or pacing burst, so the team trained models on routine clinical, tracing, and device data.

In 514 patients from two hospitals, 15 percent received appropriate therapy over about 404 days. A base model discriminated modestly, but adding short runs of fast heartbeat, called NSVT, lifted accuracy sharply, and plain logistic regression nearly matched it, showing that one signal did the heavy lifting. A separate hospital cohort of 220 patients confirmed the performance without retuning, a rare outside check.
pmc-13346847:
Le Na Lau and colleagues test whether a chitosan coat helps zirconia implants bond with bone, in cell and animal work issued in 2026. Coated and uncoated discs were grown with bone-forming and gum cells. While implants went into rabbit shin bones and were checked at two and eight weeks for bone contact and bone area.

In dishes the coat supported cell growth and raised genes linked to bone formation and early attachment, which looked promising for the modified surface. In rabbits that gain did not appear, and coated implants failed to bond with bone at all in the reported groups. The split shows why lab promise alone cannot guide implant design.
pmc-13347047:
Mahya Ramezani, Mahsa Bazargan, and Mandana Sattari measure three gene signals in gum tissue across health, gingivitis, and advanced gum disease, in a study from 2026. Biopsies came from 23 healthy people, 18 patients with gingivitis, and 19 patients with moderate to severe long-term periodontitis. Lab tests compared two tissue-cutting enzymes with a natural defence peptide.

One enzyme, MMP-1, was clearly higher in periodontitis tissue than in healthy tissue, which fits its role in breaking down gum support. The defence peptide HBD-3 varied across groups and rose with attachment loss inside the disease group, while MMP-9 showed no clear split. The authors present MMP-1 as a candidate marker for disease activity.
pmc-13347147:
Yunpeng Liu and colleagues link early blood pressure swings after clot removal to recovery in large-vessel stroke, in a cohort study from 2026. The group held 144 patients treated from 2022 to 2024. Hourly systolic readings over the first day were split at the median swing. That split made low and high groups. Recovery was scored at 90 days.

Good recovery came to 60 percent of the low-swing group but only 29.5 percent of the high-swing group in the reported shares. The swing measure alone predicted outcome with fair accuracy. Harm from wide swings looked stronger in patients who already had high blood pressure, so the authors urge steadier control in the first day after the procedure.
pmc-13348847:
Laura Gianolio and colleagues survey school life for Italian children. Their national study came out in 2026. It covers children with bowel disease. A patient-led survey ran through the national association. It drew 362 replies in total. The window ran from February to November 2024. Most pupils sat in secondary school. Topics covered disease openness at school. Teacher understanding was covered too. Toilet access, bullying, and attendance also featured.

Most pupils liked school life. Most had told someone there about the disease. Yet felt understanding stayed low. Only 30 percent often felt understood by teachers. Toilet fear ran high at 71 percent. Over half attended while ill. Criticism was the reason they gave. Few could catch up on missed work. Training, toilet access, and absence rules top the fix list.
pmc-13351947:
Jiading Xie and colleagues build a 2026 deep learning model to tell a rare mucinous lung cancer apart from inflamed lung nodules on CT scans. Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma often looks like benign inflammation, which delays correct care. Records held 443 patients treated from January 2021 to December 2023, with tissue results as the truth standard.

A total of 1,409 scan slices trained a dual-attention network that weighs both space and channel features. In the held-out group, the model reached an area under the curve of 0.990 and accuracy of 96.6 percent. Sensitivity was 100 percent and specificity was 94.1 percent. Scores beat a standard ResNet50 baseline, supporting non-invasive sorting before surgery.
pmc-13352047:
J.T. Crawmer and co-authors measure how knee position affects joint space readings in osteoarthritis in 2026. Small shifts in how the knee sits during X-rays can mimic or mask true joint change. Data came from the Osteoarthritis Initiative, covering 1,612 knees in 806 people with no arthritis grade at baseline and a 12-month follow-up.

Fixed-flexion scans gave minimum and fixed-location joint space widths, plus a position measure. Models adjusted for age, sex, race, and body mass index. Position change linked clearly to width change for both measures. The link was stronger in females for the fixed-location measure, with a slope of 0.19 versus 0.11 in males. A smaller 4-year check found responsiveness held despite poor position values.
pmc-13355647:
Mariam Ait Oumelloul and co-authors searched in 2026 for gene variants that shape blood chemical levels in people with HIV. People with HIV age faster and face more age-related illness despite good virus control, for reasons not fully known. The team linked genome data to about 1,930 blood chemicals in 1,244 people in a Swiss cohort.

They found 27 chemicals tied to 12 gene regions, including genes for metabolic enzymes. Most known links from general studies were confirmed, and gene activity data overlapped strongly with chemical levels. Further analysis hinted that some chemicals may cause age-related diseases. The authors see paired genome and chemical profiling as a path to personal care.
pmc-13355847:
Amy Pham and co-authors report a 2026 case of acetaminophen overdose in one of the smallest premature infants yet described. The baby was born at about 24 weeks and weighed 640 grams when a medical record error led to two intravenous doses ten times too large. Overdose in such tiny infants is rare, with only four prior cases in print, and their drug handling differs from older children.

Blood tests showed high drug levels and brief clotting problems, but no liver cell injury. Treatment with the antidote N-acetylcysteine brought clotting back to normal and cleared the drug. The authors urge study of safe limits for this age group as the drug's use grows in newborn units.
pmc-13358847:
Jinbing Liu and co-authors test a traditional plant remedy against flu in a 2026 study. Fagopyrum acutatum, a buckwheat relative, has long been used in Chinese medicine for lung and breathing complaints. The team asked whether its extract can calm the inflammation that influenza A virus triggers, which can injure the lungs badly.

They identified 103 compounds in the extract and tested it in cells and in animals. Gene and protein checks traced which pathways the extract quiets, while animal tests measured survival, lung damage, and inflammatory signals in blood and lung tissue. The results support the plant's traditional use and point to compounds worth isolating.
pmc-13359847:
Giulio Cantù reviews the unsettled questions around salivary gland tumors in a 2026 paper. These tumors are uncommon but come in many types and grades, which makes firm rules scarce. Drawing on about 100 past and recent studies, Cantù separates what the field knows, what it doubts, and what it merely believes.

Debates include how to grade the most common cancer type. Another asks whether one reported cancer form truly exists, or is usually a spread from skin cancer. A third concerns how much of the parotid gland surgeons should remove for each case. The review gives clinicians a clear map of where judgment, not evidence, still rules.
pmc-13360047:
Kevaun Altamon George Wilson and co-authors review a delivery idea for animal feed in a 2026 paper. Sulforaphane, a healthful compound from cruciferous plants, fights oxidation and inflammation but breaks down easily, so little survives in feed. The review examines wrapping it in tiny particles made by ionic gelation from two natural polymers, chitosan and alginate.

The shell should shield the compound through the stomach and release it where it can be absorbed. The authors cover particle size, loading efficiency, release control, and safety rules, and weigh the potential for poultry, pigs, and cattle. Most proof so far comes from human and rodent work, a gap they flag for farm studies.
pmc-13360147:
Ting Li and co-authors published a 2026 study of breath acetone as a painless way to track ketones in the body. Ketones are chemicals the body makes when it burns fat, and high levels can be a risk in diabetes. The team tested 4,000 people with normal blood sugar, prediabetes, or diabetes. They compared breath acetone with ketones in blood and urine.

People with ketones in their urine had higher blood ketones and higher breath acetone. Breath acetone rose step by step as urine ketone levels rose. The link between breath and blood ketones was strong in people with diabetes and moderate in the other groups. The team also set early breath cutoff values for spotting ketones in blood. They say breath tests could one day offer a needle-free way to watch ketone levels.
pmc-13361047:
Boyeon Kim and Jee-Hyung Lee review the inner diversity of pancreatic cancer in a 2026 paper. This cancer, called PDAC, is among the hardest to treat, with only about one in ten patients alive at five years. It almost always resists immune checkpoint drugs. The authors blame two partners: the tumor's own patchwork of cell types and a surrounding tissue that shuts immunity down.

Drawing on multi-omics data and maps of gene activity across the tumor, they show how layers of difference let the cancer adapt and hide. Dense scar tissue and suppressive immune cells add physical and chemical walls. The review ends with plans for precision immune therapy tuned to each tumor's makeup. It aims to guide researchers hunting for cracks in this cancer's defenses.
pmc-13361447:
Małgorzata Ponikowska and co-authors tracked a biologic drug in children with severe eczema in a 2026 study. Dupilumab is a shot that calms the immune signals driving atopic dermatitis. Long-term results in children, outside of trials, are still scarce. The team looked back at 55 young patients with moderate to severe disease treated at one center.

They followed skin scores, affected body area, and quality of life across the whole course of treatment. The main goal was the share of children reaching a 75 percent cut in a standard eczema score, and how fast that gain came. Deeper gains, safety, and how long the drug kept working were also tracked. Real-life paths show families what to expect over years, not just trial months.
pmc-13362247:
Nga Ngoc Quynh Nguyen and co-authors fortified tofu with a wild termite mushroom in a 2026 food study. Termitomyces albuminosus is a valued edible mushroom that grows with termites. Its dried powder was added to soy tofu at three levels, either mixed in directly or swapped for part of the soy. The team measured yield, color, texture, inner structure, nutrition, and antioxidant power in fresh, cooked, and lab-digested tofu.

More mushroom made the tofu darker, softer, and lower in yield, as the protein network grew coarser. The swaps hurt quality more than the straight additions at high levels. Still, every sample kept its gel-like spring. The lowest swap level held up best overall. The work tests whether a prized wild mushroom can lift a staple food's nutrition.
pmc-13362347:
Ivana Herak and co-authors describe who gets a collapsed lung and what their care involves in a 2026 Croatian study. Pneumothorax lets air leak around the lung so it partly collapses. The team reviewed 60 hospitalized patients over three years at one center. Cases struck mostly older men. Chest drainage, a tube that lets the air out, was used in about three quarters of admissions and in every case caused by medical care itself.

Age 60 or over was the only trait that independently predicted who received drainage. Dependency at admission and sex did not. Nursing workload was heavy: each patient carried on average about two formal nursing diagnoses, and nearly a quarter left hospital functioning worse than they arrived. The authors say care plans should build nursing dependency in from the start.
pmc-13364147:
Chenxi Liu and colleagues present a 2026 field study on drip fertigation for dense summer maize in Shandong, China. Over two years, two hybrids grew under border flooding or drip lines that deliver water and nitrogen together, across eight planting densities up to very tight stands. The team tracked where nitrogen sat in the soil and how plants moved it from leaves to grain.

Drip fertigation raised yield for both hybrids and lifted water and nitrogen efficiency by larger margins. It kept nitrogen in the top root zone, left less nitrate deep down, and pushed more nitrogen into grain after silking, while uptake efficiency itself barely changed. The gain, the authors say, comes from better placement and remobilization, not from pulling in more nitrogen.
pmc-13367147:
Wu and colleagues discuss glycosylated RNAs, RNA molecules decorated with sugar chains, as a sorting signal for the tiny parcels cells exchange, in a 2026 commentary on extracellular vesicle biology. Cells load RNAs into exosomes, vesicles that carry messages between cells, but how particular RNAs get chosen was unclear. A recent study using sugar-tagging found these RNAs enriched inside exosomes rather than on the cell surface, as earlier work had suggested.

Experiments showed glycoRNAs enriched in membrane-bound compartments in the cytoplasm and inside the exosome lumen, the vesicle's interior. The ESCRT machinery, the cell's vesicle-building apparatus, sorts them there for protected long-range delivery. Wu lists three glycoRNA classes by location: surface-displayed, exosome-luminal, and surface-associated on vesicles. The commentary argues RNA chemistry itself, not just RNA sequence, helps decide what cells send, opening a layer of communication biology.
pmc-13375947:
Zhongwei Cao and co-authors model HIV with cells that hide in a 2027 math study. Some sick cells rest and hide the virus from drugs, then wake and seed it anew. Air-like swings in the body's state can sway those wakes, the team holds.

Their model lets growth and wake rates swing in a way that pulls back to a mean. Math proves one true path for the sums and gives cut lines for the virus to stay or to die out. Strong swings can kill the virus off in the sums, even when a still model says it would stay. The work is sums alone, a guide for next lab tests.
pmc-13377147:
Vankova and colleagues ask whether sex hormones or sex chromosomes set the anti-inflammatory power of HDL, the good cholesterol particles, in 2026 heart research. Hormone therapy offers an experiment: 14 transgender men and 17 transgender women were tested at baseline, after hormone suppression, and after 11 months on hormones. The assay measured how well each person's HDL suppressed an inflammatory signal in blood vessel cells grown in the lab, alongside detailed lipid profiling.

The HDL anti-inflammatory capacity stayed largely unaffected by the hormone changes across all time points. Neither HDL cholesterol level nor particle number correlated with function. Instead, composition mattered: rises in core lipids tracked with worse anti-inflammatory function, while rises in membrane lipid species tracked with better function, each at the significance threshold. Vankova concludes neither sex chromosomes nor hormone shifts fundamentally determine this HDL function; what it carries does.
pmc-13378047:
Mukta T Killedar and Suraj B Kanase describe a 2026 case report on shoulder problems after stroke. Their patient was a 45-year-old man whose left side was weak after bleeding inside the brain. Four months later he had shoulder pain, stiff and tight muscles, limited movement, and the shoulder had slipped partly out of place.

The gap between the shoulder bone and the arm bone measured 18 mm at the start. Over four weeks he did active shoulder exercises using a sling for support, plus exercises to steady the shoulder blade and activities that put weight through the arm. The program was stepped up over time, and the report follows his individual response in detail.
pmc-13378147:
Xinqi Guo and co-authors report a 2026 study on a brain pathway that may drive high blood pressure. Certain nerve cells in a small brain region release a hormone that raises activity in nerves controlling the kidneys and blood vessels. In rats bred to have high blood pressure, those cells were overly active.

The team traced the problem to a chain of proteins that controls chloride, a salt component, inside the cells. Too much chloride made a calming signal act in reverse, so the cells fired more.
