Mice lacking the sensor's gene lost all nitrate-driven browning, while nitrate feeding improved fat heat production and wider metabolic measures in obese mice without adrenaline-like stimulation.
pmc-13408747:
Weijian Pang, Jun Zhou, Jingwen Xu, and Xinian Zhi tackle in 2026 a spacecraft problem: spotting thermal faults aboard a microsatellite when only a trickle of data reaches the ground. Thermal control telemetry arrives through one or two downlink passes a day, channels are numerous and redundant, and labelled fault examples barely exist. Supervised tools starve, while single-sensor checks miss how channels move together.

Their framework first scores how strongly temperature channels inform one another and keeps only the informative few, cutting dimensionality by more than four fifths. A two-level seasonal decomposition then separates orbital rhythms from daily cycles, and paired convolutional and memory networks predict each component. Weighted prediction errors feed an adaptive alarm threshold. On real satellite telemetry the system flagged several fault types accurately within a single day of data, beating existing approaches.
pmc-13409547:
Michalina Nowakowska and Leszek Szalewski survey Polish dentists in 2026 about their feelings toward artificial intelligence entering the surgery. AI tools increasingly read dental radiographs, assist diagnosis and planning, and run practice administration, yet attitudes in Central and Eastern Europe were undocumented. One hundred eighty-three licensed dentists answered fifteen attitude statements through professional social media groups.

Acceptance landed in the moderate middle overall, though enthusiasm ran highest on two items: AI's potential to improve how a practice is managed, and openness to adopting it in dentistry generally. The questionnaire itself proved highly consistent, and the analysis probed whether sex, age band, or specialty shifted the answers. For policymakers and vendors, the picture is of a profession willing in principle and waiting for tools that earn trust in the clinic rather than the brochure.
pmc-13410547:
Mengyi Shan and colleagues simulate in 2026 how an enzyme unravels collagen, the tough protein of bone and skin. The enzyme, cathepsin K, is unusual: with help from a sugar-like partner it can unwind collagen's triple helix and cut it up. Blocking it is a hope for bone disease drugs, yet the unwinding steps were unclear.

Computer runs lasting millionths of a second followed the enzyme pair, a collagen segment, and the sugar partner in water. Unwinding began when six key links between the collagen strands broke. The sugar partner curved across both enzyme and collagen, holding the trio steady. Two enzyme spots helped pry strands apart, offering targets for future drug design.
pmc-13410647:
Yumin Dai leads a long author list in 2026 on a soft contact lens that watches eye pressure through the night. Pressure inside the eye often rises during sleep, when clinic checks cannot see it. That blind spot matters for glaucoma, a disease of slow vision loss.

A flexible circuit built into a standard soft lens bends with the eye and turns pressure shifts into readable signals. The team reports the highest sensitivity yet for such a lens, with steady readings while wearers lie flat with eyes closed. Trials in rabbits and dogs, plus pilot wear by healthy and glaucoma patients, showed the lens was tolerated and could track posture-linked pressure rises. Home night monitoring is the goal.
pmc-13410947:
Klein, Kronfli, and Young argue that hepatitis C elimination has a doing problem, not a knowing problem. The world has curative drugs and 2030 targets, yet progress stalled. Thirteen countries are on track for the World Health Organization goals, and two of the twenty burden countries are among them. Their 2026 commentary lays out the stalled numbers, then replaces target talk with a stepwise list along the cascade, starting with prevention and testing.

New infections in 2024 ran near the number cured that year, and deaths from hepatitis C liver disease stayed high, down only slightly since 2015. Injection drug use drives cases, so the authors push opioid agonist therapy first where neither it nor needle programs exist, and prison needle programs as drug use shifts beyond opioids. Later steps press testing and treatment access for people current programs miss. Political will and funding, they conclude, are the intervention.
pmc-13411047:
Jing Chen leads a long author list in 2026 sorting polymer electrolytes for solid-state batteries into three honest families. Such batteries promise more energy with better safety, using plastic-like materials instead of flammable liquids. Papers, though, lump very different materials under one label, which muddies comparisons.

The families split by how ions actually travel: soaked gels, nearly solid mixes with some liquid help, and true solids run by the polymer alone. Each family has its own transport route, surface behavior, and built-in limits. Priorities differ by family, from gel stability to solid contact with electrodes. Clear labels and tests matched to real use would make claims across studies comparable at last.
pmc-13411147:
Dianlong Hou and co-authors examine in 2026 whether kidney function and a neuron injury marker together flag thinking problems in type 2 diabetes. Brain decline is a common, under-spotted complication of the disease. Kidney and brain share delicate small vessels, so damage in one may mirror damage in the other.

Eighty patients were split evenly by a standard thinking test score into groups with and without cognitive dysfunction. Blood measures included the kidney estimate eGFR and neuron-specific enolase, a protein that leaks from injured neurons. The analysis weighs how each marker relates to test performance and whether pairing them sharpens detection. Such a blood-based pairing could help clinics screen diabetic patients earlier without brain scans.
pmc-13411647:
George Galea and co-workers uncover in 2026 a holding bay for DNA repair: the Golgi apparatus, the cell's shipping hub, parks a repair protein until damage calls it into the nucleus. How the Golgi and nucleus coordinate was poorly understood. Systematic screening of proteins living in both places exposed a whole repair network.

The repair protein RAD51C sits anchored to a Golgi giant called giantin during quiet times. DNA damage flips a signal through the ATM kinase, cutting RAD51C loose for nuclear import. Timing and place thus gate genome protection, with the Golgi acting as a regulated reservoir. Disrupting the anchor or the release signal would predictably leave cells exposed, a vulnerability the study maps for future work.
pmc-13412147:
Anaïs Delhomme and colleagues present in 2026 a fast DNA test for parasitic worms hiding in krill. Anisakidae nematodes pass through zooplankton before reaching fish and, sometimes, people who eat them raw or undercooked. Krill are thought to be major hosts, yet checking them has been slow and fiddly, leaving an ecological blind spot. The team calibrated a PCR assay followed by sequencing, practising on krill they had deliberately seeded with larvae.

Applied to North Sea krill, the assay found infection rates between 2.5 and 4.5 percent, higher than older reports gave. The authors credit the method's sensitivity, while allowing that ecosystem change may also play a role. They offer the test for wider parasite surveys.
pmc-13412547:
Yiwei Chen and co-authors compare the safety of immune checkpoint inhibitors in melanoma in 2026 by pairing trial evidence with real-world harm reports. These drugs work well against melanoma, yet their side-effect profiles differ and head-to-head safety data are thin. A Bayesian network meta-analysis covered 31 randomized trials with 11,937 patients, and a parallel search mined the United States FAERS database for reports filed between 2004 and 2023.

Ipilimumab, nivolumab, and pembrolizumab ranked lowest for treatment-related harms of any grade in the trial network. The reports database held 5,974 adverse events among 4,599 treated melanoma patients, with 236 event terms significantly tied to the drug class. The authors offer the signals for monitoring, not firm prescribing rules.
pmc-13413947:
Yibo Zhang and co-authors coat a fibre-optic interferometer with silicone film in 2026 to make a thermometer that thrives below freezing. Electrical sensors struggle where interference, tight spaces, or wiring burden measurements, while fibre sensors shrug those off. Their device sandwiches multimode fibre between single-mode leads, its sides polished flat with a carbon dioxide laser, then wraps the sensing stretch in a temperature-sensitive silicone blend.

Polishing more sides steadily sharpened the response: sensitivity rose from 0.73 to 2.15 nanometres per kelvin as polished facets went from one to four across the tested range of 223 to 273 kelvin. The sensor stays compact and cheap to build in their design. Biomedicine, aerospace, and energy storage are named as candidate homes for it.
pmc-13414447:
Haili Wang and co-authors fine-map in 2026 the exact spots where antibodies grip p54, a surface protein of African swine fever virus used in diagnosis and vaccine design. With no vaccine available, early blood detection carries the fight against this near-uniformly lethal pig disease. The team built the protein, raised three monoclonal antibodies in mice, and shaved the target down residue by residue with mutant proteins.

Two minimal epitopes emerged: one shared by two antibodies, a seven-residue stretch starting at position 56, reported here for the first time. The third antibody pinned a stretch at positions 108 to 114 in their mapping. Ten single residues proved critical for recognition. Both epitopes stay conserved across at least the two major virus genotypes, suiting them for tests and epitope-based vaccines.
pmc-13416447:
Jingran Liu and colleagues review patient journey maps as a tool to keep people with several chronic diseases on treatment, in a 2026 narrative review. Journey maps draw the patient's path through care, exposing where adherence breaks. Searches of three databases plus reference lists yielded eight studies on chronic comorbidity care.

Four barrier zones stood out. Care lacked combined management pathways, and continuity broke when patients moved between institutions. Chances were missed at key care moments. Stigma and poor pain control pushed special groups to leave care. The map gives nurses a clear picture for designing fixes at each weak node.
pmc-13417347:
Sohaib Arshad Mayo and co-authors present a transformer model that picks its own frequency focus for diagnosing gearbox faults under noise, in a 2026 engineering study. Fault signals live in certain frequency bands, while noise spreads everywhere. Fixed filters cannot adapt to each fault or noise level, so their model learns a soft frequency mask for every sample.

Filtered signals pass through attention across sensor channels, with signal statistics injected at each layer. On one benchmark with nine fault types, accuracy held above 95 percent at very high noise, and clean accuracy neared 100 percent on two datasets. The model also runs fast on small edge graphics hardware.
pmc-13417647:
Jian-Yong Wang and co-authors link bone thinning patterns to thinking problems in Parkinson disease, in a 2026 clinical study. Brain and bone signal to each other, yet which bone pattern matters for cognition was unclear. Bone density was measured at the hip, wrist, and spine in 120 patients, alongside symptom checks.

A grouping method split patients into spine only thinning and whole body bone loss clusters. Cognitive problems were far more common in the whole body group, with roughly ninefold adjusted odds. The link ran stronger in older and male patients and in longer illness. Protecting bone broadly might also help protect thinking, the authors suggest.
pmc-13418047:
Jing Wu and colleagues pair two kinds of nucleic acid drugs to treat pancreatic cancer in patient derived tumour models, in a 2026 study. One drug switches tumour suppressor genes back on, while the other silences cancer driving genes. Single target nucleic acid drugs often fail in complex cancers, so the team profiled each tumour's genes and proteins to pick personal combinations.

Tailored pairings beat single agents through coordinated control of several genes at once. Certain pairings also worked across different tumours sharing genetic features, hinting at broader use. The flexible design shows how personal and shared combinations can coexist in precision cancer care.
pmc-13418147:
Erica Mascarenhas and colleagues outline how United States health care can cut its large climate footprint as federal rules roll back, in a 2026 article. The sector leads the world in per person health emissions, and its 2022 output was tied to heavy losses of healthy life years. Cuts are grouped under buildings, supply chains, and daily operations.

Proven steps include renewable energy, less medical waste, and lower emission anaesthetics, inhalers, and food services. Two overlooked sources get fresh attention: conference travel and the growing energy appetite of artificial intelligence. Cleaner care also promises better air, lower costs, and stronger resilience for vulnerable groups.
pmc-13418747:
Olivier Bergeron-Boutin and colleagues measure how much content from untrustworthy sources reached adults on two large social platforms during 2020. Their study covers all active adult users in the United States on Facebook and Instagram. Sources counted as untrustworthy had shared misinformation again and again, as judged by outside fact-checkers of that period.

Exposure turned out to be tightly packed among a small slice of users rather than spread across everyone. Most people rarely met such content in their feeds at all. Those who saw the most of it often held firm views before they ever logged on. Surveys tied to the platform data showed no clear shift in attitudes from the exposure itself. The results suggest that reach alone overstates the power of low-grade sources to move public opinion.
pmc-13419347:
Lubin and colleagues analysed in 2026 how malpractice litigation around suicide shapes Israeli healthcare policy. The team searched national court databases for psychiatry malpractice cases and pre-trial settlements about suicides from 1985 to 2023. They recorded patient, lawsuit, and care-quality details for each case.

Over 38 years they found only twenty court lawsuits over patient suicides, seventeen deaths and three life-threatening attempts. Plaintiffs won three in five of those cases. Fourteen suicides happened in inpatient units and six in community care. Settlements before trial rose sharply over time, from seventeen in the first period to fifty-six in each later period. The authors warn that rising legal pressure may push psychiatrists away from high-risk public-sector work. They propose stronger safety systems, clearer documentation, and less adversarial compensation routes to protect both families and prevention work.
pmc-13419847:
Alejandro Cortés-Meda and colleagues follow households in a dengue-endemic town in Oaxaca, Mexico, to learn what keeps the dengue mosquito living around homes. The mosquito thrives in urban and suburban yards, above all in poorer areas with stored water. Their year-long cohort study ran seven indoor and outdoor checks for the insect.

Teams made 476 visits in total and found 494 breeding sites holding larvae or pupae across the rounds. House traits, resident habits, and season were each tested against how often the mosquito appeared and how long it stayed. Standing water habits that families can change stood at the center of the analysis. Season-aware control aimed at the flagged household factors could cut spraying waste and dengue risk together.
pmc-13420347:
Zhang and Liu studied in 2026 a gene switch called SPI1 in age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of sight loss in older people. The disease damages the retina's support layer, whose cells can undergo a harmful identity shift known as EMT. Using patient data and a cell model stirred up with an inflammatory signal, the team traced levels of SPI1 and two linked factors, ALKBH5 and NURR1.

Zhang found SPI1 and ALKBH5 ran high in the stressed cells while NURR1 ran low, and SPI1 levels in patients tracked age and disease stage. Turning SPI1 down restored the cells' epithelial marker, lowered a mesenchymal marker, cut harmful reactive oxygen, and slowed cell migration. The chain runs in order: SPI1 raises ALKBH5, which uses a chemical RNA tag to lower NURR1. Restoring either downstream step partly undid the benefit of silencing SPI1, confirming the axis as a candidate drug target.
pmc-13420847:
Tshegofatso Seabi and colleagues describe a training strategy for the staff of 17 health and demographic surveillance centers across sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. These centers track births, deaths, and movement house to house in regions where civil registration is weak, producing rare long-run population data. Their value depends on the data, analysis, and writing skills of local teams.

The program targeted data managers and analysts, the staff who turn field rounds into publishable findings. Pandemic disruption sharpened the need, since sites with strong pre-crisis counts could measure the crisis itself. Rounds every three to twelve months capture deaths, pregnancies, and migration in the covered populations. Stronger local analysis means findings reach policy while they are still current.
pmc-13421247:
Kenji Miyazawa, Hojjat Bazzazi and Wei Gao built a whole-body mathematical model, reported in 2026, that follows lipid nanoparticle mRNA medicines through the body. Such medicines instruct cells to make a protein inside the body, yet their journey involves tissue entry, cell uptake and several steps inside the cell that are hard to measure directly.

Calibrated on detailed rat data covering both the mRNA and the protein it produced, the model includes liver uptake, lymph circulation and the fate of mRNA inside cells. Sensitivity tests showed that breakdown inside cellular compartments, mRNA stability and translation efficiency mattered most for liver protein output. Scaled to humans by body-size rules, the model matched published clinical blood measurements.
pmc-13421347:
Manzano and Mars developed in 2026 a mathematical framework for studying horizons, the null surfaces in spacetime that bound regions such as the edge of a black hole. A horizon carries a chosen direction field, and its deformation pattern sets how isolated the horizon is from its surroundings. Their formalism encodes that pattern and its first sideways change on the surface itself, detached from any surrounding spacetime.

Manzano introduces two tools: a tuple that captures the pattern's base level, and a non-isolation tensor that measures departure from perfect isolation. That tensor vanishes for the classic horizon types. From it they derive a general near-horizon equation linking the tensor, a torsion term, and curvature, which recovers known equations for special cases. They also prove two existence theorems giving exact conditions for a horizon with any chosen isolation profile to sit inside a spacetime obeying given field equations.
pmc-13422247:
Anne F. Klassen leads a ten-author team introducing, in a 2026 paper, a short questionnaire built for valuing obesity treatment outcomes in patients' own terms. A global consensus had named eight domains that matter — from self-esteem and body image to stigma and excess skin — yet standard economic measures skip several of them.

Drawing items from the established BODY-Q questionnaire, the team built the BODY-Q-7D and tested it in an international online sample. Statistical modelling trimmed the instrument to seven items that fit well, with reliability above the usual bar across three coefficients. Most of their validity and responsiveness checks passed. The next step is attaching preference values so the scores can feed cost-effectiveness decisions.
pmc-13422847:
Ibrahem-Altwijri and colleagues test in 2026 DizzyVR, an immersive virtual reality system for vestibular rehabilitation, the balance retraining used after inner ear disorders. Standard exercises bore patients, and boredom kills adherence.

Ten patients with various vestibular disorders each completed eight weekly sessions in the headset. Attendance and completion stayed high, above ninety percent of scheduled sessions in this small group of ten participants who finished the program and rated it afterward. Usability and satisfaction ratings came out good to high. Three participants reported mild nausea or disorientation that eased over time. Before-and-after comparisons showed exploratory gains in walking speed, balance confidence, and gait stability, while the dizziness handicap score improved only as a trend. The authors call the system feasible and safe, and ask for larger controlled trials.
pmc-13422947:
Stian Andersen leads a seven-author team explaining, in a 2026 Norwegian study, why so many adults have a heart murmur despite healthy valves. Systolic murmurs without significant valve disease are common and commoner in women, yet what makes a murmur audible was unsettled.

In the Tromsø population study, 1,680 adults without significant valve disease had echocardiograms and heart-sound recordings; about a fifth had an innocent murmur. One factor dwarfed the rest: the pressure gradient across the aortic valve, with murmur odds rising steeply as it grew and passing fifty percent in the six-to-eight millimetre range. Female sex more than tripled the odds, and age, blood pressure and haemoglobin contributed smaller effects. The authors say the sex gap tracks physiology, not disease.
pmc-13423047:
Chucai Peng and colleagues examine the soil pressure acting on inclined support structures built close to existing buildings, a common problem in crowded excavation work. Their 2026 study pairs laboratory model tests with fresh theoretical derivation, varying the support angle from upright to 20 degrees while holding the soil width-to-height ratio fixed.

Cameras tracking particle movement and pressure sensors mapped how failure surfaces formed in the confined soil. The team then split the soil into zones and wrote balance equations for thin horizontal slices in each zone. Their formulas for pressure size, total force, and force position matched the measurements well, especially in the main compression zone low in the soil mass.
pmc-13425647:
Nathalia Bordeira Chagas and colleagues refined hormone cutoffs for nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 2026 diagnostic accuracy study of children with premature pubarche. Early pubic hair prompts endocrine testing, and 5 to 20 percent of such children carry 21-hydroxylase deficiency in its nonclassic form. The cohort held 203 children with median age 7.5 years, most of them girls, all receiving ACTH stimulation testing.

Genotyping of CYP21A2 served as the reference standard and confirmed the condition in 32 children. Basal 17-hydroxyprogesterone showed excellent discrimination, and genotype-based thresholds should reduce both missed cases and unnecessary follow-up testing. Clear cut points help staff spare most young kids long tests while still catching the few who need full care and close watch.
pmc-13426347:
Fares Alrefai and coauthors studied keratoconus severity and follow-up in a tertiary referral cohort in a 2026 analysis of Pentacam records from 2014 to 2021. Screening 21,157 charts used corneal shape thresholds to flag the cone-shaped corneal disorder, followed by manual review to confirm diagnosis and grade severity. The focus included self-identified minority patients, risk factors for progression and surgery within two years, and loss to follow-up.

Regression and mixed models linked demographic, socioeconomic, and clinical factors with presentation severity and later outcomes. Eye services gain equity-relevant evidence on who arrives with advanced disease and who disappears from care. Some young men and women reach the chair with eyes far gone, and the facts here may help staff find them at a far earlier stage.
pmc-13426447:
Li and colleagues reported in 2026 on a membrane, a thin selective barrier, that can switch which gas it lets through more easily. Gas plants need to separate carbon dioxide from hydrogen to make cleaner hydrogen fuel, but the two directions of separation normally rely on opposite methods. The team built the membrane from a water-rich gel combined with tiny zirconium cages that have a defined pore structure.

Li found that the wet membrane strongly favoured carbon dioxide, with a separation factor of 44 and very high gas flow. When the membrane dried, it shrank and the cages shifted, exposing tight sieve-like openings that favoured hydrogen instead, with a factor of 798 in that direction. The switch could be reversed and also tuned by acidity, which points to one device that can serve both separation tasks.
pmc-13427047:
Coelho and colleagues describe a 2026 surgical technique for rebuilding the medial patellofemoral ligament. That band keeps the kneecap from slipping sideways, a common problem in young active patients. Their approach uses the patient's own gracilis tendon but leaves its lower attachment in place, preserving the graft's blood supply.

The graft is routed behind the adductor magnus tendon, which acts as a pulley copying the ligament's natural path on the thigh bone. That trick avoids drilling a tunnel in the thigh bone and needs no implants. At the kneecap, the graft is fixed through two converging bone tunnels with high-strength sutures. The authors present the method as less invasive and biologically favorable, especially for patients whose bones are still growing and cannot tolerate large tunnels or hardware.
pmc-13427247:
Cook and team crossed mice lacking one copy of the progranulin gene with mice expressing human TDP-43. The cross mimics the human cause of frontotemporal dementia. TDP-43 is the protein that clumps in that disease. They asked whether low progranulin triggers TDP-43 clumping. Or does it instead worsen the damage TDP-43 causes through other routes?

Progranulin shortage never switched on clumping in mice whose TDP-43 levels stay clump-free. It did not increase clumping in high-expressing mice either. But it deepened social dominance impairment beyond either single condition. It also brought joint effects on dendritic spines in the medial prefrontal cortex. The shortage altered the RNA splicing changes driven by TDP-43. And it skewed inflammation, raising markers of disease-linked microglia while dulling signs of adaptive immunity. The authors point to prefrontal neuron dysfunction and scrambled inflammation as forces that drive the disease forward.
pmc-13427447:
Taylor Wilcox, Julie Hansen, Andrew Blanker, and Michael E. Widlansky review disrupted mitochondrial quality control in atherosclerosis in a 2026 article. Heart muscle needs constant ATP to contract and keep ion balance, and vessel cells need efficient energy to preserve lining integrity and tone. Mitophagy, the selective recycling of damaged mitochondria, sits at the center of that upkeep, governed by several pathways still being mapped.

When recycling falters, dysfunctional mitochondria accumulate and drive vascular injury in the authors' synthesis. Pinpointing which regulatory steps fail in atherosclerotic tissue could reveal drug targets beyond cholesterol lowering. Heart and vein cells burn fuel at a high rate all day and all night, so worn fuel plants hit them first and hit them hard in this ill state.
pmc-13427647:
Qianlong Li and a large team use, in a 2026 study, machine learning to read which animal a dangerous bacterium came from, based only on its genome. Pasteurella multocida causes fowl cholera in birds and other diseases in cattle, pigs, and cats, and it can infect people. The team gathered 814 checked bacterial genomes from those four hosts in a public database. Family trees built from the genomes grouped largely by host.

Five learning models then predicted host origin from tiny genetic letter changes, scoring high accuracy on held-out strains. A method that credits each clue showed which changes mattered most, pointing to genes for metabolism, cell signaling, and drug resistance. Some strains looked misclassified because they may truly have crossed between hosts. Early host clues could warn farms before an outbreak spreads.
pmc-13427747:
Sheikh Sunzid Ahmed and colleagues design, in a 2026 computer study, candidate vaccines against tularemia, a highly infectious disease carried by animals. The bacterium's Schu S4 strain is the most dangerous form, and no licensed vaccine exists. Rather than growing the germ, the team mined its proteins for short pieces, called epitopes, that immune cells recognize. Two target proteins tied to virulence supplied most of the pieces.

Two stitched-together vaccine designs, TulaVac1 and TulaVac2, scored well on predicted safety, stability, and immune strength in simulations. Their parts are nearly identical across strains, and predicted population coverage reached high levels worldwide. Docking and motion simulations suggested firm binding to immune sensors, with the first design ahead. Everything here is computational, so lab and animal testing must follow before any claim of protection.
pmc-13428147:
Wang and colleagues gathered real-world results in 2026 for surufatinib, a targeted pill, in advanced grade 3 neuroendocrine tumors, a fast-growing cancer of hormone-making cells. The drug was proven in slower grades of this cancer, but grade 3 disease lacks clear treatment standards. The team asked how long the drug holds the cancer back and which patients gain most.

Records covered 77 patients treated at fifteen Chinese centers. The middle time before the cancer grew again was just over nine months, and about one in five patients saw tumors shrink. Patients whose Ki-67 index, a measure of cell division speed, sat at or below thirty percent stayed progression-free far longer. Adding other drugs raised shrinkage slightly but did not extend control.
pmc-13428247:
Hotmaria Julia Dolok Saribu and co-authors map, in a 2026 scoping review, how digital tools and standard routines work together to keep hospital patients safe. Falls, drug errors, and missed deterioration still harm many inpatients. The team searched five databases for studies from 2006 to mid-2025 that paired a digital technology with a set protocol. Twenty studies made the final cut across many hospital types.

Four themes emerged: early warning algorithms for decline and sepsis, barcode and electronic systems for drug safety, digital checklists for handovers, and electronic monitoring for hand hygiene and fall prevention. Reported results covered deaths, stays, errors, and rule-following. Since the review mapped evidence without grading study quality, its findings read as a landscape, not a verdict. Hospitals gain a menu of pairings that multidisciplinary teams can adapt.
pmc-13428447:
John Pooley and colleagues tracked where a gene therapy virus spreads inside the brain's fluid spaces after injection into one side chamber. The target was the choroid plexus, a tissue lining those chambers that makes the fluid bathing the brain.

The team tested an engineered virus shell in mouse, rat, and pig tissue, and in living mice. It homed to the choroid plexus lining cells in all three species, carrying a glowing marker gene. Loaded with gene-editing tools, the virus also cut levels of a water channel protein in those cells. Spread was uneven, favouring the injected side's main chamber over the middle and rear chambers, a dosing problem Pooley flags.
pmc-13428547:
Jeannine Diur Yav and colleagues assess, in a 2026 study, what caregivers and health workers know about tuberculosis in children in one Congolese health zone. Childhood TB is often missed where resources are thin, and late care-seeking makes it worse. Interviews in 2024 covered 163 caregivers and 27 health providers in the Kabondo-Dianda zone. A structured questionnaire scored knowledge of spread and prevention and asked where families turn first when a child falls ill.

Caregivers scored poorly, averaging under 3 of 11 knowledge points, while providers averaged above 8. Many caregivers blamed evil spirits or household animals for transmission. Only about half went first to a health facility, and nearly two thirds delayed seeking care. Half used informal care at some point. The authors see community teaching and faster referral habits as the clearest levers for earlier diagnosis.
pmc-13429047:
Ibrahim Abubakar Abdi writes, in a 2026 commentary, that child malnutrition in Somalia will not yield to endless emergency aid. An estimated 1.7 million Somali children under five faced acute malnutrition in 2025, including nearly half a million severe cases. Decades of conflict, climate shocks, and weak institutions keep levels at emergency marks despite large aid flows. The author argues the response model itself is part of the problem.

A proposed framework joins stronger health systems, changed food systems, social protection with nutrition in mind, gender-responsive programs, and community-based treatment. Each strand targets a structural driver rather than the latest crisis spike. Funding would shift toward national strategies built to last. The piece frames child nutrition as a foundation for national development, not a side program of relief work, and calls on partners to fund accordingly.
pmc-13429547:
Francesco Maria Carrano and a large team follow, in a 2026 study, hernia repair done alongside sleeve gastrectomy for up to ten years. A hiatal hernia lets the stomach slide upward through the diaphragm, and it is common in severe obesity. Records covered 111 patients operated at several centers in 2014 and 2015, with 108 patients assessable at follow-up averaging nearly eight years. Recurrence meant the sleeve had migrated upward by more than two centimeters.

About 13 percent of patients had an anatomical recurrence. Of those, about two thirds were managed without another operation. Large hernias at the first surgery and reflux disease afterward each multiplied recurrence odds about fivefold. About one in ten patients overall needed reoperation, always tied to reflux symptoms rather than anatomy alone. Freedom from recurrence looked near total at five years but fell by ten, a late estimate the authors treat cautiously.
pmc-13432547:
Sethmi Ranasinghe and co-authors trialed a new nose adaptor in 2026 that lets a measured-dose puffer spray steroid mist for hay fever and for sinus disease after surgery. Standard nose sprays work well, yet drip down the throat and raw noses push many users to quit. Two swap-over trials each held sixteen users, who tried both tools for three weeks apiece.

Symptom gains tied between the two tools. In both groups, eleven of sixteen users picked the puffer with adaptor, citing fewer harsh feelings. The sinus group also logged a sharper jump in satisfaction scores with the new tool. Users said they would more likely keep up daily use with the adaptor. The authors read the warmer welcome as a path to steadier long-term control.
pmc-13434047:
Bingfeng Wu and co-authors built a shoot-in gel in 2026 that hunts gum disease germs both outside cells and in their hiding spots inside cells. Gum disease wrecks teeth roots through germ fire plus immune drift. Lead germs sneak into cells and jam the cell's waste pits, which lets them dodge stock care.

The gel self-builds from three parts: a body collagen, a germ-cut chain, and a plant drug. Loose build lifts the plant drug's melt and pass rates. Outside cells, the chain and drug team to tear germ skins and stall their fuel. Inside cells, the drug pools in waste pits, cuts harsh oxygen stress, and resets pit sourness. Live tests showed calmer gum tissue and fresh repair.
pmc-13435647:
Jenet Narzary, Sayed Golam Mohiuddin, and Aslan Massahi uncover a cleanup enzyme that helps E coli survive cell wall drugs in 2026. A wide screen for active promoters flagged several cutting enzymes. Knocking out one, called Tsp, sharply cut survival under beta lactam drugs.

Without Tsp, wall building proteins pile up and the cell skin weakens. One piled protein, MepS, harms survival when too high or too low. Some skin leaks did not cut survival, so leak and death part ways here. Balance, not bulk, guards the wall during drug attack. New drugs might tip that balance on purpose.
pmc-13437647:
Valentina Daponte and co-authors deleted a signaling gene in mouse bone-eating cells to learn how they help build bone. Strength comes from teamwork: osteoclasts dissolve old bone while osteoblasts lay new, and the two swap chemical messages. Their 2026 study removed the WNT5A gene only from the osteoclast line, leaving the osteoblast supply intact, then read bone structure, cell counts, gene activity, and cell movement.

Knockout mice lost spongy bone volume. The surprise was where the fault lay: osteoclast numbers and eating power stayed normal, while osteoblast numbers and activity fell. Gene readings in builder cells showed tangled programs for sticking to surfaces and talking to neighbors, plus stress signatures. Direct tests confirmed builder cells gripped poorly, moved badly, and matured a weaker matrix without the osteoclast signal. The authors crown osteoclast WNT5A as a true coupling factor.
pmc-13439247:
Xiaobing Zhai and colleagues ask whether blood metabolites can sort people with obesity by their future risk of major depression, in a 2026 analysis. Obesity raises depression risk, yet risk varies widely between people with similar weight. The team followed more than 41,000 adults with obesity for a median span beyond fourteen years. Blood profiles were fed into several machine learning methods to forecast depression at three, five, and nine years.

About 3,600 new depression cases appeared during follow-up. The best model, a gradient-boosted tree method, sorted future cases well and beat standard clinical scores, though accuracy eased in later checks. Genetic analyses suggested some metabolites sit on the causal path from obesity to depression. The authors propose blood-based sorting to aim early help at the people most likely to benefit.
pmc-13440047:
Piotr Fabrykiewicz and colleagues chart how an unusual magnetic pattern in the crystal DyFeO3 changes with temperature, reporting neutron work in 2026. DyFeO3 is the sole rare-earth orthoferrite known with a ground state whose magnetic order does not match the crystal grid, a so-called incommensurate state. That state appears below about four kelvin and brings strong coupling between magnetism and electric polarisation. How its higher harmonic ripples evolve with warming was the open question.

Their measurements follow those harmonics across temperature and set them beside published results on a cousin material, TbFeO3. In that cousin, an applied field organises the ripples into a soliton lattice, a train of spaced magnetic kinks. The comparison helps separate traits driven by the dysprosium ions themselves from traits any such lattice would show. The work sharpens the low-temperature magnetic map of a model multiferroic crystal.
pmc-13442647:
Arshpreet Kaur and colleagues map a gene family that feeds scent and pigment paths in orchids in a 2026 computer study. The genes make an enzyme called 4CL, a gate step for a broad plant chemical path. Searches across eight orchid species found 29 such genes in total.

All 29 proteins sat in one cell part, the peroxisome, and shared a set of built-in motifs. A family tree split them into three groups. Switch zones ahead of the genes held 54 types of control marks, which hints at wide roles across plant life. Root tissue showed high use for 11 of the genes. The authors frame the map as groundwork for lab tests that tie each gene to its chemical goods, work that may guide orchid breeding in time.
pmc-13442847:
Seung Ju Kim and colleagues show tiny ion devices that hum at the edge of chaos in a 2026 paper. Brains may gain their thrift from that edge state, where order and wildness meet. Past chips reached the edge through heat shifts that burn much power. Their devices move ions through a film, much as nerve cells move ions.

At currents near a hundred nanoamperes, the devices showed sharp drops in flow ease, noise gains, and self-born pulses. A compact model tied those signs to ion drift, thread growth, and circuit play. Power thrift beat heat-based edge devices by more than a thousand-fold in the report. The authors pitch the parts as low-power bricks for brain-like chips. Much work stays ahead, from part spread to circuit tests at scale.
pmc-13443047:
Xiaochen Huang and colleagues vet a kefir microbe strain, Pediococcus pentosaceus K6, for food use in a 2026 study. The strain came from Tibetan kefir, a fermented milk. Gene maps and dish tests checked both safety and guest-gut skills that mark a good probiotic.

Safety screens came back clean, with no blood harm, no bad waste goods, and no move-ready drug defense genes. The strain lived through acid at a survival share of 83.83 percent after two hours at pH 3.0 in dish tests. It also stuck to its kin at high rates and curbed Listeria growth with a clear zone near 29.83 mm wide. Gene clusters for microbe goods may explain that punch. The authors back K6 as a food-grade lead.
pmc-13443647:
Daniel Ashipala and colleagues ask health students in Namibia how joint team work feels in real wards in a 2026 study. Team care across trades lifts patient results, yet Namibia held little work on student views. Sixteen health science students at the national university sat for deep one-on-one talks in the Khomas region.

Three themes rose from the talk records. Students read team work as a joint learn and care chance that builds skill. Blocks spanned weak trade ties, poor talk, and rank walls in wards. Fixes named by students spanned shared tasks, early team drills, and staff who model joint care. The authors say the will is there, while ward culture lags. Schools and hospitals must fix ties between trades to cash the gains students see.
pmc-13445347:
Zachary Grand and colleagues test whether an artificial intelligence scribe shortens visits and eases workload in a busy hip and knee replacement clinic, in a 2026 study. Note writing eats a large share of clinic time and feeds doctor burnout. One surgeon ran the trial at a single center from late 2024 into early 2025.

Timers watched one hundred twelve visits, split between the AI scribe and standard note taking by doctor and assistant. Visits with the scribe ran about a fifth shorter on average. Workload ratings, scored on an index first built for flight research, leaned lower with the scribe across all six fields, though that gap fell short of firm proof. The gain in time was clear even at one site.
pmc-13446347:
Georgina Fröhlich and colleagues describe a program that turns radiotherapy into a heroic mission for children, run across seven Hungarian centers, published in 2026. Treatment with big machines, tight masks, and time apart from parents frightens young patients and can force sedation. The program wraps preparation in story and play, with a hero named Brave at its heart.

From May 2023 to May 2026, two hundred fifty-six children took part. Each got a themed box with a toy model of the treatment machine, storybooks, games, a mask to decorate, comfort items, and markers for milestones passed. Staff from many trades ran the plan together. In five cases, growing ease with the steps removed the need for general anesthesia altogether.
pmc-13446647:
Berken and the Transpacifier Endoscopy Research Group tested a 3D-printed pacifier that guides an ultrathin endoscope through a baby's mouth. It lets doctors inspect and biopsy the upper gut of young infants without general anesthesia. Anesthesia worries delay infant endoscopy. The transnasal route used in older children is impractical at this age.

In the single-center study at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, six infants aged 2 to 6 months underwent the unsedated procedure using their own suck reflex. All procedures were completed with adequate views and diagnostic-quality biopsies. Findings changed management in two of the six cases reported. No major adverse events occurred during or after the examinations in this early series. Parent and provider feedback supported the approach. In a related survey, over 85 percent of clinicians agreed performing endoscopy outside the operating room is a major advantage.
pmc-13447147:
Xiuling Luo and colleagues report a 2026 trial of ongoing nursing care after stroke. Many survivors leave hospital with lasting limits in movement, thinking or self-care, and family carers often lack training. Care that continues at home through linked community services might improve recovery and cut return trips to hospital.

Sixty patients with after-effects of stroke were split evenly between routine ongoing care and a model using community medical teams at home. The community group scored higher on daily living tasks, quality of life and satisfaction with nursing. That group also had fewer complications, fewer readmissions and lower medical costs. The authors present the linked model as a practical way to support recovery while using shared local resources more fully.
pmc-13447247:
Juan Carlos Chávez-Autor sets out a teaching framework called the System 3 Method in a 2026 conceptual analysis of deep learning. Students now reach vast information and smart tools, yet access alone does not build durable understanding or transfer. The method aims to train learners to build, check and reshape their own knowledge in cycles, with creativity kept in view.

Cycles move among gut orientation, active construction, rational checking, integration and transfer, under both quiet and deliberate self-monitoring. A five-step classroom routine gives the idea practical form, from generation through reflection to time-aware control. Creative progress is judged on novelty for the learner, usefulness and diversity, alongside mastery. Artificial intelligence may serve as a scaffold or critic only when a human keeps charge of authorship and checking, the author insists.
pmc-13448547:
Maren Landsem, Gunnar Morken and Morten Schou audit first antipsychotic choices in first-episode psychosis at a Norwegian university hospital in a 2026 cohort study. Guidelines advise against starting with drugs carrying high weight-gain risk, since weight gain distresses patients and drives stopping treatment. Yet reported starting rates for such drugs run high internationally, and local practice plus its predictors needed checking.

All two hundred thirty-eight patients treated from 2012 to 2016 were traced through records at start, one year and two years. Over half began on a high weight-risk drug, about a third on a lower-risk option, and the rest on none at initiation. Older age, emergency referral and greater illness severity each raised the chance of a high-risk start. Focused effort on those groups is urged to bring practice in line with guidelines.
pmc-13449347:
Huaze Ding and colleagues engineer in 2026 a nanoparticle treatment for acute kidney injury that rebuilds two depleted energy molecules inside mitochondria. Injured kidney tubule cells lose NAD+ and see their coenzyme Q oxidized, driving a flood of damaging reactive oxygen species. Supplying either molecule alone fails in practice: NAD+ breaks down fast and crosses membranes poorly, while coenzyme Q lacks a homing signal for mitochondria.

Their carrier-free particles co-assemble NAD+ with a pre-reduced, mitochondria-targeted form of coenzyme Q. Small enough to pass the kidney's filtration barrier, the particles gather in injured tubules and release their cargo in response to reactive oxygen. In cell oxygen-deprivation and cisplatin injury models, treatment cut reactive oxygen buildup, restored mitochondrial energy production, raised protective autophagy, and eased iron-driven cell death. The authors offer the approach as a platform for other mitochondria-linked diseases.
pmc-13450447:
Edith Yeung and colleagues demonstrate in 2026 a chip-scale device that coaxes single photons out of a quantum dot in two directions at once. Reliable single-photon sources are basic currency for quantum information, and semiconductor dots inside grown nanowires already emit excellent photons, but usually upward, off the chip. The team set a dot-bearing nanowire across a gap in a curved silicon nitride waveguide, letting the wire's glow leak evanescently, through its fading near field, into both waveguide arms.

Correlation measurements at the device's output facets confirmed true single-photon emission from both ends, for neutral and charged excitonic states alike. In a further flourish, the two photons of a cascaded pair, the biexciton and exciton emissions, were collected from different facets, physically separating the cascade on chip. The authors present the geometry as groundwork for architectures that route quantum light in several directions across a photonic circuit.
pmc-13450747:
Andrew Medford and David Sholl ask in 2026 whether learned computer models of atom forces will replace quantum chemistry or simply speed it up. Quantum methods give true energies and forces for groups of atoms, yet they cost so much time that many real problems stay out of reach. Learned models promise near-equal accuracy at a small share of that cost.

Speed gains could reach a million fold, which would open far larger and longer simulations to chemists. The authors weigh what that shift means for materials and drug work, and where learned models still fall short, such as new kinds of chemistry far from their training data. They close with a research plan for using the tools with care.
pmc-13452147:
Mukherjee and colleagues assess in 2026 what circulating tumor DNA, fragments of cancer DNA in the blood, can and cannot do in gastrointestinal cancers. The evidence is strongest in colorectal cancer. Finding tumor DNA after surgery marks patients at high risk of the cancer returning, and clearing it over time refines that risk.

Trial results are mixed on acting on the signal. One trial supported safely reducing chemotherapy in stage II colon cancer, while another found that escalating treatment for positive patients in stage III did not improve outcomes. A newer trial hinted at benefit in a stage II subgroup, though its main endpoint missed significance. The authors blame uneven assays, variable shedding, and timing problems, and they demand proof of patient benefit before wider use.
pmc-13452547:
Bruno and colleagues turn lavender leaf waste, left after essential oil is drawn out, into a catalyst for making a bio based fuel additive called solketal. A catalyst speeds a chemical change without being used up. Their 2026 study cooks the waste in hot water under pressure, then adds acid groups to the carbon that forms. Tests with X-ray and infrared tools confirmed the acid groups had attached to the char.

The catalyst converts glycerol, a surplus product of biodiesel making, plus acetone into solketal under mild heat. It reached a 97 percent conversion of glycerol with a 98 percent share going to solketal, the product wanted. Best results came at low heat for just half an hour. After seven reuse rounds, the catalyst still converted more than 96 percent of the glycerol, showing that farm waste can anchor a durable, reusable tool for greener fuel chemistry.
pmc-13453047:
Thomsen and a multinational team tested whether blocking the alpha-2A adrenaline receptor can ease liver scarring and portal hypertension. Portal hypertension is the dangerous pressure buildup in advanced liver disease, driven partly by an overactive sympathetic nervous system. They combined a cirrhotic rat model, human liver stellate cells, and tissue from 15 patients with fatty liver fibrosis. A diet-induced disease model was also used.

In cirrhotic rats, the blocker BRL44408 cut portal pressure from 18 to 12 millimeters of mercury while preserving overall arterial pressure in the acute experiments. Treated livers showed restored protective enzyme phosphorylation, less inflammation, and quieter Kupffer immune cells compared with untreated cirrhotic animals. The receptor's gene was switched on more strongly in patient tissue and in the fatty liver rats, and long-term yohimbine treatment reduced collagen-measured fibrosis in those rats. Stimulating the receptor made human stellate cells contract more, an effect the blocker reversed.
pmc-13453947:
Paul Yohan George and six co-authors describe a mesh repair for the groin and pelvis after wide removal of tumors in that region. Cutting out these sarcomas often takes flat muscles and the inguinal ligament with it, leaving a weak spot where a hernia can push through. Their 2026 paper sets out a repair that places mesh outside the belly lining to rebuild the region's natural opening.

Thirteen patients treated from May 2017 to February 2025 form the review set. Most wounds closed directly, while two needed a rotated tissue flap for cover. Standard polypropylene mesh served in 11 cases, with a titanium coated version in two. Four patients got a wound infection and two a fluid collection, yet only one developed a hernia in the long run. The authors call the method simple, cheap, and repeatable.
pmc-13454047:
Peng Xue and nine co-authors probe why some Candida yeasts shrug off echinocandin drugs, the first line cure for blood stream Candida infection. Their 2026 study compares tolerant and resistant strains of two species, Candida glabrata and Candida krusei, across gene, protein, and metabolite layers. The focus falls on mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

Tolerant and resistant strains carried higher ATP, the cell's energy coin, and showed distinct metabolic rewiring. Protein scans flagged changes in mitochondrial and energy proteins, while metabolite scans tied resistance to shifts in purine handling and the main energy pathway. Gene reads found mutations in ATP binding genes in the resistant strains. The authors present the power plant changes as fresh targets for drugs against hard to treat yeast.
pmc-13454247:
Limin Hu and five co-authors open a journal collection on the tumor microenvironment in solid cancers with this 2026 editorial. Solid tumors, they stress, are ecosystems of cancer, support, and immune cells plus vessels, matrix, and chemical signals. That setting shapes how tumors start, spread, dodge immunity, and resist drugs.

The collection gathers 15 studies, reviews, and analyses across target discovery, immune and stromal control, matrix remodeling, stress adaptation, and biomarker work. Machine learning for patient sorting and translational platforms also feature. The editors frame a field wide shift: away from hunting single driver mutations and toward treating the whole tumor ecosystem. Earlier reviews often took one path or cell type; this set aims for the integrated view. The pieces run from cell level faults to clinic ready tools.
pmc-13454347:
Zhenyu Du, Siyuan Cheng, Qi Zhao, Xiongfeng Ma, and Xiao Yuan prove, in a 2026 theory study, fresh limits on copying groups of quantum states. Modern labs can steer single quantum systems along set paths, which opens new effects tied to measurement. Reading the fine details of such systems, though, amounts to cloning a whole ensemble of states.

The team first proves a general ban: no method can clone an arbitrary ensemble, even given extra copies of a linked purification state. A loophole then appears for ensembles made by finite-time processes, where the ban can be dodged in principle. Yet the authors also prove that such tasks stay beyond practical computing reach, even when the full preparation recipe is known. The results set new ground rules for probing quantum systems.
pmc-13454547:
Tian and colleagues ask whether body shape measures can act as a clock for aging, much as blood tests now do. Their 2026 study used a 3D body scanner to take 171 measures from 302 adults in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. A machine learning method picked the measures that best predicted real age. The team then compared each person's body based age with their true age, with follow up over about twenty years.

The model found 22 measures that predicted age well, with error near four and a half years, and thinner thighs and calves marked older age. People whose body age ran ahead of their true age had worse thinking scores tied to motor planning, weaker physical function, and less leg mass. Over time they also lost dexterity, balance, and muscle strength faster, and shed more leg lean and fat mass.
pmc-13457047:
Mohammadreza Kariman, Christoph M. Augustin, and Gernot Plank show, in a 2026 computer study, that judging heart pacing by one number can crown the wrong winner. Pacing therapies for a heart whose chambers beat out of step are usually graded by the surface ECG alone. The team instead simulated a detailed four-chamber human heart and graded two pacing styles with three families of measures.

One style, biventricular pacing, prettied the ECG, narrowing its main spike from 120 to 90 milliseconds, and sped activation. Yet its activation maps strayed furthest from the natural pattern. The rival style, conduction system pacing, drew maps close to a healthy heartbeat while hiding leftover unevenness in its speed profile. The authors conclude that each metric tells a partial truth. They propose patient-specific simulation with many measures as the honest way to choose and tune pacing.
pmc-13457147:
Jingke Cao leads a twelve-author study, from 2026, of heart-lung bypass support for preterm infants across China, where experience with the smallest babies remains thin. The therapy, ECMO, rests the heart and lungs of newborns in collapse. Records came from a national alliance registry covering January 2018 to November 2025.

Only six of twenty-three centers had tried ECMO in preterm infants, treating twenty-two babies in all. The median baby was born at thirty-four weeks and ran on the machine for about 112 hours. About 82 percent were weaned off, and about 77 percent survived to go home. Complications were rare beyond the cannula site. Worryingly, over half the survivors showed brain injury on later scans, and about 41 percent had developmental delay by age two. Results did not differ clearly by whether birth came before or after thirty-four weeks.
pmc-13458447: small-scale biologists find how a long noncoding RNA drives kidney cancer growth. XIST lifts TGF-beta-induced renal cancer via microRNA control. The 2026 Europe PMC paper elucidates the deep workings. It reveals treatment targets for treatment. Noncoding RNAs regulate cancer profoundly. Insight enables new treatments. Research progress.
pmc-13459047:
Xinyu Li and co-authors ask in 2026 whether blood uric acid predicts new hardening of blood vessels in people with type 2 diabetes. Their hospital cohort in Dalian followed 665 patients who began with no visible calcification on chest scans and later had repeat imaging. Over a median follow-up a little beyond two years, 315 patients developed new calcification in the coronary arteries, the aorta, or both.

Higher uric acid tracked with higher risk in a fairly straight line, and patients in the top quarter faced roughly twice the risk of the lowest quarter after adjustment. Adding uric acid modestly improved prediction. A cutoff near 300 micromoles per liter is offered only as a starting point needing outside confirmation.
pmc-13459347:
Xiaoxia Zeng and co-authors report the first known case linking antibodies against contactin-2, a protein at the gaps between nerve insulation segments, to an autoimmune nodopathy mimicking Guillain-Barré syndrome. Their 2026 case report describes a 48 year old woman admitted to intensive care unconscious with high fever after heat stroke and blood clotting failure. Cooling, ventilation, and fluids revived her. When the ventilator stopped, she showed limb weakness and slurred speech. Nerve testing revealed axonal type peripheral nerve injury.

Cerebrospinal fluid showed the classic protein cell dissociation pattern, protein raised without extra cells. Antibody testing identified anti-contactin-2 as the culprit, an association never before documented anywhere. The authors argue that limb weakness, speech and breathing problems, fluid findings, and early axonal damage on electrical testing should prompt thoughts of this diagnosis in antibody positive patients. The case expands the known spectrum of autoimmune nodopathies.
pmc-13459447:
Elif Ayşe Tamtekin Erdoğan and co-authors compared two ways of teaching preschoolers dental care: live demonstration on a model versus an educational video. Their 2026 trial enrolled 282 children aged three to five at six private kindergartens in Istanbul, Turkey. Children were assigned to model teaching, video teaching, or no training. Dentists examined the children's teeth and gums with standardized indices and surveyed parents at the start. Both checks were repeated six months later to see which method changed habits and reduced new cavities.

Both methods produced significant positive changes in the children's oral health behavior and knowledge compared with baseline. Improvements in dental and gum health measures also appeared after the education period, the authors report. The head to head comparison favored the hands on approach for the hardest outcome: model education proved more effective than video in reducing new caries over the six months.
pmc-13459647:
Mylavarapu and a large team pool studies on heart risk in women with endometriosis in this 2026 meta-analysis. Endometriosis, where womb-lining-like tissue grows elsewhere in the body, affects roughly five to ten percent of women of reproductive age and causes chronic inflammation. Because earlier reviews disagreed, the team systematically gathered studies comparing cardiovascular outcomes in women with and without the condition.

In the pooled data, women with endometriosis had about a 21 percent higher risk of cardiovascular disease overall. Their risk of major adverse cardiovascular events was about 23 percent higher than women without the condition. Risks were higher still for ischemic heart disease, at about 57 percent, and for the combination of angina and heart attack. The authors conclude endometriosis should count as a sex-specific factor when judging a woman's heart risk.
pmc-13459847:
Isheeta Madeka and colleagues asked in 2026 whether patients whose lung cancer vanishes completely after pre-surgery treatment live longer depending on which treatment they received. Using the National Cancer Database, the team found 584 patients treated between 2017 and 2020 whose resected non-small cell lung cancers showed a pathologic complete response, meaning no cancer remained. Most had stage three disease and underwent lobectomy.

Five-year survival after chemotherapy plus immunotherapy reached a level in the mid-eighties percent, significantly above chemoradiation at 70 percent. Chemotherapy alone, however, posted a similar survival figure to the combined immune approach, with no significant gap. The authors conclude that complete response after chemoimmunotherapy carries an especially strong survival association, while cautioning that treatment groups were not randomized.
pmc-13460047:
Ziyang Zhang, Yunxia Li, Tie Li, Hongfeng Wang, and Yanxin Wang mapped in 2026 two decades of research on artificial intelligence in heart failure care. Bibliometrics counts and networks publications rather than testing patients. Searching the Web of Science for work from 2005 to 2025, the team screened more than four thousand records and charted output, countries, journals, and keywords with visualization software.

Publication surged after 2019 and passed a thousand papers in 2025 alone. The United States and China led production, and hot topics clustered around machine learning, medical image analysis, and extracting features from clinical records. The authors recommend stronger multicenter validation and better sharing of multimodal datasets so models prove themselves beyond the hospitals that built them.
pmc-13460347:
Shuhui Li and a large team examined in 2026 how the mitochondria, the cell's energy factories, malfunction in blood cells from people with schizophrenia. Quality control for these parts involves building new ones, reshaping them, and clearing damaged ones. The study compared 42 patients with 43 healthy controls using imaging, gene activity, DNA checks, and oxidation measures, plus a neuron model damaged with peroxide.

Patient mitochondria appeared fragmented into many small pieces. Building signals were turned up while the clearance receptor was suppressed, and their DNA copies ran low despite extra damage. Defenses against oxidation, including coenzyme Q10 and an enzyme called SOD, were depleted, and energy metabolism faltered. The authors trace this imbalance largely to oxidative damage.
pmc-13461447:
Patrick Manser and five co-editors introduce in 2026 a research collection on whether serious digital health technologies can finally move physical activity habits. Global inactivity keeps rising despite a World Health Organization target of cutting it by fifteen percent by 2030, proving that generic advice fails. The collection's central claim is that apps, wearables, and games are delivery platforms, not interventions in themselves, so their worth depends entirely on design and support.

Evidence gathered across the papers shows self-monitoring alone fades, while well-timed, personal, interactive coaching built on behavior theory produced more durable gains. Technologies can build habits at scale when they supply clear cues, quick rewards, and repeated practice. A bibliometric anchor paper charts nearly three thousand articles and the wearable boom of the 2010s.
pmc-13461547:
Mark Katson and co-authors present a 2026 comparison of three ways to score hand-drawn spirals in people treated for essential tremor. Essential tremor causes shaking, often in the hands, and the treatment studied here uses focused ultrasound guided by magnetic resonance imaging to treat one spot in the brain. Clinicians rate spiral drawings by eye, so the team tested whether computer measures could match those ratings.

The analysis used 410 spiral drawings from 106 patients treated with the ultrasound procedure. Two newer image-based scores showed no clear link to the clinician ratings. A far simpler measure, the total length of the drawn line, did track worse ratings, with longer lines going with more severe tremor. Improvement after treatment appeared only in the treated hand, and the authors suggest simple, clear measures deserve more testing against daily function.
pmc-13461847:
Binbin Yu, Shimin Zhao, and Jun Wang report, in a 2026 cell study, how a protein around tumor cells lowers a protective molecule inside mouth cancer cells. The cancer type is oral squamous cell carcinoma, which starts in flat cells lining the mouth. The protective molecule, glutathione, shields cells from oxygen-based damage, and tumors lean on it. The outside protein, OSF-2 or POSTN, is common in many cancers and helps spread.

Treating cancer cells with POSTN cut glutathione levels, while its spent form and harmful species rose. A second protein, PRKRA, fell after treatment. Forcing cells to make PRKRA raised glutathione and lowered harmful species, yet POSTN reversed that protection. Gene and chemical surveys pointed to pathways behind the shift, including cell death signaling. The authors conclude POSTN drains glutathione by lowering PRKRA. They suggest glutathione control could become a treatment angle for this cancer, pending more work.
pmc-13462047:
Shu Yan and Fei Zhou survey, in a 2026 review, metal-based nano-drugs designed to strengthen cancer immunotherapy. Such therapy helps a share of patients, partly because tumors hold immune cells back. Metals such as iron, manganese, copper, and zinc shape how immune cells work, a field called metalloimmunology. Free ions reach tumors poorly, can poison the body, and clear fast.

The review maps designs that release their load on tumor conditions, home in on targets, or combine jobs in one particle. Metal ions can kill cancer cells in ways that alert the immune system, switch on an alarm pathway, STING, and rewire the tumor's chemical setting. Pairing nano-drugs with checkpoint drugs, heat therapy, or light therapy may add gains. The authors link each immune pathway to the design it needs. They flag safety hurdles: the safe window and the body's habit of balancing metal levels.
pmc-13462147:
Yibei Yu and colleagues test, in a 2026 imaging study, whether extra scan measures can sharpen a risk score for ovarian growths. The score, O-RADS, sorts such growths into five risk levels using magnetic resonance imaging traits. Sorting matters: ovarian cancer is a leading cause of cancer death in women. The team added measures of how water moves in tissue, drawn as a spread of values, plus a blood marker.

Records covered 196 patients with 235 growths, all checked against tissue results. Most water measures differed between harmless and cancerous growths. The score alone sorted risk strongly. Adding the mean and shape of the water spread, plus the marker CA-125, lifted accuracy and caught more cancers. Sensitivity rose while false alarms held steady. The authors conclude the added measures improve how the score classifies these growths, helping teams decide who needs surgery and who can be watched safely.
pmc-13462847:
Minseok Kim and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, the first Korean detection of Japanese iris necrotic ring virus in Narcissus plants, the daffodil family grown from imported bulbs. Bulb imports into Korea rose over fivefold in a decade, and infected bulbs carry viruses silently into new fields. The team screened 75 Narcissus plants with gene reading and tests. The virus turned up in 22 samples, all from the Shinan area, where over half the local plants carried it.

One isolate's full genome was read: just over 4,000 letters with five working genes. Narcissus isolates matched each other exactly in coat protein, while differing more from older iris isolates abroad. Rubbing infected sap onto squash plants passed the virus on, proving mechanical spread. Every positive plant carried other viruses, a sign of the mixed infections common in Narcissus. The authors expect the work to support bulb quarantine checks and cleaner planting stock.
pmc-13462947:
Congcong Ma and colleagues map, in a 2026 literature analysis, global research on gut microbe interventions for children, from autism to obesity and poor nutrition. The field has grown fast, yet its structure and gaps were unclear. The team searched a citation database for work from 2010 to mid-2025 and charted it with mapping tools. 1,915 articles by over twelve thousand authors across 546 journals were found.

Output accelerated after 2018. China and the United States formed a dual core of production. Fewer than three in ten studies crossed national borders, showing thin international teamwork. Hotspots centered on autism, obesity, and nutrition disorders, while development and behavior outcomes sat in the shadows. Rising themes included personal nutrition plans, links between gut microbes, brain, and behavior, and gene and chemistry profiling. The authors urge wider multinational collaboration and fuller attention to developmental endpoints in future trials.
pmc-13463047:
Venkata V. B. Yallapragada and colleagues built a design-build-test pipeline for synthetic proteins that seek out targets in the body and glow on arrival. Each protein joins a tiny antibody piece, which steers it, to a light-making reporter enzyme.

The team designed proteins against two targets: a staph germ surface factor and a cancer marker called MUC1. Computer screening picked the best designs, which were then made in the lab and confirmed to bind their targets. Injected into mice, the proteins gathered at infection and tumour sites, glowing in proportion to dose and target cell count. Yallapragada presents the platform as a fast route to imaging agents for infections and cancers alike.
pmc-13463247:
Raeesah Fakier and colleagues map, in a 2026 scoping review, the factors that help or hinder good pain control after surgery. Pain after operations stays poorly managed despite better treatments, suggesting the problem lies beyond drug strength. The team searched three databases for work published through September 2025, with two reviewers screening and extracting data. Barriers and enablers were organized with a behavior framework, then matched to intervention strategies.

Enablers included patients who feel empowered and take part in their pain care, good rapport between clinicians and patients, and structured support from teams and policy. Barriers ran wider: poor knowledge and false beliefs about pain, skill gaps in judging and treating it, weak talk between professions, thin policy, and short staffing. Urban, Ermert, Schmid, and co-authors show that neutrophil extracellular traps carry calprotectin, a protein linked to defence against Candida albicans. Neutrophils are the first immune cells to reach an infection site. They kill microbes by swallowing them, by releasing stored proteins, or by casting out web-like traps.

Those traps were already known to ensnare microbes. The team found calprotectin, a protein complex from inside the cell, as part of the traps' killing cargo. The result ties a known antifungal protein to a newly found immune weapon, sharpening the picture of early defence.

Cuthbert and Insel outline a new future for psychiatric diagnosis through the RDoC framework. Current diagnostic systems for mental disorders rely on presenting signs and symptoms. As a result, their definitions do not adequately reflect the underlying brain and behavioural systems involved.

That mismatch impedes research on causes and mechanisms, and slows development of better treatments. The authors present seven pillars for building diagnosis around dimensions of brain function instead of symptom checklists alone. RDoC reshaped how funding agencies frame mental health research, even as clinical diagnosis changes more slowly.
pmc-3969247:
McCambridge, Witton, and Elbourne published a systematic review in 2014 on the Hawthorne effect. The term names the idea that people change how they act when they know they are being studied. The review asked three things: does the effect exist, when does it appear, and how big is it.

The authors gathered and weighed all the evidence they could find under a broad definition. Their work shows the evidence is mixed and the concept is used in loose, conflicting ways. They argue that research needs clearer ideas about how taking part in a study shapes behavior, so future trials can be planned and read with more care.
pmc-4230647:
Hooijmans, Rovers, de Vries, and their colleagues built a risk of bias tool for animal studies in 2014. Systematic reviews of animal experiments were still uncommon, though their value was gaining notice. Animal studies differ from human trials in many ways, so trial tools do not fit them well.

Their tool, from the SYRCLE group, checks animal studies for the flaws most likely to bias results. Items cover how animals were assigned, housed, and assessed, and whether all outcomes were reported. Fair checks like these help reviewers judge whether animal findings are solid. Better appraisal can cut wasted follow-up work and improve translation to human medicine.
pmc-4700047:
McCormack, Dunn, Desai, and their team reported the PROUD study results in 2016. Earlier blinded trials showed that daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, lowers the risk of HIV infection. A worry remained that users might take more risks and cancel out the benefit.

PROUD was a pragmatic open-label trial, meaning participants knew they received the drug. Its pilot phase tested effectiveness under real-world conditions in clinics. The results addressed whether PrEP works when people know they are taking it. Evidence of this kind shaped national programs that offer PrEP to people at high risk of HIV.
pmc-4866047:
Pereira, Chin, Rueda, and their colleagues profiled mutations in breast cancers in 2016. Breast cancer genomes are highly varied, and that variety, within and between tumors, makes treatment hard to plan. The team sequenced a panel of genes in a very large set of primary breast tumors.

By combining mutations with copy number and gene expression data, plus long-term outcomes, they refined the genomic and transcriptomic landscapes of the disease. Patterns in the combined data separate tumors into groups with different behavior. Such maps help doctors predict which cancers will return and which drugs fit each type. The study is a reference cohort for breast cancer genomics.
pmc-5481147:
Wick, Judd, Gorrie, and their team made Unicycler in 2017, a tool that builds bacterial genomes from mixed read types. One major platform gives reads that are short but near-exact, so genomes built from them are sound but broken into chunks. Other platforms give long reads that can span a whole genome, but with more errors.

Unicycler blends the two. It uses short reads for exactness and long reads to bridge gaps and close the genome into its full circle. Whole, closed genomes let labs track outbreaks and resistance genes with no missing pieces. Work that once took days of hand fixing became a single automated run.

The tutorial shows how to estimate such networks from data and how to judge whether the result can be trusted. It warns that busy-looking networks can rest on shaky numbers. Worked examples guide readers through checks for accuracy and stability. For researchers tempted by network plots, the paper sets a careful standard for what claims the data can support.

Ruben Sanchez-Garcia and colleagues presented DeepEMhancer in 2021, a deep learning tool that cleans up three dimensional maps from cryo-electron microscopy. These maps are a prized source of information for building models of protein structures. They usually arrive blurred at fine detail, because contrast fades at high resolution, so they need post-processing before modelers can read them well.

Older fixes adjust the whole map with one global correction, which can leave local detail uneven. DeepEMhancer instead learns from examples how a sharpened map should look, and applies that judgment throughout the volume. The authors show it improving the readability of real maps, helping structural biologists place atoms with more confidence.
