Pranavi Koppula, Li Zhuang, and Boyi Gan reviewed in 2020 a protein that many cancers lean on, the cystine transporter known as SLC7A11 or xCT. This transporter pulls cystine into the cell, where it feeds production of glutathione, a key part of the cell's antioxidant defenses. It is switched on at high levels in multiple human cancers.

The authors explain how that extra supply helps tumors grow and, at the same time, creates a dependency doctors might exploit. Blocking the transporter can starve cancer cells of antioxidant protection and push them toward ferroptosis, an iron linked form of cell death. The review connects basic transport biology to a concrete strategy for therapy.
prescott-conquest-mexico-vol-2-1847:
William Hickling Prescott published Volume 2 of his History of the Conquest of Mexico in 1847, part of his classic four-volume history of the Spanish conquest. Prescott, a Boston historian who worked with failing eyesight, drew on Spanish archives and chronicles. Volume 2 carries the story forward from the first volume.

Hernán Cortés and his small force press deeper against the Aztec world, facing alliances, battles, and reverses. Prescott told the tale with a novelist's pace while grounding it in letters and reports of the time. His history set the English-language account of the conquest for generations. This volume keeps the drama of the march and the siege at the center.
prescott-conquest-mexico-vol-3-1847:
Volume 3 of Prescott's History of the Conquest of Mexico appeared in 1847, continuing his four-volume account of the Spanish conquest. Prescott built the work from Spanish documents, soldiers' letters, and Aztec accounts in translation. The story now moves toward its climax in the Aztec capital.

Readers follow Cortés through flight, regrouping, and the long siege of the great lake city. Prescott weighed the cruelty and courage on both sides and described a world being destroyed in detail. His narrative was praised for fairness as well as style. The volume brings the conquest nearly to its end and shows why his history stayed a standard work for so long.
prescott-conquest-mexico-vol-4-1847:
Volume 4 of Prescott's History of the Conquest of Mexico, published in 1847, completes his classic four-volume history of the Spanish conquest. Prescott closed the story he had built from archives in Spain and Mexico. The fall of the Aztec Empire and its aftermath fill these pages.

Cortés rules a conquered land, faces rivals and royal inquiries, and ends his career under a cloud. Prescott judged the conquest's violence honestly while admiring the daring of its leaders. He also traced the early years of Spanish rule that followed. With this volume the first great English history of the conquest reached its end, and it shaped views of Mexico for a century.
prescott-conquest-peru-1847:
William H. Prescott published History of the Conquest of Peru in 1847, a companion to his Mexico volume. Francisco Pizarro and a small band of Spaniards confront the Inca Empire. Atahualpa's capture at Cajamarca, after a massacre in the square, opens the conquest. Civil war among the conquerors follows the empire's fall.

Prescott describes Inca roads, temples, and rule with romantic admiration. Gold, greed, and daring drive his narrative as in the earlier work. He worked, as before, from Spanish chronicles with the help of readers. The two conquest histories made American historiography respected abroad. Peru remains a gripping, if dated, epic of empire's violent birth.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol4-1847:
Further papers and the old chronicles fill Quicherat's fourth volume, printed in 1847. The rehabilitation record runs on here, past the witness testimony of the third volume. To it Quicherat adds chronicles written in Joan's own century.

The chronicles tell her campaigns and capture as news and memory of the time, not as court proof. Set beside the trial files, they show how her fame spread while she still lived. The volume rounds out the picture of Joan beyond the courtroom walls. It gives the whole edition its depth in the wider record of the age.
reynolds-wagner-the-wehr-wolf-1847:
George Reynolds sends a cursed man through old Italy in Wagner, the Wehr-Wolf, his serial of 1846 to 1847. Wagner is a sage who sells his soul for youth, wealth, and a dark gift: he turns wolf when the moon is full. Love, crime, and the stake crowd his path through courts, woods, and the grip of the church's sleuths in a rich, wild plot.

The tale ran in cheap parts that crowds bought by the stack. It made the wolf man a star of mass print. Its zest and gore set the tone for cheap horror. It still reads fast.
savage-gorilla-description-1847:
Thomas Savage, a missionary and naturalist on the Gabon coast, named the gorilla to science in 1847. His paper, Notice of the External Characters and Habits of Troglodytes gorilla, gave the beast its first full learned account. The wild man of the woods of sailor tale became, in his hands, an animal of record.

Savage tells the gorilla's size, build, and ways from skins, skulls, and the tales of hunters he trusted. He sets the new ape beside man and the chimpanzee and marks where it stands apart. The paper founded the science of the gorilla at a stroke. All later study of the great ape starts from Savage's page.
schoolcraft-notes-on-the-iroquois-1847:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft worked as an Indian agent in the Great Lakes region and married into an Ojibwe family, giving him rare access to native knowledge. His 1847 book gathers what he learned about the Iroquois confederacy, the powerful league of nations in New York.

Schoolcraft covers Iroquois government, the council system, and the condolence council that mourned dead chiefs and raised new ones. He retells myths and traditions and prints Iroquois pictographs, the picture records used to hold memory. Though later scholars corrected some of his claims, the book shaped American views of the Iroquois for generations.
schwann-microscopical-researches-1847:
Theodor Schwann was a German scientist who studied living tissue under the microscope. His Microscopical Researches appeared in English in 1847, in a version by Henry Smith. The book set out a bold claim about how plants and animals are built.

Schwann argued that all living things are made of cells. He showed how cells form, grow, and work in both plant and animal bodies. That single idea gave biology a firm base and still shapes how life is taught today. Few books have changed a whole science so deeply. Doctors and students across Europe read the work with care.
schwann-microscopical-researches-smith-1:
Theodor Schwann announced the cell theory in his Microscopical Researches, Englished by Henry Smith in 1847. The Sydenham Society published Smith's translation of the German work. Schwann argued that all living things, plant and animal alike, are built of cells. Structure and growth follow the same plan in both kingdoms.

He compares tissues under the microscope and traces how cells form and change. Eggs, embryos, and adult parts all fall under his single scheme. The book founded cell biology as a shared field. Its claim unified two sciences that had grown apart. Readers still cite it as a founding document. The evidence is patient and close.
snow-ether-inhalation-1847:
John Snow turned to surgical anesthesia in his 1847 pamphlet on inhaling ether vapour. Ether had just entered surgery, and doses were guesswork. Snow made the first scientific study of how much vapour a patient needs. He built an inhaler to give a measured, steady dose.

Case reports from operations show the method at work on real patients. Snow records pulse, breathing, and depth of sleep with care. His aim was to make painless surgery safe as well as possible. The pamphlet marks the birth of anesthesia as a measured craft. Snow later became the queen's own chloroform doctor. The first edition holds the founding study.
thackeray-vanity-fair-1847:
William Makepeace Thackeray published Vanity Fair in 1847, a long novel of English society during the Napoleonic Wars. Becky Sharp is a poor, clever orphan set on rising in the world. Her friend Amelia Sedley is kind, gentle, and far less worldly. Their fortunes rise and fall through love, marriage, war, and money troubles.

Thackeray calls his setting a fair where vanity is bought and sold. The Battle of Waterloo changes several lives at the midpoint. No character is a pure hero, as the subtitle warns. Thackeray narrates with wit, pity, and sharp social insight. Vanity Fair stands among the great panoramic novels in English.
the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-intere: Another edition of Hawthorne's "most interesting stories": world fiction at its best, from all nations and ages. Each tale chosen for pure storytelling power. An ideal bedside anthology for the omnivorous reader. From Poe to the continentals, the masters of the short story parade past.
theophilus-essay-upon-various-arts-1847:
Theophilus was a monk and metal hand of the 1100s in Germany. His work, De Diversis Artibus, tells how the arts were then done. Robert Hendrie gave it English dress in 1847 as An Essay Upon Various Arts. The book is the chief text on the craft shops of the mid ages.

Paint, glass, and metal form the three great heads of the work. The monk tells how to grind hues, blow glass, and cast bells and cups. Each step is set down as a hand at the bench would need it. Few books bring the mid age shop so close to life.

Apuleius wrote The Golden Ass in Latin in the ancient Roman world, and William Adlington's 1566 version was its first English translation. No other complete Latin novel survives from Rome. Its hero, Lucius, is a curious young man whose dabbling in magic goes badly wrong.

Instead of power, Lucius gets the body of a donkey. Kicked, beaten, and sold from master to master, he watches human greed, lust, and folly at close range and cannot speak to stop it. Release comes only when the goddess Isis restores him. Bawdy comedy and genuine religious feeling sit side by side throughout his misadventures.

Jacques Collin de Plancy published his Dictionnaire Infernal in France in the early nineteenth century and kept enlarging it. The dictionary covers demons, magic, omens, and the occult in short entries. Later editions added the demon portraits that made the book famous.

Entries give each demon's rank, form, and powers, drawn from older grimoires and folklore. The engravings show horned, winged, and beast-like figures that still define how demons are drawn in popular culture. De Plancy wrote first as a skeptic and later as a Catholic, and the shift shows in the text. Part reference work, part show, it remains a rich source on demon lore.

Nikola Tesla told his own life story in My Inventions, a set of six articles printed in 1919. The Serbian-born inventor had changed electrical power with his work on alternating current. Late in life, famous and short of money, he looked back.

Tesla recalls boyhood in Croatia, the flash of insight that gave him the rotating magnetic field, and his huge tests at Colorado Springs. He describes his habit of building machines whole in his mind before touching metal. The articles blend hard fact with bold claims, in a voice as odd and bright as the man himself.
tob-13147: John C. Street published The Hidden Way Across the Threshold in 1887, a work of the spiritualist age. Street writes as a believer explaining a hidden path across the boundary between the living and the dead. The book survives as a period piece of the seance era, of interest to readers who study nineteenth-century occult and spiritualist belief.

William Blake published Songs of Innocence and of Experience as paired poems showing two contrary states of the human soul. Innocence sings of the Lamb, laughing children, and a piper piping joyful songs. Experience answers with the Tyger's burning symmetry, poison trees, and chimney sweepers whose waking misery indicts the world that made them.

Blake etched and hand-illuminated the originals himself, wedding text and image as one visionary work. The same titles recur transformed across the divide, a child of joy becoming a voice of accusation. Deceptively simple in form, the Songs remain the most visionary children's poems for adults in English, short enough to memorize and deep enough to argue over for life.

The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Hindus know it as their book of the dead.

Volume two of Goodwin's Moralia carries on Plutarch's essays on the conduct of life. One famous piece weighs superstition and finds it worse than unbelief, since fear of the gods poisons every joy. Others praise brotherly love and ask why divine justice sometimes seems slow.

He writes as a wise friend rather than a stern judge. Goodwin's dignified nineteenth-century English suits the material well. Readers gain a full picture of Greek moral thought at its kindest.
turgenev-jew-and-other-stories-1847:
Constance Garnett translated the early tales in The Jew and Other Stories from Ivan Turgenev's first years as a writer. twelfth-night-pg2247: Malvolio's downfall delights in this edition: the puritan steward, tricked by the forged letter, smiles himself into the dark room. Meanwhile Viola loves Orsino, who loves Olivia, who loves Cesario. The most musical of the comedies, melancholy and merry together.
twining-memo-1947:

Twining tells of craft that climb and turn past any plane of the age, as pilots had sworn to him. He asks for a full study, and Project Sign was born of that ask. The memo stands at the head of the whole Air Force UFO file. No later paper in the line counts for more.
ueber-den-verfall-der-alchemie-und-die-h: Ueber den Verfall der Alchemie und die hermetische Gesellschaft, 1847. The decline of alchemy. This book preserves that work. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
ueber-die-alchemie-ein-vortrag-im-wissen: Ueber die Alchemie, 1847. The Berlin lecture. This book preserves that lecture. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it.
un-ga-res-1747:
Southern Rhodesia, a British colony in southern Africa run by a white minority regime, came before the UN General Assembly in Resolution 1747, adopted on 28 June 1962. The Assembly had weighed the report of its decolonization team. It notes that most people in the colony had rejected the 1961 constitution forced on them.

The text deplores the denial of equal rights and votes to the African majority. It faults Britain for not yet handing all powers to the people of the land, as the 1960 call for an end to colonial rule requires. The fight over Rhodesia would run at the UN for two more decades.
un-ga-res-47:
Thanks close out the story of Resolution 47, passed by the General Assembly on 11 December 1946. A year before, the Assembly had formed a team to drum up support for UNRRA, the relief agency feeding a war-torn Europe, in its final stage. The team now reports back: member states had backed the agency's work to a large degree, and the aid had helped rebuild lands laid waste by war.

The Assembly warmly thanks the team's chair and members for their work. It notes that a small share of the pledged sums had still not come in. The chair is asked to press the states concerned to complete their gifts, so the agency can finish its task in full.
un-ga-res-a-69-47:
Standard arms, the guns and tanks of daily war, do their worst harm close to home. Resolution A/69/47, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, argues that control of such arms must be sought first at the level of regions and sub-regions. Most threats to peace since the Cold War, it notes, flare up between states that share the same corner of the map.

The text recalls a long chain of yearly votes on the point, back to 1993. It holds that keeping a fair balance in the defense strength of states in a region serves calm. Arms control built on local trust, in this view, beats rules imposed from far away.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1747 (XVI) was adopted on 28 June 1962. It took up the question of Southern Rhodesia. The Assembly backed the findings of its Special Committee on decolonization. It stated that the territory was a Non-Self-Governing Territory under the Charter. Its people had mostly rejected the constitution set in December 1961.

Britain, as the ruling power, was asked to call a conference of all political parties at once. The conference was to write a new constitution based on one person, one vote. The text also asked Britain to restore the rights of the non-European population. It asked Britain to end laws built on racial discrimination and free political prisoners. It asked Britain to work toward a free African state.

General Assembly Resolution 47 was adopted on 11 December 1946, at the fifty-fifth plenary meeting. It concerned the closing stage of UNRRA, the relief body for lands wrecked by war. The Assembly thanked its UNRRA committee for drumming up support. It noted that most pledged gifts had arrived, but a small share had not. It urged the member governments concerned to send in the balance. That way UNRRA could finish its task with the full sum its council had set.

General Assembly resolution 69/47 (2014) argues that conventional arms control belongs mainly at the regional and subregional level, because most post-Cold War threats arise between neighbors. The Assembly decides to give urgent consideration to regional conventional arms control. It asks the Conference on Disarmament to formulate principles that could frame regional agreements. It requests the Secretary-General to collect member states' views and report to the seventieth session. Keeping a balance of defence capabilities at the lowest possible level is treated as the goal.
un-sc-res-1347:
Judges for the Rwanda war crimes tribunal were the business of 30 March 2001. The Security Council had received nominations for the International Tribunal for Rwanda. Under the tribunal's statute, the Council forwards a shortlist to the General Assembly. The Assembly then elects the judges. The names sent forward came from five African states. They were Benin, Zambia, Lesotho, Malawi, and Madagascar.

The one-paragraph act is a standard step in building the court. The tribunal, based in Arusha, tried those accused of leading the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Its bench needed judges from many legal systems. Forwarding the list kept the election timetable on track.
un-sc-res-1447:
Iraq's oil-for-food programme was extended by the Security Council on 4 December 2002. The programme, set by resolution 986 (1995), let Iraq sell oil to buy food and medicine under United Nations control. The Council said it remained a temporary measure for the civilian needs of the Iraqi people. It pointed to the Secretary-General's report of 12 November 2002 on the programme's working.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the programme's provisions in force for a new 180-day period starting on 5 December 2002. It promised to weigh changes to the Goods Review List, which screened contracts for items with military uses, within thirty days. The Secretary-General owed a full report at least a week before the period ended. He also had to assess how the goods review was working in practice. The extension came weeks before the invasion that ended the programme altogether.
un-sc-res-1547: Adopted in 2004, Resolution 1547 is a Security Council decision preserved through English Wikisource's transcription of the official record. Council resolutions range from short statements to long mandates, but all are voted the same way. This entry keeps the voted wording whole, so the decision can be read and cited exactly as issued.
un-sc-res-1647:
Liberia sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1647, adopted on 20 December 2005. Peaceful elections had just chosen a new president, set to take office in January. The Council praised the vote as a big step toward calm. Still, it found that Liberia had not yet met the terms for ending sanctions.

The text renews the arms and travel bans for twelve more months. Bans on diamond and timber exports run six more months. The incoming government is urged to reform the forestry office and seek outside advice on diamond income. The expert panel that tracks the sanctions returns until 21 June 2006.
un-sc-res-1747:
Iran's nuclear program reached the Council's table and drew Resolution 1747, adopted on 24 March 2007. The atomic energy agency reported that Iran had not obeyed earlier Council orders. Iran had refused to halt enrichment work. Six powers kept an offer of talks on the table.

The Council widens the sanctions set in December 2006. More people and firms tied to the nuclear and missile work face asset freezes and travel watch. Iran may not sell or send out any arms at all. States should hold back on heavy weapons sales to Iran. Banks and lenders should make no new grants or soft loans to its government. A fresh agency report is due within sixty days.
un-sc-res-1847:
The Security Council's Resolution 1847 on Cyprus was adopted on 12 December 2008. Full reunification talks had opened on 3 September that year. Both sides had also dropped planned military exercises as a sign of goodwill. Hopes for a lasting settlement ran higher than they had in years.

The text extends the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, called UNFICYP, until 15 June 2009. It urges the leaders to seize the moment and speed up the talks. The two sides must keep working with the force on marking out the buffer zone. The Secretary-General had to report on progress by 1 June 2009.
un-sc-res-1947: From 2010, Resolution 1947 records a formal decision of the Security Council in official-record form. English Wikisource supplied the transcription held here. The document's paragraphs show the genre's range in miniature, from welcoming and noting in the preamble to deciding and requesting in the operative part, each verb carrying a distinct weight.
un-sc-res-247:
Spring 1968 found the Cyprus force due for a new term, during a calmer spell on the island. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 9 March, said the force was still needed to keep the peace. Cyprus's government agreed it should continue beyond 26 March. Resolution 247 was adopted unanimously on 18 March 1968.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They also had to make good use of the current favorable climate and keep their joint efforts going. The force's stationing was extended for three months, ending on 26 June 1968. Like the renewals before it, this text kept the peacekeepers in place while talks between the communities made slow progress.
un-sc-res-2647:
The Council adopted Resolution 2647 on Libya on 28 July 2022. Elections planned for late 2021 had collapsed, leaving rival bodies claiming power. The 2020 ceasefire still held, but foreign fighters and mercenaries had not left. The mission in Tripoli also lacked a confirmed chief envoy.

The Council extends the support mission, called UNSMIL, only until 31 October 2022. The short term presses Libyan leaders to agree a path to presidential and parliamentary votes. The Secretary-General must name a special representative without delay. All sides must honor the ceasefire and pull out foreign forces. Reports on progress come every thirty days.
un-sc-res-347:
Lebanon and Israel traded charges after deadly attacks in April 1974. Palestinian gunmen had killed civilians in an Israeli town. Israeli forces then raided villages in southern Lebanon. Civilians died on that side as well. On 24 April 1974 the Security Council voiced deep disturbance at the continuing violence. Lebanon's foreign minister and Israel's envoy had both spoken. Such acts, the Council warned, could wreck efforts toward a just peace.

It condemned Israel's violation of Lebanon's sovereignty and land. Israel had to stop military actions and threats against Lebanon. The Council also condemned all acts of violence, above all those killing innocent civilians. Israel had to free abducted Lebanese civilians and send them home at once. Every government had to honor the Charter and the law.
un-sc-res-447: The library catalogues Resolution 447, a Security Council decision, under the year 1979. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-47:
Kashmir's fate should rest with its people, holds Security Council Resolution 47, passed on 21 April 1948. India had brought the fight over the state of Jammu and Kashmir to the Council. Both sides had been heard. Peace and order in Kashmir must be restored at speed, the text holds, and both states must do their utmost to halt all fighting.

Both India and Pakistan, the Council notes with pleasure, hold that Kashmir's choice of state should be made by a free and fair vote of its people. The Kashmir team set up in January is grown from three members to five. Its task, to ready and watch such a vote, forms the heart of the text. The vote itself has never been held. The catalog year of 1947 is off by one.
un-sc-res-647:
The Geneva accords on Afghanistan needed military observers in 1990. The Secretary-General proposed borrowing officers from other United Nations missions. They would serve for a time in Afghanistan and Pakistan. On 11 January 1990 the Security Council confirmed its agreement to his plan. His letters of 1988 and a January note set out the scheme. The Council had blessed the observer idea in resolution 622.

The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed of progress. The work rested on the Geneva Agreements of April 1988. Those deals covered the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan. The observer mission, UNGOMAP, checked that the pullout terms held. Its borrowed officers were a cheap way to field a mission fast.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Five names for the Rwanda court's bench fill this text of 2001. On 30 March, the Council adopted Resolution 1347 without dissent. The court, sitting in Arusha, tried the planners of the 1994 genocide. Its judges are elected by the Assembly. The lists they are picked from come through the Council.

The text sends five nominees for stand-in judge seats. Mouinou Aminou of Benin leads the list. Frederick Mwela Chomba of Zambia and Winston Churchill Matanzima Maqutu of Lesotho follow. Harris Michael Mtegha of Malawi and Arlette Ramaroson of Madagascar complete it. Shortlists like this were the steady pipeline of the court. They kept its benches full as the case load grew.

Iraq's oil-for-food program is renewed in Resolution 1447, adopted unanimously on 4 December 2002. The program let Iraq sell oil under UN supervision and spend the proceeds on food and medicine for civilians, while sanctions stayed in place. The Council described it as a temporary measure until Iraq met the disarmament demands in earlier resolutions.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the program's core rules in force for another 180 days, starting 5 December 2002. The renewal rested on the Secretary-General's November report on the humanitarian situation. It was among the last extensions of the program: the invasion of Iraq three months later ended the sanctions order on which oil-for-food rested.

Dahomey, the land now called Benin, entered by this line of 1960. On 23 August, the Council adopted Resolution 147 without dissent. The same sitting handled the bids of Chad and Ivory Coast. The Republic of Dahomey had won freedom from France on 1 August. It was a French West African land reaching self-rule that summer.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Dahomey. It was seated in September of that year. Dahomey arrived in the busiest admissions season the UN has known. African freedom redrew the Assembly in a single autumn. The new states found a shared voice for the first time.

An advance team is sent to Sudan on 11 June 2004, ahead of an expected peace deal. Sudan's government and the Sudan People's Liberation Movement had just confirmed agreement on six protocols in Nairobi. Only the final stages of talks toward a full peace deal for the south remained.

The United Nations Advance Mission in Sudan is set up to prepare for a future operation. The Secretary-General's staffing plans for the team are backed, and he is asked to prepare groundwork, including early logistics, so a mission could deploy quickly once a Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed. That operation would help watch compliance with the deal and support the transition that followed.

Liberia's sanctions stay in place under Resolution 1647, adopted on 20 December 2005. Peaceful, orderly elections had been held, and the incoming government pledged to rebuild the country. The expert panel reported that the conditions for lifting the measures in Resolution 1521 (2003) were not yet met. UNMIL was helping the government take hold in diamond and timber areas and along the borders.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms and travel measures for 12 months and the diamond and timber measures for six months. It stands ready to end them once the conditions are met. It urges forestry reform, outside advice on diamond management, and full use of the Governance and Economic Management Assistance Program. The asset freeze under Resolution 1532 remains. The Panel of Experts is re-established until 21 June 2006, to report by 7 June 2006.

Iran's sanctions are widened in Resolution 1747, adopted on 24 March 2007. The IAEA's February 2007 report found Iran had still not suspended enrichment or complied with resolutions 1696 and 1737 (2006). Six governments plus the EU's foreign policy chief kept a negotiated settlement offer on the table, first made in June 2006.

Acting under Article 41 of Chapter VII, the Council applies the asset freeze and other measures of Resolution 1737 to the additional persons and entities in its Annex I. They cover nuclear, missile, and Revolutionary Guard-linked bodies and a state bank. It bans Iran from exporting arms and forbids states to procure them. It calls for vigilance and restraint on selling Iran heavy conventional weapons, and for no new grants or concessional loans to Iran's government except for humanitarian and development purposes. Iran is told to comply without delay; an IAEA report is due within 60 days.

Fresh Cyprus negotiations frame Resolution 1847, adopted on 12 December 2008. Fully fledged talks had opened on 3 September 2008, the first in years, and the two leaders had made joint statements and announced confidence measures, including cancelled military exercises. The Ledra Street crossing had opened, and the island stayed generally stable with fewer incidents. Demining funding beyond 2008 was urgently needed.

The Council extends the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, until 15 June 2009. It urges both sides to seize what it calls an unprecedented opportunity: speed up the talks, keep the atmosphere of trust, and work openly toward a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality. It welcomes the confidence measures and pushes for more crossing points, including Limnitis. It again asks the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. A report is due by 1 June 2009.

How the United Nations helps countries recover after a war is the subject of Resolution 1947, adopted on 29 October 2010. The text follows a review of the United Nations peacebuilding system. That system is built around the Peacebuilding Commission, created in 2005 to advise countries coming out of conflict.

The Council welcomed the review report. It told all United Nations bodies to carry out the report's recommendations within their own areas of work. The goal was to help the Peacebuilding Commission work better. The Council said peacebuilding needs steady support and enough resources. It asked the Commission to report each year on progress with the recommendations. Another full review of the system was called for five years later.

Hopeful words about a deal mark this Cyprus renewal of 1968. On 18 March, the Council adopted Resolution 247 without dissent. The Secretary-General had reported that the peace force was still needed. Cyprus agreed it should stay past late March.

The text restates all prior Cyprus decisions. It urges the parties to act with the utmost restraint. It asks them to seize what it calls a hopeful climate for a deal. The posting then runs three more months, to 26 June 1968. One hope is voiced again at the end. Progress by then might let the force shrink or leave. Later renewals repeat the same wish.

Libya's political mission gets a short three-month rollover in Resolution 2647, adopted on 28 July 2022. The Libyan Political Dialogue Forum's roadmap had missed its deliverables. Elections still had no agreed constitutional basis. The Special Representative post stood vacant. The October 2020 ceasefire remained only partly implemented.

The Council extends the United Nations Support Mission in Libya, UNSMIL, until 31 October 2022 under its Resolutions 2542 (2020) and 2570 (2021) mandate. It calls on the Secretary-General to appoint a Special Representative promptly. It urges Libyan institutions and stakeholders to agree a pathway to free, fair, and inclusive presidential and parliamentary elections as soon as possible. It demands full implementation of the ceasefire. That includes the 5+5 Joint Military Commission's plan for withdrawing foreign forces, fighters, and mercenaries. It requires thirty-day implementation reports. It also recalls that oil must stay under the National Oil Corporation's exclusive control.

Resolution 347, adopted on 24 April 1974 by thirteen votes to none, responds to violence along the Lebanon-Israel frontier. Lebanon and Israel had both written to the Council, and ministers addressed it directly. The Council said it was deeply disturbed by continuing acts of violence that could wreck efforts toward a fair, lasting peace in the region.

The Council condemned Israel's breach of Lebanon's sovereignty and borders. It demanded an end to further raids and threats. It condemned all violence, especially attacks killing innocent civilians. It also called on Israel to release and return abducted Lebanese civilians at once, and urged every party to avoid steps that might endanger negotiations.

Angola reported another round of South African invasions in March 1979. The attacks came once more from occupied Namibia. Civilians and Namibian refugees were killed. The raids seemed timed to wreck the settlement talks then under way in southern Africa. Resolution 447 was adopted on 28 March 1979.

The Council strongly condemned South Africa's invasions of Angola. They were planned in advance and kept up over time, the text says. The use of Namibia as a springboard was condemned as well. The invasions had to stop at once. Angola's independence, sovereignty, and territory had to be respected. Member states were asked to give Angola and the other front-line states urgent help for their defenses. Casualty and damage figures were requested by 30 April 1979, so the Council could weigh sanctions.

India brought a complaint about Jammu and Kashmir to the Council in 1948, and Pakistan answered with counter-complaints. Both new states told the Council that the state's future should be decided by its people. Both also declared that peace and order had to be restored early. Resolution 47, adopted on 21 April 1948, lays out a plan to settle the dispute.

The Council enlarged the commission created by Resolution 39, from three members to five. The commission was sent to the subcontinent at once to mediate. The plan began with Pakistan. It had to work to withdraw the tribesmen and Pakistani nationals who had entered Kashmir to fight. India would then pull back most of its forces in stages. A special administration would be set up in Kashmir to hold the vote. The vote on joining India or Pakistan had to be free and fair.

Soviet troops had left Afghanistan, but peace work went on. The 1988 Geneva pacts framed the pull-out. A small band of UN men in uniform watched the deal. Their chief's term was near its end. A new note from him came on 9 January 1990. Resolution 647 passed with no dissent on 11 January 1990.

The Council agreed to his plan in full. Men in uniform would be lent from other UN posts. They would aid the good offices work in both lands, Kabul's and Pakistan's. The loan would last two more months. News of fresh steps had to reach the Council as they came. The text is a clerk's nod, but it kept a thin UN watch in place as a hard war wound down.
william-malmesbury-chronicle-kings-engla:
William of Malmesbury wrote his Gesta Regum Anglorum, the Deeds of the Kings of England, in the 1120s, and it runs to the year 1127. J. A. Giles translated it into English in 1847. William is judged the greatest English historian of the twelfth century, a monk who read widely and weighed what he read.

From the Saxon kings to Henry I, he tells of courts, bishops, wars, and wonders with a fair and curious mind. He collected tales at first hand and marked what he doubted. His portraits of William the Conqueror and his sons still anchor the story of Norman England. Giles's version made the Latin monk a household name for English readers.
wirnt-wigalois-pfeiffer-1847:
Wirnt von Grafenberg sang of Wigalois, the son of Gawain, in a romance of the early 1200s. Franz Pfeiffer's 1847 edition prints the medieval German poem in full. Wigalois leaves Arthur's court as a young knight with a wheel of fortune for his sign.

His quest takes him against Roaz, a sorcerer whose dark realm has swallowed kings and knights. Monsters, magic, and hard fights line the road as the young hero grows into his name. The tale was a favorite of late medieval readers and was oft retold. Pfeiffer's text gives the poem whole, as its first hearers knew it.
wood-choir-gaure-stonehenge-1747:
John Wood, the Bath architect, turned his eye to Stonehenge in 1747 and produced Choir Gaure. Wood measured the ring on Salisbury Plain and set down what he found in careful detail. He also offered his own bold reading of what the stones had been for.

Wood held that Druid priests built the ring as a temple tied to the moon. He tried to show how the stones might once have stood, in effect restoring the ruin on paper. His answer pushed back against William Stukeley, the best known Stonehenge writer of the age, and gave readers a rival, richly drawn account.
zoist-vol-05-1847:
Volume five of The Zoist spans March 1847 to January 1848. Elliotson's journal carries mesmerism into its fifth year of print. Surgery under trance still fills reports, though ether now rivals the method. Cerebral physiology articles tie brain form to mental traits, as phrenology taught.

Somnambulist wonders and plain cures stand side by side in the record. Contributors argue over what the trance state truly is. The journal remains the English movement's chief archive, bound to reach thirteen volumes. Volume five shows a cause adapting to a changed world. Its case files preserve practice that journals of rank ignored. The primary detail is the value.
